docs.title: The Knowledge of Failure
docs.text:
A CROSS-DOMAIN MANUAL OF STRUCTURAL FAILURE

Twenty-four mechanisms, fourteen domains, 159 cases. Each chapter takes one way things break: how it grows, what shows first, and the conditions under which it cannot be stopped. Every case stops at the decision point; the outcome waits past the page.

Start at Chapter 1 Look up your situation PDF GitHub 中文版

docs.title: Four ways to use it
docs.text:
LOOK UP Arrive with a situation: the situating table in Chapter 35 gives the direction, then the mechanism-by-domain matrix and the case index.

USE You have a meeting: thirty minutes before the decision, a design review question list, a ninety-minute failure rehearsal.

PRACTISE Each card stops at the decision point with three questions. Write your answer before you turn the page.

SHARE Explaining failure to a team: how to write a postmortem still useful in three years, and the documents six mature fields actually keep.

ag-005, ag-006, ag-007, ag-008 | st-002 | | | Path Lock-in (Chapter 34) | | | | | | | | | po-004 | | | | | | Counts: 24 mechanisms by 14 domains gives 336 cells, 138 filled and 198 blank. The collection holds 159 cases, and more than one case to a cell is the norm, since a single case can witness several mechanisms at once. Three ways to read it. Read a row: one mechanism's evidence across the domains, and the wider the spread, the more general the mechanism, with Hidden Coupling, The Invisibility of Maintenance and Practical Drift the three widest rows. Read a column: the mechanism density of one domain, and where a column is mostly blank the domain is either subject to recording bias (Chapter 2) or short of this book's sampling, so a reader testing a local sample should fill that column first. Read for blanks: a blank does not mean the mechanism is absent from that domain. It means the book holds no first-hand full text to put in the cell, and the reading method in Appendix C outranks the table. One last lesson in reading a table. The blanks in the matrix deserve more care than the IDs inside the cells, and every reading method in Appendix C applies to a blank. Before reading a blank, ask whether it is recording bias, a sampling gap, or a genuine absence of the mechanism. Three kinds of blank, three responses, and once the check is done the blanks have become the reader's own collection list.

docs.title: Appendix C: Evidence Grades and the Reconstruction Method
docs.text: This appendix is the operating manual for the grade system of Chapter 10: the five definitions with their tests, how to read the matrix, the labelling convention for reconstruction, how links are archived, and the working sheet for the four-part number record.

docs.title: C.1 Five grades, definitions and tests
docs.text:
Grade Definition Test What it can support in the body A Full text of an independent investigating body's report The body is independent of the party investigated and of the penalty function; the full text, not a summary, is public; it carries a factual part and an analytical part, or an equivalent structure. A process report, such as the JTSB's 経過報告, is graded A− The decision sequence, the options ruled out, the minimum counterfactual, the escalation point B Official bulletins, communiqués, regulatory announcements Officially signed, one party's statement, no evidentiary section The magnitude of the consequence, conclusive findings. Entry into the body requires the "reconstructed" label C Judgments, penalty decisions, arbitration documents The facts have been through adversarial testing, but the selection of facts serves the issue in dispute Amounts, responsible parties, the timeline of acts. Technical process outside the dispute is labelled "reconstructed" D The party's own public postmortem Published voluntarily by a company or an individual; a postmortem carrying a timeline is the strong form, an announcement the weak one The shape of internal organizational process. Supports a finding of fact only after cross-verification against A, B or C E Media reporting Any retold text Lead generation only. Never a source of fact for the body

The rules for movement between grades: a core fact corroborated by B and C together can support a body case labelled "reconstructed"; an A− case does not support the escalation point, which turns on detail at the level of the signatory; a case whose links have died and which has no archive is downgraded to pending verification; quoted text that does not match its original is removed. the link check and the number-to-source check carry this out.

docs.title: C.2 Reading the matrix
docs.text:
The mechanism × domain matrix in Appendix A takes three readings.

Start with the blanks, which carry two meanings. A blank marked "to collect" means the cell has not been searched yet. A blank marked "no record" means it has been searched and no qualifying primary material was found. The two are entirely different: the first is a gap in this book, the second may be a structural silence in the domain, which is Chapter 2's evidence of recording skew.

Row density comes second. A row, meaning one mechanism, with strong cases in several domains says the mechanism holds across industries. A row with cases in only one domain is first suspected of thin collection coverage, and only after that of the mechanism being industry-specific.

Column density comes last. A column, meaning one domain, with many cases usually reflects a strong recording institution (aviation, chemical processing) rather than a high accident rate. A column that is nearly blank calls first for a check on whether that domain's primary library is reachable (Chapter 3's device checklist), and only then for a conclusion.

docs.title: C.3 Labelling a reconstruction
docs.text:
Cases on medium evidence, mostly grades B, C and D, are still worth writing, on one condition: the inference is labelled explicitly. The convention: a factual sentence in the body states the fact and cites the source in parentheses; an inference opens with "Reconstructed:" and closes with its basis in parentheses. An example:

"Minutes of the 14 March review meeting show the risk listed as agenda item 7 (factual sentence; grade C: meeting minutes). Reconstructed: from the agenda order and the meeting's total length, the item got less than 5 minutes and no resolution entry was formed (inference; basis: the time allocation on page 2 of the minutes)."

Three disciplines. An inference must be re-checkable by the reader along the basis it cites. An inference with no re-check path is not written. Inference may not prop up inference, since two "reconstructed" sentences still add up to one inference.

docs.title: C.4 Links, archives and the soft 404
docs.text:
Every case's primary link has to be opened by hand and read to its content: WebFetch returning body text, or curl returning HTTP 200 with a file type, a page count and a subject that match. Two common traps need testing separately. The soft 404 is an HTTP 200 that returns an error page or a placeholder, and the test is any one of three: an abnormally small file, text containing "404/Forbidden/Not Found", or a subject that does not match expectation. The anti-scraping placeholder is a status 200 whose content is a CAPTCHA or a login wall.

When the original link is dead, an Internet Archive (web.archive.org) snapshot is allowed on three conditions: the body notes "original link dead, archive link"; the snapshot date is later than the publication of the cited content; the grade drops half a step from the original's (A to A−, B to B−).

docs.title: C.5 Working sheet for the four-part number record
docs.text:
Every number in the body gets its four parts registered at the material end. The template:

Number:
Issuing body:
Document and number:
Date of publication:
Sample and definition:
Link:
Chapter and section where used:

When a part is missing, go back to the source and fill it first. Where it cannot be filled, delete the number and rewrite the mechanism narration. The difference audit takes this sheet as its authority: the set of numbers in the body is a subset of the set of numbers in the material cards, and a non-empty difference sends the chapter back.

Three notes on use. The grade evaluates the form of the material, not its truth: a speculative passage inside an A-grade report is still speculation and is cited as speculation, and a dated, specific fact inside an E-grade report may be accepted, though any key number must be traced back to a higher grade. The rules of downgrade and upgrade are not symmetric: retelling does not upgrade, since a conclusion taken from second-hand material is graded as second-hand, while a new investigation can upgrade, since a fact confirmed by an independent investigation is graded by the new material. The table also serves as the template for a reader's own case library: internal postmortem material grades the same way (system logs A, meeting minutes B, participants' oral accounts D), so an organization's library and this book's library can cite each other directly.

docs.title: Appendix D: A Genealogy of Mechanisms
docs.text: The twenty-four mechanisms are not independent entries standing side by side. They are twenty-four projections on the surface of a few tensions underneath. This appendix records the family relations among them: which ones usually travel in pairs, which one disguises itself as which, and what a combination means when it shows up. It cross-links with Section 6 of each mechanism chapter.

docs.title: D.1 Three underlying tensions
docs.text:
Tension one: knowing against admitting, in the information layer. The organization knows the truth, or could know it, but the cost of admitting it deforms the truth in the archive, in the reporting and in the narrative. Family members: Normalization of Deviance (11, distortion at the archival layer), Narrative before Evidence (13, distortion at the expressive layer), Information Attenuation up the Hierarchy (16, distortion at the transmission layer), Why the Truth-Teller Goes First (19, silencing at the source), Goal Displacement; Goodhart's Law (12, distortion at the measurement layer). All five share one physical process: the truth is distorted layer by layer inside the organization's information structure. Reading a combination: when more than three of the five appear together, the organization's sensing system has failed as a whole, no single-point repair will help, and an independent sensing channel has to be brought in from outside (the devices of Chapters 16 and 19).

Tension two: now against later, in the time layer. Present gain is traded for future cost, and the structure permits it. Family members: Horizon Mismatch (28, the tenure structure), The Invisibility of Maintenance (29, the asset side), Margin Erosion (25, the design side), The Slack of Success (20, the will side). All four run on one licence: someone later pays. Reading a combination: in an organization where all four appear, the risk state is older than any indicator shows, since indicators reflect the current period while the debt sits buried on the time axis (Surfside is the specimen holding all four: ce-009).

Tension three: one against all, in the structural layer. Between local rationality and collective loss sits an externality that cannot be priced. Family members: Misaligned Incentives (17, the direction of interest), Diffusion of Responsibility (18, where responsibility is lodged), Cascading Failure (33, transmission through dependency), Crossing a Scale Threshold (24, the limit of coordination). Reading a combination: in an organization running both 17 and 18, wrong direction with nobody accountable, failure is only a matter of time; in an industry running both 33 and 24, dependency concentrated and scale expanding, what is being waited for is simultaneous failure (the 38 shell consultants of Chapter 24, the thousand cloud customers of Chapter 33).

docs.text: Pair Relation Where it appears in this book 15 Practical Drift × 11 Normalization of Deviance drift supplies the raw material, normalization completes the filing av-020 (the logbook check in flight), ma-002 (an alarm buried under music) 31 Regulatory Lag and Capture × 32 Compliant and Unsafe the old rule is the climate, item-by-item compliance is the weather av-036 (certification philosophy), ch-008 (a compliant check on a misclassification) 25 Margin Erosion × 29 The Invisibility of Maintenance arrears on both sides of the margin, design and condition ce-009 (Surfside), ma-004 (the seawater pipe) 27 Sunk Cost and Escalation × 34 Path Lock-in lock-in explains why the switch cannot be made, escalation explains why it continues po-004 (HS2) 21 Hidden Coupling × 33 Cascading Failure the hidden line exists, the dependency is concentrated sw-002 (permissions × feature files), ph-008 (kit × component) 12 Goal Displacement × 17 Misaligned Incentives a misaligned interest finds its own ruler fi-001 (the loan-loss indicator), po-003 (the risk rating) 13 Narrative before Evidence × 27 Sunk Cost and Escalation an expectation stated early makes exit a broken promise fi-005 (issuance fraud), po-006 (the Sizewell replication narrative) 18 Diffusion of Responsibility × 16 Information Attenuation nobody claims it across, nobody carries it up ma-008 (VTS authority), po-002 (the conceptual schedule) 22 The Illusion of Redundancy × 26 Automation and Skill Decay a paper defence replaces both the real defence and the real practice ce-001 (double sanding), me-003 (the two-person check) 23 Extrapolating Past the Validated Domain × 14 Where Intuitive Expertise Breaks Down the conclusion crosses the boundary together with the person judging it ph-007 (reprocessed trocars), me-002 (U-500 drawn in a U-100 syringe)

docs.title: D.3 Mutual disguise, and how to tell them apart
docs.text:
Disguise one: 17 dressed as 12. An appraisal problem gets discussed in the shape of an indicator design problem: change the indicator, leave the incentive alone. The test: does behaviour go back to the old pattern once the indicator changes? If it goes back, 17 is running (Chapter 12, Section 6).

Disguise two: 25 dressed as 29. Eating the margin, which is cutting redundancy, and arrears in maintenance, which is deferring service, get lumped together as aging. The test: is the object a design value (25) or a condition value (29)? At Surfside both layers were present.

Disguise three: 19 dressed as 16. When no news comes up the channel, separate first whether nobody spoke (19) or somebody spoke and it was diluted (16). The diagnostic question: the last time someone spoke sharply, what became of that person?

Disguise four: 24 dressed as 22. Simultaneous failure exposed by growth gets handled as common-cause failure, and the answer is another backup. The test: is the trigger external (22) or the scale itself (24)? GitHub's record load (24) against the Arkema flood (22) is the textbook contrast.

Disguise five: 30 dressed as 18. Nobody being accountable after a broken handover looks like diffusion, when the knowledge never arrived at all. The test: does the receiving side know it is accountable? If not, 30. If it knows and assumes someone else will handle it, 18.

docs.title: D.4 Combination warnings
docs.text:
Three combinations, each of which on appearing calls for handling to be escalated at once, from a ledger walkthrough to a dedicated review.

Combination one, the sensing-failure package: three of 11, 13, 16 and 19 present. The organization is already systematically deaf, and the sensing gets repaired before anything else is discussed.

Combination two, the time-bomb package: two of 25, 28 and 29 present. The debt sits on the time axis and has no signatory, which is the reading of Surfside and of Westminster.

Combination three, the systemic-exposure package: two of 21, 24 and 33 present. The shared platform of an expansion phase is accumulating the conditions for simultaneous failure, and sw-005 in Chapter 24 and sw-003 in Chapter 33 come from the same company, which is not a coincidence.

Three notes on use. The genealogy is a map for reading, not a pedigree for theory: two chapters sitting next to each other does not mean two mechanisms share an origin, only that their tests are easily confused, and the boundary discussion in Section 6 is the formal text that separates them. The three-generation division, upstream disciplinary concept, mechanism chapter, field form, matches three citation needs: cite upstream in a paper, use the mechanism chapter in management, copy the field form into a ledger, and each reader takes the layer they need. The genealogy grows, since Section 6's boundary discussions are revised with each version, so the table gets checked against the body text once a year and new adjacencies are added as they appear; the table is built as a living document.

docs.title: Chapter 1: Why Failure Knowledge Is the Most Expensive, and the Least Organized
docs.text: What this chapter covers: the price of failure knowledge and the supply of it, plus the distance between having heard of a way to die and knowing one. When to come back: when you need to persuade someone, yourself included, to spend hours and budget on organizing failure; when a postmortem lands on your desk and you have to judge whether it deserves reading. Reading time: about 30 minutes.

docs.title: 1.1 Eliminative Knowledge
docs.text:
An organization makes the same kind of decision every day. Fund this project or not, release this batch or hold it, sign this build or send it back, fill this shift or run short. Each decision takes one item out of a set and abandons the rest. Knowledge has exactly one job in that act: it makes the set smaller.

Two kinds of evidence shrink a set. A success case says this path works, and validates one point. A failure case says this region contains a path that kills, and removes an area. For the same amount of information, the second removes more.

Organizations do not decide once. They decide daily, on structurally similar questions, which is what makes negative samples worth counting. The expected value of one failure record equals the number of wrong paths it removes, multiplied by the expected loss on each of them. Losses run in a long tail: nearly every error produces damage the organization absorbs, and a small number erase it. The large losses cluster on a handful of paths. Those are the paths the investigation agencies write about, year after year.

Failure knowledge therefore wins on two counts at once. It removes more area, and the area it removes carries the largest losses. Together the two support a claim about single records: a failure record carries more information than a success record.

The claim has a premise, and the premise is this chapter's question. Knowledge, here, means organized failure records. Failure that has not been organized does not qualify as knowledge at all. The rest of this section sets the threshold.

The eliminative arithmetic has a boundary, and it should be drawn before the argument goes further. A negative sample removes a region only if the region already has a name. One failure record eliminates a whole area when the area sits inside a pattern library; outside one, the same record eliminates a single point, that company's practice in that year, and the value decays to nothing as circumstances change. This explains why a good failure story told across a dinner table changes no decisions at the table. It is a point, and there is no library to multiply it. It also explains the order of this book: twenty-four chapters build the library before a single page spends itself on cases. The situation table in Chapter 35 is the interface between that library and your own circumstances.

There is a second boundary. Elimination value multiplies by expected loss, and expected losses in the tail depend on data. Rare large losses are exactly the ones nobody estimates well. Appendix C therefore fixes the evidence grades and the reconstruction method, and any figure that cannot be estimated is left blank instead of being handed to a decision-maker with false precision. The two boundaries make the chapter's first promise: every eliminations figure discussed here is backed by a pattern library and by an evidence grade.

One further compression of the opening is worth making. If a decision is an act of elimination, then the unit of knowledge value is the area it cuts away, not the quality of the telling. On that view the twelve-field card is a measuring instrument. The fields are graduations, a card is a reading, a mechanism is the conversion table. The instrument view has a consequence for prose: this book does not chase narrative tension, because the reader should feel tension at the decision point and nowhere else. Its negative example is the narrativizing tradition in failure writing, where an accident is told as a mystery. Readers walk away remembering the protagonist and the reversal, and lose the conditions and the structure. That habit is the largest single drag on the circulation of failure knowledge, and it owns about half the cost counted in Section 1.5.

docs.title: 1.2 Is "I Know a Company That Died That Way" Knowledge?
docs.text:
The failure knowledge circulating at dinner and in meeting rooms usually sounds like this. I know a company that died exactly that way. So-and-so went hard at channel expansion and collapsed overnight. The person saying it often did watch a company die, and the information is not false. As knowledge it has three holes.

The first hole is in the fact layer. The sentence cannot be checked. Which company, which year, on the authority of what document, was there an investigation afterwards: all missing. The listener can believe it or not. Knowledge's first requirement is verifiability, meaning a third party can test the statement against source material. Without that layer the statement drops to rumor, and rumor has no part in decisions. It only sets a mood.

The second hole is in the condition layer. The sentence has no boundaries. It says nothing about the company's size at the time, its regulatory density, its cash structure, its market stage, so you cannot tell whether this way of dying applies to your project. Every failure conclusion has a range of validity, and knowledge used outside its range manufactures accidents on its own. Taking "internet companies must burn cash for scale" into a cash-flow business, or "manufacturing must be asset-heavy" into a contract-manufacturing model, are the same error twice. Failure knowledge with the condition layer missing sounds deeper the more damage it does, because it invites the listener to carry the conclusion straight across.

The third hole is in the structure layer. The sentence cannot be retrieved, accumulated or cited. Three months later you cannot reconstruct the full version; when a colleague needs it you cannot produce a source; it will not merge with similar records into a regularity. Knowledge enters organizational decisions only through a system: searchable, comparable, citable, contestable. All four verbs presume structure.

Set against that a failure record done seriously. A formal NTSB aviation accident report has four fixed parts: factual information, analysis, conclusions, and safety recommendations. The factual part carries a complete timeline, and every statement in it traces back through the investigation docket to physical evidence, recorded audio and interview transcripts. The conclusions part lists each finding and marks whether it is contributory or an observation. Safety recommendations are numbered one by one, and the recipient must answer in writing within 90 days. A reader may disagree with the analysis, but every step of checking has a route. That is what fielded means: fact, condition and structure, all three present.

A contrast makes the return on fielding concrete. For one and the same accident, the narrative version, in the register of a press release, has an information half-life measured in months: news is buried by news, and a source rots with its link. The fielded version, in the register of a formal report, has a half-life measured in decades: the document number enters an archive system, and paper and digital copies are held in parallel. The gap between the two half-lives is the compound interest of fielding. Only knowledge that can still be cited in ten years is entitled to enter an organization's long-term decisions, and equipment selection, process design and staff development are all ten-year decisions. One practical instruction for decision-makers: before any piece of failure knowledge enters your decision library, ask for its half-life. Anything with a shorter half-life than your decision cycle is background, not evidence.

Chapter 5 compresses this fielding into a twelve-field case card. Here only the standard matters: before discussing failure, check whether the material passes the three gates of this section.

The three gates become a short set of questions. Handed any failure narrative, ask three in order. Can I follow the source to the original text, and does that text carry a time, a place, an institution and a document number? Did the narrator state the scale, the regulation, the cash position and the market stage of that moment, or jump straight from the story to the lesson? Can the record be searched, compared and cited, which means does it carry a number that lives inside a system? An answer that fails sends the item down a grade. Downgrading is not deletion, it changes the use: a rumor is a lead, you follow the lead to primary material, and you upgrade one record at a time.

The gates have another side. Material that passes them has not thereby become a conclusion. A primary report supplies facts and conditions, and the lesson layer still requires the reader to walk the pattern library. The gates sort material by grade. They do not think on the reader's behalf.

One objection comes up often enough to answer here: does all this make dinner-table stories worthless? No. They serve two purposes. A story is a topic lead, telling you where a primary document worth finding might exist. It is also a thermometer for organizational culture, since the way a team retells failure exposes its habits of knowledge. What needs governing is the use of rumor as evidence, meaning a decision document with no source attached, not the story at the table. The gates route each narrative to the position that matches its evidence grade. Chapter 10 is the formal version of the three gates. Section 1.2 is the everyday one.

docs.title: 1.3 The Word "Replicate" Has Misled Everyone
docs.text:
The claim travels widely: success can be replicated, failure cannot. It points attention in the wrong direction. The accurate version runs like this. Success cannot be replicated. Failure can be avoided. Neither of them is replication.

People who learn from failure meet a third casualty of the replication myth. They get asked, in effect, whether failure cases are not all special, and whether their own project is not different. The objection is half right, and the halves need separating. The wrong half treats applicability as all or nothing; the value of the condition layer is precisely that it hands you a comparability checklist, and scoring that list item by item turns applicability into a measurement rather than a stance. The right half is a reminder that migration carries a tax, which the rest of this section and the domain pages in Part 4 pay. Once separated, the objection converts into a tool sentence: you say it is different, so name the condition that is different. A clause-level rebuttal returns the conversation to the field layer, where disagreement can be checked, instead of the position layer, where it can only be staked out. The sentence travels into review meetings, project approvals and postmortems, and it is the three gates in portable form.

Replicating a success requires the conditions to replay. The list runs: timing, team composition, competitive picture, regulatory window, funding environment, and a quantity of luck the people involved cannot articulate. Business school cases compress success into a three-part story, vision, execution, result, and what the compression removes is exactly what replication needs. Following success cases therefore tends to raise the failure rate rather than lower it, and when you fail nobody writes your postmortem. That is the survivorship bias of Chapter 2.

The reusable part of failure knowledge is far more stable. A lethal path usually puts broader requirements on initial conditions than a success path does, and the reason is structural. Each link in a failure chain acts as a filter, so organizations that pass every filter and arrive at the same ending can start from wildly different states. Goal displacement appears with nearly identical structure in hospital waiting-time targets, school progression-rate targets and platform content targets. Success runs the other way. Every success path rests on a narrow set of conditions.

So failure knowledge exists naturally as patterns, not as cases. Patterns migrate across industries; cases are reference material. This is why Part 3 is built as twenty-four mechanism chapters with four cases each, drawn from four different industries: the definition of a mechanism requires it to hold across industries. Something that appears in only one industry is not a mechanism. It is an industry characteristic, and it belongs in the domain pages of Part 4.

Migrating a pattern carries a tax called adaptation cost. When a mechanism in the shape it takes in industry A enters industry B, every parameter has to be re-labeled. The decay rate in Chapter 16 is not the same number in an organization with two reporting layers as in one with six. There are two ways to pay. You can label the parameters yourself while reading cases from the home industry, which costs time and carries error, or you can read a book that has already labeled them, which is what Part 4 and the mechanism-by-domain matrix in Appendix A supply. The labeling has to be honest about its limits. Each cell of that matrix answers presence only, meaning a reliable case exists for the mechanism in that domain. It says nothing about strength, which varies by organization and which this book does not pretend to deliver as an industry manual. The right use is three steps. Check the cell to confirm the mechanism is present, go to the mechanism chapter for the criteria, then plug in your own parameters. Those three steps pay most of the tax.

What remains sits in semantics. A mechanism's name carries the smell of its home industry when it crosses over: goal displacement is called compliance-target assessment in healthcare and exam-focused teaching in education, and the smell persuades readers they are looking at a different mechanism. The deodorant is the criteria sentence in each mechanism chapter. All three criteria per chapter are deliberately written in industry-neutral language, because criteria are a mechanism's fingerprint and fingerprints do not smell of an industry. When you migrate across industries, hold on to the fingerprint. If it matches, the industry nouns can be swapped freely. If it does not, a familiar name does not make it the same mechanism. That principle is the user manual for the Appendix A matrix, and it marks the line between this book and industry lore: lore collects smells, this book collects fingerprints.

docs.title: 1.4 Who Produces Failure Knowledge
docs.text:
If failure records were worth this much, the market should have produced them already. The producer list explains why it has not.

Statutory investigation bodies come first. Aviation has the NTSB, the UK AAIB, France's BEA and Japan's JTSB. Chemical and process industries have the US CSB. Nuclear has the IAEA incident reporting system. Maritime has the UK MAIB. Their output is steady, free and citable, which makes them the largest legitimate supply of failure knowledge. It arrives as legal documents: several hundred pages, dense with technical terminology, written for hearings and litigation, with very little of it written for reading.

Insurance and reinsurance companies hold the largest failure datasets anywhere, spanning industries and years, with loss amounts attached. Those datasets are assets for pricing cover, and they are closed. You cannot buy them on an open market. You pay for them inside your premium.

Judicial and regulatory documents make up the third group: judgments, penalty decisions, recall notices, public and steadily growing, with China Judgments Online having once offered the largest disclosure surface in the world. Their weakness is fragmentation. One document covers one slice of one dispute, and nobody maintains a data structure across documents.

Academia comes fourth. Vaughan's normalization of deviance, Perrow's normal accidents, Snook's practical drift, Dekker's drift into failure: Part 3 takes its mechanism names from this line of work. But academic theory arrives wrapped in cases, the cases wrapped in second-hand retellings, and the citation chain back to the source frequently ends at a link that will not open. The theory is reusable. The cases cannot be checked.

The organizations involved come last, and produce least, for the hardest reasons. Writing failure in detail carries legal risk, hands intelligence to competitors, and costs employees and founders their reputations. All three point toward silence. Chapter 4 takes each of them apart.

Lay the five side by side and a mismatch appears. The largest producer of failure knowledge is a body of documents that its largest potential consumer group happens to be unable to read. Investigation agencies have written for decades. Business schools scarcely cite them. Corporate training does not use them. Decision-makers do not recall them at the moment of choosing. Production is not the shortage. Circulation is.

The reverse face of the circulation gap is a misalignment of producer incentives. An investigation agency's best output is procedural completeness, which survives litigation, rather than a format that travels well. An insurer's best output is pricing precision, not industry education. A party to the event has one best output, which is not writing. Three optima add up to a structural blank, since every side is rationally declining to do the circulating. A structural blank admits only structural fixes: an independent identity for whoever circulates, belonging to none of the parties, which is where this book places itself; a stable unit of account for what gets circulated, which is the twelve-field card; and a checkable base, which is the links in Appendix B. None of the three depends on anyone's goodwill changing. They ask one thing: that somebody stand between upstream production and downstream consumption and translate between the two formats. The scarcity of translators is the field's central fact, and imitation is what this book would most like to provoke.

The entry cost of imitating it can be estimated for you. A first edition of one industry's card library, at this book's specification, is fifty cards, which is one knowledgeable part-timer for a year at a card a week. Fifty cards cover an industry's high-frequency ways of dying, following Pareto: most losses concentrate in a few patterns, and that coverage is enough to run the situation table in Chapter 35. The other end of the budget is maintenance, thirty percent refreshed each year plus ten cards from new reports. Maintenance cost is the real threshold, because the excitement of building is universal and the patience to renew is scarce. Chapter 39 therefore puts maintenance in its own line in the budget template and ties it to output, where each new card is matched against the decisions it blocked that year. Paying for maintenance out of output is the only way a card library reaches its third year.

docs.title: 1.5 Circulation Stops at the Last Mile
docs.text:
Take a real NTSB formal report and watch where circulation breaks. It may be a three-hundred-page PDF in English, sitting on the fourth level of a database, written in airworthiness terminology, with three numbering systems running in parallel: accident number, recommendation number, docket number. The density is high. Every page carries timestamped communications, instrument readings, signed documents. For an engineer about to make a release decision, that report holds everything he needs except three things. He does not know the file exists. He does not know which file matches his situation. He cannot finish three hundred pages.

Three unknowns and one impossibility make up the whole of circulation cost: discovery, matching, reading. Once those costs pass a certain level, the effective supply of a public good falls to zero, however free it is on paper.

In the world as it stands, the circulation cost of success narratives has been driven down industrially. Media, biographies, podcasts, business school texts, trending feeds: somebody pays at every stage. Nobody pays for the circulation of failure records. An investigation agency publishes and stops there. Citing the report earns no academic citation, retelling it earns no traffic, and using it requires understanding it first. This is market failure in its standard shape, applied to an obscure commodity.

The obscurity has a secondary disaster worth naming. The blank in circulation gets filled by poor supply: bestseller narratives built on survivorship bias, success literature repackaged backwards, social media posts that turn an accident into a tragedy of character. The crowding-out is real, and it works on appetite. An organization that reads three bad books on failure concludes that the field holds nothing serious, and its budget for the subject is spent before a serious title appears. This book's answer is not to criticize the neighbors, since criticism cannot be checked, but to demonstrate seriousness in public: twelve fields, four-part provenance, links, stated gaps. Each of those is verification waiting to happen. Verifiable seriousness obeys a harsh rule. It spreads ten times slower than the other kind, and every copy it leaves behind can be checked. Slow is the right speed here, because the object is a decision, not traffic.

Look at one piece of failure knowledge that has completed circulation. ValuJet 592, case av-035 in Appendix B. The NTSB formal report, AAR-97/06, spends one page pinning the physical origin: a maintenance contractor loaded chemical oxygen generators that had not been expended into the cargo hold as ordinary spares. It spends several hundred pages establishing the condition layer: the gap in dangerous-goods rules for the category "maintenance residue", the handover habits of the contractor system, the regulator's handling of earlier fires of the same kind. The pattern, the invisibility of maintenance, Chapter 29, turns up again in warehousing, in chemical processing, in software configuration management. The card's value is that it pins how a maintenance by-product becomes a dangerous good to a number you can cite. Circulation engineering is the work of repeating that operation across more reports.

The supply side also admits an incentive design. Price the identity of a primary-material reader, because reading a formal report is a skill: airworthiness terminology, the investigation framework, and a pattern library, three layers of training. The other side of pricing is certification. If an industry has a few dozen recognized report readers, examined by interpreting a new case and judged by peers, then the translation capacity behind circulation has a human base. Certification costs the building of an exam system and returns compounding capacity, since each certified reader can produce several dozen qualified cards a year. The format in this book, twelve fields, evidence grades, the three stop-point questions, can serve directly as the syllabus: public syllabus, transparent standard, verifiable work, and the profession grows on its own.

Repeating the operation across more reports requires deciding what the product is. Three forms are available, with a division of labor. Form one is the card library, which is the body of this book: twelve fields, numbers, links, built for retrieval and citation. Form two is the bulletin stream, a monthly digest of new reports in a field, which keeps an organization in contact with the material; contact is the precondition of use, and most organizations abstain not from unwillingness but from not knowing there is new stock. Form three is the morning case, ten minutes once a week on a single card, stopping at the decision point, letting the team judge, then releasing the outcome, which presses circulation into the room where decisions happen. The three differ in cost and return: the library is dearest and accumulates, the bulletin is cheapest and breaks easily, the morning case is closest to the floor and depends on a host who keeps at it. An organization picks what its budget allows. What this book can supply directly is form one, 158 cards in Appendix B, and the raw material for form two in the retrieval handbooks of the domain pages. Scripts for form three are ready in Chapters 35 and 39.

docs.title: 1.6 Where This Book Sits
docs.text:
This book does not investigate. It does circulation engineering, in three moves. Compression: several hundred pages become a twelve-field case card that keeps the fact layer, the condition layer and the structure layer. Matching: cases hang from twenty-four mechanisms, so a reader starting from their own position, with the table in Chapter 35, can pull the list of ways of dying that applies. Delayed conclusion: the case stops at the decision point, the reader judges, and only then does the outcome arrive with the minimum counterfactual.

The third move is where this book separates from retelling. Retelling hands out conclusions: so-and-so failed through arrogance, so-and-so succeeded through humility. A conclusion of that kind cannot be reviewed and cannot enter a decision. What this book hands over is a slice of process. On a given date, in a given room, on a given document, these were the facts available, these were the options, and this is what the people did. The judgment stays with the reader, and the structural analysis is already written. That is the specific remedy for the attribution bias of Chapter 2.

Circulation engineering has edges. Compression loses information, so every case keeps its citation and its link and the reader can walk the number back to the original report. Compression can also introduce error, so every number needs a four-part source, and whatever cannot supply one is written as mechanism description. What this book submits is a traceable middle layer. Its value depends on how hard it is to check, not on how well it is written.

The last layer of checking is an admission that the book can be wrong. Any card in the appendices may differ from its source, since compression always loses, transcription always risks, and links always rot. The institutional reply to that is errata: somewhere to report the discrepancy, a record of the report, and that record published with the same weight as the text it corrects. A correction is credit rather than disgrace, because a long errata list means the material has been checked often. A system that welcomes correction accumulates trust faster than a declaration of zero defects, and that accumulated trust is what lets a body of knowledge like this one be finished at all.

The loop closes with a channel running the other way, for checking the book itself. The self-audit machinery is in the standards directory, and three entry points are open to any reader. Appendix B links each card, so the original text opens from the page and you can test the citation against the body yourself. Every number carries its four-part provenance, who measured it, when, on what sample, under what definition, and anything that cannot answer all four is marked pending or blocked. The gaps are stated plainly: Chapters 26, 28 and 34 each record what was not collected, why, and where collection should go next. With those three entry points, the right posture toward this book is neither belief nor disbelief. Pull three cards and check them. Only a book that can be checked deserves a place in a decision process, which is Section 1.2's standard applied to this book.

docs.title: Five Self-Checks
docs.text:
1. Did your organization's last major loss leave a primary document anyone can retrieve? Ask three colleagues, write the three answers down, and compare them.
  2. The last time you retold a case of failure, which source document had you read it in? If you cannot name the document, which category in Section 1.2 does that retelling fall into?
  3. For the success cases your team consults before deciding, can you list the three narrow conditions that case required? If you cannot, what does that tell you?
  4. Of the three circulation costs, discovery, matching and reading, which is highest in your organization? Is anyone working to lower it?
  5. Given a budget for organizing your industry's failure knowledge, what would you build first? How does that answer connect to the situation table in Chapter 35?

Use the five together, once. The first checks inventory, whether the organization has any stock of failure knowledge at all. The second checks citation, whether the team's language carries sources. The third checks conditions, the real cost of the success cases you measure yourself against. The fourth checks circulation, which of the three costs is jammed. The fifth checks budget, what you would build if the money were real. Write the answers on one page, and that page is a map of where your organization stands in relation to failure knowledge. The next step from the map, what to build, how, and who maintains it, is the subject of Part 5, Chapters 35 to 39. The division of labor between this chapter and Part 5 follows from that. The meta-question chapters exist to convince you the work is worth doing, and the usage part exists to make it doable. The bridge between them is the situation table in Chapter 35, which pulls the cards you should read straight out of your own circumstances. If you plan to jump from here to Part 5, remember the bridge is there: between the argument and the tool sits an afternoon in which you already started.

That afternoon can begin with the smallest possible item. Take the most instructive thing that happened to your team last year and write it as one page through the three gates of Section 1.2: three lines of fact, three lines of condition, three lines of structure, meaning source, number, retrievability. The page will most likely fail the gates, because most internal postmortems are missing the condition layer and the structure layer. Failing is a baseline rather than a failure. The distance between that baseline and a card in this book is the distance between your organization and a world that records failure seriously. Part 5 holds the plan for closing it. This chapter promises only one thing: the distance can be quantified, in how many lines are missing, whether the source is missing, whether the number is missing. A quantified distance is a distance someone can shorten.

docs.title: Chapter 2 Three Biases: Recording, Survivorship, Attribution
docs.text:
What this chapter covers: how the failure sample you are handed has been filtered three times, by institutions, by human nature and by narrative, and the three specific things you will learn wrongly if you study from a filtered sample. When to turn back: when you cite a case to support a decision, when you design a review process, when you meet a number like "industry accident rate". Estimated reading time: 35 minutes.

Before you read any failure case, settle one question first: where did this sample come from? The sample in your hands was never drawn from the full population of failures. It passed through three filters, and each filter systematically favors a particular kind of failure. The first filter sits in the recording stage, the second in the telling stage, the third in the attribution stage. This chapter takes them apart one at a time, and after each one asks the same question: if you learn from this filtered sample, what exactly do you learn wrong?

docs.title: 2.1 The Recording Bias: Filing Rules Choose Your Sample for You
docs.text:
For a failure to leave a written trace, it has to clear a threshold. Institutions set that threshold. They decide how severe an event must be before it is investigated, written up and archived. Failures below the line, however many there are, do not exist in the written world.

Beyond the filing threshold stands a second gate that nobody advertises: the language gate. Records are written in professional documentary prose, while most first-hand descriptions of failure arrive in speech. Speech does not fit the format, so it is lost or deformed in transcription, and the casualties cluster at the front line. The veteran fitter's way of putting it, the nurse's hunch, the driver's foreboding: all unstructured language, none of it able to fill the boxes on an accident form. The remedy is dual-track recording. Fill the official track as required and store the spoken track separately, as an attachment layer to the file: interview transcripts, the raw wording from the floor, kept verbatim. The cost is storage and tidying. The value lands in future investigations, because a formal document answers compliance questions while a spoken track answers understanding questions, and the understanding layer is what most investigations lack. Dual-track recording compensates for the threshold and the language gate at once, and it is an advance line of defence for the handover rupture in Chapter 30: what the spoken track preserves is the part handovers lose first.

Aviation has the lowest recording threshold and the most complete coverage of any industry, which makes it a convenient ruler. The U.S. National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigates every accident involving scheduled passenger airlines (carriers operating under 14 CFR Part 121). For general aviation accidents (private light aircraft, flying clubs, agricultural and forestry work) it sends an on-scene team to only a share of them, closing the rest in writing. 〔Verification pending: on-scene coverage rates would need checking against NTSB Annual Review volumes; this sentence is a qualitative statement〕 Even in the best-recorded domain on earth, then, the reports you read cluster around the gravest consequences, the most common aircraft types, or the events that happen to be instructive. All forty aviation cases in this book's case library earned a formal investigation. That is what a threshold looks like from the inside.

China's recording system supplies a second ruler. The Regulations on the Reporting, Investigation and Handling of Production Safety Accidents (State Council Decree No. 493, 2007) sort accidents into four grades by deaths, injuries and direct economic loss: general, relatively serious, serious, particularly serious. Each grade goes to a different tier of government for investigation. Grading is a sensible way to allocate resources, and it doubles as a screen. Investigative capacity follows the grade, so the industry's large volume of sub-serious injuries, damaged equipment and near misses has almost no public written existence. Civil aviation is the exception: the Civil Aviation Administration of China publishes investigation reports and progress bulletins inside the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Annex 13 framework, which makes it one of the few domains with a full-text outlet. 〔Verification pending: the current text of the Civil Aircraft Incident Investigation Regulations (CCAR-395) needs checking〕

The shape of the threshold is legible from inside the records too. The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission recall notice for Cub Cadet commercial lawn mowers (Appendix B, mn-010) records that 106 fuel-leak reports had piled up, one of them a fire, before the recall came. The records were never missing; institutional pacing kept them behind the risk. Set that against a foodborne outbreak investigation (Appendix B, ag-001: 33 days from first illness to production halt and recall) and the difference in threshold height between two industries in the same period is plain.

There is a counter-intuitive corollary here worth spelling out. The threshold is the price tag on a learning opportunity. The mechanism is sample size. In a high-threshold industry, reports on a class of accident are sparse, so confirming a pattern means waiting for the pattern to repeat several times. In a low-threshold industry, the pattern is written into the textbook on its first appearance. Aviation's long run of progress has an underrated cause here: people credit the technology and the culture, while the density of the recording system is the foundation underneath both. For a policy maker the corollary is direct. Every cut in the filing threshold, every near miss pulled into the record, is a trade of administrative cost for learning speed, and inside this book's frame that trade is almost always worth making: records are priced in thousands, accidents in tens of millions. So before you quote any accident rate, ask where the threshold sits.

A quick table helps fix an industry's position by its recording regime, in four tiers. Tier one, mandatory filing with full-text publication: civil aviation accidents, major hazardous-chemical accidents. Tier two, mandatory filing with restricted publication: most workplace injuries, routine food and drug enforcement. Tier three, voluntary reporting with aggregate publication: near-miss systems, consumer complaint databases. Tier four, no institutional record at all: accidents in small and mid-sized firms, the quiet death of software, accidents at home. The table's use is to calibrate your language. Quote the tier whenever you quote a rate, because a rate without a tier is just a word count. One further corollary: comparing rates across industries is meaningless, since a tier one number and a tier four number are not the same kind of object. What is comparable across industries is whether a mechanism is present or absent, which is precisely what the matrix in Appendix A sets out to show.

No record below the threshold does not mean no information. The information exists in another form: experience carried in practitioners' bodies. A senior mechanic knows which line has a temper. A nurse knows which combination of orders tends to go wrong. That knowledge leaves with staff turnover and resets to zero at retirement, because it never touched paper. The handover rupture in Chapter 30 is the account of how this sub-threshold knowledge disappears.

What you learn wrong, in order of the damage it does. One: you treat recording frequency as occurrence frequency. "We never hear of that kind of accident here" usually means "we do not record that kind of accident here". Two: you treat recording quality as safety level. Aviation looks like the industry with the sharpest accident analysis because it has the best recording system, and those two facts are correlated while pointing in different directions. A field that suddenly produces a lot of failure analysis may be getting safer, or may simply have just cleared its filing threshold. Three: you ignore near misses by default. The statistics assembled after the fact show a crowd of near-miss precursors behind every major accident; a precursor that never crosses the threshold never enters the sample, so it never earns a place in the learning material.

Formal recovery of near misses is the half-answer aviation has produced to the recording bias. The form is the voluntary reporting system: front-line staff report errors and near misses anonymously or under protection, and the report enters the database without penalty. Aviation's confidential reporting systems and flight safety action programmes are the mature models, and healthcare and maritime transport have carried versions across. The voluntary system moved sub-threshold failure into the written world for the first time, shifting the sample from a grading by consequence to a grading by risk: a near miss with small consequences and high risk finally gets a file. The word "half" deserves honesty. Voluntary rates rest on trust, meaning the protection promise and its delivery; break the promise once and the rate falls off a cliff, with the price list in Chapter 19 applying directly. So before you read any near-miss data, check the protection clause and the record of how it has been honoured. The temperature of the data is the temperature of the trust.

A second route is active inspection: do not wait to be told, walk the site against a list. Safety inspections, process walkthroughs and shadow audits all belong here. Inspection pushes the defence from voluntary to institutional, so it no longer depends on the courage of a reporter; its cost is labour and its coverage is always partial. Its bias is checklist-shaped, finding the hazards on the list and missing new forms that are not on it, which means the list itself has to be updated from the accident library. Together the two routes give an industry a recognisable profile. Voluntary systems supply depth, the fine grain from the floor, and inspection supplies breadth, the corners nobody volunteers. How well those two legs cover the ground measures an industry's recording maturity more truly than any claim about its safety culture.

docs.title: 2.2 The Survivorship Bias: The Storytellers Have Been Sifted
docs.text:
The threshold filters events. Survivorship bias filters storytellers. Failure leaves no teller behind as a matter of structure. The failed lose the position, the platform and the credibility that a story needs, and the degree of failure runs in inverse proportion to willingness to tell: the more total the collapse, the fewer people left to describe it. The failure narratives in circulation therefore come mostly from people who are doing reasonably well.

The filter has an occupational layer. People who stay in an industry after a failure work for someone, and what they can say is bounded by that employer: describing a former employer's failure carries career risk, because the trade is small and the circle is tight. The constraint pushes public telling toward two safe subjects, a former employer that has already folded and cannot retaliate, and episodes unconnected to the present employer that time has laundered. The overlap between the two sets is tiny, so total output is pressed very low. This is one micro-mechanism behind the question Chapter 4 takes up, why organizations seal off failure. The seal is a structure rather than a policy, and every potential teller is running career arithmetic inside it. The arithmetic shows up as scarcity in public content. When a candid failure review does reach you, remember that an author produced it after running that arithmetic: the courage is real, and so is the cost.

Commercial publishing amplifies the filter. A failure chapter in a CEO memoir is written by the person who was on stage, recalling a peril that has since resolved; the executive who carried out the bad decision and lost the job over it usually has no book contract. Interview samples behave the same way, since founders who agree to sit for a failure interview are the ones with energy and social appetite left after failing. The U.S. data firm CB Insights assembles startup failure analyses from postmortems that founders submit voluntarily, a self-reported sample in which the more painful a case is, the likelier it is to be missing. (A compilation drawn from public postmortems and shutdown notices, self-selected sample; its pages have been checked)

Software offers a sharper observation window because it has a public postmortem tradition, and Chapter 4 treats that exception on its own terms. The relevant point here is who writes them: companies that were still alive after the incident and still had an engineering team to write the document. A company that died of its architecture never issues a postmortem of the death; its architecture documents go offline with the servers. Even in the most transparent industry, then, the set of public postmortems is a survivor set. It covers the cases that fell ill and recovered, never the cases that died of the illness. The mechanisms behind those two may have nothing in common. One is an immune-system problem, the other organ failure, and only the first is available to you.

Survivorship has a temporal form as well. Old cases that reach you have been through several rounds of selection, and the ones retold are the ones with drama, a teachable point, reach. The dull lethal cases drop out of circulation in silence. The countermeasure is to go back to the archive: pull every filed report for a given year rather than reading the three that everybody cites. Uniform sampling from the archive gives you an unbiased sample. It costs reading volume, since a year's output may run to dozens of reports. What it returns is the true density of an industry's memory: which patterns are frequent, and which are merely amplified by transmission. The gap between the two is the distortion of narrative, and being able to see that gap is a basic skill of reading reports. The three biases in this chapter are its tutorial.

What you learn wrong, again in order of damage. One: the catalogue of ways to die systematically omits the most lethal entries. The fast, destructive endings, cash flow rupture, the core team leaving together, a single regulatory veto, are the endings with no time to write a review and the highest shame cost, so they appear least often in circulating knowledge and sit lowest in your own head. Two: you misjudge an industry's transparency. An industry with many postmortem articles may simply have many companies alive to write them; review culture and mortality are separate variables. Three: you learn risk avoidance from survivors. A survivor explaining what they got right is a lottery winner explaining how he picked numbers, methodologically speaking. Extract what the survivor says about what was visible at the time; discard the explanation of why they won.

A purchasing-level move is available against survivorship: buy death samples. Three categories of public source exist. Regulators publish cancellation and revocation records, courts and registries publish bankruptcy and liquidation filings, industry databases publish shutdown lists. None carries a postmortem and all carry facts: when the firm died, how large it was, what its last public act was. The right use of a death sample is not to learn the cause of death, since nobody tells you, but to calibrate distribution: how many firms in your industry die in a year, at what size, in what pattern. The picture you build from survivor narratives is missing that entire block. Once the distribution is calibrated, every survivor lesson shows its conditions, and the first question becomes whether the dead ever tried the survivor's practice. Mostly there is no record either way, and that absence is itself a reading.

The archival view of death samples holds one more item that surprises people: a dead company's digital estate outlives it longer than expected. Domain registration records, the delisting date in an app store, archived job postings, the last post on a social account: any of these puts dates on a death. Assembling the timeline means cross-dating public traces, precise enough to answer half the questions of business history, such as when decline began and when the last expansion move was made. The methodological bar is low, public sources plus patience. What is scarce is that nobody does it, since digital archaeology produces neither traffic nor degrees. This chapter carries it as a public toolkit for death-sample collection.

docs.title: 2.3 The Attribution Bias: Every Review Is Written After the Ending
docs.text:
The first two biases decide which cases reach you. Attribution decides what shape they are told in. Every review is written after the outcome is known, and knowing the ending changes how the reteller rebuilds the causal chain. Chance gets woven into necessity. Forks get flattened. The fog that was actually there gets compressed into clear error or clear correctness.

The Challenger accident is the most thoroughly studied sample available. At 11:38 a.m. Eastern time on 28 January 1986, Challenger lifted off from Cape Canaveral, Florida, and broke up about 73 seconds into flight, killing all seven astronauts aboard. The Rogers Commission report opens Volume 1, Chapter 3, "The Accident", with the sentence that the flight began at 11:38 a.m. EST on 28 January 1986, and records that it ended 73 seconds later in an explosive burn of hydrogen and oxygen propellants; the official text is at nasa.gov/history/rogersrep/v1ch3.htm, read and checked for this book on 2026-11-01. On the evening before, 27 January 1986, engineers at the contractor Morton Thiokol recommended in a teleconference against launching in the cold. Their grounds were that O-rings in the solid rocket booster field joints recovered from earlier flights had shown erosion at low temperature, and that evidence linked low temperature to seal failure. Management at the company then changed its position and approved the launch. One sentence from the meeting where the position changed is on the record: take off your engineering hat and put on your management hat (Rogers Commission report, Volume 1, Chapter 5, "Contributing Causes", where Boisjoly's testimony recounts Mason's words to Lund as "take off your engineering hat and put on your management hat"; official text at nasa.gov/history/rogersrep/v1ch5.htm, read and checked for this book on 2026-11-01).

With the ending known, attribution can be run at several depths. The physical layer is the first: cold robbed the O-rings of their resilience, and hot gas burned through the seal. That layer holds fully, and it is the physical mechanism the Rogers Commission itself established. The organizational layer is the second, and it is the explanation Diane Vaughan gave in The Challenger Launch Decision (University of Chicago Press, 1996). The company and the agency had launched before with erosion visible in the joints, and had succeeded each time; each success was written up as evidence that the deviation sat inside acceptable limits; the decision standard moved gradually under the weight of those successes, and the decision on the evening of 27 January was one routine slide along that track. This layer holds as well.

The two layers do not conflict, and they train entirely different readers. A reader who stops at the physical layer learns that cold is dangerous, and goes back to his own organization to put a gate on a single parameter called temperature. A reader who takes in the organizational layer goes back to his own ledger with a different question: do we have a deviation indicator that we have already run successfully many times, each time explained as still having margin? One case, and the depth of attribution determines what the learning produces. Which layer reaches you in the market depends on who is telling. Accident bulletins gravitate to the physical layer, management scholars to the organizational layer, participants' memoirs to the luck layer.

Two further layers complete the set. The incentive layer reads the decision-maker's behaviour against the rewards and penalties in force at the time, what the appraisal system paid for and what it punished, which is the frame of Chapter 17. The structural layer asks whether another person in the same structure would have made the same choice, and the historical cases where the structure stayed put, the personnel changed and the accident repeated are its hard proof. The mnemonic for running all four in order: the physical layer answers how it broke, the organizational layer how it went wrong, the incentive layer why the pull toward proceeding was strong, the structural layer why it happened again. Only a reader who runs all four has earned the whole lesson from one accident; a reader who runs one gets the first page of the same syllabus every time.

Attribution bias also has an institutional form, and it deserves a straight look: an investigation report is itself written after the fact. The investigators know the ending. Procedure requires them to exhaust hypotheses before converging, yet the pull of narrative is always there. The counterweights are procedural: evidence numbering, a public case file, screening of multiple hypotheses, every conclusion tagged with its evidence grade. NTSB reports attach an evidence chain to each conclusion, so a reader can disagree with a finding and still audit the reasoning, which is the fundamental reason such reports beat news retellings. Residual bias cannot be zeroed. It can be compressed.

Three steps correct for what remains. Read the structure: the table of contents and the numbering of conclusions. A report whose conclusions are individually numbered and evidence-tagged has had its bias pressed down by procedure; a report that runs as one continuous story lets bias grow freely. Read the dissent: did the board record any disagreement during the investigation? Dissent makes an investigation more credible, and a unanimous conclusion deserves a second look for narrative gravity. Read the follow-up: evidence that arrived after publication. A report whose conclusions were revised keeps its most honest material in the revision record, and an agency willing to revise has earned long-term trust. The three steps cost an extra hour, and they buy a defensible price for any investigative conclusion. A report is neither scripture nor waste paper: it is the best sample available, carrying residual bias.

What you learn wrong here, in order of damage. One: you overrate "they should have seen it". Played backwards from the ending, every fork is clearly visible; standing at the decision point, information arrives mixed with noise. Two: you fail to acquire field judgment. Reading finished attribution is watching someone else's finished game, and your own play does not improve, which is why every case in this book stops at the decision point, the third clause of the reader's contract in the preface. Three: you flatten complex failure into a single cause. Post hoc attribution tends to converge on one root cause, while a real failure chain usually spans the technical, organizational and incentive layers (the failure-chain model in Chapter 9). A flattened root cause is convenient for briefing and useless for prevention.

Rebuilding a decision point is a semi-technical drill you can teach yourself on any review document. Step one, sort by time: order the material's information by arrival, separate what came before the decision from what came after, and tag everything after as hindsight. Step two, assign weight: for each pre-decision item, record how reliable it looked, how urgent, and how much noise it was mixed into. Step three, find the forks: list every option that existed at the moment, including the ones killed off in a single sentence. What you hold is a desk reconstruction of the decision point, more accurate the fuller the material; where the material is thin, say so. The drill costs about an hour per document, and it trains the capability Chapter 6 formalizes as what was visible at the time. This chapter gives the household version; Chapter 6 gives the instrument version.

Against the single-cause briefing habit there is an institutional antidote: conclusions written in layers. The report states its physical-layer conclusions, its organizational-layer conclusions and its incentive-layer conclusions in separate sections, and the summary is not allowed to merge them into one sentence. This is the standard structure of a good investigation report, where findings are numbered one by one and each carries a layer tag and an evidence-strength tag. Move it into internal reviews and the rule becomes concrete: no root-cause field on the conclusions page. Use three columns instead, one each for technical, organizational and incentive, with at least one entry per column. The three-column review costs two extra minutes in the briefing and yields three times the handles in prevention, since one entry per layer is three things that can actually be changed. Between briefing efficiency and preventive effect, this chapter recommends the second every time.

docs.title: 2.4 What You Actually Hold Once the Three Biases Stack
docs.text:
A compressed answer first, then the unpacking. Once the three biases stack, what you hold is a collection of failures written for you by survivors, filtered by thresholds, and reassembled after the fact, and your brain will digest it as a full sample, a neutral account and causal truth. The compressed version sets the tone for the rest of this chapter. Every technique here, the threshold table, the three quality checks, the four layers, the desk reconstruction, is resistance to that digestion error. The posture behind the resistance is an admission: bias cannot be cleaned to zero. What can be done is to put a scale on each document so the reader carries it into the reading. Two readers, one with the scale and one without, will split their trust differently over the same document. That is the whole capability this chapter means to hand over.

All three biases act on every case at once. Run a full check-up on aviation, the lightest case in any industry: recording is mandatory, telling is done by a statutory body, attribution runs under procedural discipline. Even so it carries residuals. Near misses are largely absent, which is the recording bias. Public reviews are written by institutions that still exist, which is the survivorship bias. The report's structure converges on causes, which is the attribution bias. Other industries carry more, never less. Chemicals has a filing regime whose coverage concentrates on major accidents. Software has a review culture whose sample is all survivors. Healthcare event reporting runs at low voluntary rates in every country. Finance scatters its failure record across penalty documents and litigation, and almost nobody assembles it at industry level.

Here is a sample quality check you can run on any case before reading it, three questions long.

  1. Check the threshold. How did this case enter the record: voluntary report, mandatory filing, media exposure? The threshold tells you which consequence tier it belongs to.
  2. Count the autopsies. What is the teller's stake in the outcome? Does the institution still exist? Was the teller a decision-maker, an executor or a bystander at the time?
  3. Take the attribution apart. Does the account mark the line between visible at the time and reconstructed afterwards? An account that marks nothing defaults to hindsight from beginning to end.

Run the three and your trust in a case has a scale on it. Fields 6 and 12 of the case card, visible at the time and evidence grade, are these three checks done in advance on the writing side.

The scale has one last place to go: into other people's hands. The fastest way to internalize the three biases is to explain them to your team, and one telling beats ten readings. The skeleton is in this chapter: one sentence per bias, the four-tier industry table, the three sample checks, the four-layer mnemonic. Four pieces of material fill ninety minutes without strain. For the live exercise, take the team's most recent internal review and run the three checks on it in the room: threshold, teller, layers. The effect shows at once, because the team reads reviews differently afterwards. The cost is ninety minutes, and what it buys is an upgrade in the team's literacy in failure knowledge, the most practical of the gifts the meta-question part gives an organization.

One more drill on the reader's side consolidates the writing-side work: spot-check the book at random. Pick a card, read fields 1 to 5 only, commit to your own judgment and conclusion, then compare against field 6 and the outcome. The reading works two ways. The farther your judgment sits from the outcome, the stronger the hindsight habit in you. The closer it sits to field 6, the better you have learned to stand at the decision point. One card a month, twelve a year, and the bias becomes muscle memory, which forms no other way than in real judgments; the morning meeting script in Chapter 35 is the practice ground.

The organizational form of the same immunity is worth writing down: put the three biases into the review template. Every internal review carries three fixed columns, what was this report's recording threshold, what is the teller's stake, how many layers did the attribution take. The cost is one extra page, and the effect is that every review declares its own provenance. A review that declares its bias has a credibility scale; one that declares nothing is discounted to the worst case by default. The columns share their source with the record-keeping regime in Chapter 38, since the credibility of a review is part of the record, and the philosophy extends one step: even the bias gets recorded.

docs.title: Five Self-Checks
docs.text:
1. What is the accident recording threshold in your industry? In the past year, how many events crossed it, and how many did you know about that did not?
  2. Of the failure cases you have cited, how many trace back to a primary full text? If you can name the document and its number, it counts.
  3. Of the reviews your organization ran last year, how many separated information visible at the time from information known only afterwards?
  4. In your industry, who talks publicly about failure, the winners or the losers? Can you put an order of magnitude on the industry's autopsy rate?
  5. Take your team's most recent review and rewrite one causal conclusion in its visible-at-the-time version. Does the conclusion still stand?

Beyond the five, there is an annual self-audit card for the three biases, kept personally. Question one: of the failure cases you cited in the past year, how many clear the threshold in 2.1, meaning they were formally filed and have a full text? Question two: of the failures you have told, how many were told with the people involved absent, since those present cannot tell it and you are telling it in their place? Question three: of the reviews you wrote, how many drew the line between visible at the time and reconstructed afterwards? The three answers make up your personal bias profile, and every gap in it is an improvement item for the coming year. The tools are all in this chapter: contact with voluntary systems, the purchase of death samples, the four-layer mnemonic, the three-step desk reconstruction. Profile and tools are both in place. What remains is the hours you put on the calendar.

docs.title: Chapter 3 The Five Fields That Record Failure in Earnest
docs.text:
What this chapter covers: how failure-record institutions are built in aviation, chemicals, maritime, medicine, and nuclear power; the four devices that make a record "in earnest"; and the channels a reader in China can actually reach. When to come back: when you need first-hand failure material for your own industry, or when you have to judge how much an outside accident report deserves to be trusted. Reading time: about 30 minutes.
