Failure knowledge does not accumulate out of conscientiousness. It accumulates out of institutions. Worldwide there are only about five fields that keep failure records at scale, and although none of them ever compared notes with the others, the machinery they grew looks strikingly alike. This chapter takes that machinery apart into four parts, then checks how far each of the five fields has assembled them, and finishes on the channels a reader in China can reach today.

docs.title: 3.1 What "In Earnest" Means: Four Devices
docs.text:
A field's failure-record system earns the word "earnest" only if four devices are in place at the same time.

Device one: mandatory reporting. Statutes must state which events carry a reporting duty and what happens when a report is withheld. Where the duty is optional, the reporting rate tracks individual willingness from month to month, and the sample stops meaning anything.

Device two: independent investigation. The investigating body answers neither to the party under investigation nor to the enforcement arm that issues penalties. Its product is a statement of what happened and why. Allocating blame is a separate trade. Merge the two and the party under investigation will buy safety with silence.

Device three: publication in full. Reports must be obtainable whole, numbered, and citable. A field that issues press releases and nothing else has headlines and no body text.

Device four: liability separation. What is written in a report must, as a matter of principle, stay out of proceedings against individuals, and the statements of those involved must carry no threat of prosecution (gross negligence excepted). Take this one away and the other three collapse together, because nobody writes into a report the details that would put him in prison.

The four devices lock into one another. Without the second, the fourth has no institutional carrier. Without the third, the output of the first two cannot circulate. Without the first, the sample facing the other three is defective at the source.

One further criterion belongs in front of the inspection, and it is a criterion about criteria: redundancy. For each device, is a second body keeping a backup copy of the function? Beyond the NTSB there is the FAA's continuing oversight, the insurance industry's investigation teams, and the industry's own voluntary reporting systems. An agency that is the only one doing its job is a candidate for Chapter 22 no matter how good it is. Redundancy varies enormously between fields. Aviation's four devices each stand on several legs; most industries have one leg per device, sometimes one leg across all four. The number of legs is what decides how a record system survives a budget crisis, a political intervention, or the departure of the one person who cared. A reader scoring his own field should add a fifth column to the four: how many legs does each device stand on. The five-column total is the operational definition of the word in this chapter's title.

The interlock also has a direction, and the direction is worth drawing as a dependency graph. Let liability separation fail and report content self-censors, a failure that propagates downstream from device four. Let publication fail and independent investigation works for nothing, propagating from three to two. Let independent investigation fail and mandatory reporting loses its point, propagating from two to one. The repair order is that graph read backwards: first the holes in mandatory reporting, then the independence of investigation, then publication, and liability separation last. The value of the order is diagnostic. When a field's record system has gone to seed, find the worst device and start there; repair anywhere else has no leverage. The lever is checked with one question: in this field's reports, does the person involved dare write the truth? On that question the first priority is always device four.

docs.title: 3.2 Aviation
docs.text:
Aviation is the prototype of this system, and it earned the role through accumulation. Aviation's record institutions were not designed in one sitting; they were bought layer by layer with disasters, and behind each reporting duty and each independent agency sits a famous investigation report. For a designer the stratified history is a free course: each founding document records the correspondence between the accident shape of its moment and the gap it exposed. The stratification continues, with record rules for unmanned aircraft and the airworthiness framework for electric vertical take-off and landing vehicles being written now, which makes new vehicle categories a live sample of institution-building. Anyone pushing for better records at home can treat aviation's history as the most complete set of construction drawings available. The drawings are aviation's; the mechanics of the structure are general.

At the international level, ICAO Annex 13, Aircraft Accident and Incident Investigation, sets three principles. The state of registry and the state of occurrence both carry an obligation to investigate. Investigation is separated from judicial accountability, and the report is not used to apportion blame. Reports should be published as promptly as possible. Major states have set up independent agencies under Annex 13 and produce a steady output: the NTSB in the United States, the AAIB in the United Kingdom, the BEA in France, the JTSB in Japan, the BFU in Germany, the ANSV in Italy, the AESA in Spain (with the CIAIAC under it), the ATSB in Australia, and the TSB in Canada. Reports are published in full and numbered, as with NTSB AAR-10/01 or AAIB AAR 1/2023, and major investigations open a public docket in which physical evidence, interview records, and transcripts of communications are itemized entry by entry.

China's civil aviation runs inside that international framework. The Civil Aviation Administration of China organizes accident investigations and publishes reports under the Annex 13 structure. Major accidents appear as progress bulletins: the March 21, 2022 crash of China Eastern flight MU5735, in which all 123 passengers and 9 crew members died, produced a progress bulletin from the CAAC on March 20, 2024. How fast the final report arrives and how complete it is are questions the reader can settle from the case library (see the av-038 entry in Appendix B).

Aviation produces a second thing that gets overlooked: follow-up. Every NTSB safety recommendation carries a number, the recipient must answer in writing, and whether the recommendation was adopted is a matter of public record. Failure knowledge is not only the analysis. It is also the ledger of what changed after the analysis.

The ledger has cross-industry value. The adoption-rate curve is a direct indicator of safety governance: sustained high adoption means a working channel from recommendation to practice, and a slide means fatigue or financial strain. The data are public in the NTSB's recommendation status database and on the CSB's recommendation tracking pages, and the reading belongs to Chapter 19's landing-rate logic, where the landing rate is what an organization charges for the truth. The two chapters interlock exactly here. A reader outside aviation should still memorize the mechanism, because it is portable: any regulator's recommendation deserves a number, a named recipient, a response deadline, and a public status.

The cost of the aviation system is on the record too: investigations run long. Take the January 2, 2024 collision at Tokyo Haneda between a Japan Airlines A350 and a Japan Coast Guard aircraft. Five people died aboard the Coast Guard aircraft and its captain was seriously injured; all 379 people aboard the airliner were evacuated, with one passenger seriously injured and four lightly injured. The JTSB's second interim report, released December 25, 2025, still came without a final report, close to two years after the event (av-037, Appendix B). Deep investigation is priced in years. That is what "in earnest" costs.

The other half of the price list is that speed is tiered. Aviation's graduated publication is the mature pattern: a preliminary report within days, an interim within months, a final when it is ready, safety recommendations at any time. The effect is to break the information flow into timestamped statements, each declaring what is known and what is not at that moment, which serves public information and investigative rigour at once, two demands usually treated as opposites. The cost of transplanting it is publication discipline, since every interim must separate the confirmed from the pending in its wording. The return is credibility: public patience with progress bulletins comes from bulletins that never claim more than the evidence holds. The Haneda interim reports are a working sample, and a reader can study them as a template.

docs.title: 3.3 Chemicals and Process Industries
docs.text:
In the United States the chemical sector's investigative device is the Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board (CSB), created under the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990, independent of the enforcement agencies OSHA and EPA, and restricted to investigation with no power to penalize. (The CSB began actual operations in 1998; checked against the About page of its website.) Its output comes in two parts: full investigation reports, which include animated reconstructions of the event and are unusually public-facing for an investigation agency, and execution tracking of its safety recommendations.

The institutional difference from aviation is coverage. Aviation's investigator has jurisdiction over every major accident in the field. Chemical investigation resources concentrate on the worst events, while small and mid-sized releases and near misses are left to company management and local regulators. The UK's HSE system and the continental European arrangements are comparatively complete. In most developing countries, chemical accident records depend on press coverage and full texts are scarce. In China, chemical accident investigation reports are issued by the Ministry of Emergency Management and by provincial and municipal emergency management departments; major accidents get a public report, smaller ones get a bulletin, and completeness varies (Chapter 31 carries the channel details).

A further dimension of chemical recordkeeping sits inside the fence line: the internal records of a process safety management (PSM) system. A mature PSM system keeps three families of record alive year round, covering process hazard analysis, management of change, and mechanical integrity. Their quality sets the pace at which the company learns, and in an investigation they form a key evidence layer. Internal records and public investigation are complements: the report yields the industry's lesson, the internal record yields this plant's specifics. How well the layers are connected is a gauge of learning capacity, and at most companies they are not connected at all. The report is read and filed, the records stay locked in the system, and nobody does the translation. That post, mapping an industry report's lessons onto the facilities on your own site, has a ready tool in Chapter 35's locating table.

docs.title: 3.4 Maritime and Transport
docs.text:
Maritime failure records are built from the rule framework of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) plus the accident investigation bodies of individual states. The UK's MAIB is the model agency: reports published in full, independence from maritime justice, and an investigative stance aimed at safety improvement rather than fault-finding.

What makes maritime distinctive is fragmented jurisdiction. The state whose flag the ship flies leads the investigation, and the flag state, the coastal state, and the state of the crew's nationality may be three different agencies. Report quality therefore tracks the institutional level of whichever flag happens to be involved. The same accident under a different flag may leave no public full text at all, which is a warning worth carrying: in the maritime field, the absence of a report frequently says nothing about the absence of an accident.

The industry has a consensus model for this: a lead investigating state with assisting states, jurisdiction concentrated in one body while the others help as needed. How well it works depends on the good faith of the assistance, meaning how fast data are shared and whether access to witnesses is granted, and gaps in that good faith are the largest single reason maritime investigations are slow and incomplete. Hence a cheap reading habit: look twice at a report's acknowledgements. The list of assisting states and technical assistance is the report's collaboration network, and the wider the net, the more complete the perspectives inside.

A second line of repair runs through the industry's own records. Safety management system rules require ship operators to keep maintenance and event records aboard, which gives a second layer of documentation beneath the flag state's paperwork; the cross-checking value of reading the two layers side by side was set out in Chapter 16. And fragmentation has a search implication. A single accident can leave several documents behind: the lead state's investigation report, the flag state's position paper, the coastal state's administrative record, the insurer's survey report. They fill in different parts of the picture, with the lead report giving the process, the insurance report giving the loss, and the administrative record giving the penalty. The complete search move is document genealogy, pulling the existence of the other documents out of one report's references, and A maritime reader should practise it until it is a habit.

One more public channel in this field deserves registration: port state control detention records. Which ships were detained and why are public, and the record works as a health check on the state of a hull, in a form that rewards batch analysis.

docs.title: 3.5 Medicine and Devices
docs.text:
Medicine's device takes a different shape. What it records is not the accident but the adverse event and the adverse reaction. The FDA's MAUDE database collects medical device adverse event reports, with mandatory reporting duties on manufacturers and on user facilities; the drug side runs on the FDA's Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) and on the European Union's pharmacovigilance system; China's counterpart is the National Medical Products Administration's (NMPA) bulletins and recall announcements together with the drug adverse reaction monitoring system. 〔Verification pending: the NMPA site loads dynamically in JavaScript; annual report figures to be checked once access is in place; this sentence is qualitative.〕

Score medicine against the four devices. Reporting is mandatory, so device one is present. The investigation side has no aviation-style independent accident body, so device two is missing, with post-market "investigation" replaced by signal detection and safety updates. Publication is half there, since the databases are queryable while individual records vary in quality. Liability separation is present, because the device adverse event reporting rules state explicitly that a report is not a determination of liability (see the language of 21 CFR Part 803, with the manufacturer duty at 21 CFR 803.50, checked against the current eCFR; user facility reporting has its own provision in the same part).

That structure produces a skew peculiar to medical data. Reporting rates move with how recent an event is and with how hard the causal link is to judge, and the same adverse event can arrive several times through several channels or never arrive at all.

Duplication and undercount together give the data user an operating rule: aggregate by event rather than by report count, merge the several channel reports of one event, and declare the gap left by under-reporting when you interpret anything. Aggregation needs event identification fields, a composite key of product, time, and symptom; records missing them, typically free text in older systems, must be read by hand, and that reading is the main cost of medical data analysis. Cross-border advice for readers from other fields: whenever you cite a medical figure, state that it counts reports, not cases. The distance between the two numbers is a function of the reporting system, and every loosening or tightening moves the ratio. One line of disclosure blocks nine tenths of the misuse. To Chapter 2's threshold checks add one rule: read medical data as signals, and treat any use as evidence as requiring separate epidemiological verification.

There is a further direction worth adding, about the gap between signal and evidence: the absence of a signal is itself a signal. A device that has been on the market for years and shows zero reports in MAUDE may be safe, or may reflect an absent reporting habit, since compliance with user facility reporting duties is low worldwide. The correct reading of a zero is uncertainty, which is neither proof of safety nor evidence of a hidden problem, and the action it prompts is active checking: follow-up literature from clinical trials, comparable data from other jurisdictions. Misreading the zero is the common cold of medical data use, taking a quiet database for a clean product. This chapter files it under the medical edition of record skew. The phrase to keep on hand when citing medical data is: what grade of quiet is this quiet?

docs.title: 3.6 Nuclear Power and Energy
docs.text:
Nuclear power has the deepest international sharing of any field.

One detail of that sharing deserves study by other industries: the grading of events. The International Nuclear Event Scale (INES) puts events on a single 0 to 7 scale with explicit criteria at every level. Its governance value lies in the language, since a common scale lets insiders and outsiders talk: the public understands that a 6 outweighs a 5, and the press no longer invents its own explanation. The cost is coarsening, because differences within a level are flattened and two level 1 events can carry wildly different risk. Coarse and fine is a permanent trade-off; coarse serves public communication, fine serves professional analysis, and running both at once is the mature arrangement. Any field building event grading can copy the two-layer structure, coarse outside and fine inside, with INES's public documents as a model for writing the criteria.

The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and the OECD Nuclear Energy Agency jointly operate the Incident Reporting System (IRS). Operating organizations in member states report operating events, and the database is shared among member states. The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission requires licensed operators to submit operating event reports (regulatory location: 10 CFR Part 50.73, the licensee event report system, checked against the current eCFR). The World Association of Nuclear Operators (WANO) runs a further reporting and assessment system inside the industry that is not open to outsiders. Nuclear events also carry an INES rating, published on the 0 to 7 scale.

The weak point in nuclear's assembly is publication. IRS detail is restricted to member states, WANO is entirely closed, and what the open world can obtain is whatever each national regulator chooses to publish. This is the first sample in the book of a system that is institutionally serious and externally sealed: how deep a reader can go depends on the openness of his own country's regulator.

The sealed side has an open substitute inside the industry. Some of WANO's technical material is published as ordinary documents, training material and summaries of operating experience analysis, shallower than the database but usable. The way to use it is to borrow across fields: a reader from another industry can read nuclear's public output as a textbook, because nuclear operating experience analysis is among the most rigorously written public material in process industries. The direction of the borrowing is worth naming plainly. Nuclear is missing device three and its internal rigour is the ceiling for the whole industrial world. The gap between inside and outside is a fact of the institution, and the spill of internal material into publications is a ride the reader can take for free.

docs.title: 3.7 Assembling the Four Devices
docs.text:
Field Mandatory reporting Independent investigation Publication in full Liability separation Notes Aviation Full Full Full Full (Annex 13 principles) The prototype; the most complete tracking ledger Chemicals Medium (major accidents) Independent in the US through the CSB; uneven elsewhere Medium Medium Small and mid-sized accidents rest on internal records Maritime Full Split (follows the flag state) Medium Full Fragmented jurisdiction Medicine and devices Full (adverse events) Missing (replaced by signal detection) Medium (individual database records vary) Full Read the data as signals Nuclear power Full Full Split (international systems closed; national regulatory documents vary in openness) Full External publication is the weak point

The first use of the table: find the row for your own industry, or the nearest neighbouring row. The gaps in that row are the discount to apply when you read outside cases.

The second use: find the device your field is missing and borrow cases from a field that has it. Chemicals has no public sample for small accidents, so a chemical reader borrows maritime individual reports; the mechanism is the same and the parameters are converted on your own desk. The borrowing rule is in Section 3.9 below and in Chapter 23, which requires extrapolation to be declared: name the source industry, state the conversion assumptions, keep the account visible.

The third use is for institution builders. If you get a seat at the design of a record system, this table is the parts list: copy aviation's full set, de-specify to the budget, and declare what you de-specced rather than hiding it. All three uses rest on one stance. The table grades no field; it tells each reader where he stands. In chemicals, major accidents give you CSB-grade full texts and small ones give you nothing public, so your study of small accidents runs on analogy from aviation or maritime, and how much to discount that analogy is a number you write down yourself.

docs.title: 3.8 Where China Stands
docs.text:
A reader in China has five channels to failure records, and they differ sharply in availability and in quality.

Channel one: accident investigation reports. Under the Regulations on the Reporting, Investigation and Handling of Production Safety Accidents (State Council Decree No. 493), serious and especially serious accidents are investigated at the provincial level or by the State Council. Reports on major chemical and industrial accidents are published by the Ministry of Emergency Management and by provincial departments, with completeness varying from case to case. Against the four devices: mandatory reporting is present; independent investigation is weak, because the investigation team is government-led and staffed from several departments, leaving investigators and the people who allocate blame heavily overlapping; publication is incomplete, with plenty of bulletins and few full texts; liability separation is weak, because reporting and accountability run as one process, and a sequence that assigns blame before it finishes investigating steers every statement toward self-protection. 〔Verification pending: the original State Council gazette, Article 19 onward, needs checking.〕

A secondary phenomenon of missing liability separation deserves its own entry: language drift. A report written under accountability pressure drifts toward the unfalsifiable. Timestamps lose precision, descriptions of actions turn into characterizations, names turn into job titles. The drift is measurable. Compare the reports of a single institution across years, and the annual change in linguistic precision works as a thermometer of accountability pressure. The measurement has governance value, since the year the language shifts is usually the year the accountability procedure changed, and that correlation points the repair at procedure design rather than at individuals. The use of linguistic evidence in this chapter is institutional diagnosis: take the language's temperature first, then talk about amending the institution.

A reading exercise for this section: take one published major accident report and work through it section by section, asking which section corresponds to which device. Facts map to device one, analysis to device two, the manner of publication to device three, the accountability section to device four. What comes out is a credibility map of that report, showing which sections can be cited freely and which need a second look, because accountability and facts often carry different weight. Three reports are enough to learn the drawing, and the skill lasts a working lifetime, since any investigation report, Chinese or foreign, can be priced quickly with the same frame. Making that pricing ability common is this chapter's central delivery to Chinese readers: the number of channels is a fact of where you were born, and pricing what they produce is trainable.

The comparison also gives a company reader a place to start on his own organization. Score your internal reporting system against the four devices. Is internal reporting a duty or a virtue? Where does the internal investigation team sit relative to the department it investigates? How granularly are findings published to the whole staff? What written protection does a reporter have? Most companies come out short on devices two and four, with internal investigation and HR running on one line and no written protection for the person who speaks. Chapter 19 covers external intake and exemption clauses and Chapter 30 covers handover protection, and both carry ready designs. This chapter's only job is the reminder: internal systems and national systems run on the same mechanics, and what a state can learn, a firm can learn.

Channel two: civil aviation. The CAAC works within the ICAO Annex 13 framework, which makes this the channel that meshes best with the four devices of the five. The MU5735 progress bulletin came through it.

Channel three: drugs and devices. NMPA recall announcements, bulletins, and the annual report on drug adverse reactions are standardized public outlets. The depth of any single record is limited, but retrieval works.

Channel four: court judgments. China Judgements Online once offered the largest public body of judgments in the world, and tort, product liability, and labour dispute documents carry a great deal of detail about organizational failure. Availability has changed in recent years. 〔Verification pending: the Supreme People's Court's annual work reports and judicial statistics need checking; this sentence is qualitative.〕

Channel five: exchange and regulatory documents. CSRC administrative penalty decisions, exchange inquiry letters and regulatory letters, and audit reports cover financial and governance failure at listed companies, in full text, publicly available, in a uniform format.

Stack the five and the conclusion is this: readers in China have usable full-text channels in civil aviation, in drugs, and in listed-company compliance. In chemicals, public safety, and several other areas, full texts are scarce, bulletins and press paraphrase carry the load, and the grade of the learning material drops below B (grade definitions in Chapter 10).

One combined technique with the five channels deserves teaching on its own: cross-channel corroboration, where documents about the same matter check one another. A CSRC penalty decision and a court judgment corroborate the detail of financial fraud; an NMPA recall announcement and a judgment corroborate a product quality dispute; a CAAC bulletin and a judgment corroborate an operational dispute. The output is an upgrade in evidence grade: B-grade material from a single channel can support a reconstruction tag once its core facts are corroborated through a second channel, under the rules in Chapter 10 and Appendix C. The cost is one search. The return is material promoted a grade, and corroboration is the retrieval move a Chinese reader should practise until it is automatic. It is the dividend this five-channel structure pays to the careful. The same structure sets the distribution of evidence grades among this book's China cases, and explains why most of them are tagged "reconstructed".

docs.title: 3.9 Putting the Map to Work
docs.text:
Three moves.

Move one: find the nearest primary library for your own industry. That means a specific database and a specific report numbering scheme, not a search engine.

Move two: read three recent full-text reports from your industry and note, for each, which of the four devices is present and which is missing. The missing one is the extra caution to carry into every page.

Move three: if none of the five fields is close to your industry, then before you set the strength of any analogy from a neighbouring field, run Chapter 2's three sample checks.

A fourth move sits outside those three: build the table of Section 3.7 for your own industry, with a column per device, a mark for present or missing, and a count of legs. The criteria are this chapter's and can be copied straight across. Building it is itself a survey of your field's record institutions, with the question list already supplied above, and it costs an afternoon. What it produces is a map of your industry's learning infrastructure as it stands, and the gaps on that map are the agenda for a proposal to your trade association or regulator. An agenda beats a complaint: a proposal that arrives with an assembly table is the only kind taken seriously at an industry meeting.

docs.title: The Five Self-Checks
docs.text:
1. Which of the four devices is missing from your field's accident reporting system? Last year, how much detail did that gap cost in one specific case?
  2. Your industry's most recent major failure: at what address does the full investigation report sit? How many minutes do you need to find it?
  3. Beyond regulatory inspection, does your organization keep its own failure records? How would you estimate the reporting rate?
  4. If only one could survive, the regulatory report or the internal postmortem, which would your organization keep? What follows from that choice?
  5. Of China's five channels, how many have you used? For the ones you have not: did you not know the entrance, or did you search and come away empty?

A weekend assignment goes with the five questions, one full tour of the channels in half a day. In the morning, run channels one and two: a full text of a major accident report, and an aviation bulletin. In the afternoon, run channels three through five: an NMPA recall announcement, a court judgment, and a CSRC penalty decision. Read every document with the same question in hand: how many of the four devices show in this text. The output is five sets of reading notes plus a quick-reference table of China's record institutions drawn by you, closer to your own use than the table in Section 3.8. A reader who finishes the assignment has converted the map of Chinese failure records from something heard about into something walked. That sense of footing comes before any retrieval work: the map comes first, and the tools only bite once the map is there.

docs.title: Chapter 4 Why This Method Did Not Spread
docs.text:
What this chapter covers: five domains proved that failure can be turned into an institution, so why has that institution stayed inside them for sixty years, and what special conditions let software become the one exception. When to come back: when you are about to propose "let's build a postmortem system" to management, or when you need to judge whether an industry's failure knowledge can be expected to grow on its own. Reading time: about 25 minutes.

None of the four devices listed in Chapter 3 depends on advanced technology, and none is expensive to legislate. Aviation had the full set installed by the middle of the twentieth century. In the seventy years since, no industry outside safety regulation has copied the set whole. The reason is structural. It sits in the incentive structure, and no one's negligence is required. This chapter counts the five gates in the way, takes apart the software exception, then hands over a framework for judging your own industry: whether it could grow this system, and whether you should wait for it.

The chapter's place in the book is worth stating once. It works as a pressure valve. A reader who finishes Chapter 3 tends to ask why, if the arrangement is this good, their own industry does not have it. The answer this chapter gives is that the absence is not a verdict on your industry. It is the mechanics of five gates.

Relief is followed by a turn, from waiting for an institution to building one. The templates in Chapters 38 and 39 exist for people who will not wait. The psychological threshold on that turn is loneliness. An organization that builds its own system is a minority inside its industry, and a minority does not need encouragement. It needs proof that peers exist. Software and the five precedent domains supply that proof: building your own was never naive, because it has precedents, tools, and an endpoint.

This chapter hands over all three. Precedents are in Chapter 3. Tools are in Part 5. The endpoint is in Chapter 40, which draws the boundary of a self-built methodology.

docs.title: 4.1 The Five Gates
docs.text:
Gate one: liability. Writing down the details of a failure amounts to organizing the evidence for a lawsuit nobody has filed yet.

The five gates do not weigh the same, and the weight distribution varies enormously across industries. Aviation carries a light liability gate, because statutory liability isolation exists, and a heavy cost gate, because the public does not read accident reports. Software carries the lightest liability gate of any industry and the heaviest institutional gate, since nothing is legislated. Manufacturing carries the heaviest competition gate, because process detail is intelligence. A reader can score the five gates for their own industry, one to five each, and treat the two highest scores as the principal obstacles. Resources belong there. Spreading effort evenly across all five is the standard waste of institution building.

The distribution also moves. Technology changes the weight of the competition gate, since digitized process information lowers the threshold for arming a rival. Changes in the legal environment move the liability gate. Re-scoring once a year is routine work for anyone who keeps an industry's records.

Where the liability gate sits for internal postmortems is a question every legal department knows cold, under the discovery rules that govern what must be produced in litigation. The clearer the document, the harder the defense later. The rational choice is to write the postmortem vaguely, or to leave it unwritten. Compliance documents such as inspection records and training sign-in sheets have mandated formats and must exist. A causal postmortem carries no such obligation, and is better not written at all. That is the real legal position of postmortem culture in a great many organizations.

There is a mature line of remedy for the liability gate, and it lives inside the law. Privilege and protection regimes already exist in various forms across legal systems: privilege attaching to audit workpapers, statutory protection for quality assessments, immunity clauses covering investigation reports. The design point is to pin down what a document may be used for, safety improvement only, never liability or litigation. Pinning it down takes a written clause plus usage discipline, and the clause has to specify where each part of the document is allowed to travel.

Protected documents already exist in regulated industries, which shows the route works: operating event reports in nuclear power enjoy limited protection under the laws of several countries. Resistance to transplanting the idea comes from an instinct inside legal departments, since every newly protected document is one more object that can be challenged. The trade-off between resistance and benefit is best settled in one three-party legal meeting, with corporate counsel, industry association counsel, and the regulatory line arguing it out together. Loosening the liability gate has always been talked through by lawyers. It has never been shouted through by engineers.

A document management protocol is the second tool on this gate, and it complements protection. Most jurisdictions have well-developed means for handling internal documents: labeling the purpose, restricting distribution, applying retention rules. The purpose is not to destroy evidence, which is a serious offense, but to keep causal discussion and compliance records under separate management during normal operations, before any litigation starts.

The protocol has to be signed jointly by legal and safety. Safety understands what the content is worth. Legal understands where exposure begins. A protocol designed by one side alone will be defective on the other side. The output is a single document: which class of postmortem text carries which purpose label, how long it is kept, who may read it. The cost is one cross-department meeting and half a page of text. What it buys is a downgrade of the liability gate from absolute barrier to manageable constraint.

The boundary clause goes in the first paragraph. The protocol covers causal analysis written voluntarily; it does not cover records under a statutory retention obligation. Once that boundary is clear, the protocol survives scrutiny from both legal and the regulator. 〔Verification pending: a cross-jurisdiction comparison would need legal databases; this passage is a qualitative statement〕

Gate two: competition. Failure detail is concentrated competitive intelligence. A crash investigation report names the component, the fuel line, the checklist that failed. A postmortem of a commercial failure names the supplier, the parameter, the channel that failed. The first is read by the whole industry. The second is read by your competitors, among others. The patent system protects technical solutions. It does not protect lessons. Lessons lie in the rubble of the loser, and only competitors go digging there.

One economic exit exists for this gate: the alliance scale of a shared pool. The competition gate is tight between two rivals and loose among forty, because competitive intensity is diluted by scale. The more members a pool has, the less any single firm exposes and the more it gains.

A pool needs two mechanisms. A contribution threshold, meaning you submit cards to get in. An access rule, meaning you see as much as you contribute. Both exist to stop free-riding, since read-only members will kill the pool. Precedents are everywhere once you look: insurance loss pools, and shared engine fleet data in aviation, which is a mature model. The model rests on two conditions, member homogeneity and a trusted third-party custodian, usually an industry association or a reinsurer. If competition in your industry is too fierce to share anything, the first question is whether a custodian has been found.

Gate three: face. The organizational narrative is an asset.

The deepest layer of this gate is individual psychology, where admitting error collides with narrative identity. A manager's professional identity is built on the correctness of past decisions, and a postmortem that looks directly at error is a direct challenge to that identity. At the individual level, the face gate runs on the motivated reasoning of Chapter 13.

The individual remedy comes out of psychology as identity expansion: fold the ability to write postmortems into the professional identity itself, so that a manager's image moves from never wrong to good at correction. Redefinition turns the postmortem from a threat into a stage. The driver of that redefinition is almost always the top of the organization, because only modeling from the top gives it credibility. Chapter 19's endpoint criterion, senior people admitting error in public at no cost, functions here as a cultural switch again.

A listed company's prospectus carries a section headed "Risk Factors", and any reader can run an experiment on it. Pull ten prospectuses at random and compare how the risk factors are written. The language comes out heavily templated. Disclosure specific enough to say "this accident happened in our history, and it cost us this much" is rare, because that would be using a statutory document to characterize your own past. 〔Verification pending: systematic testing would require sampling full prospectus text on SEC EDGAR; this is an operational suggestion the reader can check in an afternoon〕

The face gate reaches well past listed companies. Founders' public narratives, anniversary celebrations, government achievement reports, all of them run in the same direction. Failure has no column inches in that direction.

Inside the organization the gate has a human resources variant, since the space for failure in the internal narrative is just as scarce. The annual meeting tells success stories. The internal newsletter profiles excellent teams. Promotion defenses report achievements. Internal memory skews toward success exactly as the external narrative does. The consequence is quiet: failure knowledge can only circulate as gossip, passed by word of mouth and private aside. Gossip has no structure, fails all three tests of Chapter 1, and the more of it circulates the lower the quality of the organization's failure knowledge.

The remedy is to give failure a formal slot: a standing item on the monthly review meeting agenda, a lessons column in the internal newsletter, a failure section in the internal knowledge base. All three share one requirement, a named-credit system that makes writing about failure an achievement that can appear in a promotion file. The cost of the arrangement is opening an agenda item and a column. What changes is the ratio of the organizational narrative, and a ratio held for one year changes the failure literacy of a generation inside that organization.

A communications exit exists as well: turn failure into an honor narrative, finance it from the opposite direction. An industry award for the best postmortem makes writing about failure an act that earns standing. The design point is the judging standard, which should score by this book's card quality criteria, the completeness of fact layer, condition layer, and structural layer, and not by how good the story is. The supplier of such an award should be an industry association or a foundation, a third party with credibility. The output is an annual selection, and that selection is the industry's first batch of qualified cards.

Loosening an honor gate has plenty of precedent in human experience. Medicine's morbidity and mortality conference turned public discussion of death cases into part of professional honor. The M&M conference is a ready template for industries outside healthcare to copy, and its charter, its blameless culture, and its conventions of frequency are all documented in public literature.

Gate four: institutions. The most expensive of the four devices is the independent investigation body, and it needs legislation. A body without investigative powers cannot write the full process. Reporters cannot obtain the docket, scholars cannot get onto the site, insiders cannot publish the whole text. Investigative power is a public power, and public power is generally paid for by a disaster large enough. Section 4.3 takes that up.

A lighter substitute sits in the middle: an industry joint investigation panel. No standing institution, no permanent staff. An association convenes it, member firms supply experts, and the team forms per event. Independence and expertise land between an internal postmortem and a national agency. The panel fits industry-level accidents of medium size, the ones too small for a national case and too murky for an internal review. Its institutional cost is very low, a charter plus an expert roster. Its credibility rests on two clauses: recusal, so that no investigator has a material interest in the company involved, and a commitment to publish the report in full. Prototypes of the joint panel can be found in industry bodies of the Flight Safety Foundation type. The distance from prototype to working model is one charter meeting and five live investigations.

Gate five: cost. Writing a postmortem consumes hours. Reading one consumes capability. Indexing and maintaining the collection consumes headcount.

One remedy on this gate is underestimated: let students and newcomers make the cards. Card production is unusually good entry training, since it drills reading a report, extracting fields, and mapping to mechanisms in a single pass. The channel is a course partnership with a school, with the accident analysis course using real cards as assignments and the best of them entering the industry library under the student's name. The design point is the quality gate. The inclusion standard does not drop because the author is a student. A single standard is what keeps a library alive.

The economics work out on both sides: teaching needs real material, the industry needs throughput, and cards are the medium of exchange. Of all the remedies on the cost gate this is the most elegant. The education system is the circulation partner this field should always have had and never did.

Circulation works for success because a media industry pays for it. Failure has no business model. Nobody subscribes to accident reports, nobody pays for a postmortem, and retelling one generates no traffic.

The cost gate has a hidden dimension, an asymmetry in capability. Writing can be made cheaper with a template. Reading cannot, because reading needs a pattern library: without the twenty-four mechanisms as a frame, what comes off the page is a story. That half of the capability is the reason this book exists. The routes to building it are laid out in Chapters 35 to 39, through the morning meeting, the positioning table, the playbook, and the budget. This chapter only needs to explain why the capability belongs on the cost ledger. Teaching one person to read postmortems well takes dozens of cards read closely, and those hours are a real cost. If the cost never enters a budget, the capability never gets built.

Writing reading capability into job descriptions and the training budget, which the budget template of Chapter 39 carries as a line item, is the enterprise-side remedy for this gate. An enterprise can treat exactly one of the five: cost. The other four sit at industry and legal level. Enterprise readers should therefore put all of their attention here.

Of the five gates, the first four are incentive problems. The fifth is plain market failure.

A technical exit on the cost gate is maturing: make the reports machine-readable. Regulatory documents are trending toward structured data, and XBRL in financial reporting proves that a document can be read by a person and by a machine at once. Machine-readable failure knowledge pushes reading cost down by an order of magnitude, since retrieval, comparison, and aggregation become automatic. Reading three hundred pages by hand and extracting fields by machine belong to two different eras.

The precondition is a field standard for the document. This book's twelve fields are one candidate: if regulatory reports were labeled to a comparable scheme, the reading cost of circulation would drop a tier at once. The promoter of such a standard can be a user alliance, with financial institutions, insurers, and research bodies jointly proposing structure to a regulator. Collective user voice is the strongest force behind document standardization, and the model is the history of financial data users pushing XBRL into place.

docs.title: 4.2 The Software Exception: How the Public Postmortem Survived
docs.text:
Over the past decade and a half, the software and internet services industry grew the only large-scale body of public failure knowledge in the world with no statutory basis behind it: the public postmortem, and the methodology built around it. A landmark is the methods literature that Google's Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) team published openly in 2016, whose operating discipline for the blameless postmortem has been widely paraphrased since. Earlier practice took shape inside several leading internet companies, and the name itself is usually traced to the engineering blogs of a handful of those firms in the early 2010s. The representative public text is the SRE handbook at sre.google, verified as accessible. Earlier texts that carried the name as it spread have been lost or migrated, and are not cited here.

The exception deserves a device-by-device dissection, because it shows how four devices get assembled with no legislation at all.

The substitute for device one, mandatory reporting: changes and outages are high-frequency events, monitoring systems generate event records automatically, and the on-call regime requires a postmortem. The ticket does not close until the write-up is done. No statute exists, but a workflow does.

The substitute for device two, independent investigation: the postmortem is moderated by an engineer from a team that was not involved, on a fixed pattern. The people involved narrate, the moderator probes, the conclusions are anonymized. Independence comes from rotating the process, with no institutional headcount behind it.

The substitute for device three, publication of the full text: status page culture and incident notices to customers. Public postmortems cover only outages with a wide blast radius, yet the public libraries of the leading firms have accumulated several hundred entries, all of them searchable in full.

The substitute for device four, liability isolation: the blameless principle. The output of a postmortem is defined as a set of system improvements, never as a list of human errors. Whether the performance system actually quarantines incident records varies from company to company. This is the device most often honored in name only across software's postmortem institutions: the institution is called blameless, and the incident history still counts in a promotion defense.

There is a blunt way to test whether the name matches the practice. Trace where one incident record flows after it is written. Who read it, whose file it entered, whose evaluation it affected. Tracing the flow is the measurement.

The measurement usually produces embarrassment. The readers turn out to be management rather than the improvement group, and the attachment turns out to be review material rather than a work ticket. That embarrassment is the starting point for governance, because unless the flow changes, blameless is decoration. The design work for flow governance is set out in full in Chapter 19, covering external custody, immunity clauses, and archive separation. This chapter sets one test: a postmortem that cannot answer where it goes means the postmortem culture around it sits somewhere between the name and the practice.

The substitutes hold together because of four conditions in the industry.

A portability test is a small tool worth carrying away: score your own industry against the four conditions, present or absent. An industry missing one or two cannot copy the software model whole, but it can copy its parts. The blameless moderation process, the change-linked method of attribution, the output definition inside a postmortem template. Parts do not need the full set of industry conditions, and the parts-level transplant list is laid out in the templates of Part 5. What this chapter owes the reader is the reason parts detach and still work: their conditions are an order of magnitude looser than those of the assembled system. Parts solve the technical side of a postmortem, how to moderate, how to attribute, how to define the output. The industry conditions constrain the incentive side, why anyone writes at all and who reads the result. Technical parts carry no incentive precondition. Only the incentive side needs the conditions. Keep the two apart and the transplant budget goes to the right place.

Condition one: the object of failure is infrastructure. A service outage has no criminal dimension, the loss is capped by service level agreement (SLA) payouts, and the legal exposure of writing a postmortem is far smaller than in other industries.

Condition two: the industry has a written culture. Design documents, code review, change tickets. An engineer's ordinary work already lands on the page, and a postmortem is one more document type among familiar ones.

Condition three: failures are frequent and causally traceable. Canary releases and change management systems let the link between a given change and a given outage be drawn automatically. The sample size and the attributability are things other industries do not have.

Condition four: talent moves quickly. Engineers pass between companies and carry postmortem practice as a job skill, so the norm standardizes across the industry without any legislation.

Those same conditions mark the boundary of the exception. Software postmortems cover availability failures. Security incidents, data breaches and intrusions, hardly ever get a public postmortem, because the text itself is an attack manual and the legal liability is nowhere near capped. Product failures, meaning the wrong feature was built, and business failures, meaning the wrong market was chosen, sit outside this tradition altogether and fall back under the five gates of section 4.1.

A further boundary is a trend. In recent years the complete public postmortems from leading companies have grown fewer, status page disclosure has grown briefer, and the public libraries have slowed their rate of update. 〔Verification pending: a quantitative trend would need year-by-year counts of the public libraries; this is a qualitative judgment〕 The exception has no legislative moat. It is a function of industry conditions, and when the conditions shift, the exception contracts.

The contraction can be read in the other direction too, and that reading should be stated plainly. Contraction is market behavior rather than decline. The volume of public postmortems rises and falls with the cost-benefit calculation of the industry publishing them. It follows the market.

That reading carries a warning for anyone who cites these libraries. Do not treat any industry's transparency as a permanent feature. The library you quote may stop updating in five years, so cited knowledge needs a local copy. The knowledge pack principle of Chapter 30 applies here: an external library will walk away, your own card library will not. The same discipline serves researchers and procurement people alike. Archive a snapshot whenever you cite an external postmortem, because the archiving rules in Appendix C are as necessary in software as anywhere else.

docs.title: 4.3 The Institution Is the Price a Disaster Paid
docs.text:
Look back at the legislative history of the four devices and one pattern repeats. They are almost always written after a major disaster.

In chemicals, the U.S. Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board (CSB) was established under the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990. The legislative backdrop included the pressure from events such as the December 1984 toxic gas release at the pesticide plant in Bhopal, India, where thousands died; the count of immediate deaths is a matter for later investigations and government statistics. 〔Verification pending: the official figure would require Indian government archives; estimates vary widely, and the text keeps the qualitative "thousands"〕 In finance, the Sarbanes–Oxley Act of 2002 followed close behind the 2001 bankruptcies of Enron and WorldCom.

In aviation, the international investigation framework ratcheted upward through a run of accidents in the postwar jet age. After the collision of two aircraft at Tenerife on 27 March 1977, which killed 583 people and was investigated by the Dutch, Spanish, and American sides with the final report issued by the Spanish authorities, the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) moved revisions through on radio phraseology and cockpit communication procedure. 〔Verification pending: the official archive page for the Spanish investigation report remains to be located; this sentence has been written as a qualitative statement〕 〔Verification pending: the original ICAO Doc series texts need checking〕

Disaster pays first and the institution is written afterwards. That order tells you institutions are not created because someone recognized their importance. They are forced into existence by the pricing of loss.

The order has an observable byproduct. An institution built after a disaster usually fixes only the class of problem that disaster belonged to, which is what targeted legislation looks like: chemicals after Bhopal, financial audit after Enron. Targeting makes legislation fast, since the problem is clear and the pressure is concentrated. It also fragments the record system. Each disaster yields one agency or one act, and the institutions share no infrastructure with each other. The five precedent industries cannot exchange anything.

The direction out of fragmentation is to make the institution's infrastructure. Shared field standards for reports, shared retrieval infrastructure, mutually recognized evidence grading. One build at the infrastructure layer would serve every targeted institution at once. The promoter of that can only be a cross-industry user alliance, with insurance, academia, and media as natural members, and the object of the push is a shared tool of the kind this book is. If the twelve-field standard gets adopted by card libraries in several industries at once, infrastructure has begun to exist.

Three uses follow for the reader.

Use one: assess your industry. If your industry has no failure record system, the meaning is that losses have not yet grown large enough to force legislation, or that losses are absorbed by many small parties whose aggregation never becomes legislative pressure.

Use two: look for cheaper substitutes. Waiting for a disaster to buy the institution is the most expensive route there is. Industry self-regulatory alliances, shared postmortem libraries with liability immunity clauses, and insurer-led data pools have all been used as substitutes in the past, and section 4.4 gives the conditions under which each one stands.

Use three: the timing problem for whoever builds institutions. The disaster-buys-institution model has a corollary that runs against intuition. The window after a disaster is very short, since a legislative window usually closes before public memory fades. The operational answer is to pre-draft: an industry body keeps a finished legislative proposal on the shelf year round, so that when the disaster arrives, while everyone else is mourning, it has text.

Pre-drafting has precedent throughout legislative history. Most of the provisions that pass quickly after a disaster existed as proposals before it. The cost of keeping text ready is one drafting pass and an annual update. The return shows up in the catch rate at each window. The case format and the appendix system in this book are half of that pre-drafted text for your industry. The other half has to be filled in with your industry's own parameters.

docs.title: 4.4 Will Your Industry Grow This System?
docs.text:
Three criteria. Score each one.

Criterion one: the externality of failure. Does the failure hurt you, or the public? A failure that hurts the public eventually draws regulation, and regulation will sooner or later be pushed into building a record system. All five precedent domains are high-externality industries. A failure that hurts only you will never grow an institution, and self-discipline is the ceiling.

Criterion two: the rate of technical iteration. When the rules update more slowly than the technology, a regulator's record system cannot keep up with its own object. Fast-iterating industries are more likely to spread the norm through practitioner mobility, which is the necessary condition of the software model. Slow-iterating industries get there through legislation, which is the nuclear model.

Criterion three: practitioner mobility. Talent flow is what turns a case lesson into industry common knowledge. In low-mobility industries, utilities and some monopolies among them, lessons stay trapped in the original organization until that organization disappears.

An industry scoring on all three can expect a software-style postmortem tradition to grow on its own. An industry missing two of the three should build internally and stop waiting for the industry, and Chapters 38 and 39 supply the templates. The judgment is itself a form of prevention: knowing which kind of disaster your industry is waiting to pay the bill means at least knowing the shape of the invoice.

One addition at the level of use: read the three criteria dynamically. All three parameters move with time. Mobility rises and falls with the industry cycle, externality heats up as a regulatory issue gains prominence, iteration speed shifts with each technology generation. The operational form is to fold the three criteria into the annual industry scan, which the intelligence function of Chapter 33 can do in passing: rescore once a year.

The movement of the scores carries more information than the level of the scores. An industry whose mobility has turned from rising to falling is losing the conditions for the software model. The window is not only legislative. It is also cultural. The annual scan of windows is the last lesson this chapter has for an industry observer: institutions do not wait indefinitely, and they have a flowering season.

The shape of the invoice can be drawn as a prediction table from your industry's parameters. Score the three criteria, then lay the combination against the history of the five precedent industries and ask which way your industry's institution would arrive. The columns of the table are institutional forms: a national investigation body, an industry joint panel, an insurance data pool, an enterprise-built system, or nothing ever. The rows are combinations of scores.

The table is not fatalism. It gives a baseline, meaning the default trajectory with no intervention, and the value of a baseline is that it makes the need for intervention calculable. If the baseline says nothing ever appears, and you judge that the industry needs a record system, then the material for your argument is the difference row.

The difference row is the strongest opening a policy discussion can have: by baseline our industry will never grow a record system, and our loss curve says we need one, which is why there is a proposal on the table.

A ready comparison is the Indian cryptocurrency exchange Koinex, case st-002 in Appendix B. The founders' shutdown postmortem put the cause of death on banks freezing payment channels. Regulatory uncertainty travelled through financial infrastructure, and the industry made no wrong product decision at any point. This is the startup-shaped sample of criterion one, with the externality landing outside the practitioner: the disaster your industry is waiting for is sometimes one you did not make.

docs.title: Five Self-Checks
docs.text:
1. In your organization's most recent internal postmortem, did legal take part in reviewing the draft? What did the review change?
  2. In your industry, how much is failure detail worth as competitive intelligence? Name one specific field where writing it down amounts to arming a rival.
  3. In your industry's prospectuses, annual reports, or public materials, how templated is risk disclosure? Compare two of them and count the places where disclosure gets as far as a number.
  4. Of the four software conditions, infrastructure as the object of failure, a written culture, frequent and attributable failures, and talent mobility, which does your industry lack? The missing conditions decide whether you copy the software model or the nuclear model.
  5. The last time your industry's disaster bought an institution, what did it buy? If that invoice were issued again, where would your organization rank among the claimants?

docs.title: Chapter 5 The Twelve Fields of the Case Card
docs.text:
What this chapter covers: the twelve fields of the case card, the analytic unit this book uses everywhere, defined one at a time, each with one badly written example and one corrected version. When to come back: when you write a postmortem of your own, review someone else's, or need to compress an investigation report onto one page. Reading time: about 40 minutes.

A three-hundred-page investigation report holds almost everything and reads badly. A postmortem article reads well and holds fragments. The case card is the layer in between: one page, twelve fields, a hard requirement attached to each field, and no case admitted to the main text until the fields are filled. This chapter defines the fields one at a time and gives each one a bad example. The bad examples come from real postmortem and briefing prose. You will find the same species inside your own organization.

One term of use before the table. The twelve fields are an engineering format, not an academic one. Every field is on the card because something downstream consumes it: the ID feeds citation, what was visible then feeds training, the minimum counterfactual feeds a work order. A field with no downstream consumer has no claim on a line of the page.

Engineering formats are strict, and the strictness is the point. An engineering drawing carries tolerances because a dimension without a tolerance cannot be built to. The field requirements below are tolerances of the same kind, and "maybe good enough" quietly removes the use the field existed for.

Read with a pen in hand. Take your organization's most recent postmortem and fill each field as you reach its definition. By the end you hold one completed card. A reader who only reads ends up with a list of format facts, which is not the same thing as the skill.

The twelve fields at a glance:

# Field Hard requirement 1 Case ID domain code plus serial, unique across the book 2 One-line summary 30 characters or fewer, states only what happened 3 What and who organization plus equipment or project, nameable down to model and registration number 4 When and where year, month, day plus location 5 Domain and mechanism domain code plus main mechanism, 1–3 attached, main mechanism first 6 What was visible then information the actors held, with timestamps, at the moment they decided 7 Options ruled out options tabled and rejected, and options that never reached the table 8 The decision point who did what, in which meeting or on which document 9 Point of no return the action after signature, go-live, takeoff, or pour 10 Scale of consequences figures from primary material; where none exist, "no public quantification" 11 Minimum counterfactual one action changed avoids the event; write one 12 Evidence grade and sources grade A–E plus full citation plus link

docs.title: 5.1 Definitions and Examples, Field by Field
Field 1: Case ID
docs.text:
Definition: domain code-serial. Aviation av, chemicals ch, nuclear nu, healthcare me, pharmaceuticals ph, construction ce, maritime ma, software sw, finance fi, startups st, public policy po, military mi, manufacturing mn, agriculture ag.

The scheme travels. An organization building its own library may change the format and draw the prefix from its own industry vocabulary. Three governance rules do not travel, because they are what keeps any citation system alive: append only, keep state separate, reserve ranges. Formats can vary because an ID means something only inside its own system; your av-037 and this book's av-037 may point at different events, and carrying the title when you cite resolves it. The rules cannot be dropped because a broken link or a collided number kills a library outright. Take the three rules and the field definitions and use them as needed. Permission to take them is why this chapter exists.

Bad example: "Accident Case No. 3", or "Compilation of Typical Cases in Our City, Volume XI". The serial hangs off a table of contents. Revise the contents and the serial is void, and every citation into it snaps.

Good example: av-037. Three years later, after a contents revision, this ID still points to the Japan Airlines A350 record and its collision with the Japan Coast Guard aircraft. The ID is the anchor between this book and other material, and the primary key of the master case table in Appendix B.

Three engineering rules decide how long a scheme lives. Appending is the only permitted edit: when an ID turns out to sit under the wrong mechanism, add a correction entry and leave the number alone, because citation integrity outranks catalogue tidiness. State is a separate field, so revisions, v1 and v2, and errata never enter the ID. Ranges are reserved, with hand-collected, bulk-imported, and externally exchanged records given their own blocks of serials, so a merge cannot collide. The cost is one line of explanation in the register. The return arrives ten years out, in a system with no broken links, no duplicate numbers, and no silent renumbering, which is the credential a knowledge base needs before it can talk to outside material at all.

docs.title: Field 2: One-line summary
docs.text:
Definition: 30 characters or fewer, stating only what happened. The test is negative: no cause, no judgment, no adjective.

Bad example: "Due to inadequate safety management and weak employee safety awareness, an avoidable serious accident occurred." Six information slots, four of them judgments (inadequate, weak, avoidable, serious) and none of them fact.

Good example: "737-9 door plug separates in climb; rapid depressurization; return." Fifteen characters in the Chinese, one action sequence: component, phase, consequence, outcome. The reader knows what happened and does not yet need to know why.

The method is to find the first moment on the timeline when something went wrong physically and write it as subject, verb, object. "Door plug separated." "Ball-nut thread worn to failure." "Oxygen generator caught fire." Evaluation gets its turn later.

The field has a second use as the catalogue index line. A catalogue page carries nothing but IDs and one-line summaries, and one page then scans the whole stock of ways things die. Its standard is the scan test: fifty lines in thirty seconds, after which the reader can say roughly which families of death the library holds. A summary that fails is too long or too clever. Put the page on the wall of the decision room rather than the canteen, updated monthly as new cards arrive, since the readers of a death catalogue should be the people deciding.

Three sentence rules hold the field down. Verbs beat nominalizations: "door plug separated" beats "a door plug separation event", since nominalization hides the action inside an abstraction and is where bureaucratic prose starts. Quantifiers stay conservative: the 30-character limit forbids piling up, yet writers still squeeze in three parallel actions, so write the first physical event and leave the rest to the body. Names stay out: no personal names, no characterizations, because the summary is public-information layer while individual accountability belongs in field 8 and in the investigation documents. All three serve one purpose. The summary is a retrieval tag, a thing that exists to be found rather than read to the end.

docs.title: Field 3: What and who
docs.text:
Definition: whose thing failed. Organization name, equipment model, any identifier that can be named: flight number, registration number, construction section.

The field carries a second layer. Write the subject on two levels, the operating level and the owning level. Ask whether the crew sailed for the owner or was hired with the hull, whether the plant runs its own staff or a contractor's. Responsibility and the landing point of remediation usually sit between the two, so write a subject chain of brand owner, operator, facility. Every name on the chain holds a decision point, and primary documents usually write the subject by level, which means the chain can be copied from the report's subject section. The chain pays off in tracking: a requirement handed to one level has to be executed and verified at another, and a card with no chain gives tracking nothing to hang on.

Bad example: "an aircraft operated by a certain airline". One word, "certain", and the case drops to a fable. It cannot be checked, extended, or confirmed at the level of conditions.

Naming is also a weapon against survivorship bias. Narrated failures tend to lose their subject, and once it is gone the reader cannot check whether that company still exists, how it has done since, or whether the accident recurred. A named case allows the full verification pass, and the result is often more instructive than the story. The action is to look up what happened to the organization afterwards: its remediation, its later record, its events of the same kind. Doing this repeatedly is the advanced drill of card reading and the technical form of Chapter 2's instruction to go out and buy the death samples. Enough passes and a reader develops an instinct for the time depth of failure. An accident occupies a stretch of an organization's history; its single day is only the visible part.

Good example: "Alaska Airlines 1282, Boeing 737-9 (N704AL)." Checkable, citable, condition layer complete: the model fixes the airworthiness background, the airline fixes the maintenance system, the registration number lets anyone walk the aircraft's history in public databases.

Where naming carries legal risk, with a judgment not yet final or a penalty not yet published, drop one level: name the industry and the category, and state why the subject is not named.

One recurring argument deserves an answer. Are small subjects worth naming, the sole trader, the one-person company? Yes. Small operators account for most of the statistical mass, and anonymizing them teaches readers that risk belongs to large organizations; naming restores the distribution to its real shape. The privacy boundary is prior publication: where the subject information is already public in a primary document, the card copies it, and where it is not, the card follows the document. Beyond that boundary there is an emotional cost, and it is real. A small operator's failure, written into a book, will be read by the people involved or their families. Write only the facts the documents contain, with no characterization of anyone. Characterization is the sugar of narrative and a second injury to the people in it.

docs.title: Field 4: When and where
docs.text:
Definition: the event's year, month, day and location, precise to the day. The investigation's publication date belongs to field 12.

The field carries a geographic discipline. Write the location to the level where it can be found on a map: country, city, facility. Where the facility can be identified, name it; where it cannot, name the administrative area. The level decides whether the reader can place the case in its geographic and regulatory context, because the same mechanism in another jurisdiction carries a different condition layer, and location is the reader's first evidence about the regulator. Where a case cannot be located at all, for open sea or a facility that cannot be disclosed, say why. A stated reason distinguishes a limit from laziness.

Bad example: "early 2024", or "last summer". Early and late in a year are eleven months apart, enough room for a full maintenance cycle.

Good example: "2024-01-05, Portland, Oregon, USA, about 20 minutes after takeoff" (NTSB AIR-25-04). The date anchors the information environment: weather bulletins from before that day, maintenance records, meeting minutes all fall inside what was visible then; anything dated after is hindsight.

Precision has three more rules. Keep one time basis in a card, with event times in local time and the zone marked, and publication times in the issuing body's local time, because a mixed timeline steals the reader's sense of sequence. Distinguish an instant from a window: the minute where a minute is known, the window where only a window is known, with the source's precision marked, since false precision misleads as much as vagueness. Mark the genealogy of the timeline: where a preliminary bulletin and the final report disagree, follow the final report and note the difference, which is itself a record of how the investigation moved.

docs.title: Field 5: Domain and mechanism
docs.text:
Definition: the domain code plus the main mechanism. Up to three mechanisms may be attached, the first being the main one. Names come from the twenty-four-term vocabulary in Chapters 11–34. Do not invent one.

Bad example: "management problems", "human factors", "systemic risk". These three phrases turn up in the conclusion paragraph of most postmortems. They can hold anything, and so they explain nothing.

Good example: "av; The Invisibility of Maintenance; Practical Drift." Attaching a mechanism is an act of attribution, and an inaccurate attachment is worse than a single accurate one.

The ratio is one main mechanism and at most two companions. Three or more says the attribution has not converged; go back to the mechanism chapters, compare against their criteria, and attach again. The ratio protects the index, since a card that attaches five mechanisms has voted in five rows of the matrix and thinned the signal-to-noise ratio of every search through it. It also prevents drift. The main mechanism declared here may not change in the body text: a case can be cited in several chapters, and every citation presents it under the same main mechanism. Stable identity is part of what makes a case citable, and it is the specific defence against a case retold in each chapter as a story supporting that chapter's thesis.

docs.title: Field 6: What was visible then
docs.text:
Definition: the timestamped information the actors held when they decided. Only records whose phase can be fixed from the material are admissible: meeting minutes, work orders, the issue time of a weather forecast, the previous shift's handover notes. Anything learned only afterwards stays out, without exception.

Bad example: "hidden hazards had long existed, and management cannot escape responsibility." The phrase "long existed" erases every piece of time information. Existing for how long? Who saw it, and when? Did the person who saw it have a duty to report it?

Good example: in the Alaska Airlines 261 case (NTSB AAR-02/01), what was visible then included the inspection records from before the lubrication and end-play check intervals were extended, the application for the extended intervals with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) approval, and the accident crew's reports of abnormal jackscrew position and unusual cabin noise.
