Each item carries the date it entered someone's field of view. The thread wear found when the nut was opened after the accident is post-event information and cannot enter this field.

This is one of the two fields with the highest value density in the book, field 11 being the other. Its purpose is to keep Chapter 2's attribution bias outside the reasoning: only what the actors could see is admitted. Chapter 6 is given over to operating it.

One implicit standard needs stating. Visible does not mean noticed. The field collects information that was reachable, meaning it sat on the desk, in the system, or in the minutes; whether the person saw it is a separate question and belongs to the reader. Conflating the two lets the card quietly excuse or convict, since a thing unseen may be an attention problem or a presentation problem. Keep them apart by recording how the information was reachable: in the system, on paper, or by word of mouth. The three modes carry different attention costs. Once the mode is written, field 6 becomes the material from which a reader rebuilds the desk of that day, and every judgment made from it is the reader's own.

docs.title: Field 7: Options ruled out
docs.text:
Definition: the options on the table at the decision point that were rejected, plus the options that should have appeared and did not. Record both and mark which is which.

Bad example: "had they been more careful, it would not have happened." More careful is an option that does not exist. No action, no cost, no decision-maker. Writing it is writing nothing.

Good example, with the format shown on Challenger (Rogers Commission report, 1986). On the teleconference of the evening of January 27, 1986, the options on the table were: launch on schedule on January 28, which was selected; delay until daytime temperatures recovered, rejected on schedule pressure; and honor the engineers' proposed threshold of no launch below 53 degrees Fahrenheit (about 12 degrees Celsius), rejected because launches had already succeeded several times at lower temperatures. The absent option was any reopening of why the launch temperature threshold had been sliding downward launch by launch. Volume 1, Chapter 5 of the Rogers Commission report records that Thiokol engineers recommended against launch below 53 degrees Fahrenheit, resting largely on blow-by data from flight 51-C; the official text is at nasa.gov/history/rogersrep/v1ch5.htm, and this book read it on 2026-11-01.

Ruled-out options are valuable because they expose the structure of the decision: how options were generated, how they were rejected, who was entitled to put them on the table. Most postmortems record what was chosen and omit what was choosable, and the same option-generating machinery then produces the same menu at the next decision.

Absent options need restraint. The evidence for one is a process document. An option that procedure required and the record never shows is a legitimate absence; an option the reviewer thought of afterwards is an invention. Restraint is needed because absent options are the easiest thing in the card to write with hindsight, turning what the actors never considered into what they should have considered, which is Chapter 2's attribution bias returning through the side door. The evidentiary standard is a comparison: the step exists in the procedure, its counterpart is missing from the minutes, and the gap is the evidence. Where the evidence is thin, write the absence weakly: "the procedure appears to have offered this path; no record of discussion appears; unresolved." A weak entry costs nothing. An invented one costs the card.

docs.title: Field 8: The decision point
docs.text:
Definition: four elements, person, meeting, document, action. Who decided what, in which meeting or on which document. The date falls on a day.

A discipline is buried in that definition. A decision point has to be an identifiable human action: who, when, in what form, doing what. Automatic system actions and physical processes do not occupy this field; automated actions are recorded in the failure chain, and Chapters 21 and 22 cover the paths taken by things and by systems. The reason is what the field is for. Postmortems improve the environment in which people decide, which covers how options get generated, how information arrives, and how a signature comes to be given; with no identifiable action there is nowhere for the improvement to land. The more automated the system, the fewer human decision points remain and the more each one matters. The takeover moment in Chapter 26 is the scarce form of the decision point, and scarcity raises the standard of description, because those points are everywhere a human being can still intervene.

Bad example: "company management made the wrong decision." No name, no meeting, no document. The sentence can be neither contested nor cited.

Good example: Alaska Airlines 261 (NTSB AAR-02/01, executive summary). Alaska Airlines extended the lubrication interval and the end-play check interval for the horizontal stabilizer jackscrew assembly, and the FAA approved both; the investigation found that the extended intervals let a lubrication shortfall the old schedule would have caught develop into excessive wear and then failure (text from the executive summary, in the portions I read myself). All four elements present: the company as who, the documents and approvals as the vehicle, the interval extension as the action, the FAA approval as the gatekeeping act.

docs.title: Field 9: Point of no return
docs.text:
Definition: the moment after which the event's main consequences can no longer be undone by ordinary means. The test is in Chapter 7: money can undo it, time can undo it, a public announcement can undo it; a signature and a go-live cannot.

The register links to the duty to notify. Information arriving after the point of no return, a weather update after takeoff or a test report after the pour, is post-event information, and what it does is open a new decision point: continue, turn back, stop work. At the point of no return the question changes from whether to do the thing to whether to rescue it. Cards handle that phase as a separate entry, the post-irreversible decision, and it carries high value in review because it tests the ability to lose less in a bad position. Most postmortems only train the ability not to lose at all.

Bad example: "from the moment the project started, failure was already certain." Fatalism is not a definition of the point of no return. It folds every decision point into one and erases every position in between where intervention was still possible.

This chapter registers position only: which step, once passed, cannot be walked back. Chapter 7 owns the typology, where incremental, one-way valve, and compound types call for different interventions. The division of labour keeps the card's density manageable, since a list of positions already carries large engineering value; most organizations cannot state the irreversible points in their own key processes. Chapter 7 gives the method for compiling the list the first time, walking the process node by node and asking at each one whether the step can still be reversed. The cost is a single process walkthrough. The output is a register covering every key process, and every row should carry a named custodian, which is where Chapter 18's single-responsible-person clause comes in.

Good example: in the Japan Airlines 516 event (av-037), the point of no return formed when the Coast Guard aircraft entered the runway while the A350 crew held landing clearance. From that combination onward, the two aircraft's speeds and the remaining distance made the collision an event most operating paths could not avoid. Assembly-type cases are cleaner: the door closes, the concrete is poured, the reactor is synchronized to the grid, and every minute of work afterwards is paying the fare for that action.

docs.title: Field 10: Scale of consequences
docs.text:
Definition: the figures in the primary material. Deaths, injuries, money lost, hours of downtime, units recalled; write whatever exists and name its source. With no figures, write "no public quantification".

Bad example: "caused enormous economic loss and severe social impact." Enormous is how much? Severe to what degree? The sentence's only function is to hold a place.

Good example: "0 deaths; 7 minor injuries (all passengers); 169 uninjured; aircraft substantially damaged" (av-030, NTSB AIR-25-04). Four figures, each with its own basis, all from one report.

"No public quantification" is a legitimate answer. It means the consequences never entered any primary document. It does not mean they were zero.

Casualty figures follow an official basis and carry its version. Preliminary and final counts often differ, since an initial bulletin gets revised as identities are confirmed, and the card takes the final adjudicated basis while preserving the revision trail. The reason is respect as much as law: every number in a casualty count corresponds to particular people and families, and a careless basis does harm to the people behind the digits. The operation is to date the number, as in "7 minor injuries (adjudicated, 2025-03)". Number and adjudication date travel together, and the reader knows which version is in hand. Version management looks fussy. It is the minimum courtesy this book extends to this field.

docs.title: Field 11: Minimum counterfactual
docs.text:
Definition: the one action which, changed, would have avoided the event or sharply reduced its consequences. Work backward from the latest action that did not depend on luck. Book-wide discipline: write exactly one.

Bad example: "had management been strengthened, systems perfected, awareness raised, and oversight tightened, the accident could have been avoided." Four actions amount to none. The reader cannot tell which comes first, and so does none of them.

Good example: Alaska Airlines 261 (AAR-02/01). Leave the end-play check interval unextended and inspect on the original schedule, and the wear had a chance of being found before it reached failure. One action, at the latest position on the chain of decisions actually taken, resting on no luck of the "happened to be spotted" kind. (AAR-02/01 executive summary p. 4, and the Safety Board's statistical study of end-play data in section 1.18.2; PDF verified.)

The field is a training device. Writing it forces the author to answer where the minimal intervention point lay along the whole chain. Chapter 10 gives the backward-walking method. Two counterfactuals amount to none, because the reader remembers the easy one, and the easy one is rarely the minimal intervention point.

One test is gold. Write the counterfactual as an instruction: who, by what date, does what, at what cost, approved by whom. Fill all five and it is usable; fail any and it is a wish. The test pulls the lesson down from the moral layer to the operating layer. "Tighten oversight" fails it; "change this check from annual to semiannual" passes, and the gap between the two is the gap between a lesson and a slogan. Organizations can use the test at scale by turning every passing counterfactual straight into a work order. A counterfactual that reaches a work order is closed. One that stays on the page is decoration.

docs.title: Field 12: Evidence grade and sources
docs.text:
Definition: grade (A, full independent investigation report; B, official bulletin or communiqué; C, judgment or penalty document; D, public postmortem by a party involved; E, media lead), a full citation, and a link. Rule: E-grade material may never be the sole source for a case in the main text.

Bad example: "compiled from multiple media reports." When several outlets retell one wire story, "multiple" is a fake number.

Good example: "Grade A. NTSB, Aviation Investigation Final Report DCA21FA085, 2023; link at Appendix B, av-006."

A citation has to resolve to a document name and number, and the link has to have been opened by hand. No exceptions, because this is the collateral behind every credibility claim the book makes.

Readers need a conversion table. Read the grade first; it tells you how the card may be used. Grade A: all details quotable, down to signatory-level actions, and a postmortem can benchmark against it directly. Grade B: the event frame and official conclusions quotable, with detail discounted, since a bulletin carries limited resolution. Grade C: the facts legally established are quotable, and a judgment's fact section has been tested in adversarial proceedings, which is the distinctive value of the grade, though the disputed issues may have shaped which facts were selected. Grade D: frame only, no details, because a party's own postmortem has not been adversarially tested. Grade E: a lead only, to be followed toward primary or secondary material and not cited until something is found. The table also sets house rules: an organization can decide that only A through C cards enter the library used as a basis for decisions, and with that rule standing, the library has a gate.

Link rot needs a policy, because rot is the norm. Sites get rebuilt, agencies merge, PDFs come down, in batches every year. Three layers answer it. Snapshot at first reading, archiving the page or keeping the local PDF. Register the dead link on the errata page with a substitute entry point. Downgrade where no substitute exists, following Appendix C, or convert the entry into a checkpoint. All three belong to the reading routine, and their cost is small: archive while collecting, click the batch once a year. They keep the book's citations checkable five years out, and checkability is the difference between a card library and a scrapbook of news.

docs.title: 5.2 Why Three Fields Carry the Value
docs.text:
Of the twelve, fields 2, 3, 4, 5, and 10 supply coordinates, fields 8 and 9 supply structure, and fields 6, 7, and 11 supply training. Strip 6, 7, and 11 from a card and what remains is indistinguishable from news. News tells you that something happened. Those three let you rehearse what you would have done.

Be honest about the cost. The three take more than sixty percent of the hours in one card: field 6 means checking phases along a timeline, field 7 means digging rejected options out of documents, field 11 means the full backward walk. Tooling answers it. Phase markers for field 6 come from a timeline template, the absence record in field 7 from a process comparison table, the backward walk in field 11 from the four questions in Chapter 10, and good tools compress the sixty percent to thirty. Tooling has a second payoff in consistency: cards by different authors reach the same level on the fields that matter, and a library that reads as though one person wrote it becomes possible. Templates sit in Part 5. This chapter's job is to say that the expensive part is expensive for a reason, and that it has tools.

The three relate in a fixed order. Field 6 fixes the information environment, since you can only decide with the cards on the table. Field 7 lists the real options that were on it, including the one never played. Field 11 points at the card whose replacement wins the hand. Together they make one repeatable drill: read field 6, write your own field 7, make your own choice, then turn the page and compare against the actors' choice in field 8 and the minimal intervention point in field 11.

The drill grades by difficulty, and one card can be worked three times. In the first round the card is open: field 6 gives the full information set, and what gets trained is the imagination of options. In the second the card is half covered: fields 7 and 11 are hidden, field 6 and the situation are given, and what gets trained is the handling of information. In the third the card is closed: only time, place, and subject are given, and the reader reconstructs what was visible and what the options were from industry knowledge before comparing, which trains the actual stock of that knowledge and usually stings most. Space the rounds a month apart, since repeating a card too soon contaminates memory and a longer gap keeps the comparison honest. The card is a dumbbell, the weights come in steps, and different weights work different muscles. This is the specific remedy for Chapter 2's attribution bias, and the reason every case in this book stops at the decision point.

Two variants serve readers at different levels. Solo: read field 6 and the situation, write your option list and your choice on paper, then compare. Writing is the point, since an unwritten choice is an imagining while a written one can be tested. Group: split a morning meeting in two, hand out the front of the card, keep the back with the facilitator, discuss the options, then reveal. The group variant buys option diversity, because a room generates a fuller list than one person and absent options surface more easily in company. Both cost about ten minutes per card, and both are the basic forms of the morning meeting script in Chapter 35, which is nothing more than the variants fixed into a procedure.

docs.title: 5.3 How to Use the Fields
docs.text:
Three uses. Writing a postmortem: Chapter 38 turns the twelve fields into a template and attaches a paragraph-by-paragraph rewrite of a "strengthen management" style postmortem. Reviewing: the question lists in Chapter 37 are grouped by mechanism, and their answers backfill fields 6 and 7. Building a ledger: an organization indexes its industry's cards by mechanism under field 5, sorts them onto a timeline by field 4, and distils check items out of field 11; that ledger is the ammunition for the rehearsal meeting in Chapter 39.

Two more uses are worth adding. External communication: when an event description goes to a regulator, a customer, or an insurer, the twelve fields are a complete materials list, and a party that prepares by field always has a page number ready when a question comes. The value is that failure knowledge becomes a negotiating asset, and the posture of a party with complete materials in accident communication, claim negotiation, and regulatory inquiry is a different posture. Teaching: an industry induction course can be taught from that industry's cards, which carry three parts less drama and seven parts less bias than an accident story, and ten parts more structure. A newcomer learns how the industry dies faster from cards than from legend.

The five uses converge. The twelve fields are the working language of the field, and someone who has learned them saves a layer of translation in every conversation with this book, with their own organization, and with outside parties.

One caution on the other side of the standard: the twelve fields are a floor, never a ceiling. Additions should still be governed. Use the twelve for three years before considering a thirteenth, and put a candidate through three gates: it has a clear downstream consumer, it has a fill standard that can be executed, and the cost of producing a card stays bearable with it added. The gates stop field inflation, the geriatric disease of every format, since each added field is a tax on every card already written. The exception to the tax is the optional field, marked optional, with no backfill of old cards and no obligation on new ones. Version the field set as Chapter 1 governs IDs, with v1 holding the twelve and v2 listing the optional additions. A format can stay alive, provided it stays disciplined.

Blank space on a card can hold any supplementary material. A case that cannot complete any one of the twelve is demoted to the appendix matrix, which accepts an ID, a domain, a mechanism, and consequences. The main text accepts nothing less.

Demotion runs both ways. A matrix card returns to the main text when the twelve fields are complete, the sources reach grade A through C, and the three key fields are written, and the return is reviewed on the same standard as first admission. Because the clause runs both ways, the matrix is a bench rather than a bin, and the bench matters because it keeps the route back open. Maintaining that route keeps a library alive: once a year, go through the matrix and ask which cards are close to promotion, which fields they lack, and what the path to filling them is. The review produces the work order for the next collection round. Chapter 28 makes the same argument about lists in general, that a list needs a destination. A bench means demotion is not an ending.

docs.title: Five Self-Checks
docs.text:
1. Write a twelve-field card for your organization's last major loss. Note which fields the first card cannot fill.
  2. In your postmortem documents, which passages are information known only afterwards, written as though it were known at the time? Rewrite one passage.
  3. At your last significant decision, which options were on the table? For each rejected option, who supplied the reason, and where is it recorded?
  4. Can your organization state the point of no return for each of its key processes? Do the people who can state it hold rank enough to call a halt?
  5. Take your industry's most recent investigation report and restate it using only the content of field 6. Has your conclusion changed?

One graduation standard sits beyond the five questions: complete one full card alone, from choosing the report to checking the citation, asking no one for help. Hand it to someone who has read this chapter and have them review it field by field against the requirements here. Their feedback is the final list of gaps between you and this chapter. A reader who clears that list can build a card library for any organization. What the skill is worth in the market, which Chapter 4 discussed as the scarcity of the circulating translator, and in governance, since the postmortem template in Chapter 38 takes this as its skeleton, is argued later in the book. Get the skill into your hands first. The occasions for using it will announce themselves.

docs.title: Chapter 6 Visible at the Time
docs.text:
What this chapter covers: how to drive the hindsight perspective out of your postmortems and out of your reading. Three operating disciplines, one test, three worked examples. When to turn back: when writing a postmortem, reading one, reviewing a design, or catching yourself saying "they should have seen it". Estimated reading time: 45 minutes.

The main enemy of the postmortem is a fact about memory: a person who knows how something ended can no longer think the way they thought before they knew.

The fact applies to the case card as well. Every card is written after the outcome is known, and no card can eliminate hindsight; the discipline has to be forced into the fields. Field 6, what was visible at the time, stands alone in the left column while the analytic fields are held back during composition. One rule follows: fill Field 6 first, and read the outcome section only after it is complete. An ordering discipline is imperfect and better than nothing. It rests on the writer's self-control, and self-control fails, so every card library needs a fallibility statement and an errata channel alongside it.

What follows compresses the contamination to a minimum, and states its ceiling in the same breath: these disciplines cannot return a postmortem to zero bias. Bias can be compressed, never zeroed. Memory and the narrative instinct reintroduce the outcome perspective at every layer of writing. Chapter 2 made that claim. This chapter is the compression manual.

Teach the three disciplines to your team. One person compressing their own bias still leaves a team postmortem with bias in it. Only when the whole team carries the disciplines does an organization's postmortem turn collectively. The teaching material is this chapter: forty minutes to read, an afternoon to practise.

The three rules: use only timestamped material; use only information the actors could obtain; list separately everything learned later. Executed together, they hold hindsight outside the door.

Whether the door is actually shut can be tested. The exchange test hands your left column to someone who does not know the outcome and asks them to infer what happened. The distance between their inference and the real ending is the purity of your column. A short distance means the column leaves the right blanks and leaks nothing from the future. The tester should if possible be a new colleague, who carries none of the organization's existing narrative and so measures more accurately. The test returns a purity score and a recording of the tester's reasoning, which shows what path your column led the reader down. Run it on a sample of postmortems once a quarter. Half a day of a newcomer buys an objective third-party reading of postmortem quality.

docs.title: 6.1 Why the Rearview Mirror Cannot Be Shut Off
docs.text:
Psychological experiments in the 1970s gave the phenomenon its name. Baruch Fischhoff's classic study had two groups read the same historical situation, one told how it turned out and one not told. The group that knew judged the outcome to have been systematically more likely all along, and did not realize that knowing the ending was why (Fischhoff, "Hindsight Foresight: The Effect of Outcome Knowledge on Judgment under Uncertainty", 1975; full citation: Fischhoff, 'Hindsight-foresight', Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance 1(3): 288–299, 1975, bibliographic record verified via Crossref).

One laboratory detail carries a sharper implication for organizations. People who know the outcome do not merely raise their estimate for the outcome that happened. They lower their estimates for the others. The whole probability distribution is dragged toward the ending, and a distribution dragged that way is useless for risk work. The historical risk list written inside a postmortem has already been reshaped by the outcome, so using it to identify future risks is measuring new events with a bent ruler.

The correction is to write intervals instead of points. A risk retrospective records the several outcomes that seemed possible at the time, each with the basis it rested on. That spreads the bent distribution back out. The difficulty is evidential: probability judgments made at the time were almost never written down. That is the gap the decision record of Chapter 7 fills. Write the distribution at the moment of decision, and a future postmortem inherits a draft the ending has not touched.

The draft does not need to be elaborate. Line 2.5 of the three-line decision record covers it: the main alternative outcomes then believed, and roughly how much confidence each carried, in words rather than numbers. "About seventy percent confident" is enough for a later comparison. Verbal probability is unintimidating, since numerical probability demands calibration training while anyone can write down how confident they felt. Vagueness beats absence, because a postmortem with no draft can only be reshaped by the ending. File it in the same repository as the decision record. Half a line added to the Chapter 7 system saves a chapter's worth of archaeology later.

Later research gave the effect a plainer name: creeping determinism. Once the ending is known, memory rewrites the process into a single road running to that ending.

Inside an organization the consequences are worse than in a laboratory, because postmortems are written by people who know the ending, for readers who will know it too. Three layers of contamination stack up: the author knows, the reader knows, and both find it obvious that anyone at the time would have known.

Each layer has one counter. The author's is a writing-order discipline: left column first. The reader's is a reading-order discipline: left column alone, form a judgment, then read the right column and compare. The editor's is a layout discipline: columns physically separated, the entry point to the right column at the end of the left column, behind an explicit button. All three cost layout work and process discipline, and none is technically difficult. The difficulty is persistence, which comes from template fixation, Chapter 38's subject. The template hard-codes where the columns sit, so an editor who wants to interleave them has to fight the tooling.

Layout discipline sounds like housekeeping. It is the only one of the three that keeps working after the author leaves. Institutionalized layout outlives personal conscientiousness. Without it, postmortems train no judgment at all. Every fork in the road looks like open highway on paper, the reader concludes he would have seen it too, and back at his own desk he finds information arriving mixed with noise.

Accident investigation bodies maintain a whole procedural defence against this, and five of their devices can be lifted directly. Facts and analysis are published as separate parts, and the boundary between them is the boundary between the columns. Evidence is numbered item by item, so the analysis cites numbers and the citation chain can be checked. Competing hypotheses are worked through before any conclusion, and the report lists the hypotheses it excluded with the grounds. Conclusions are graded, each annotated with the strength of the evidence behind it, reusing the grade table in Chapter 10. Dissent is recorded: disagreements inside the team go into the report, because the presence of dissent is a mark of honesty.

All five have been verified as transferable, since they recur across industries in the better investigations. Resistance is measured in working hours. Together they add roughly thirty percent to the time a postmortem takes, and what that thirty percent buys is a generation of difference in credibility. Put a postmortem with all five beside one missing three, read both, and the gap needs no argument.

The anti-forgery principle deserves one more step. A structured document's verification path closes because every number it carries walks down to a physical object in the file. The report cites an investigation number, the number resolves to an interview record number, and the interview record carries a signature page. Three levels down, and forgery would have to be committed at one of the three.

The organizational version of that landing is an evidence chain of numbers. Each fact number maps to a number in the source record, which can be a work order number, a log ID, a page number in meeting minutes, anything that lands on a physical object. A postmortem whose numbering chain closes gains anti-forgery and anti-forgetting at once, because retrieval runs on the numbers. Three years later, the factual basis of a conclusion takes about five minutes to reach.

Reports of the NTSB type split facts and analysis into two parts. The facts part admits only material that carries a source and a phase. The analysis part annotates each statement with the fact it rests on. The structure's deeper function is chronological sorting: for any statement, the first question is whether it happened before the accident or after.

For readers who work in investigation, that question has an upgraded form. Tag each statement with three moments: when the event occurred, when the information about it was recorded, when the author used it. Three-phase tagging makes recording delay visible, and recording delay is itself an object of postmortem. A record system with long delays produces a left column that is incomplete by construction. One more column than two-phase tagging buys an evaluation dimension for the record system, and gives improvement a precise target under Chapter 38's trace-keeping requirements: the link with the longest delay gets rebuilt first.

This chapter's discipline is that whole procedure compressed into three rules a person or a team can execute on Monday.

The scope has to be drawn before the rules are applied. They constrain the writing and reading of postmortems, whose purpose is to preserve the training value of judgment. They do not constrain the conduct of an accident investigation, which should exhaust every piece of evidence available after the fact. An investigation establishes what happened; a postmortem re-enacts a decision. The two document types face different directions, so their disciplines differ.

The two meet at the reading of an investigation report: facts part under this chapter's discipline, analysis part as conclusions, the switch between the two readings being the section heading. With the scope drawn this way, no reader need fear that the discipline turns a postmortem into a crippled version of the truth. The right column, the post-hoc reconstruction, is where the truth is kept. The discipline asks only that the two worlds be labelled.

docs.title: 6.2 Discipline One: Timestamped Material Only
docs.text:
The operational definition: every item admitted to the visible-at-the-time set must answer when it entered whose field of view. Only items that can answer it may stand as inputs to the decision.

Timestamped material includes meeting minutes, with date, attendees and the order of the agenda; work orders and checklists, with completion time and signatory; the publication times of weather and market data; the timelines of recordings and chat logs; the sequence of steps in an approval flow.

One digital-age caution belongs on that list. System timestamps are not automatically trustworthy. Server clocks can be reset, clocks across machines drift out of sync, log time zones can be a mess. Judgment about sequence across systems needs clock alignment first. Record the clock source and the time zone for each class of log, in the system configuration, so that at postmortem time the clocks are checked before the timeline is ordered. Cross-system accidents are where this trap bites hardest: two systems five minutes apart in their logs will invert the order of events, and an inverted order drives the analysis in a completely different direction. Synchronize the watches, then read the cards.

Material without timestamps includes the recollections of participants, summary reports, retellings in the press, and undated statements like "hidden dangers had been found repeatedly before this".

An aviation case shows how hard the discipline bites. In the fact chain of Alaska Airlines 261 (NTSB AAR-02/01), the items that can carry timestamps include the application documents for extending the lubrication and end-play check intervals, with the dates on which the FAA approved them; the accident crew's reports to the ground about abnormal jackscrew position on the horizontal stabilizer, with call times; and cabin reports of unusual noise, with times. The thread wear morphology of the nut found in the teardown after the accident, and the laboratory metallurgical analysis, have no moment at which they entered anyone's field of view. They go to the hindsight column whole.

Once the columns are separated, the reader sees what the decision-makers held: the interval had been extended by their own organization, and the aircraft had begun reporting abnormal position. What they were not holding was any card showing the condition of the nut.

The method asks something cruel of the writer. Every clever insight has to pass four questions, and most fail, because they are thoughts available only after the ending is known. The cruelty pays. The thinner the left column, the more real the reader's immersion, and fewer cards on the table means the judgment being trained is closer to the judgment the field demanded.

The method extends outside postmortems. Split a history book's account into what was visible then and what was learned later, and you will see at once how much of what gets called foresight was assembled afterward. The demystification of historical reading comes free with this discipline.

The frequent error in practice is to treat the existence of information somewhere inside the organization as visibility to the actor. Between existing and visible lie four gaps: channel, format, timing, language. A test report buried on the ninth directory level of a shared drive does not exist for the engineer making a release decision at two in the morning.

Judging visibility takes four questions. Did the item enter the channel the actor actually uses? The duty room reads the duty system, not the shared drive. Can the format be read on the spot? An original English report handed to a night-shift assembler may not be. Did it arrive before the action or after it? And can the magnitude be grasped on the spot, when the one number that matters sits inside a hundred pages?

Institutionalized, those questions become an information accessibility audit: an annual sample of key decision points, drawn from every major decision the organization made that year, audited by postmortem-style walkthrough. It produces an annual accessibility report that lists the decision points where accessibility failed and classifies the causes, channel missing, format wrong, timing late, magnitude hidden, with counts for each. The report goes to the annual budget for information infrastructure, Chapter 39's line item, where accessibility spending and its returns are reconciled. The audit costs about two working days a year, sampling plus walkthrough. An individual discipline governs the pen; an annual audit governs the system.

The four questions also compress into a pocket card, taped to the monitor while a postmortem is written: channel, format, timing, magnitude. Read the four words in order. If any word fails, the item moves to the right column.

From the pocket card the next step is organizational: an information accessibility matrix, key decision points as rows, the four questions as columns, the actual situation at the time in the cells, maintained annually by Chapter 33's intelligence function. Its output is an accessibility terrain map. The depressions on it, information that should have been visible at a key decision point and was not, form the construction list for information infrastructure. That list's budget line exists in Chapter 39. From terrain map to budget, the chain is complete except for a first move.

docs.title: 6.3 Discipline Two: Only What the Actors Could Obtain
docs.text:
The direct corollary: any "data at the time" cited in a postmortem must state whose hands it was in.

Where the same information sits in an organization determines what it is worth. Risk control knew that customer concentration had passed its limit, but the lending decision belonged to a branch manager whose system displayed only a ranking of customer contribution. A postmortem that writes "the bank knew concentration was over the limit and lent anyway" has placed the risk department's knowledge inside the branch manager's field of view. The accurate version reads: "the branch's lending system interface carries no customer-concentration field; that field appears only in the head office risk monthly report, dated the fifteenth of each month." Both sentences describe the same organization. The first invents a decision-maker who never existed.

A companion field belongs beside the distribution note: the people who should have known. Record which positions, by design, were supposed to have this information, then record who actually knew. The designed side comes from process documents, job descriptions and flow charts that specify the intended scope of knowledge. The actual side comes from systems and records, which show who could really see. Put the two columns side by side and the difference is a symptom of the information system.

A distribution table built this way serves two later chapters at once: information attenuation up the hierarchy (Chapter 16) and lateral information gaps (Chapter 21). Draw it once and both analyses have ground under them.

The Challenger case shows why the discipline is necessary, and shows it most completely. On the teleconference of the evening of January 27, 1986, the engineers' hand held this: O-rings recovered from booster joints on earlier flights had shown erosion and blow-by, with flight numbers and photographs on record; those signs correlated statistically with low temperature; the joint had performed worst at the lowest launch temperature reached so far. Their hand did not hold the on-site high-speed imagery, which came into existence only after the accident; nor the precise order in which the joint failed, reconstructed afterward; nor data on how the second seal behaved dynamically at low temperature, supplied by later experiments. The decision in that meeting was made with the first hand only. The Rogers Commission report can support attribution at the organizational layer precisely because its evidence chain keeps the two hands strictly apart. (Each item checked: the flight-numbered records of erosion and blow-through, and the Morton Thiokol engineer's memorandum of July 31, 1985 warning of "a catastrophe of the highest order", both appear in Volume 1, Chapter 6, "An Accident Rooted in History"; the conduct of the meeting, with the engineers' photographs and diagrams entered as evidence, appears in Volume 1, Chapter 5. Official full text at nasa.gov/history/rogersrep/, read and verified for this book on 2026-11-01.)

The material leaves an advanced note for postmortem writers. Split the actors' hands by person. The engineers and the managers in that night's meeting held different cards: the engineers held cards leaning on data, the managers held cards about schedule and precedent. Only when the hands are split does the source of the disagreement become readable.

The technique is a seat-by-seat card chart, one column per attendee, recording what he brought into the room, what he received there, and who received what he sent out. The cost is a few more columns per person. The return is that a meeting postmortem stops being a blur and becomes a card game analyzable seat by seat: whose card was suppressed and never played, whose was played at the wrong moment. Chapter 19's price list for speaking and Chapter 16's attenuation analysis both run on that chart.

docs.title: 6.4 Discipline Three: What Was Learned Later Goes in Its Own Column
docs.text:
On the page, Discipline Three is two columns. The left column is visible at the time. The right column is reconstructed afterward, and every right-column entry states how it became known: teardown, interview, experiment, data analysis.

The right column carries a source discipline of its own. The means by which post-hoc information was obtained must be named as a tool: which instrument performed the teardown, whom the interview spoke to, what parameters the experiment ran. Tool information is what makes the right column's evidential strength assessable. Spoken post-hoc information and measured post-hoc information differ by an order of magnitude.

The execution standard is one line of source per entry, abbreviations acceptable: teardown report number, the interviewee's position, the experiment's parameter table number. The benefit is that the right column becomes checkable in its own right. A postmortem with both columns checkable is the highest definition of a postmortem this book offers.

The columns may not be interleaved. Any sentence that borrows from the right column to support reasoning in the left gets rewritten or deleted.

Visible at the time (left column) Reconstructed afterward (right column) Around 20:00 on January 27, contractor engineers on the teleconference recommended against launching below 12 degrees Celsius Launch imagery shows gas leakage at the joint beginning around the 58th second after liftoff [pending: page number awaits the official Rogers report text] Erosion records from O-rings recovered on earlier flights, flight numbers checkable Laboratory low-temperature elasticity test data, run after the accident Contractor management reversed its position after a recess of roughly 30 minutes and agreed to launch Vaughan's 1996 quantitative reconstruction of the successive lowering of launch temperature thresholds

The value of the two columns lies in the existence of the right one. It admits on paper which content is post-hoc knowledge, and in doing so exposes an illusion the author and the reader share. A postmortem with interleaved columns never writes the word "afterward" and depends on hindsight in every sentence. The two-column version drives those sentences into the annotation column, where anyone can see them.

One maintenance rule: keep the growth history of the right column. An early draft's right column is thin and thickens as the investigation goes deeper. Keeping the two versions side by side leaves a live record of how the postmortem's understanding evolved. That record has teaching value. Where the draft judgment and the final judgment differ is the trace of an author's cognition being corrected by evidence, and such a trace is unusually good material for training judgment.

The organizational application is a postmortem of the postmortems. Once a year, sample the differences between first draft and final version across everything the organization produced, and look for the pattern. Which class of problem is always misread in the first draft is the organization's systematic blind spot in judgment. That list is the target paper for the next training cycle, and Chapter 39's rehearsal meetings should pick their topics from it first.

docs.title: 6.5 The Test: Three Signal Classes and One Dissection
docs.text:
A quick test for readers. When a piece of narration contains any of the following three classes of signal words, the hindsight perspective is doing the talking.

The first class is the counterfactual inside a process account: "if only, at the time, they had". A counterfactual appearing there means the author is filtering the process through the outcome.

The list has to keep growing as the genre's style evolves. Three phrases have come into fashion and belong on it: "essentially", "in the final analysis", "when it comes down to it". They almost always land where attribution is converging, and they work as rhetorical tools for compressing a complex failure, which is the flattening disease of Chapter 2, section 2.3. The mechanism for growing the list is a team blacklist of signal words, kept in a shared document and extended after each month's postmortem meeting. The longer the list, the stronger the team's immunity. The blacklist is for marking, not banning: writing does not have to avoid these words, but where one appears the author checks the perspective. Marking trains self-awareness. It does not censor vocabulary.

The second class is the vocabulary of surprise and retrospection: "had they known", "to everyone's surprise", "unexpectedly", "nobody imagined", "and yet". The subject of these words is a person who knows the ending, not an actor in the event.

The third class is "in fact, by then it had already". Behind every "in fact" sits a piece of information with no timestamp. Interrogate it: who saw it, when, through which channel.

For a deeper check, dissect. Break the narration into event cards, each card carrying two lines: the moment the event happened, and the moment the information reached the decision-maker's field of view. The difference between the two lines is the post-hoc content.

The tool version is a dissection table with three columns, event, event time, information arrival time, and a fourth that computes the difference. Every row gets filled. Where arrival time cannot be established, the row is marked N/A with a note. The N/A rows become a list of record gaps, which is also a map of where the trace-keeping system is missing pieces.

The payoff usually arrives about thirty minutes in, when the person filling the table first sees, physically, how many rows carry a large gap. Those rows are where hindsight is concentrated, and they get rewritten or moved to the right column. The template belongs in the postmortem toolkit of Chapter 38, alongside the two-column template and the signal word list. Those three pieces are the complete set of implements for this chapter's discipline.

Do it once and you will find that in most of your own cards the two lines carry the same moment. As you wrote, you promoted the ending into the information environment of the time.

More phrases are worth collecting, and the acknowledgements and closing paragraphs are where they cluster: "if only it had been a little earlier", "thankfully", "a blessing in misfortune", "fortunately". Words of that kind in a closing paragraph mean the author's perspective was suspended over the outcome from beginning to end.

The correction for a closing paragraph is to return to the beginning. What the ending should answer is this: if we did it again, which items on the list of decision points would change? That question forces the author from the endpoint back to the start, and the round trip is itself a full self-check of the three disciplines across the document. An alternative honest ending states the limits of the judgment: "this postmortem's reconstruction of what was visible then is limited by missing records; the following three points cannot be restored." A limitation statement tells the reader where the thin ice is. Thin ice is not off limits; it has to be crossed with the uncertainty in view.

docs.title: 6.6 Three Walkthroughs
docs.text:
Walkthrough one: rewriting an Alaska Airlines 261 postmortem.

The hindsight version reads: "the threads of the jackscrew nut were already severely worn, the safety margin exhausted, and ditching was only a matter of time." Three post-hoc components sit in that sentence. The degree of wear was known only from the teardown. "The safety margin exhausted" is an analytic conclusion. "Only a matter of time" is an inference running backward from the ending.

The visible-at-the-time version reads: "the crew of the accident flight reported abnormal stabilizer position and motor overload in succession, with call records of repeated attempts and exchanges over roughly ten-plus minutes; the component's lubrication and check intervals had earlier been extended following the company's application and FAA approval (AAR-02/01 executive summary p.4, verified)."

Both versions describe one event. The first teaches the reader to watch out for wear. The second teaches the reader to watch the decision chain that extended the interval, and the procedure for handling abnormal signals. The first cannot be acted on. The second can.

There is an extreme form of actionable writing, the decision-point re-enactment. The left column becomes a drill. The reader reaches the decision point, closes the material, writes down a judgment, then opens it again to compare. Re-enactment is the name of this book's stop-point design, and it converts a postmortem from something read into something practised.

The organizational use is a rebuilt postmortem meeting, with the agenda changed from reading the report aloud to walking the decision points. At each point the meeting stops, everyone writes a judgment, and then the discussion starts. The meeting takes twice as long and trains ten times as much. Resistance comes from the time cost, and the honest comparison is that one rebuilt meeting is worth three accidents. The account is worked out in Chapter 39's budget.

An actionable left column has a check standard: the density of executable instruction. Can the reader, after each sentence, list an action? Sentences that allow it are information. Sentences that do not are atmosphere. The strict form is one action per paragraph: every paragraph contains at least one item convertible into an action check, and paragraphs that fall short get cut or supplemented.

The organizational version is quantitative quality control. Count the executable instructions in each postmortem and send anything below threshold back for rewriting, with the threshold starting at three per page. This control and the Chapter 38 template requirements are two halves of one gate: the template governs structure, the count governs density.

Walkthrough two: the 737-9 door plug (av-030, NTSB AIR-25-04).

Among the safety issues listed in the report's executive summary is the state of work on the door area during final assembly at Boeing's Renton factory. Sorted under the two-column discipline, the visible side holds the operational fact that this door had been opened for riveting rework within the assembly flow, together with the states of the work-order records along the release chain. The hindsight side holds the laboratory confirmation made after the accident that four positioning bolts were missing and no reinstallation was recorded (AIR-25-04 PDF pp. 10, 22, 26, verified).

Standing at the release node, what the actors could see was that the records were incomplete. What they could not see was that the bolts were missing. A postmortem that writes "they knew the bolts were not installed and released the aircraft anyway" has pushed the right column's physical evidence into the left column's heads.

The accurate question sits in the left column: how did work on a critical area, with no record of reinstallation, pass down the release chain without any additional confirmation being required? That question points at structure, specifically at the rule that incomplete records for critical-area work should by themselves trigger manual review. The remedies are in Chapter 29 (the invisibility of maintenance) and Chapter 15 (practical drift). The attribution of knowing violation points at nothing.

Structure-pointing questions come in a set of five patterns, all running backward from the conclusion. How was it allowed, meaning who did the structure authorize? How was it not stopped, meaning which gate was missing? How was it not seen, meaning which information chain was broken? How was it not written down, meaning which record requirement was absent? How did nobody own it, meaning which seat was empty?

The output is a list of five structural questions, each pointing at an object that can be modified. That list is the translation layer between postmortem and remediation, and the layer is what lets a postmortem end in a work order instead of a sigh. A sigh-style postmortem leaves the reader with a feeling. A postmortem built from the sentence patterns leaves a work order.

Attribution by knowing violation deserves a specific prohibition, because it is the most harmful pattern in the genre. It disguises a structural problem as a problem of character, and writes a repairable organizational defect as an unrepairable human one.

Enforcement takes a substitution drill. Whenever the pen produces "knowingly" or "deliberately", stop and ask why a rational person inside that structure would have done this. The answers that come back are almost always structural: the appraisal system, the process, the information available, the workload.

The psychological resistance is that the drill looks like excusing the actors. Chapter 2 covered the difference. Attribution places a behaviour inside its conditions in order to understand it. Excusing wipes responsibility off the conditions. This chapter trains attribution. When it is done, responsibility is still distributed through the structure, each piece where it belongs. Fixing the structure is more useful than cursing the people.

Walkthrough three: the R44 that took off at night in fog (av-021, NTSB CEN23FA125).

Visible at the time: the pilot's night qualification and instrument experience status, checkable in person and in the records; his own visual reading of the weather at the departure point; the night visual conditions before departure and in the direction of the destination. Reconstructed afterward: the flight path rebuilt from ADS-B data, which shows ground impact within a very short distance after liftoff.

A postmortem that writes "he did not know he had entered dense fog" breaks Discipline Two. Whether he knew cannot be established from the materials. What can be established is the climb and the turn he performed at that moment. Write actions, leave the psychology out: rule 2 of the case-writing method in Chapter 5, applied here.

The rule has a companion. Gaps between actions are left blank, honestly. If forty minutes pass between two calls with nothing recorded, write that nothing was recorded. A blank is honesty toward the recording system; filling it is a deception of the reader. Mark the blank with a gap row in the timeline: forty minutes with no record, no calls inbound or outbound and no system event log. The gap row reminds the reader that every judgment in that interval is a blind spot.

Gap density is diagnostic data in itself. Many gaps along the key decision chain mean the trace-keeping system is in poor condition, and Chapter 38's trace requirements exist to treat exactly that. The psychological threshold for leaving blanks is higher than it appears. A writer's instinct is to fill the gaps with reasonable inference so the narrative runs smoothly. Smoothness is a virtue in narrative and a poison in postmortem.

docs.title: 6.7 The Limits of the Discipline
docs.text:
The three disciplines have an honest boundary. In most organizations, timestamped material does not cover every key decision. Meetings without minutes, decisions reached in a corridor, verbal instructions that left no trace: the organization's own recording gaps thin the visible-at-the-time column itself.

That is a diagnosis rather than a failure of the discipline. A key decision point in some failure carrying no timestamped record at all is itself a failure report on the organization's trace-keeping system. Chapter 38 lists the trace requirement as a standing clause of the postmortem system.

This chapter can supply a design standard for that system. The minimum requirement is three moments: when the decision was made, when it was recorded, when it was communicated. With all three present, a future postmortem has something to restore. The registration cost is tiny, since the three-line decision record already carries it under the Chapter 7 system. The maximum requirement is the probability draft described earlier: the alternative outcomes then believed, with confidence attached, in words. Between the minimum and the maximum, each organization sets its level by the risk grade of the decision. Low-risk decisions take the minimum. High-risk decisions, the ones before an irreversible point, take the maximum. Grading the requirement is what keeps a trace-keeping system from being resented, because a blanket requirement for full tracing dies in its first week.

Where the record is blank, the blank is marked as blank. Memory is not permitted to fill it.

Blank marking carries a second value. The distribution of blanks is a disease map of the organization's record system: which classes of decision carry the most blanks. Levels where verbal command dominates, cross-department coordination points, and night shifts are the three high-incidence zones.

Drawing the map takes a blank count across every postmortem of the past three years, classifying and counting the blank points in each left column. The output is a heat map, and its three hot zones correspond exactly to the handover failure of Chapter 28, the coordination problem of Chapter 18, and the night shift of Chapter 26. The remedies in those three chapters are the heat map's prescription. After the prescription comes a retest: the same blank count run again next year, against this year's. The speed at which blank density falls is the speed at which the record system improves.

The heat map is where this chapter's discipline scales. An individual's honesty, aggregated, becomes an organization's diagnosis.

docs.title: Five Self-Checks
docs.text:
1. Take your most recent postmortem and scan it with the three signal classes from section 6.5. How many hits?
  2. In your organization, what key information exists somewhere in a system but cannot be seen on the interface of the person who decides? Name the system and the field.
  3. For your last important decision, can you reconstruct the timestamped sequence of information arrival? Where you cannot, is the record missing or is your memory?
  4. Does your team's postmortem template have columns for visible at the time and reconstructed afterward? If not, whose resistance will adding them meet?
  5. Rewrite one paragraph of your industry's most recent public postmortem in two columns, three items in each.

Beyond the five, the graduation exercise for this chapter: run the whole sequence on your organization's last major postmortem, all four steps, the signal scan, the two-column rewrite, the dissection table, and the exchange test. It takes about one working day. Its four products, the scan list, the two-column version, the dissection table, and the purity score, are the first physical examination report on your organization's postmortem capability.

The report's value shows over time, in the annual comparison. Run the same sequence next year, and the improvement across the four products is a growth curve for organizational postmortem capability. What that curve means gets said again in Chapter 38, where postmortem capability is treated as the cardiopulmonary function of organizational learning.

docs.title: Chapter 7 Decision Points and Points of No Return
docs.text:
What this chapter covers: how to recognise the two most valuable positions on a failure chain, the decision point where the track can still be switched and the point of no return where it cannot, with a reversibility test table you can apply directly. When to turn back: when setting checkpoints into a process, when defining signature authority, or when judging whether there is still time to brake. A fourth use, past the three openings of the chapter: training a newcomer. These two concepts are the first lesson of induction in any industry. A newcomer who lacks them treats every moment as equally important and spreads attention like pepper from a shaker. The teaching kit is this chapter's table plus three cases from the newcomer's own industry. Fill three tables and the newcomer has the feel for where the points sit in that trade. The same kit scales to an industry association. A published checklist of points of no return, drafted once from this chapter's table plus cases contributed by member firms, gives every member's release form a common skeleton. It is the highest-yield service an association can offer: one drafting, a whole sector served. Estimated reading time: 40 minutes.

Not every moment on a failure chain deserves your attention.

Attention is the scarcest resource in a postmortem. The session runs two hours, and where those two hours land decides what the session produces. The allocation rule is the two tools of this chapter: mark the decision points first, because a fork earns the time; mark the points of no return next, because a cliff edge earns the time; run every remaining advance moment in a single line each.

Put a number on the rule and you have decision-point density. A competent postmortem carries between five and ten marked decision points. Fewer than three means the failure chain was drawn too coarse. More than fifteen means advance moments have been promoted to forks. Calibrate against good published work: the count of findings in a formal investigation report is a usable yardstick for where the density should sit.

Most moments are the event advancing. At a few of them, someone stands at a fork with the untaken roads still in hand. This chapter supplies two tools for finding those moments: recognising the fork (the decision point), and recognising, past the fork, the step from which no road leads back (the point of no return). Both tools come with one test table.

The relationship between the two tools is worth drawing on a timeline. Decision points cluster before the point of no return. A failure chain usually carries several decision points and one or a few points of no return. Decision points are opportunities; points of no return are boundaries.

The timeline has a management consequence. The last decision point before the point of no return is the most valuable position on the chain, and the minimum counterfactual of Chapter 5 usually lands there. Staffing that position is a governance question: who stands there, and does that person hold enough authority and enough information to use what they see. Chapter 18's single-owner list carries the answer.

The timeline also reads backwards. Count decision points backward from the point of no return: first back, second back, third back. The smaller the backward index, the lower the intervention cost and the more indirect the effect. Choosing among the backward indices is the whole art of the postmortem.

docs.title: 7.1 The Decision Point: Three Necessary Conditions
docs.text:
A moment that satisfies three conditions at once is a decision point.

Condition one: at least two real options exist. Real means the option carries a concrete action, a concrete cost, and could have been chosen at the time. "Be more careful" is not an option. "Delay until the next day, when daytime temperature rises" is one, and it was the option rejected in the Challenger case (Rogers Commission report, 1986).

Condition two: the person with authority to choose sits within reach. In the room, on the other end of the line, at the next node of the approval flow.

Options laid on the wrong table have a standard shape. The one who could actually veto is not present, and the ones present believe they hold no veto.

An option set can also fail before anyone enters the room. The menu was fixed in advance. The real choice happened in informal contact the week before, and the meeting is a coronation. A ritualised meeting satisfies the three conditions of condition one on paper and none of them in substance.

Detection runs on the agenda timeline. Look at how mature each item was when it reached the table. If the pre-read already carries a conclusion and its endorsements, the decision point sits before the meeting, and the search has to move backward.

Moving backward is done by reconstructing the shadow meeting: the email, the phone call, the corridor. The table in the shadow meeting is the real table. Read the shadow record beside the formal minutes. Reading two meetings together is advanced postmortem work, and it is the only way to recover a decision that was made in a room with no minutes.

Shadow material is usually absent from the file. Words in a corridor leave no trace, and that is the decision-point version of the recording gap described in Chapter 6. Move a decision point into the untraced zone and the postmortem runs out of food. Chapter 18's diffusion of responsibility has this collapse as its core symptom: everyone present, nobody holding the authority to stop.

Prevention sits at the level of the criterion, and it is cheap. Run a power pre-check when the process is designed. Annotate each decision point with three answers: who may choose here, who generates the options, who confirms a veto. Write the three answers into the process document. The cost is three extra lines at design time. What it prevents is a collapse of authority during operation, and that collapse is far more expensive to repair. Learning after an accident that nobody at a given position held the authority to stop is the most expensive way to learn it.

Review the annotations annually, folded into the process review. Every major process change updates the authority annotation in the same pass. A stale annotation is as dangerous as a stale process.

Condition three: the consequence of the choice appears later. Time sits between the decision and its consequence, and that interval is both a window for correction and a bed for illusion.

Mid-course checkpoints are the governance tool for the interval. Place one or two mandatory review points between decision and consequence, and ask a single question at each: how far does the current actual diverge from what we expected. This converts the window from passive to active. Divergence is measurable before the consequence lands, and a measurable divergence triggers a correction rather than a blame round. The institutional footing for a correction culture sits exactly here.

Density scales with the consequence cycle: one checkpoint per third of the cycle. A decision whose consequence matures in three years gets review points at nine months and at eighteen months.

Route the output into the decision record. It is the counter-document to the probability draft of Chapter 6: the expectation then, the actual now. The comparison of two drafts is the learning itself.

Deferred appearance supports two readings. "We chose correctly, which is why nothing happened," and "our turn has not come yet." Telling them apart waits for Chapter 11 on the normalization of deviance. For now, hold one line: a deferred decision is free in the mind and never free on the ledger.

The psychological accounting has a forward-facing version. Deferral does more than make the current decision feel free; it teaches the current decider a wrong way to read feedback. Nothing bad happens in the short term, the decider reads nothing-bad as positive feedback, and the misreading accumulates into the confidence illusion of Chapter 14.

The correction device is the post-decision audit. Thirty days after a major decision, review once: what did we expect, what actually happened, how do we explain the difference.

Cost, half an hour. What it buys is speed in the feedback loop. Without it, feedback waits for the consequence to cash, and a decision with a three-year consequence cycle carries a three-year learning cycle.

Give the audit a slot in the decision record template: the three lines of Chapter 38 plus a fourth, the audit date. One line of text turns every major decision into a learning loop.

Moments satisfying all three conditions appear more than once on a failure chain, which is why the list matters more than any single point on it.

The list also feeds the book's stop points. Every decision point on it is raw material for a stop point. A stop point is not a literary flourish; it is a decision point made teachable, the real fork on a real chain carried to the reader intact.

One operation converts list to stop point: lay the information that was visible at the time in front of the fork. With the information assembled, the fork becomes the reader's problem.

The craft sits in the proportion. Information too complete and the problem is trivial. Too fragmentary and the problem is unfair. Calibrate by testing the distribution of reader judgments. A problem everyone answers the same way carries no value, and a problem that splits the room is a good one.

The principle is stated here so the reader knows a stop point is not decoration. Behind every one of them sits a list of decision points dug out of a real failure chain.

The discipline for writing and for postmortems is to take the latest one. The latest decision point on the chain is the anchor of the minimum counterfactual (field 11 of Chapter 5; Chapter 10 gives the full backward-walking method). The latest decision point carries the lowest intervention cost, sits closest to the consequence, and holds the most complete evidence.

The latest-one rule has a boundary case. At the latest decision point, every option is bad. Postponement is bad; degradation is bad. A dead corner is not a good anchor for a minimum counterfactual, because an anchor should be a position that held one good option not dependent on luck. Handle a dead corner by moving forward: find where a good option appeared, and anchor there. Record the dead corner as evidence of the organisation's helplessness.

Keep both marks. The anchor is marked for the counterfactual, the dead corner for structural repair. A dead corner shows that the organisation needs a mechanism for generating new options, not better technique at choosing among the options it has.

A second boundary case: the latest decision point sometimes carries the least authority. The person who could actually stop the thing left the chain at an earlier position, so the latest position where intervention remained feasible sits with someone who holds no authority. Annotate both levels: the latest feasible position for training, the earliest position holding authority for institutional change.

Add a column to the decision point list for the authority grade of the decider at that position, one of full, partial, none. Statistics on that column expose the organisation's authorization disease. If the last feasible position at most key decision points concentrates in the hands of people with no authority, the authorization structure needs rebuilding, and the column is the proof.

One more distinction has to hold: a decision point and a point of accountability are different objects. A postmortem chases decision points, meaning where the track could be switched. Courts and disciplinary processes chase points of accountability, meaning who owes a legal duty for the consequence.

The two sit on different scales. Decision points are positions on the failure chain, distributed across the whole advance of the event. Points of accountability are legal anchors: a signature, a job title, a duty of care. They are far sparser. The sparsity follows from what law will connect, which is foreseeability and control. Law does not assign fault to a link you could neither foresee nor control.

The gap between sparse and dense is the division of labour between legal learning and engineering learning. Law teaches people to discharge duty at sparse anchors. Engineering teaches people to switch tracks at dense forks. An organisation needs both, and merging them into a single meeting loses both.

Coincidence, never necessity. The latest feasible switch point may sit with someone who holds no authority, while those holding authority narrowed the options to zero at several earlier positions. Take the accountability answer as the postmortem answer and the organisation learns "sign carefully." It does not learn who narrowed the options, in which meeting, on what grounds.

Resisting that gravity has an organisational form: an independent right to convene the postmortem. Convening does not pass through the accountability line. Safety or quality convenes directly, and the accountability line assembles its own material separately. Separating the two lines is standard in industries with mature investigation systems (Device 2 and Device 4 of Chapter 3), and it works inside a single firm.

The resistance comes from the efficiency argument: two meetings for one accident is expensive. The cost comparison is the output quality of the two meetings. A merged meeting produces a finding of responsibility. A separated meeting produces an improvement list. The two documents do not sit on the same shelf.

The answer to the efficiency argument sits in the cost table. The half-day saved by merging buys no effective improvement item at all.

A technical form of resistance: the conclusion layer of the postmortem and the conclusion layer of the legal document cite each other and never substitute for each other. The postmortem writes structural findings; the judgment's factual section is cited as an evidence source. Different readers, different purposes, different standards, and a document that mixes them serves neither reader.

The organisational form is two texts on two signature lines. Safety signs the postmortem, answering the improvement question. Legal signs the legal document, answering the responsibility question. The lines meet at the fact layer, which exists once, and diverge at the analysis layer, where the purposes part: the postmortem asks how to prevent, the court asks who answers.

Cost, one more document. Return, both kinds of learning hold and prevention learning does not contaminate responsibility learning.

docs.title: 7.2 The Three Currencies of Reversibility
docs.text:
Irreversibility is a spectrum, never a switch. Decompose "undoing an action" into the capacity to pay in three currencies.

Currency one is money. After the action, can money buy it back? Rebuild a part, switch a supplier, recall a batch. Money works while the object is unused, unconsumed, not yet grafted onto something else. A bad supplier on the approved list comes off for a switching fee. Concrete poured into a wall does not come back for any sum.

Currency two is time. After the action, can waiting undo it? Postpone a release, a departure, a construction window. Time works while the window stands open. Before it closes, postponement is a costless undo. After it closes, the same action jumps from the reversible column into the irreversible one with nothing in between.

Currency three is credibility. After the action, can it be withdrawn in public? A correction notice, a recall statement, an apology with compensation. Credibility works while nobody has yet taken an irreversible action of their own on the strength of your statement. Correcting a notice nobody followed costs little. Correcting a standard the downstream has executed for six months costs in proportion to the breadth of that execution.

What none of the three currencies can buy back forms the fourth category: the signature and the go-live. The release engineer signs the airworthiness release, the software team presses deploy, the aircraft finishes its takeoff roll, the reactor synchronises to the grid, the drug enters the formulary, the announcement goes out. The shared structure: a statement has been made about the world ("this thing is good"), the world has begun to act on the statement (passengers buy tickets, clients call the endpoint, physicians prescribe), and withdrawal no longer depends on your capacity to pay. It depends on what others have already sunk.

Split the fourth category in two tiers. The signature tier makes a single-point statement: one release, one approval. The go-live tier makes a systemic statement: a product launch, a regulation taking effect, a public announcement. The withdrawal cost structures differ. Withdrawing a signature faces the validity of a document. Withdrawing a go-live faces an ecosystem's adaptation, and that cost scales at network level with what others have built on the statement.

The tiering has a budget consequence. At the signature tier, a second confirmation slot can be a person. At the go-live tier it has to be a system, because human confirmation does not hold against launch momentum. Grey release and the canary are the engineered second confirmation slot at that tier.

That engineering is the software industry's best contribution to this chapter's table. For any go-live tier action, in any industry, one question is worth asking: where is my canary.

One-line test, expanding field 9 of Chapter 5: money can change it, time can change it, a public correction can change it; a signature and a go-live cannot.

The test carries a time dimension, because reversibility decays. Right after the action, money still works: the part is uninstalled, the stock is on hand. Three months on, money no longer saves it: the part sits in the airframe, the stock has dispersed. Reversibility has a half-life.

The management consequence is to pull the undo decision early. Every day of delay after the error is discovered burns reversibility. The escalation described in Chapter 27 burns a psychological account; delay burns physical reversibility.

Quantify the half-life by annotating each action with a reversible window: the installation cycle of the part, the turnover days of the stock. Supply chain and production systems already hold that data.
