A year where the three converge is a candidate for break resonance, and the list of such years goes to governance, because each deserves a nine-cell walkthrough in retrospect. All the data comes from ledgers you already keep, maintenance logs, change orders, budget tables. The chart costs half a day and carries more insight than ten special meetings.

Incentive lookback needs a method of its own. Configuration archaeology runs on year spans, since break three's lookback is often measured in decades: the configuration meeting, the material selection, the supplier contract from fifteen years ago. How deep you dig depends on how much archive survives. Are the minutes and the option lists still there? Where they are not, the substitute is comparison with contemporaneous projects of the same kind: what did others select? The comparison restores the sense of what the decision's boundaries were at the time. The output goes into the incentive row, with the evidence column stating the archive's condition and the method of comparison. Mark the limits of the archaeology honestly.

docs.title: 9.4 The Walkthrough: Fitting a Case into Three Layers
docs.text:
Here is the reusable checklist. For any case, answer three questions per layer, nine cells in all:

Where this layer broke in the event Dated evidence for the break Corresponding intervention Technical layer The chain of physical and system behavior Physical evidence, logs, data (the fact sections of the investigation report) Replace parts, add sensors, change the design Organizational layer Information flow and the structure of responsibility Meetings, work orders, handover records, training records Change the process, change the checkpoint, change what the handover contains Incentive layer Contract and assessment structure Assessment schemes, contract clauses, pricing and configuration decisions Change the assessment, change the contract, change the payment structure

The easiest column is the first, because everyone can tell a story. The one most often missing is the second, the dated evidence.

Column two has a width rule. Dated evidence need not be perfect: a frontline original record, an email from the time, a photograph of the duty log will do. Where the date is fuzzy, state the fuzziness, "roughly that week". Honest width beats precise fabrication, because a fabricated date collapses under cross-verification, and one collapse takes the credibility of the whole walkthrough to zero. An empty cell may not be filled with a story. It may hold "no record", and under Chapter 6's discipline "no record" is a diagnostic result.

Complex cases should use the extended version, with a column for time span: the year and month each layer's break formed. Technical breaks usually form days before the event, organizational breaks months before, incentive breaks years before. The column makes the layers' temporal depth visible, and once visible the timescale of the improvement follows: an incentive repair is measured in years, so do not expect quarterly results. Fill it from the dates of each layer's evidence, the manufacture date of the physical item, the date on the minutes, the signature date of the contract. Spans are inferred, so write the basis.

A worked example: Alaska Airlines 261 (av-034, NTSB AAR-02/01, executive summary checked). Technical layer: the Acme nut threads in the horizontal stabilizer jackscrew assembly were excessively worn, the assembly failed in flight, the aircraft lost pitch control and went into the sea, and all 88 people on board died, in the report's own wording. Organizational layer: the company extended the lubrication interval and the end-play check interval for that assembly, the FAA approved the extension, and the investigation found that the extension let inadequate lubrication develop into failure-level wear. Incentive layer: the report's conclusions place the maintenance program and regulatory oversight on the list of issues. The specific economic trade-off behind the extension, downtime cost and scheduling pressure, is discussed but not quantified to a citable degree, so this cell is marked "insufficient evidence; reconstruction requires the maintenance engineering record". No story is inserted.

The discipline of not inserting stories meets a psychological obstacle: the social pressure to fill the blank. In a review meeting an empty cell invites the question of why you did not find out, and the correct answer is to display the search process: which archives you checked, whom you asked, what came back. Displaying the process turns the blank from an embarrassment into proof of work. Auditing calls this the trace, and the trace of the search matters as much as the trace of the conclusion.

The last intervenable position in this case falls on the organizational layer, at the node where the extension was approved. That is where field 11 of Chapter 5, the minimum counterfactual, takes its value. The two routes meet at that node, which tells you something about the book's architecture: the twelve-field card and the three-layer walkthrough are two tables for one object.

One detail of the join matters. A counterfactual action must be tagged with its layer, which layer it falls on and which currency it moves. A tagged counterfactual enters the improvement list for that layer. An untagged one is an orphan: after the review meeting it has nowhere to live and the list will not take it in. One line of tagging saves one lesson.

Where the incentive row is thin, hand it to Chapter 17's principal-agent framework. The row usually gets no further than assessments and contracts, and the framework asks one level down: who is the principal, whose objective is the agent optimizing, where is the monitoring cost spent. The deeper look often rewrites the row, because what read as an assessment problem turns out to be an absent principal. Not required every time: clear contract evidence closes the case at nine cells, and the framework is for rows where evidence is vague.

Merge the two tables and you have the script for Chapter 39's rehearsal. The nine cells fix the scenario, the twelve-field card lays out the material. The join is a mapping: field 8, the decision point, corresponds to the organizational row; field 9 to the time-span column; field 6 to the evidence column. The mapping table sits in the user notes to Appendix A. Because the mapping exists, a reader who learns either table gets the other for free. The two are one instrument, one cut from the training angle, one from the structural angle.

docs.title: 9.5 What "All Three Broken" Means for Three Kinds of Reader
docs.text:
For the person writing the postmortem. A postmortem that stops at the technical layer is a fault report.

When the walkthrough is done, read the nine-cell table beside the body of the postmortem and work out which cells the narrative paragraphs correspond to. The cells the text never touches are the blind spots, and the list goes back to the author as material for the next version, without reproach. The procedure also runs in reverse: walk first, then write, with the table as the outline. Such an outline covers the three layers automatically and carries the evidence column with it.

Whether your conclusion crossed the technical layer takes one question: is the subject of the conclusion sentence a part or a structure? "Nut wear caused the crash" has a part as its subject, so it is a fault report. "The approval of the extended inspection interval let wear develop into failure" has a structure as its subject, and only now are you approaching failure. The upgraded form is the subject-chain test. Write the causal chain in full: who approved what in which year, letting whose work under what conditions develop into what result. Written in full, every link is an intervenable position and the list of links is a rich seam of measures. Chain length is postmortem depth: three links or fewer is shallow, five or more begins to touch the incentive layer.

For the person designing defences. Leave one gate on each layer.

Acceptance of the three gates should be done together. The technical gate is accepted by real rehearsal, the organizational gate by a drill, the incentive gate by a case replay. The institutional carrier is Chapter 22's annual real rehearsal plus this chapter's walkthrough. Cost is amortized by the combination and completeness rises, because single-gate acceptance cannot see problems of mutual exclusion and three gates in one room expose them.

The point of three-layer defence is independence. The organizational gate, meaning a mandatory re-check, must not take its signal from the technical gate, meaning a sensor. The incentive gate, meaning no penalty for calling a stop, must guarantee that the organizational gate dares to be used. Chapter 22 carries a case where all three gates were shared.

One failure mode of the combination deserves flagging: gates that exclude each other. When the incentive gate, no penalty for stopping, fights the organizational assessment of schedule bonuses and penalties, the organizational gate prefers not to be used, because the person who uses it loses the schedule bonus. Detection is the two-document reading of break two in section 9.3. Once detected, the repair is in the incentive layer: put gate use into positive scoring, count uses as a plus and not a minus. That reversal is the decisive switch for whether three gates work together at all.

For the person deciding on improvement measures. Which layer you can move decides which chapters of Part III you read.

Lay the measure list out in three columns, incentive, organizational, technical. The columns force every measure to show its currency, and a measure that fits none, "pay more attention" or "strengthen management", is deleted on the spot. The layout costs a table with two extra columns and its filter value shows on first use: in most organizations the first version of the list has an empty incentive column, and the empty column is itself a finding.

Frontline engineers can move the technical and organizational layers (Chapters 15, 21, 30). Middle managers can move the organizational and incentive layers (Chapters 16, 17, 18). Only those who can change contracts and assessments can move the incentive layer (Chapters 12, 17, 28). An improvement plan cannot exceed your intervention currency. Work out which currency you hold before writing the plan; this is the first parameter of Chapter 35's positioning table.

The second parameter is layer span, meaning how many layers you can coordinate across. The frontline acts within its own layer, the middle manager crosses two, the executive moves all three. An honest assessment of span sets the size of the plan. A middle manager who cannot cross into the incentive layer should not write incentive actions into the plan, or it will stay on paper. The correct way to cross is to find a bridge, an ally at executive level, and Chapter 35 describes how to choose one.

Recognizing your currency also applies at organization level: tiered sign-off on the improvement list. The list sits in three columns by currency, and each has a different signer. An engineer signs the technical column, a manager the organizational, and whoever holds assessment authority signs the incentive column. Every measure then carries a signature from someone able to execute it. A measure with no corresponding signer is deleted or transferred to someone with authority. Ownerless measures are the dead stock of an improvement list.

docs.title: Self-Check: Five Questions
docs.text:
1. Run the nine-cell walkthrough of section 9.4 on your organization's most recent significant loss. Which cells cannot be filled with dated evidence?
  2. In your organization's latest improvement list, how many measures fall on the incentive layer? If none do, how many years will the technical repairs hold?
  3. Find one concrete place in your processes where a technical signal has no organizational category word: what anomaly can occur for which the system holds no registration category?
  4. What is your post's intervention currency? Can you change a process, change an assessment, or only change a parameter? The answer decides which chapters of Part III you need.
  5. In your organization's postmortem conclusions, is the subject usually a part or a structure? Who trained that habit?

Beyond the five questions, here is the end-of-part test for the anatomy section. Take a real investigation report from your own industry at grade A and complete the full cycle from zero: draw the failure chain, mark decision points and points of no return, fill the nine-cell table, judge reversibility, walk the three signal words, write the minimum counterfactual, assign the evidence grade. The first run takes about a day, half a day with practice, and the output is one complete case card, your first grade-A card, at once the graduation certificate of Part II and the entry ticket to Part III.

One reminder above the model. The three layers are an analytical framework, not an organization chart. Departments such as engineering, operations and HR do not map cleanly onto the layers. HR is not the incentive layer. The incentive currencies, assessments, contracts and pricing, are scattered across several departments. Fill the table by currency ownership, not by department ownership, and ask what change would eliminate this event, never whose department it is.

docs.title: Chapter 10 The Minimum Counterfactual and Evidence Grades
docs.text:
What this chapter covers: the five-step backward method for the minimum counterfactual, with the three kinds that fail; and the A to E evidence grades, with the rules for moving a case up or down and for labelling it "reconstructed". When to turn back: when writing fields 11 and 12 of a case card, reviewing someone else's postmortem conclusion, or deciding whether a case may enter the main text. Estimated reading time: 35 minutes.

Chapter 5 defined the twelve fields. Chapter 6 set the discipline for one of them, what was visible at the time. Chapter 7 gave the test for the decision point. Chapter 9 supplied the framework for combining the parts. This chapter finishes the two most valuable fields on the card: field 11, the minimum counterfactual, and field 12, the evidence grade.

The recommended way to learn the craft is by doing, one chapter at a time. Build a single card and let it grow. Fill the fields after Chapter 5; add "what was visible then" after Chapter 6; add the point of no return after Chapter 7; run the nine cells after Chapter 9; do the backcast and the grading after this chapter. Five passes, and the same card is complete in every cell. The card that grew this way is your graduation piece.

Beyond the card, the rest of the book has a route. A reader who finishes Part II should treat every case in Part III as practice material: take one case per chapter, run the five-step counterfactual on it, set its grade from the table, walk it through the nine cells. That exercise runs across the twenty-four chapters of Part III, and by the end the domain pages of Part IV read as revision, with the tools unchanged and only the parameters swapped for an industry. The learning curve reaches its first plateau at the end of Part II: the reader standing there holds every tool, and every later part stacks parameters and situations on top of them.

One pace suggestion for the climb: a full run every four chapters (11 to 14, 15 to 18, and so on), six groups in all, one case per group taken through the whole set of card, counterfactual, nine cells and grade. After six groups the tools sit in the hands rather than in the notes. The test is speed. The first full run takes half a day; the sixth takes an hour.

For teachers and trainers, the five-step method and the grade table work as course material without alteration, because a training programme is a sequence of exercises. Session one: the five-step method and one demonstration. Session two: learners critique each other's counterfactuals. Session three: grade judgement, with cross-verification. Session four: a full run, one card, start to finish. The package costs almost nothing, since the material is this book's chapters plus public cases, and it produces the organization's first cohort of people who can write a card. Cards are the bottleneck on the industry's circulation of failure knowledge (Chapter 4), and a four-session course is one of the ways through that bottleneck.

The class should be mixed: one third line engineers, one third safety staff, one third middle managers. A single-composition class trains a homogeneous skill. A mixed class produces cross-layer conversation, with engineers and managers finding holes in each other's counterfactuals, and that argument is where cross-layer understanding forms. Chapter 9's theory of intervention currencies gets its first field trial in that room: each side learns what the other side's currency looks like in the hand.

The extension of the course is organizational certification. Four sessions plus a graduation card earns an internal certificate, and the roster and the card work go into the knowledge base. A certificate is a capacity marker, not a title: projects that need cards draw names from the roster, and the skill becomes visible for the first time, which is the precondition for deploying and rewarding it. Chapter 39's budget template carries the two lines that close the loop, certification training and card-writing hours.

docs.title: 10.1 The discipline of the minimum counterfactual
docs.text:
Definition, expanding field 11 of Chapter 5: the one action whose change would have avoided the event or greatly reduced its consequences.

One word in that definition needs slow reading: greatly. A counterfactual does not have to erase every consequence. Turning 110 deaths into 110 injuries is a qualified counterfactual. What it must satisfy is proportionality: the scale of the intervention has to match the scale of the consequence. Set the counterfactual for a 97-death accident at a reminder issued in a pre-shift meeting, and the reminder cannot stop a consequence of that size. The test for proportionality is magnitude coverage: does the intervention carry enough leverage to move this consequence? A counterfactual without that leverage is a toy. The way to identify a toy is to run it for real and ask whether the consequence would actually have shrunk to the magnitude claimed.

The least-cost rehearsal is a variant of that exercise. Assume the counterfactual action is executed once, and answer three questions: what does it cost, who objects, and does the process allow it. The three answers score the counterfactual's realism. A low-realism counterfactual can still be qualified, but it is only theoretically qualified. Theoretical counterfactuals mark the position; realistic ones can be executed. Keep both in the working draft, and put only the one that passes realism into the signature line.

Reduction is measured by what can be verified. State the magnitude: half the consequence, or nine tenths of it. Declaring the magnitude gives the assessment a scale. An unverifiable claim that the consequences would have been much better does not count.

Three disciplines follow, and all three have to pass. Write one counterfactual only. Test it for dependence on luck. Test it for overreach.

Why only one, argued from the author's side rather than the reader's (Chapter 5 made the reader's argument): the impulse to write several comes from a fear of omission, the worry that a better candidate is being left out. The working draft answers that fear. Put every candidate in the draft, attach the draft behind the card, publish nothing from it. The card carries one conclusion, and every candidate leaves a trace. Separating draft from conclusion is routine in academic review, and postmortem writing can borrow it as is. The serious form of the discipline: two counterfactuals sitting side by side on the table mean the backcast is not finished. Compare their intervention positions and their evidence strength, choose one, and move the loser into the draft. A reference book owes its reader exactly one conclusion.

There is a game-theoretic reason as well. When several counterfactuals stand side by side, the reader takes the cheapest as the lesson, and the cheapest is often not the most effective. The choice of lesson slides from the author to the reader's laziness, and the result is that one case yields different lessons in different hands. Randomised lessons amount to no lesson at all. A single-counterfactual discipline returns the choice to the author, whose comparison sits in the draft while one conclusion is delivered. The two layers, delivery and draft, get rigour and readability at once.

docs.title: 10.2 The five-step backward method
docs.text:
Step one: reverse the failure chain. Start from the consequence and list the nodes backwards: the consequence, the point of no return (Chapter 7), the last decision point, the earlier structural conditions. Go down to the organizational and incentive layers; the nine-cell table of Chapter 9 can be used directly for the sorting. Every node carries a date and an actor. "Management was lax" is not a node. "The 14 March review meeting put this item at position 7 on the agenda and spent 4 minutes on it" is.

Timeline software or paper will do, and the tool is not what matters. What matters is that each node is written on a card. One node, one card. A backcast is trial and error, and a wrong order gets redone; carding drives the cost of re-sorting to near zero. The physical act (writing the cards, laying out the order, drawing the lines) looks crude and beats most thinking software. The book draws one practical conclusion from this: do the postmortem and the backcast on paper.

A team version is worth adding. Tape the node cards to a wall and let the whole group sort them. The sorting disagreements mark where the group's understanding diverges, so mark the disputed cards in a different colour. The colour wall is the advanced form of the review meeting: the meeting stops being a report-reading session and becomes a sorting session, and its output is a failure chain calibrated across the group. A shared organizational picture of a failure survives handover better than any individual's picture (Chapter 30).

That picture also needs a documentary exit. Photograph the sorted wall and archive the photograph alongside a digital version of the final order, both into the knowledge base and the knowledge pack (Chapter 30). The archived wall is the permanent draft of that failure chain. A newcomer rebuilding the chain three years later compares against it, and the deviation becomes measurable. The trail of deviations is the record of how the organization's understanding evolved.

The starting level deserves its own warning. Choose which consequence to backcast from: the death, the injury, or the near miss. A different start gives a different chain. A major consequence gives a longer chain; a near-miss chain stops at the defence gate. Choose by the purpose of the exercise: to study defences, start from a near miss; to study penetration, start from an accident. Purpose comes before backcast, and this is the first appearance of Chapter 35's positioning table inside the method.

One more node criterion: a node has to be an action, not a state. A meeting being held is an action; an item's position on the agenda is an action. Lax management is a state, and so is a poor culture. Actions can be swapped, and states cannot be swapped directly, since nobody can swap in a different culture. States change through the actions that generate them, so the work is to find the decision that produced the state. States are regular guests on the incentive layer of the nine-cell table, and writing down which action generated a given state completes the reduction from state back to action.

Step two: test each node. For every node ask whether a different action there would have changed the consequence. Mark the ones that would as effective, the rest as ineffective. Use only what was visible at the time (the discipline of Chapter 6). For an action to count as a qualified intervention point, its necessity has to hold inside the actor's own information environment.

The information environment itself is a boundary case worth naming. Sometimes the actor could not see something because the system did not display it. In that situation the qualified intervention point moves up a layer, to the information system: making the information visible is the counterfactual, and making the actor cleverer is not. The logic matches the nine-cell table, where redesigning an information environment is an organizational-layer intervention. Both levels can hold a qualified counterfactual at once, each labelled with its layer, following Chapter 9's labelling discipline.

Step three: strike the luck types. Any candidate that depends on coincidence goes out. "If the inspector had looked once more that day." "If the person on site had happened to be a senior engineer." The identifying feature of a luck-type counterfactual is that the action it demands has no position in the system. Whether it happens depends on staffing and on coincidence.

Step four: strike the overreach types. A candidate that requires the actor to break procedure, defy a superior, or exercise authority he did not hold gets removed, or moved up a layer. "The shop-floor operator should have refused to release the batch" is an overreach counterfactual unless the procedure actually grants him an independent veto. Where the veto does not exist, the qualified intervention point sits in the authorisation design, and the node moves up to the meeting that wrote the procedure. Overreach is the most common defective item in postmortems, and its function is to dress a structural problem as a courage problem.

The overreach check needs a companion step. A node that has been moved up must go through the luck test again. If the repair at the authorisation layer depends on an enlightened leader, on some executive happening to care, the candidate is a luck type once more. Luck does not discriminate by layer, and it can enter a candidate at any layer. The mnemonic is one action, one question: does this action have a position in the system? If it does, carry on; if it does not, move up or strike it.

Step five: take the latest one and sign it. Among the qualified candidates that remain, take the one latest in time and write its three elements: date, location (whose ground it sits on), action. The signature format reads: "Minimum counterfactual: on (date), on the (carrier), (actor) performs (action)." If the three elements cannot be filled in, the backcast is not finished, and the answer is to go back to step one.

The signature has a quantitative use. Collect a year's qualified counterfactuals and classify each by layer, position and action type. The reading is a distribution of the organization's improvement opportunities: which layer produces the most counterfactuals. That distribution tells next year's improvement money where to go, since the layer with the most counterfactuals is the layer the budget belongs to. This path from tally to budget is the interface between the chapter's method and the budget template of Chapter 39.

It has an organizational use too: conversion into a work order. A qualified counterfactual generates a work-order draft, with the fields mapping one to one, date to deadline, location to owner, action to task. Conversion is what turns a lesson into a standing to-do item. A counterfactual that is not converted dies when the review meeting ends. The trigger for conversion is a pass at review, and the review asks the five-step questions, so passing the five steps makes the work order legitimate on its own.

docs.title: 10.3 Three disqualifying counterfactuals
docs.text:
Type Example Defect All-purpose "strengthen management, improve the system, raise awareness" No action, no actor, no date; cannot be executed and cannot be refuted Luck "if the inspector had happened to look one more time" The action demanded has no position in the system Overreach "the operator should have held out against the pressure and refused release" Requires authority the person did not hold; the qualified intervention point sits in the authorisation design

All-purpose is the most common. The test is to compress the sentence into one verb and one object. If it will not compress, it fails.

A hybrid form needs recording: the disguised specific. "Management should have recognised the fragility of the supply chain earlier" looks as though it carries an action and an actor. Take it apart. Management is a collective noun, so there is no named actor; "recognised earlier" is a state, so there is no action. A disguised specific is more dangerous than an obvious void because it passes the two-second intuition check. Only the five steps, run item by item, bring it back into view. The mnemonic for the disguised version: name a person, land a verb, give a date; missing any one of the three sends it back.

docs.title: 10.4 Evidence grades A to E
docs.text:
Every case in the book carries one of five grades, and the grade decides what that case is entitled to support.

Grade A: the full report of an independent investigating body. Independent of the party investigated and of the prosecuting function, published in full, with a factual section and an analytical section. Supports the decision sequence, the options ruled out, and the minimum counterfactual. This is the grade of the cases in the main text.

Grade B: official notices, communiqués and regulatory announcements. Authoritative, without a complete evidence chain. Supports the magnitude of the consequence and conclusive findings. Does not support the detail of a decision point. B-grade cases go into the appendix matrix; a B case that enters the main text must be labelled "reconstructed". A process report, such as the JTSB's 経過報告, is graded A− to match Appendix C.

Grade C: judgments, administrative penalty decisions, arbitration awards. The facts have gone through adversarial testing, but the selection of facts serves the legal issue. Supports amounts, responsible parties, and the timeline of acts. Does not support technical processes that never entered the dispute.

One directional hint for using C-grade material: prefer the findings that went against your own side. A fact confirmed by the court against the party that contested it has been tested hardest, so an adverse finding is the harder finding. When a postmortem cites C-grade documents, leading with the facts the party admitted is a technique for raising credibility.

Grade D: the party's own public postmortem (software industry postmortems, company statements, participants' memoirs). First-hand detail, inherently self-interested. Supports the shape of an organization's internal process. Supports a finding of fact only after cross-verification against A, B and C material.

Cross-verification of D-grade material has an efficiency trick: an order of work. Verify first the details that appear nowhere else, since only the unique ones need testing. Where the material overlaps a public report, the report has already vouched for that part, and re-verifying it wastes effort. Verify the unique, skip the overlap. This order cuts the cross-verification workload by 70%.

Grade E: media reporting. Lead generation only. Use it to find a case, then go and find A to D material on that case. The main text may never rest on E-grade material alone.

A search tip belongs here as well: media reporting has a time structure. The incident report is fast and wrong often. The investigative piece is slow and corrects more. The anniversary retrospective is slowest and adds the long view. Reading all three layers in sequence is the complete move in E-grade lead mining; stop at the first layer and the direction you take is often the wrong one. The reading list for those layers sits in's search manual, which names the deep outlets for each domain and the search strings for anniversary pieces.

Two rules govern movement between grades. Combination upgrade: a core fact corroborated by B and C together can support a main-text case labelled "reconstructed", while a single B-grade document cannot. Downgrade: a dead link with no archive drops the case to pending verification, and a quoted passage that does not match the original is removed outright. the link check and the number-to-source check carry these out.

Corroboration has one further detail: what gets corroborated is the fact, not the conclusion. Two B-grade documents recording the same fact identically establish corroboration. Two documents agreeing on a conclusion while describing the facts differently do not, because agreement on a conclusion can be a loop of retelling. This is Chapter 2's circulation skew in its evidentiary form. A cites B, B cites C, and three sources turn out to be one. The test that breaks the loop is to find the earliest source: is the first of the three an independent interview, or a retelling of the others? The mnemonic: trace it back, find the earliest, and ask whether that source saw the thing itself.

Two further states exist beyond up and down.

A frozen case: evidence grade undetermined, investigation running, litigation unresolved. Mark it frozen. A frozen card enters neither the main text nor the matrix; it waits in the knowledge base, with the reason written down and the thaw condition stated, which is publication of the final report. On thaw it is graded afresh. Freezing prevents two errors, concluding from an out-of-date process report and forgetting to come back once the final report appears.

A partial downgrade: within one card the facts carry different grades, the core fact at A, circumstantial material at C. The card does not drop as a whole. What drops is the support range of one fact, and the labelling switches to per-fact grades, so that a user of the card knows precisely which line is hard and which is soft. A coarse whole-card grade misleads on a complex case, and per-fact labelling is the mark of a mature one.

Disagreement about a grade can be arbitrated. Grading has a subjective element, and two people can grade the same document differently. The rule is to take the lower of the two, since the margin of safety in that rule belongs to the reader, who uses the material at the lower grade and loses nothing. Record the dispute in the case's errata line. The dispute is itself material.

docs.title: 10.5 Labelling "reconstructed"
docs.text:
Cases on medium evidence are still worth writing, on one condition: the inference is marked. Most organizations' internal material is B, C or D by nature, a front-line review being D, an internal investigation B, legal paperwork C. A grade system gives those materials a grammar of mutual recognition for the first time, so that an internal review can be used correctly, neither overstated nor thrown away. Teaching that grammar takes a day, and afterwards the organization's stock of old reviews turns from a pile of paper into a graded knowledge base.

The labelling convention: narrative text carries verifiable factual sentences only, and an inference opens with "Reconstructed" and states its basis.

Inference has a tone discipline of its own. Keep the modals restrained, and never write "obviously", "undoubtedly" or "of course" inside an inference. An inference is an inference, and an author who writes it as an assertion is using tone to make up for evidence. Tone runs in inverse proportion to evidence, which is a hard rule of postmortem writing: the stronger a sentence sounds, the more the reader should ask for its evidence number.

The format, by example:

"Minutes of the 14 March review meeting show the risk listed as agenda item 7 (factual sentence, grade C: meeting minutes). Reconstructed: from the agenda order and the meeting's length, the risk received less than 5 minutes of discussion and no resolution item was recorded (inference)."

The discipline for a reconstructed sentence: a reader must be able to re-check the inference along the basis given. An inference with no re-check path is not written.

Density needs self-control as well, since a case reconstructed on every page reads as a page of footnotes. When reconstruction exceeds 40% of the body text, the evidence is not yet sufficient to write the piece, and the material goes back to the matrix. The quantitative standard is a ratio of factual sentences to inferences of at least three to one. Below that ratio, the title must state that this is a reconstruction, not a report of fact.

Grades are not for life. New evidence moves a case up or down: publication of the investigation report lifts a B case to A, and a quoted original that gets overturned drops the case or removes it. The institutional carrier for that maintenance is the case library's annual review, which reads each card's evidence status in turn, asking whether a new report exists and whether the links still resolve. The output is a list of grade changes, published to readers, so that what a reader holds is always the current grade. Appendix B's case table keeps a grade column for every case. A reader's trust should follow the grade.

docs.title: 10.6 Numbers back to source, and citation convention
docs.text:
Every number in the main text carries the four-part record set out in Chapter 5: who counted it, when, on what sample, under what definition. Two execution rules are added here.

Rule one: the set check. Before a chapter is delivered, extract every number in the body and take the difference against the set of numbers in the source cards that chapter cites. An empty difference passes.

The difference can be audited in the other direction as well. Numbers in the cards that the text does not use are not a problem; numbers used in the text that the cards do not contain are. A reverse difference shows that the source cards are richer than the chapter, which is a good sign, since it means the author made selections rather than copies. Write the reason for each omission into the card's note, so the selection stays traceable. The practical meaning of the rule: no approximate numbers written on the fly. Every number in the body comes from a source card, or it is deleted.

The cost and the return of that discipline are worth stating. The cost is slower writing, since every number goes back to its card for a check. The return is that nobody has to check you. A reader can trust each number because the system guarantees them, and the trust compounds at the point of citation, where another author cites your number without re-verifying it, because you already did. Being citable is the long-run return on numeric discipline.

Rule two: a quotation keeps the language of the original, with a translation in brackets. Institution names, document titles and regulation names follow the glossary's bilingual table, and no chapter drifts from it.

The bibliographic form is fixed: (institution, document number or title, year, link at the Appendix B entry). Page numbers are completed at the checking stage. Where a page cannot be obtained, widen the cited range, writing "the report's executive summary" rather than "page 41 of the report". That is how a style handles uncertainty honestly.

The honesty principle extends to telling the reader the grade. A conclusion resting on A-grade evidence may be written as a flat statement. One resting on B-grade evidence is written as a probable statement. A reconstructed sentence always carries its marker. Grade disclosure lets the reader read at the right level of confidence, and an uncertain sentence never appears in a certain tone. The disclosure goes into the postmortem template of Chapter 38, where the template governs the format and the discipline governs the substance.

One more application: what to quote. Quote only sentences you have checked word for word. A reported quotation is marked as reported ("according to a paraphrase"). The distinction between paraphrase and direct quotation is the foundation of citation ethics. On that foundation sits one more check: every directly quoted sentence must be findable on a page. A direct quotation that cannot be found on a page is downgraded to a paraphrase. The check costs a minute a sentence and buys the book's zero-tolerance commitment, which is to quote one sentence fewer rather than one sentence that cannot be verified.

docs.title: The five self-checks
docs.text:
1. Write the minimum counterfactual for your organization's most recent loss, then run the five steps to see whether it is a luck type or an overreach type.
  2. Do your project's decision records support grade A, or only grade D? Where is the gap?
  3. Of the industry cases you have cited, how many survive the grade test in 10.4? How many conclusions still stand after the downgrade?
  4. When did an all-purpose counterfactual last appear in one of your postmortems, and how did it pass review at the time?
  5. Set a citation rule for your team: material below which grade may be cited as fact in your meeting room?

The graduation exercise sits outside the five. Write a complete case card for your organization's most recent loss: twelve fields, five-step backcast, grade labels, reconstructed sentences, the whole sequence. The work takes about half a day, and the acceptance standard is a colleague who does not know the event being able to re-check it end to end from your card and its links alone. Pass that, and you hold every component of the book's method. Writing a card is the last tool this book hands over, and every later part uses it again, the domain pages organising cases by card, the usage chapters expanding templates from cards, the boundary chapters checking against cards.

Your first card will not be good, and it is not meant to be. Its job is to expose the distance between where you are and the standard. A list of that distance is more useful than a perfect card, because the list is your study plan for the next stage. Take the finished card and check it against the field table of Chapter 5, cell by cell: which cell is empty, which cell has a story impersonating a fact, which cell's counterfactual is all-purpose. Write the result as a one-page memo. Run the memo, and your second card passes about half of it. All of Part II exists to get you to a passing second card, a fluent fifth, and a tenth you can teach from.

Before the tools are put away, run the evidence disciplines of the five chapters into one route. A reader facing a new piece of failure material passes five gates. Gate one: what grade is it (this chapter). Gate two: has it cleared the recording threshold (Chapter 2). Gate three: are the visible-at-the-time and the reconstructed-afterward kept apart (Chapter 6). Gate four: how many layers did its failure chain break (Chapter 9). Gate five: is its minimum counterfactual qualified (this chapter's five steps). Once the five are passed, the material's use is settled: cite it, refer to it, keep it as a lead, or discard it. The route fits on one sheet of paper, and that sheet is Part II's final compression.

Not every reading needs all five. Skimming the news needs gates one and two. Citing needs all five. The gates are used at levels, the way Chapter 23's releases are tiered: the use decides the depth. Material mentioned in passing needs none of them; material written into the basis of a decision passes all five.

docs.title: Closing Part II
docs.text:
This chapter is the last of Part II, and the anatomy section hands in its paper here. The chapters it collects (the fields, what was visible, the decision point and the point of no return, the escalation ladder, the failure chain, the counterfactual and the grades, six in all) form one evidence workflow. Find material, at the threshold of Chapter 2. Read it, under the discipline of Chapter 6. Take its structure apart, with the nine cells of Chapter 9. Locate the positions that matter, with Chapter 7. Give the conclusion, with the fields of Chapter 5 and the methods of this chapter. Every station on that route has a tool, a discipline and an exercise, and the route ends at one capacity: turning any failure into a checkable card. That capacity is the foundation under all of the book's analysis. Each of Part III's twenty-four chapters was built with it, and a reader who has practised it can test every stone of the foundation by hand.

The six lessons, named once more with their equipment: Chapter 5, 12 fields. Chapter 6, 3 disciplines. Chapter 7, 2 tools and 1 judgement table. Chapter 8, 7 steps and 4 devices. Chapter 9, 3 layers, 3 breakpoints and a 9-cell table. Chapter 10, a 5-step method and a 5-grade table. The arithmetic of the six comes to 12+3+3+11+15+10, which is 54 operable items. That number is Part II's entire output and the craft cost behind every case in Part III. Large, and every item usable: this is the line between a reference book and a book of opinions, and the reason the book can hand 158 cards to its readers for checking.

The whole of Part II in plain words: treat failure as something that matters, work it with method, leave a paper trail. Treating it as something that matters is the attitude, and Part II exists to show that an attitude can be converted into method. Working with method is the tools from Chapter 5 to this chapter, and method can be learned. Leaving a paper trail is the institution of Chapter 38, and a trail can be checked. None of the three is mystical, and each can start tomorrow afternoon.

The twenty-four chapters behind the door use every tool practised in these six lessons. The case cards change shape from chapter to chapter, some full, some condensed, but the skeleton is always the twelve fields, the evidence always carries a grade, the counterfactual always passes five steps. A reader who has finished this chapter meets no new tool in Part III, only the same tools in twenty-four uses. That variety is evidence the tools were designed well, and it is why the book puts them all up front. The cost of front-loading is two parts of abstraction; the return is four parts of fluency.

The other argument for front-loading is time. Learning the tools costs once: six chapters, then usable for life. Learning the mechanisms late costs continuously, with the method re-explained in every chapter. A one-time cost beats a continuing one in any long project, and Chapter 28's logic of horizons here sides, unusually, with the investment. Money spent on tools is the highest-return money in this book.

The next part visits five industries, and each has an accent. Aviation's accent is procedure, where every sentence has a number. Chemical processing's accent is layers, physical chemistry and management wound into a double helix. Maritime's accent is the international, since every case sits in several jurisdictions at once. Drugs and devices speak statistics, converting a single case into a signal. Nuclear speaks conservatively, logging even one millisievert. Each accent gets a page in Part IV, and a reader who has heard all five can pick up a report from any industry and hear where it comes from. Hearing the origin is the prerequisite skill for evaluating a piece of material.

The closing inventory of this part, in its fullest form: Chapter 5, 12 fields. Chapter 6, 3 disciplines, 1 criterion and 3 signal words. Chapter 7, 3 conditions, 3 currencies and 1 judgement table. Chapter 8, 7 steps, 4 devices and 1 self-test. Chapter 9, 3 layers, 3 breakpoints and a 9-cell table. Chapter 10, 3 disciplines, a 5-step method, 5 grades and 1 labelling convention. More than fifty operable items between them, each usable before the end of today. Part I gave the reader a view of failure, Part II gave the scalpel, and Part III takes both on rounds through twenty-four organizational failures.

For the reader who wants to skip Part II and go straight to Part III: you can. Every case card in Part III stands on its own, and the story reads without the anatomy. What you will miss is the second half of each chapter, the failure-chain analysis and the mapping from each defence to an intervention currency, and that missing half is exactly what separates this book from a collection of stories. If you reach Part III, find you need the tools and come back, Chapters 5 to 10 are here. A reference book is best opened with a question in hand; reading it in order is only its most respectable form.

Part II is also worth a second reading once you have made a card by hand. On the second pass, every counterexample in Chapter 5 is one you committed, and every discipline in Chapter 6 is one you nearly broke. All the detail invisible the first time lights up.

What marks the tools as yours is not remembering the definitions but muscle memory. Your hand splits the two columns when you write a postmortem. Your hand fills the judgement table when you decide. Your eye looks for the grade when you read a report. Muscle memory has no fast route; each tool wants ten uses by hand, and the list of ten uses is each chapter's five self-checks. Five questions plus practice is the whole training plan, and the starting point is one card.

docs.title: Chapter 11 Normalization of Deviance (Vaughan, 1996)
docs.text: What this chapter covers: how a deviation turns into standard practice on the strength of "nothing happened last time"; three trigger criteria, the shape the mechanism takes in four domains, eight weak signals and the devices that block it. When to come back to it: when someone answers a challenge with "we have always done it this way"; when you are about to approve a request to relax a standard, extend an interval or waive an inspection. Reading time: about 55 minutes.

docs.title: 11.1 What It Is
docs.text:
Definition: the first appearance of a deviation is handled as an anomaly. As it recurs and produces no consequence, it is reinterpreted as acceptable normal; the explanation stops entering the register; the inspection and release criteria move quietly. Diane Vaughan named the mechanism while studying the Challenger launch decision (Vaughan, The Challenger Launch Decision, University of Chicago Press, 1996). The coldest part of her account is this. Normalization does not happen in the explanation. It happens in the filing. Every deviant event is explained by the organization, which says why this one did no harm, and then filed, which says which category it belongs to. Explanations are public and arguable. Filings are quiet and not arguable. The substantive move of normalization is to shift a deviation out of the drawer marked "to be eliminated" and into the drawer marked "known, acceptable", and the basis for the filing is the outcome: nothing happened.

Three trigger criteria. If any one of them is present, the mechanism is already running.

① A deviation of the same class has appeared twice or more, and none of the occurrences produced a consequence. ② Each occurrence was explained as "there is still margin", "a one-off", "contained", and none of the explanations generated a register entry. ③ An inspection standard, a limit or an interval was lowered or relaxed and written into the process, or practice took the place of process.

Normalization runs through three phases, each with its own archival signature. In the anomaly phase the deviation appears for the first time, enters the register, the entry stays open, and the handling work is organized around removing the cause. In the case phase the deviation appears a second and a third time, each occurrence is explained on its own terms (margin, coincidence, special conditions), the register entries are closed one by one, and no combined statistic across entries is ever produced. In the routine phase the appearance of the deviation no longer triggers a register action at all. Handling is fixed in the process or in habit, and "we did it this way before" becomes the oral register. What separates the three phases is attention. The anomaly phase consumes attention, the case phase sustains it, the routine phase releases it. The mechanism's end product is a reallocation of attention: the attention that used to watch the deviation is moved elsewhere by the organization, while the deviation keeps running where it was.

People assume normalization needs an explicit decision to tolerate something. In most cases no such decision can be found. The "in family" clause in section 11.3, the alarms that close in seconds, the noise explanation: each is a structure that only becomes visible when a large number of small handling actions are strung together and read backwards. Standing at the moment any one of those actions was taken, the person saw a reasonable piece of work. That is the argument for the three-state register in section 11.5. Reasonableness seen from one seat cannot be re-checked by addition. Only the register can do that.

Why "no consequence" carries almost no evidential weight needs saying once, plainly. A run with a deviation that lands safely proves very little. It proves this run did not hit the tail, and nobody knows where the tail sits. Stack fifty safe landings and the evidence grows far more slowly than intuition suggests, because the runs are correlated with one another (the same people, the same practice, the same tempo) and the information they carry overlaps heavily. An organization that reads a consequence-free period as proof of safety is reading an intuitive count of independent trials. The real trials are neither independent nor repeated often enough to separate hypothesis A from hypothesis B. That is also why weak signal 8 in section 11.4 is so hard to refute. The challenger cannot produce more data, because the data only exists after the consequence. Normalization wins arguments in a peculiar way. It does not need to win. It needs to last until the data arrives.

The arithmetic core is worth setting out, because it explains why "we have always done it this way" is an understandable error rather than a stupid one. The deviation has appeared n times with no consequence, and two hypotheses are on the table. Under A the margin really is sufficient, and the absence of consequence is the structure's doing. Under B the margin is not sufficient, and the absence of consequence is luck. The organization usually holds no data that discriminates between them. Discrimination requires knowing the tail of the distribution, and the tail is precisely what has not happened yet. Normalization is the default to A when the data cannot discriminate. The cost of that default is set by the compounding of exposures. Every run with the deviation is one exposure. Under B the accident probability rises with the number of exposures; under A it stays constant. The installment-type irreversibility of Chapter 7 is this arithmetic in the form it takes at a release decision.

docs.title: 11.2 How It Grows
docs.text:
Four generating conditions, corresponding to structure, incentive, time scale and information.

Structural: the deviation is produced at the front line, and the authority to remove it sits far away. Stopping a line, changing a supplier, redesigning one detail: high cost, long process. Writing an explanation: low cost, finished on the spot. When the gap between the cost of removing and the cost of explaining is wide enough, the organization chooses explaining again and again.

Incentive: the person who explains the deviation does not carry the deviation's tail risk. The manager who signs the relaxation is usually transferred before the consequence lands (Chapter 28), or the deviation itself yields a current-period benefit in output, on-time rate or labor hours. Where the person who sees the deviation is also the person who benefits from it (Chapter 17), the explanation drifts toward hypothesis A on its own.

Time scale: the consequence is delayed. Delay breaks the learning loop. Months or years sit between the deviation and the consequence, and by the time the consequence arrives, the record of the deviation has already been overwritten with "explained". Delay has a side effect. A stretch of no consequences is itself evidence, to the organization, that hypothesis A holds. Success becomes the fuel of deviation; the slack of success in Chapter 20 is the sister mechanism.

Information: no cumulative register. Each deviation is assessed on its own, from the material of that one event plus the memory of the people involved. A list of historical deviations does not exist, or exists with every entry marked "explained". With no independent review, the hypothesis-A explanation has nothing to be confronted with.

There is one amplifier: years in the trade. Personal experience is not built like an organizational register. "I did this for twenty years and nothing happened" treats a personal exposure count as data, and its sampling bias is the microscopic version of this chapter's mechanism. It also sits on the border with Chapter 14: intuition is most confident inside its own failure zone.

One archival property of the mechanism needs adding after the generating conditions. The status of a register entry decides who reads it later, and with how much attention. An entry marked "explained" presents itself in every later search, every handover, every audit as a settled matter. The reader assumes it no longer needs judgment, only awareness. Chapter 30, handover rupture, meets this chapter exactly here. The entries on a handover sheet marked "legacy item, dealt with" are how normalization travels between departments.

The consequence-free period has a second contaminating effect: it rewrites the baseline for future assessment. Every run with the deviation produces a record that says the run was normal. Those records enter the experience base, and later risk assessments use them as their template. The sample the assessor sees has already been screened of bad outcomes. This is the survivorship bias of Chapter 2 reproduced inside the organization. The filing action rewrites the organization's definition of normal every day, and the rewriting raises no alarm.

Among the four generating conditions, the structural one is the most often misread, as "the front line is a long way from headquarters". Distance is the shell. The core is a difference in standing between two kinds of knowledge. Design knowledge is written into documents; operating knowledge is scattered among people. Documents can be searched, cited and audited. Knowledge held in people cannot, so every collision between the two ends with the document winning, and the real operating practice survives outside the documents under the name of custom. Normalization is that survival, filed. Before custom produces a consequence, the organization's official language has no word for it. The front-line representative signature clause in the device list of section 11.5 is aimed at this gap in standing. Its job is to give operating knowledge the same right to be cited as a document.

docs.title: 11.3 The Pattern in Four Domains
docs.text: The six cases below come from four domains. Following the book's convention, each stops at the decision point: you decide first, then turn the page for the outcome. Case numbers match Appendix B. Cases one, two and five are given as full cards, each backed by a grade-A full report from an independent investigation. The other three stay condensed.

docs.title: Case 1 (Spaceflight): The "In-Family" Classification of a Foam Strike
docs.text:
mi-001.

When and where: 16 January 2003, launch at 10:39 a.m. local time; 1 February 2003, entry interface at 8:44:09 a.m., loss of communication with the ground at 8:59 a.m. Locations: Kennedy Space Center, Florida (launch and imagery interpretation); Marshall Space Flight Center, Huntsville, Alabama (external tank project, flight readiness review); Johnson Space Center, Houston, Texas (debris assessment team, mission evaluation room, mission management team).

What and who: The NASA Space Shuttle Program office (SSP); the Marshall external tank project (ET Project); the Johnson engineering directorate and structures division; engineers from United Space Alliance and Boeing; the Debris Assessment Team (DAT, led by two co-chairs, one from NASA and one from United Space Alliance); the Mission Evaluation Room (MER, the project office's engineering support group); the Mission Management Team (MMT, chaired by an appointee of Johnson); and the Program Requirements Control Board (PRCB), the body that signs the flight readiness review. The STS-107 crew numbered 7 and spent 16 days on orbit.

What they were doing: On 7 October 2002, STS-112 launched and a piece of foam roughly 4×5×12 inches came off the left bipod ramp of the external tank, tearing the insulation on the solid rocket booster attach ring (CAIB p.126, figure 6.1-5). On 31 October, at Marshall, the PRCB heard the external tank project manager, Jerry Smelser, at the STS-113 flight readiness review. His briefing was titled "STS-112/ET-115 Bipod Ramp Foam Loss" and ran four pages (CAIB p.126). That loss had occurred three months before Columbia's last launch (CAIB p.124, figure 6.1-3). The briefing gave three flight rationale: the foam came off the -Y bipod ramp and exposed the bipod fitting; the current fitting had not changed since STS-54 (ET-51); and across more than a hundred external tanks only 3 significant bipod foam losses had been recorded (CAIB p.126). At the same review the NASA headquarters safety office submitted a report estimating a 99% probability that no further foam would come off that area (CAIB p.127). The review's conclusion characterized the foam loss as an "acceptable risk" rather than as "not a flight safety issue", and the STS-113 certificate of flight readiness was signed (CAIB p.127). STS-113 launched at night in November; no imagery was obtained, so whether foam came off again could not be determined (CAIB p.127). The judgment rested on a long ledger. After the first flight in 1981, 300 tiles were replaced. Of the 79 missions with imagery, 65 captured foam loss, and the orbiter's lower surface averaged 143 dings after return (CAIB p.123). STS-107, meanwhile, flew as a 16-day science mission with no robotic arm, and RCC panels 1 through 11 on the left wing leading edge could not be seen from inside the cabin (CAIB p.147).

The decision point: ① 31 October 2002, Marshall, STS-113 flight readiness review. On the table: the foam dimensions and damage photographs from STS-112, the three flight rationale from the external tank project, and the 99% estimate from the headquarters safety office. The Image Working Group had earlier recommended that the STS-112 loss be recorded as an In-Flight Anomaly; the recommendation was not adopted at the review (CAIB p.126). CAIB's re-check found the first and third rationale incorrect. The bipod ramp design had been changed at ET-76, and the 99% calculation pooled the left and right bipods and set the start of its sample after STS-112, which left out STS-7, STS-32R and STS-50 (CAIB p.127). The meeting's conclusion was written as "acceptable risk", and the certificate was signed (CAIB p.127).

② 22 January 2003, in the morning, Houston: the imaging request is withdrawn. At 8:09 the MER log records that "Engelauf wanted to know who was having the Air Force look at the vehicle" (CAIB p.154). At 8:30 NASA's Department of Defense liaison called US Strategic Command to withdraw the imaging request; less than 90 minutes separated initiation from withdrawal (CAIB p.154). After the withdrawal, a 9:33 email from Ham to Austin and Roe was still asking the same question in another form: could anyone state that no external tank foam loss could cause a flight safety problem, on grounds of density (CAIB p.155). At 10:15 Dittemore replied that someone first had to confirm that foam density could not strike a tile hard enough to affect the orbiter (CAIB p.156). At 10:37 the log records the conclusion: "Shriver, Ham, Roe have indicated they do not need Air Force look at vehicle" (CAIB p.157).

③ 24 January 2003, 7 a.m., Houston: the debris assessment team briefed the MER. That day the MER manager gave the MMT an oral summary with no data. The MMT classified the impact as a "turnaround issue" and stopped pursuing imagery (CAIB p.39).

What was visible then: On 17 January at 9:30 EST, image analysts at Marshall saw the impact at 81.9 seconds on film, and within an hour Kennedy confirmed it on higher-resolution film (CAIB p.141). Only three ground cameras could see the impact at all: one lost tracking during ascent, one was out of focus from improper lens maintenance, and one captured only the upper surface of the left wing (CAIB p.141). At 10:58 CST the same day, the MER log recorded debris "from the external tank forward bipod area, traveling down the left side, striking the left wing leading edge near the fuselage" (CAIB p.142). At 15:15 Bob Page, chair of the Image Working Group, telephoned Wayne Hale and Lambert Austin: Boeing was computing trajectory, velocity, angle and energy (CAIB p.142). At 16:28 the log records that "USA and Boeing are not working the debris problem over the weekend, waiting for film on Monday" (CAIB p.143). On 18 January Boeing produced two size estimates, 20×20×2 inches and 20×16×6 inches, with a velocity of about 750 feet per second and an incidence angle under 20 degrees (CAIB p.144). At 11:39 on 20 January the log records debris "about 20 inches, plus or minus 10 inches, similar in size to the STS-112 event" (CAIB p.147). At 9:26 on 21 January, Schomburg wrote by email: "TPS took a hit, probably not a problem" (CAIB p.150). The debris assessment team held its first formal meeting the same day (CAIB p.152). At 9:01 on 22 January, Air Force Lieutenant Colonel Lee emailed McCormack: "Austin called yesterday, requesting DoD high-resolution photos of the shuttle on orbit" (CAIB p.152). That same day Rocha wrote an email that was never sent: "in my poor technical judgment, SSP and the orbiter project not requesting additional imaging is wrong, close to irresponsible" (CAIB p.158). At 23:13 on 23 January, Stich emailed the crew: "the experts have looked at the high-speed photography, there is no concern for RCC or tile, and absolutely no concern for entry" (CAIB p.160). At 12:15 on 28 January, the safety and quality assurance seat's log mentioned debris for the second time, asking whether anyone from SR&QA had been involved in the decision that the ascent debris strike was safe (CAIB p.167). Information that became available only afterwards: the foam struck RCC panels 5 through 9, panel 8 was breached, hot gas entered the wing leading edge spar, and the aluminum structure melted. None of this appeared before the debris reconstruction that followed 1 February.

Stop here. Decide before you turn the page.

You are in that seat now, with the materials above in front of you.

  1. What would you do? Write the action, not "pay more attention".
  2. Which item here are you most likely to miss, and why does it look unimportant?
  3. If you may set one checkpoint, when is it and what does it check?

What happened: At 8:44:09 on 1 February 2003 the orbiter entered the atmosphere. At 8:59 communication with the ground was lost, and the vehicle broke up over Texas and Louisiana. All seven astronauts died. During the search a Bell 407 helicopter crashed in Angelina National Forest, killing the contract pilot and a Texas Forest Service employee and injuring 3 (CAIB p.47). Ground searchers passed 3,000 within two weeks and 4,000 within a month (CAIB p.46). Back to the three questions. The most common answer to the first is "ask for the imagery again". CAIB lists it as the 4th of eight missed opportunities: the request was withdrawn within 90 minutes, and the person who withdrew it was not an engineer (CAIB p.154, p.168). The item most often missed on the second question is the four slides of 31 October. They described a design that had already been changed as unchanged, and that sentence was the pivot of the entire flight rationale (CAIB p.127). The third question lands on 17 January. The Image Working Group had classified the strike as "out of family" that day, and under project procedure an event of that class should have been handled as a Tiger Team. What was formed was a DAT, which is not bound by the Tiger Team checklist, so the event belonged nowhere in the procedure (CAIB p.143).

Options ruled out: Have the crew photograph the left wing with a handheld camera. Rocha asked on 17 January whether the crew could inspect the wing; no response is recorded (CAIB p.168). Columbia had no robotic arm, RCC panels 1 through 11 were not visible from the cabin, and a visual check required a spacewalk (CAIB p.147). Request Department of Defense imaging. It was initiated on 22 January and withdrawn within 90 minutes (CAIB p.154). Change the entry trajectory to reduce heating. The engineering analysis concluded that no alternative trajectory would significantly reduce the heat load on that area (CAIB p.161). Upgrade the DAT to a Tiger Team. The event had been classified out of family, but that procedure was never run; the team was left "organizationally adrift" with only a date to report: 24 January (CAIB p.143). Extend the mission and wait for on-orbit imagery. Not found in any meeting record. Declare the strike a flight safety issue outright. CAIB records the actual requirement as the reverse: engineers had to prove it unsafe before management would move, while the standing expectation was to prove it safe (CAIB p.170).

Early signals: ① 18 June 1983, STS-7: the left bipod ramp lost a 19×12 inch piece of foam, leaving 25 shallow divots forward of the bipod strut and 40 divots on the lower external tank. The post-flight PRCB recorded it as an in-flight anomaly and closed it at the next review on the grounds that the orbiter thermal protection system had been repaired. Neither the closure document nor the flight readiness certificate mentioned the cause of the foam loss (CAIB p.124). Suppression reason: it was logged under procedure, so it counted as handled. ② 9 January 1990, STS-32R: 5 divots in intertank foam with diameters from 6 to 28 inches, 111 strikes on the orbiter's lower surface with 13 over 1 inch. The anomaly was closed at the STS-36 review as a "local foam void", vent holes were subsequently drilled in the foam, and the mechanism has never been confirmed (CAIB p.125). ③ 2 December 1988, STS-27R: 707 divots, 298 of them over 1 inch, one tile knocked off and structure exposed. After the ablator was replaced, the problem counted as closed before the next review (CAIB p.128). The same investigation recommended that the project "actively solicit design improvements to eliminate the source of debris or reduce the potential for damage"; 14 years later there was still no corresponding action (CAIB p.129). ④ 25 June 1992, STS-50: the third bipod foam loss, characterized in Hazard Report 37 as an "accepted risk", with the external tank project writing at the same time that it was "not a flight safety issue" (CAIB p.125). ⑤ 19 November 1997, STS-87: thermal protection damage prompted NASA to run 9 flight tests to settle the foam loss question. The fix did not work, and the in-flight anomaly was closed after STS-101 as an "accepted risk" (CAIB p.129). ⑥ 7 October 2002, STS-112: the fourth, with foam of 4×5×12 inches tearing the booster attach ring insulation. The review of 31 October passed it with two lines, "design unchanged" and "99% no loss" (CAIB pp. 126–127). The suppression reasons collapse into one sentence: this is a class of event already logged, already explained, with no consequence on record. CAIB's count is 7 left bipod losses in 113 flights, about 10% of the 72 flights with usable imagery (CAIB p.124).

The point of escalation: 31 October 2002, Marshall, where the STS-113 flight readiness review wrote "acceptable risk" into its conclusion and the certificate of flight readiness was signed shortly after (CAIB p.127). CAIB's judgment is that this decision "made it, and possibly encouraged it, easier" for members of the MMT to use the same reasoning when they assessed the STS-107 foam strike (CAIB p.126). STS-113 then launched at night with no imagery, and in November the same rationale was forwarded by Paul Shack to Rocha by email as a reference (CAIB p.151). By 17 January, an engineer arguing "this one is different" first had to overturn the conclusion of the project's most rigorous review, held a month earlier.

Failure chain: Technical layer: foam separated from the left bipod ramp at 81.7 seconds and struck RCC panels 5 through 9 at 625 to 840 feet per second at 81.9 seconds; panel 8 was penetrated and hot gas entered the wing leading edge spar. There is a design background underneath this. The thermal protection system was designed to withstand impacts below 0.006 foot-pounds, and the external tank requirement was that it produce no debris; both requirements were breached on the first flight in 1981, when 300 tiles were replaced (CAIB p.123). Organizational layer: the strike was filed as "in family", meaning within known experience, considered understood, and not a flight safety issue. The classification rested on the absence of past consequences, not on the energy and location of this strike (CAIB p.124). The same filing broke once, on 17 January, when the strike was reclassified as out of family, but the Tiger Team procedure that out-of-family should trigger was never started (CAIB p.143). Foam damage monitoring was judged inadequate by the project itself, a fuller record would have helped identify trends, and the improvement never landed (CAIB p.129). Incentive layer: STS-107 was a long-scheduled 16-day science mission, imaging would consume science time and require interagency channels, and the trade on 22 January was to stop a 90-minute request (CAIB pp. 154–155). The break sits between the organizational and incentive layers. The filing clause exists precisely so that anomaly signals can be dissolved quickly under schedule and resource pressure, and what it saves management is the cost of one more look.

Minimum counterfactual: At 8:30 on 22 January 2003, do not withdraw the Department of Defense imaging request that had already been initiated. Let it run through the procedure Strategic Command was already following. One action, ten days before the breakup. The cost was a few hours of science observing time, and it required no luck and no new technical judgment, because that morning the request had already reached the stage of identifying available imaging assets (CAIB p.153). CAIB lists it as the 4th of eight missed opportunities (CAIB p.168).

Outcome and sources: Seven astronauts died. Two search personnel died in a helicopter crash and 3 were injured. The orbiter broke up, and debris was scattered across Texas and Louisiana. CAIB found that the accident "was not a random event" and listed the way the foam loss was filed as an organizational cause (CAIB p.10, p.124). Primary source: Columbia Accident Investigation Board, Report Volume I, August 2003, NASA official PDF, link at Appendix B mi-001.

docs.title: Case 2 (Chemicals): Thirty-Two Alarms
docs.text:
ch-001.

When and where: 10 November 2014, a Monday, a mis-dilution shutdown; 12 November, an attempted restart; the morning of 14 November, the hydrate plug confirmed and a handling plan settled; 15 November, high-pressure alarm inside the building at 2:51 a.m., valves opened from 3:01 to 3:13 a.m., the last victim found between 11:15 and 11:55 a.m. Location: La Porte, Texas, the Lannate insecticide unit of the DuPont La Porte plant. The point of failure was the second-floor drain area and the third-floor vent header collection level of a multi-storey enclosed building; the control room stood outside the building.

What and who: E. I. du Pont de Nemours and Company, La Porte plant, insecticides business unit (IBU), Lannate (methomyl) unit. The shift was nights: control board operator, shift supervisor (who also served as Process Coordinator, responsible in an emergency for giving the rescue team process information), and field operator. Three plants on the site shared one emergency response team (ERT) of about 60 people, managed by DuPont (CSB p.20, footnote). The same building also handled chlorine and methyl isocyanate (MIC), both more toxic than methyl mercaptan under site standards (CSB p.13, footnote; p.28). Methyl mercaptan was detected with borrowed hydrogen sulfide detectors, with the alarm set at 25 ppm for methyl mercaptan (CSB p.14, footnote).

What they were doing: On 10 November a tank truck of 50% acetaldoxime (AAO) was being unloaded when a water dilution valve that should have been interlocked shut stayed fully open, because a jumper installed during the spring 2014 turnaround had not been removed. Water entered the tank, the AAO was diluted, and the unit shut down (CSB p.9, footnote; p.13). Water entered the methyl mercaptan feed line during the shutdown. Houston temperatures held below 55 Fahrenheit from 11 November, averaging about 40 Fahrenheit over the first 24 hours, hydrates formed in the line, and the restart on 12 November failed (CSB p.13, footnote; p.102). On the morning of 14 November the unit technical team met the day-shift supervisor, concluded that water had entered and formed hydrates, and decided to heat the line under its insulation with hot water hoses until the hydrates decomposed. The team also recognized that heating would expand the methyl mercaptan and that it needed somewhere to relieve, so operators opened three valves between the methyl mercaptan feed line and the vent header; at the time of the incident one was fully open and one was slightly open (CSB pp. 99–100, pp. 102–103). None of this work had a process hazard analysis, a written procedure or a management-of-change review (CSB p.100). Execution began at the tank and feed pump section and moved along the feed line toward the reactor system, with pressure gauges on the three connecting valves used to locate the plug and track progress (CSB p.103). In the early hours of 15 November the hot water melted the hydrate, and liquid methyl mercaptan passed through those three valves into the vent header, a line built for vent gas and designed never to carry liquid (CSB p.104). At 2:51 a high-pressure alarm came from equipment inside the building. The board operator treated it as condensate accumulation, as custom dictated, and sent the shift supervisor and operator 1 to drain the third floor (CSB p.15). Third-floor low-point draining had been written into the daily work instructions since 14 January 2014, once per shift (CSB p.108).

The decision point: ① 2011: the $20 million NRS incinerator project went into service. The vent header running to the incinerator had not been designed with liquid accumulation properly in mind. The line has low points, there is no engineering measure such as a knockout drum, and accumulated liquid could only be removed by hand from the low points (CSB p.106, p.108). CSB records that this was not considered in design; no individual signature for project approval or acceptance appears in the report. Over the following three years, several pieces of equipment connected to that header had repeated high-pressure events, and the fixed response was manual draining (CSB p.107).

② March 2010: a corrective action closed. A second-party PSM audit in 2009 found that the site held no documentation showing the building ventilation system had ever been tested for supply effectiveness, and recommended a periodic test procedure.
