The site configured an automatic work-order generator in the computerized maintenance system and closed the corrective action on that basis in March 2010, without assigning an owner (CSB pp. 97–98). The first test should have run in November 2010 and was actually delayed to 2012. The dry end was measured for airflow but never analyzed and had no acceptance criteria. The wet end, the side that failed in 2014, was never tested at all (CSB p.98).

③ 14 January 2014: the daily work instruction. Area management required operators, in the daily instruction book, to drain accumulated liquid from the third-floor vent header "low point" once per shift. A paragraph was added later: attach a hose and drain the liquid under an open floor safety shower until it stops flowing (CSB p.108). The instruction came with no management of change, no dedicated procedure, no line-breaking permit, and no requirement for additional protection (CSB p.108, p.111). The instruction book had no per-item signature block, and CSB names the approving source only as "area management" (CSB p.108).

④ The morning of 14 November 2014: the meeting of the unit technical team and the day-shift supervisor. The meeting settled on external hot water heating with three valves connected to the vent header, with no management of change and no written procedure. The hot water heating also exceeded the heat input design value of the system's thermal expansion relief valve (CSB p.104).

What was visible then: 32 methyl mercaptan alarms at the control panel over 17 hours (CSB p.14). The detector range was 0 to 25 ppm and the alarm was set at 25 ppm, which is 2.5 times the OSHA limit of 10 ppm and 50 times the NIOSH recommended value of 0.5 ppm; readings appeared only on the DCS and never entered the historian (CSB p.15, footnote). The high-pressure alarm at 2:51 on 15 November arrived with the "condensate" custom attached to it (CSB p.15). The odor threshold of methyl mercaptan is about 2 ppb, one five-thousandth of the OSHA permissible exposure limit of 10 ppm, so smelling it says nothing about a low concentration, and prolonged exposure brings olfactory fatigue (CSB p.14, footnote). Two shift suggestion meetings, in February and October 2014, both recorded the low-point accumulation and both proposed changing the piping to eliminate the low point (CSB p.112). A management-of-change review started weeks before the incident stated in its own text that third-floor draining "was not a good practice, because the line is sometimes nitrogen-purged, which could release nitrogen inside the building" (CSB pp. 108–109). The only written note on the shift turnover record was one line: "Unplugging M[e]SH Header." (CSB p.113, footnote). An "urgent" work order had been opened on 20 October after another roof fan stopped with an abnormal noise, and a second fan had been down since June (CSB p.85). The ventilation system had no scrubber or incinerator of its own; exhaust went straight to atmosphere (CSB p.97, footnote). The 2009 audit finding and the March 2010 closure were on file (CSB pp. 97–98). Information that became available only afterwards: the concentration gradient on each floor, the release rate and the dispersion, all reconstructed by CSB modeling, with a total of about 24,000 pounds (CSB p.7, p.24).

Stop here. Decide before you turn the page.

You are in that seat now, with the materials above in front of you.

  1. What would you do? Write the action, not "pay more attention".
  2. Which item here are you most likely to miss, and why does it look unimportant?
  3. If you may set one checkpoint, when is it and what does it check?

What happened: Four people died: 3 operators and 1 shift supervisor, from the combined effect of asphyxiation and acute methyl mercaptan inhalation (CSB p.7, p.24). At 3:30 operator 1 radioed for help, and different listeners understood the wording as "we need help" or as "I need help on the fourth floor" (CSB p.17). Operators 2, 3 and 4 went in without respiratory protection. Operator 2 died on the third floor. Operator 4 advanced about 10 feet, hit what he later called "a wall" of methyl mercaptan, and fell back (CSB p.18). Operator 6 entered with three 5-minute escape respirators, put one on operator 4, went up to the third floor for his brother, and was overcome before he could connect the mask to the air cylinder (CSB pp. 19–20). The ERT was called at 3:50, and the other party understood "rescue" as high-angle and confined-space work, so it brought harnesses and rope (CSB pp. 20–21). At 4:05 the incident commander asked for blast suits and SCBA. The small pumper truck carrying the SCBA would not start, and it stood more than 2,000 feet from the control room (CSB p.21). The first team wearing SCBA entered the building at 4:25 (CSB p.24). About 40 minutes passed before the control room understood how serious things were inside the building, and full control took more than six hours (CSB p.27). The pump was not stopped until 6:02, and the tank and the leaking line were fully isolated at 10:07 (CSB pp. 25–26). On the three questions: the most common answer is "go into the building and look", and operator 4's ten feet is that answer. The item most easily missed is the fans, two "PSM critical" machines with one down five months and one down nearly a month (CSB p.85). The third question does not land on alarm handling. It lands on why that header had a low point in 2011 at all.

Options ruled out: Stop draining and evacuate. The emergency plan required that a release be reported to the shift supervisor, that the site toxic gas alarm be sounded, and that SCBA be worn during response; what happened was confirmation followed by continuation (CSB p.29). Start the ventilation. Neither roof fan would turn (CSB p.85). Confirm at the valve mouth with a portable detector. Personal methyl mercaptan monitors existed on site and were never issued to field operators to wear (CSB p.28). Work under a line-breaking permit. By DuPont's own standard, opening a valve to atmosphere is line breaking and requires a written work plan; the people on site did not regard a drain hose as line breaking (CSB p.111). Remove the low point by engineering. Raised at the shift suggestion meetings of February and October 2014, never opened as a project (CSB p.112). Wait for the management of change to finish before draining. That review had started only weeks earlier, and draining went on (CSB p.108). Add technical support to the night shift. The handling plan gave the night shift no adequate technical resource (CSB p.95).

Early signals: ① The 2009 second-party PSM audit: ventilation never verified; the corrective action closed in March 2010, the first test slipped to 2012, the wet end never tested (CSB pp. 97–98). Suppression reason: the entry's status already read "closed", and CSB calls this kind of closure a paper closure (CSB p.97). ② The 2011 process hazard analysis: hydrate plugging was ranked consequence C-1 and frequency F-1, the lowest rung of both scales, risk level IV, "no mitigation required", so there was neither heat tracing nor any procedure for decomposing hydrates (CSB p.94). Suppression reason: the matrix had already answered, unlikely and minor. ③ Text left behind by the 2012 safety perception survey and the July 2014 front-line supervisor interviews: "our safety passion has slipped over the past ten years"; "we are just not as good as we thought we were... a long slow decline, and we may not have noticed how far we had dropped" (CSB p.84). Suppression reason: a culture survey is not a deficiency entry and does not enter the corrective action register. ④ The daily drain instruction from 14 January 2014, which turned a known design defect into a per-shift action (CSB p.108). Suppression reason: ten months in writing, nothing had happened. ⑤ Both shift suggestion meetings in 2014 identified the low-point accumulation and proposed changing the piping (CSB p.112). Suppression reason: it had been discussed in a meeting, which counted as handled. ⑥ 32 alarms in 17 hours, at an alarm value of 25 ppm (CSB pp. 14–15). Suppression reason: they coincided with maintenance, so they were maintenance-related.

The point of escalation: The morning of 14 November 2014, when the unit technical team and the day-shift supervisor settled on hot water heating with three valves connected to the vent header. From that point liquid methyl mercaptan had a route into the building (CSB pp. 102–104). CSB's own words: an effective management-of-change review of the heating and of this abnormal line configuration "could have identified and controlled the hazards that led to the incident" (CSB p.104). After that step the only interception point left was confirming what the line contained before the valves were opened, and sampling was written into the daily instruction and never carried out (CSB p.108).

Failure chain: Technical layer: the vent header to the 2011 incinerator has low points and no knockout drum, and liquid was removed by hand (CSB p.108); building ventilation was designed to 25% of the lower explosive limit for combustible gas with no allowance for toxicity, while 25% of the LEL for methyl mercaptan is 65 times the immediately dangerous to life or health concentration of 150 ppm (CSB p.8, footnote); both roof fans were unavailable at once (CSB p.85); the detector alarm sat at 25 ppm and displayed only in the control room (CSB p.15, footnote). Organizational layer: the 2009 audit finding was closed by building a procedure, with no test performed (CSB p.98); the 2011 hazard analysis rated hydrates as the lowest risk (CSB p.94); draining had no management of change, no procedure and no line-breaking permit (CSB p.108, p.111); turnover was oral, with a single written line, "Unplugging M[e]SH Header." (CSB p.113); the definition of line breaking did not match field understanding, and a drain hose was not treated as line breaking (CSB p.111). Incentive layer: the $20 million project of 2011 was for more output and lower emissions, and Lannate was a full-rate product (CSB p.106); the 2014 bonus plan, LPBC, was tied only to OSHA recordable injuries, deducting 5% per injury up to a cap of 50%, with no process safety metric in it (CSB pp. 115–116). The break sits between the organizational and incentive layers: making the accumulation into an engineering fix requires a project and a shutdown, while writing it into a daily instruction requires one line.

Minimum counterfactual: At the meeting of 14 November 2014, run a management-of-change review on "hot water heating plus three valves connected to the vent header". One action, available the same day, needing no new data. CSB found that this step "could have identified and controlled" the hazards that led to the incident (CSB p.104).

Outcome and sources: Four dead and about 24,000 pounds of methyl mercaptan released. In May 2015 OSHA issued 11 citations for this incident; on 9 July it issued 8 more for the adjacent unit and placed DuPont in the Severe Violator Enforcement Program; a settlement was reached on 17 July 2017 (CSB p.62, footnote). EPA proposed 22 risk management program violations after its inspection, the Department of Justice filed a complaint with a consent decree on 23 July 2018, and DuPont paid a $3.1 million civil penalty without admitting liability (CSB p.65). DuPont announced in spring 2016 that the Lannate unit would not restart, and it was demolished in 2017 (CSB p.10). Primary source: CSB, Investigation Report No. 2015-01-I-TX, June 2019, link at Appendix B ch-001.

One detail in this case deserves a second look from the chapter's angle. The maintenance work order for the failed exhaust fan sat in the system for nearly a month with the status "urgent", and CSB's text uses that word in English, where it means handling within two to three days. The work-order system was not wrong, and the person who set the priority had a reason: ventilation plays no part in the reaction, and a stopped fan does not affect output. The gap sits between the status language and the handling. "Urgent" reads, in this chapter's archival sense, as the maintenance edition of "explained": a known defect formally logged as urgent, with nobody asking why it had not been handled within two or three days. What arrived was that defect becoming the condition that turned a release into a poisoning on the night of the incident. Device 1's three-state register, ported to a work-order system, is a one-line patch. A defect in equipment that carries a safety function may only be given the status "remediation by date", and the date is set by a party whose appraisal does not depend on output. An "urgent" with no time standard is an adjective.

docs.title: Case 3 (Aviation Maintenance): Interval Extensions, Approved One Signature at a Time (condensed)
docs.text:
av-034. Alaska Airlines 261, an MD-83 (N963AS), 31 January 2000, 2.7 miles north of Anacapa Island in the Pacific. The NTSB final report (AAR-02/01; this book downloaded and read the PDF): the lubrication interval and the end-play check interval for the horizontal stabilizer jackscrew assembly had been extended at the company's request with FAA approval (executive summary p.4, verified). The report found that the extensions allowed inadequate lubrication to develop into excessive wear, that the jackscrew nut threads failed in flight, and that the 2 pilots, 3 cabin crew and 83 passengers on board all died. The decision point is the moment the FAA signed the extension. Minimum counterfactual: do not extend the end-play check interval, and check at the original interval. Primary source: NTSB, AAR-02/01, 2002, link at Appendix B av-034.

The condensed version is worth a second look because it shows normalization's most ordinary carrier: a relaxation document with unimpeachable wording. The application came from the operator, the approval from the regulator, both acting inside their own authority, and every step is compliant when read alone. The mechanism leaves one trace. Almost all the information the approval rested on came from the applicant's own records. NTSB's executive summary sets out the path between the extension and the development of wear plainly; in hindsight, the separate reasonableness of each extension request adds up to putting the wear process of the jackscrew nut inside a sparser inspection window. Devices 2 and 4 in section 11.5 are built to this shape: numbers must be measured, and a signature must have a second pen.

docs.title: Case 4 (Finance): Alarms Closed in Seconds (condensed)
docs.text:
fi-013. Moors & Cabot, a broker-dealer, anti-money-laundering (AML) monitoring. FINRA disciplinary decision of August 2026 (this book downloaded and read the monthly summary PDF): a large number of AML alerts were closed within seconds with no corresponding review, after an earlier independent AML test had flagged the alert backlog and no remediation followed. The decision point is the moment the independent test report reached management and named the backlog. Minimum counterfactual: when the report arrived, add staff and systems as it recommended. Primary source: FINRA, Disciplinary and Other FINRA Actions – October 2026, 2026, link at Appendix B fi-013.

The condensed version hides the standard form this mechanism takes in finance. The handling action for an alert is closing it, the reason field is a structured dropdown, and the menu has no option reading "needs more time". The choice architecture has paid for the normalization in advance: each closure taking seconds is, on its own, a non-compliant act, but the interface makes non-compliance the default path. Once the independent test had flagged the backlog, the entry should have moved into remediation. It moved into the next audit calendar instead. A reader in financial services can carry Device 1 back unchanged: alert entries get three states only, and a closure measured in seconds must be filed under "running at risk" with a signature attached.

docs.title: Case 5 (Aero Engine): The Low-Amplitude Indications of 2016 (full card)
docs.text:
av-006.

When and where: 20 February 2021, departure from Denver International at 13:04 local time, failure in the climb at 12,500 feet at 13:09, return and landing at 13:28, about 24 minutes from takeoff to touchdown (the flight was bound for Honolulu); the failure occurred above Broomfield, Colorado. The inspection that matters happened in April 2016, at the Pratt & Whitney overhaul shop (NTSB pp. 19–20).

What and who: United Airlines flight 328, a Boeing 777-222 (N772UA, manufactured September 1995, 400 seats, maximum takeoff weight 545,000 pounds), with two Pratt & Whitney PW4077 engines rated at 77,000 pounds of thrust each. The right engine was manufactured in 1995 and installed on the aircraft in August 2016; its most recent inspection before the event was a continuing airworthiness inspection on 16 January 2021, with airframe total time 96,814.41 hours (NTSB p.9). The maintenance program was United's FAA-approved engine maintenance program, built on the Pratt & Whitney PW4000 112-inch maintenance planning document (NTSB p.19). Fan blade overhaul was done at the manufacturer's overhaul shop and included fluorescent penetrant inspection, visual inspection and thermal acoustic imaging (TAI) (NTSB p.19).

What they were doing: The aircraft was climbing at 12,500 feet at about 280 knots, with moderate turbulence forecast between 13,000 and 23,000 feet, and the crew increased thrust to shorten the time in it. Five to seven seconds after the thrust increase, the cockpit voice recorder captured a thump; the flight data recorder showed an uncommanded shutdown of the right engine, followed by a fire warning (NTSB p.6). The engine had accumulated 2,979 cycles and 12,384 hours since overhaul, and 15,262 cycles and 81,768 hours since new (NTSB p.9). The blade that failed was number 19, fractured transversely across the full span at the root platform plane (NTSB p.14). That blade had been through two overhauls, one in 2014 and one in 2016; the April 2016 TAI left two low-amplitude indications on the record (NTSB pp. 19–20). The overhaul interval in force at the time was 6,500 cycles (NTSB p.19). The blade failed at less than half the interval, and the next TAI was scheduled at 6,500 cycles (NTSB p.3). TAI works like this. The blade airfoil is coated with a thermally radiative paint, a transducer at the root vibrates the whole blade, the faying surfaces on either side of a crack rub at high frequency and generate heat, an infrared camera reads the temperature signature at the surface, and software amplifies it for an inspector to interpret (NTSB p.19). Inspectors do meet suspicious indications and have to judge whether a real crack or a benign cause produced them, the benign ones being paint debonding at the surface or sand trapped in the internal cavity, neither of which justifies removing the blade (NTSB pp. 19–20).

The decision point: ① April 2016, the overhaul shop, the TAI interpretation. The software flagged two low-amplitude indications on the convex side, in the mid-chord flowpath region, and both fell inside the fatigue origin area that later fractured. The inspector classified them as extraneous, judging them to come from camera sensor noise or from loose particles inside the cavity (NTSB p.20). Under nondestructive inspection procedure NDIP 1065, then in force, an indication of that amplitude required one of two actions: strip the coating, re-spray and run a second TAI, or escalate the ambiguous indication to a team review. The report states that "there was no evidence that either of these reviews occurred", and the blade was released for continued service (NTSB p.3, p.20). The interpretation left one word behind, extraneous, and no second opinion (NTSB p.20).

② 13 February 2018: another PW4077 on a United 777-222, over the Pacific, released a fan blade in the same way, NTSB case DCA18IA092. NDIP 1065 then went through revisions B, C and D, which added process controls and sharpened the illustrations of acceptable and unacceptable indications (NTSB p.20). The same passage records that after the 2018 event the April 2016 thermal data were pulled for review, that "the reviewers accepted the previous interpretation", and that the blade stayed in service (NTSB p.20).

③ The 6,500-cycle overhaul interval itself. The figure comes from the manufacturer's maintenance planning document, applies uniformly to PW4000 112-inch stage 1 fan blades, and was executed through United's maintenance program with FAA approval; NTSB lists the manufacturer's insufficient inspection interval frequency among the contributing causes (NTSB p.4, p.19). After the event the TAI interval went from 6,500 cycles to 1,000, one sixth of what it had been (NTSB p.4).

What was visible then: The hierarchy of the maintenance program: United's engine maintenance program approved by the FAA, resting on the PW4000 112-inch maintenance planning document, under which a blade continues in service as long as it passes the prescribed inspections (NTSB p.19); this set of blades had been overhauled in 2014 and again in 2016, both at the manufacturer's shop (NTSB p.19). The April 2016 TAI images, and the two low-amplitude indications the software flagged on its own (NTSB p.20). The NDIP 1065 criteria then in force, under which an ambiguous indication is either redone or escalated to a team review (NTSB p.20). The cycle counts for that blade since new and since overhaul, and the 6,500-cycle interval set by the maintenance planning document. The work cards from the 2014 and 2016 overhauls, covering fluorescent penetrant, visual and TAI, with April 2016 the second shop visit at which this set of blades received TAI. The procedure requiring that an indication an inspector cannot clearly interpret be referred, with the images and the blade, to a process engineer (NTSB p.20). Information that became available later: the fracture originated on the internal cavity radius surface about 6.6 inches above the blade root and grew from 0.063 inch to 0.199 inch over about 3,150 cycles of stable low-cycle fatigue; the two low-amplitude indications sat "very close" to that origin, and the report concludes they "most likely" are the images of the initiating fatigue crack (NTSB p.18, p.20). Two manufacturing reasons for the short blade life also only hold after metallurgical analysis: carbon contamination on the cavity surface accounts for about two thirds of the total difference, and a contour discontinuity left by machining for about one third, the latter raising local steady stress by 30% and cutting fatigue life by 50% (NTSB p.4, pp. 18–19).

Stop here. Decide before you turn the page.

You are in that seat now, with the materials above in front of you.

  1. What would you do? Write the action, not "pay more attention".
  2. Which item here are you most likely to miss, and why does it look unimportant?
  3. If you may set one checkpoint, when is it and what does it check?

What happened: At 13:09 the fan blade fractured across its full span. The inlet cowl lip, the fan cowl support beam and thrust reverser components separated, and debris fell over about 40 acres that included a park and a residential area; one vehicle and one house were damaged, and the 239 people on board were unhurt, as was everyone on the ground (NTSB p.1, p.7). Blade 18, next to 19, fractured about 25 inches above the platform with overload features; the remaining blades were intact but their tips were bent against the direction of rotation (NTSB p.14). The fire warning came seconds after the fracture, and both fire bottles discharged without putting the fire out. K-flange bolts failed under the high dynamic loads, hot compressed air escaped and ignited leaking high-pressure fuel, and the lower thrust reverser strut area burned through about 6 to 9 minutes after the fracture, while the airworthiness requirement for that area is at least 15 minutes of fire resistance (NTSB pp. 2–3). The fire had a second, independent path: the engine-driven hydraulic pump supply shutoff valve did not close as commanded because of silicone grease contamination on the motor brushes and commutator, and hydraulic fluid leaked into the engine compartment and fed the fire (NTSB p.3). Certification standards do not allow the inlet cowl and fan cowl to separate when a blade is released. Boeing changed the inlet cowl structure, adding metal to raise strength and ductility, and the FAA mandated the change by airworthiness directives 2022-06-10 and 2022-06-11 (NTSB pp. 1–2). Back to the three questions. The most common answer is "re-test the signal", but the problem here was not a reading that drifted. It was two indications that nobody chased. The item most easily missed is the number 6,500, because it decided that between April 2016 and the failure there would be no mandatory second look. The third question lands on the filing. The noise explanation could stand, but the entry belonged in "remediation by date" with a review deadline, and what it got was a one-time closure (NTSB p.3, p.20).

Options ruled out: Strip the coating and re-spray for a second TAI. NDIP 1065 says so; it was not done (NTSB p.20). Escalate the ambiguous indication to a team review. NDIP 1065 says so; it was not done (NTSB p.20). Treat the indication as a suspected crack and remove the blade. No record shows it was considered. Register the indication as a trackable item with a re-check required before the next overhaul. The NDIP of the time offered two paths only, redo and escalate, with no tracking tier (NTSB p.20). Shorten the inspection interval for this blade type. After the 2018 event only the procedure document changed and the interval stayed where it was, until airworthiness directive 2022-06-09 on 15 April 2022 moved TAI from 6,500 cycles to 1,000 (NTSB p.4, p.20). Screen the fleet for the manufacturing anomaly. Pratt & Whitney moved to a dedicated clean argon system in 1997, the failed blade was hot-formed in 1994, and no screening aimed at pre-1997 blades appears (NTSB p.19).

Early signals: ① April 2016: the software flagged two low-amplitude indications, both inside the crack origin area (NTSB p.20). Suppression reason: judged to be camera noise or cavity particles, a "known benign cause". ② 13 February 2018: a full-span fracture on an engine of the same type (NTSB p.20). Suppression reason: handled as a procedure revision, which changed the interpretation text and not this engine's record; the 2016 images were pulled and the original call was upheld. ③ The first PW4000 fan blade separation came in 2010, when about 50% of the airfoil came away; 2018 brought one full-span fracture; this event is the fourth of its type (NTSB p.2). Suppression reason: each handled as its own case, and the four never merged into a trend. ④ From the first confirmed cracked blade in December 2004 to 31 January 2023, 17 blades were confirmed cracked, 7 of them found by TAI, 1 visually and 9 by the new ultrasonic inspection (NTSB p.21). Suppression reason: found meant replaced, and the count never entered the interval assessment. ⑤ Two on the manufacturing side, cavity surface carbon contamination and contour discontinuity (NTSB pp. 18–19). Suppression reason: part of the manufacturer's process history, outside the operator's inspection scope.

The point of escalation: After the fracture of another PW4077 on 13 February 2018, the thermal data from April 2016 were pulled out for review, the reviewers accepted the original interpretation, and the blade stayed in service (NTSB p.20; the report gives no date for the re-review itself). The engine that fractured in 2018 was of the same type, also a PW4077, also on a United 777-222 (NTSB p.20). After that step the same images had been read twice with the same result. The only chance left to open the question was the 6,500-cycle overhaul, and the blade broke at 2,979 cycles before reaching it (NTSB p.3, p.19).

Failure chain: Technical layer: a fatigue crack initiated on the internal cavity radius of blade 19 and grew stably from 0.063 inch to 0.199 inch over about 3,150 cycles, then the blade separated across its full span; the blade's own life was short because of carbon contamination and the contour discontinuity (NTSB p.18). The growth rate from detectable size to through-wall thickness was relatively stable and predictable across this fracture and the earlier ones, because the initiation sites were all at the surface (NTSB p.4). The fan case did contain the blade fragments, but the displacement wave from the impact deflected the case into the fan cowl hinge, and the damage moved out into the nacelle (NTSB p.1). Damage also reached the nacelle by a second route: the inlet cowl and aft bulkhead of the event engine were carbon-fiber honeycomb sandwich, and simulation showed it could not dissipate a blade release the way the aluminum cowl used in certification testing could. Predicted displacement for the 2018 event was 0.55 inch, past the sandwich's compressive rupture strain, while the aluminum certification article was predicted at 0.47 inch with only local yielding (NTSB pp. 20–21). Organizational layer: two low-amplitude indications filed as extraneous, with the second TAI or team review that the procedure required never happening and no record of why (NTSB p.3, p.20); a 6,500-cycle interval that did not match the blade's actual life, named by NTSB in its probable cause as insufficient inspection interval frequency (NTSB p.4). Incentive layer: a second TAI means stripping and re-spraying and consumes overhaul hours, and a shorter interval means more inspections across the fleet. Both costs land in the current period, and the crack risk lands five years out (NTSB pp. 20–21). NTSB's findings read "scheduled maintenance inspections: inspection inadequate" and "organizational issues: manufacturer equipment design" (NTSB p.5). The break sits in the organizational layer, where a filing action turned an entry the procedure said needed a re-check into a one-time closure.

Minimum counterfactual: April 2016: run the second TAI that NDIP 1065 specifies on those two low-amplitude indications, after stripping and re-spraying. One action. The procedure existed, the equipment existed, the criteria existed, and NTSB's words are that the blade "should have" received a second TAI or a team review (NTSB p.3, p.20). At the stable growth rate of 3,150 cycles, there was at least one chance to see it within five years.

Outcome and sources: Nobody died. The inlet cowl and fan cowl support beam separated, the nacelle burned, and property on the ground was damaged. The FAA issued emergency airworthiness directive 2021-05-51, grounding every 777-200 and 777-300 powered by PW4000 112-inch engines; from 15 April 2022 TAI runs every 1,000 cycles and ultrasonic inspection every 275 cycles (NTSB p.4, p.21); Pratt & Whitney's service bulletin also required an immediate fleet-wide TAI, with the new ultrasonic inspection covering three high-risk areas (NTSB p.21). NTSB's probable cause: fatigue failure of the right engine fan blade, with the blade inspection's failure to identify low-level crack indications and the manufacturer's insufficient inspection interval frequency as contributing factors (NTSB p.4). Primary source: NTSB, Aviation Investigation Final Report DCA21FA085, published 7 September 2023, link at Appendix B av-006.

Where this sits against the mechanism: No relaxation in this case was pushed in bad faith, and no explanation in it was absurd. The whole work of the mechanism was done by one default action, explain and close. The opening against it is not a better class of explanation. It is Device 1's rule that every entry carry one of three states.

docs.title: Case 6 (Nuclear Power): Tagging With No Verification (condensed)
docs.text:
nu-002. Unit 3 of the Gravelines nuclear plant, France. The ASNR event notification (October 2026, this book read the page): a tagging error disabled an existing compensatory measure, the affected equipment was unavailable for 7 hours 45 minutes, and the event was rated INES 1. Tagging is one of the most frequent routine actions on a site: performed several times a day, with no consequences for years, its execution carried by custom. From this chapter's angle the decision point is the verification step after the tag is applied. No second pair of eyes checks the correspondence between the tag and the compensatory measure, and the error walks into an undefended interval. Minimum counterfactual: make independent verification mandatory once tagging is complete. Primary source: ASNR, 2026, link at Appendix B nu-002.

Set the six cases side by side and the common structure appears. None of them lacked a procedure. Spaceflight had a classification clause, chemicals had an SCBA response clause, aviation had established inspection intervals, finance had an alert handling process, nuclear power had a tagging system. What all six lacked is the same thing: a mechanism that forces the procedure and reality to meet. Foam came off, alarms sounded, signals arrived, alerts piled up, tags were hung, and none of those meetings produced a review action, because the entry's status, the alarm's calibration and the signal's handling had already supplied the answer "no further thought needed". Normalization is that "no further thought needed" accumulating item by item in the archive. The signal list and the defenses in the two sections that follow are aimed entirely at that accumulation.

One more observation belongs at the end of the case set. In all six cases the procedure text was in place before the event, and a paper compliance check would have looked at it and seen nothing. A checklist verifies that a procedure exists. The three-state register verifies that the procedure met reality. Separating those two jobs is the first operational distinction this chapter offers.

docs.title: 11.4 What Can Be Seen Earliest
docs.text:
Weak signals, each with the reason usually used to push it aside. The list runs from earliest to latest.

  1. The register of same-class deviations is missing, or every entry in it carries the status "explained". The reason it is pushed aside: "we have already dealt with that."
  2. The number of anomaly reports falls while the number of problems raised at the front line stays the same. Reason: "safety is improving." (A falling report count is more likely to mean the reporters gave up.)
  3. The wording of an inspection standard or an acceptance clause is rewritten from "must" to "in principle". Reason: "for workability."
  4. "We did it this way before" enters meeting minutes for the first time, as a basis for a decision. Reason: "respect for practical experience."
  5. A request to relax a limit, an interval or a threshold comes from the user, and the review is carried out by the user's usual collaborator. Reason: "standards should fit reality."
  6. A newcomer's question about existing practice is answered with a statement of custom rather than a statement of grounds. Reason: "old hands training newcomers is the best training there is."
  7. The same problem has two or more formal explanations in circulation, and they do not cite each other. Reason: "a difference of wording, nothing more."
  8. "No consequence so far" is used as safety evidence for the first time, rather than as a statement that the data are insufficient. Reason: "let the results speak."

Signal 8 deserves its own paragraph. It marks the fully formed stage. By the time it appears, the mechanism's output is a system of argument with "nothing happened" as its evidence, and any later challenge has to refute that system before it reaches the facts. Most misuse of black swan rhetoric (Chapter 41) grows on this foundation.

Put the eight signals back against the cases in this chapter and their landing points show. Signal 1, a missing register or one where everything reads "explained", lands on fi-013: the independent test had already written the alert backlog up as a finding, and the entry never moved into a remediation status. Signal 4, "we did it this way before" written into minutes, lands on mi-001: the STS-113 review formally recorded the foam loss flight rationale as safe to fly (CAIB p.126). Signal 5, an application by the user reviewed by a collaborator, lands on av-034: the lubrication and end-play check intervals were extended on the company's application with FAA approval, on a single information source (NTSB AAR-02/01, executive summary p.4). Signal 8, absence of consequence used as safety evidence, lands in two places at once. In mi-001 it is twenty years of foam loss without a catastrophe read as the system working, and the per-flight table at CAIB p.124 is the ledger of that argument. In av-006 it is every normal inspection result read as support for the explanation, once the anomaly had been explained and closed.

There is an order of use worth writing down. Check the register first, then talk to people. Half the eight signals (1, 3, 5 and 8) can be confirmed from the register alone; the other half need interviews and site observation. Run it the other way round and the interviewee's "explained" narrative arrives first and explains away the fork that was sitting in plain sight on the register. The order of the audit is itself part of the defense.

Who runs the audit matters too. The best candidates often sit outside the organization chart: internal audit, a third-party assessor, or a newcomer less than six months in post. What those three share is the absence of stock memory about the "explained" archive. They ask the questions that a stock reader has stopped asking. That also explains why the same register gets quieter the older the organization is: every reader has already accepted the "explained" entries. The list of questions a newcomer raises in the first year is usually the best index of what the register actually contains.

docs.title: 11.5 How to Prevent It
docs.text:
The four devices share one principle: take the filing action out of the hands of the explanation and give it to the register and the signature.

Device 1, the three-state deviation register. An entry may carry one of three statuses only: eliminated (with evidence of elimination), remediation by date (with a date and an owner), running at risk (with a risk assessment and a signature). A fourth status, "explained", is prohibited. Explanations may go in the remarks field, but the status must land in one of the three. Device 1 in Chapter 8 is the same register used in an escalation setting.

Device 2, margin quantified. Any statement that "there is still margin" must be written as a number together with its data source, and the source may not be the consequence-free history itself. Evidence for hypothesis B cannot be used to prove hypothesis A. A margin statement with no numeric source counts as no margin.

Device 3, the exposure audit. Every running-at-risk item carries two numbers: the current exposure count, and the exposure increment added by each release. The audit has one question. Is the operation of this deviation a finite exposure that we authorized, or an infinite one? This is the register form of the installment-type irreversibility in Chapter 7.

Device 4, two signatures for any relaxation. Approval to relax a standard, extend an interval or waive an inspection requires two signatures: the head of the requesting party, and a representative of the risk-bearing party who has no interest in the deviation and whose appraisal is not affected by current output. The FAA approval in the Alaska 261 case could not act as independent gatekeeping because its information source was single. The two-signature rule pins the information source down: the material required for approval must include inspection or test records from outside the user.

The weak signals of normalization share one cross-industry property. None of them needs technical expertise to see. All of them need a register. An auditor with no industry experience who is handed a deviation register can count the share of entries marked "explained" and make a reliable judgment about how far the mechanism has run. Defending against normalization therefore does not require industry experts. It requires an honest register and someone willing to read it.

The signature requirements across the four devices add up like this. The register is maintained by a safety engineer, not a production engineer. Margin figures are written by the user's engineer and reviewed by the safety engineer. Exposure increment reports go directly to the technical director. Relaxation approvals carry the signature of both the user and the risk-bearing party. What the four roles share is the absence of any interest in current output, and that is the organizational base the whole defense stands on.

Each device has one most direct application in the cases of this chapter. Device 1 on fi-013: on the day the independent test report arrives, the alert backlog entry must land in one of the three states; on the facts it can only go to "remediation by date", with a date and an owner attached, and the quarterly audit after that looks at one thing only, whether this entry has closed. Device 2 on av-034: a statement in an extension request that lubrication remains adequate must carry a measured jackscrew lubrication condition and measured end play; without the measurement the request returns automatically. Device 3 on av-006: had the 2016 anomaly been registered as "remediation by date", the entry would have rolled into every inspection with a review deadline attached, and the blade that broke in 2021 would have had several chances to be looked at again. Device 4 on mi-001: had the STS-113 review run on two signatures, the second pen signing the safe-to-fly rationale would have had to come from a party with no interest in the launch schedule. CAIB calls that review a "key decision" (p.126), which shows how completely the second pen was missing.

None of the four devices can be installed once the drift has matured. Registers, numbers, audits and second signatures are slow variables, and they work only if the organization configures them during the consequence-free period. Install them as the consequence approaches and the mechanism has already passed into the routine phase; what the defenses then face is the whole "explained" archive. That is why these items belong in a standing budget rather than in a special remediation project. Slow variables need a standing carrier.

The failure modes of the four devices are worth naming, because each one has a dignified way to die. The three-state register dies when a "remediation by date" comes due and nobody asks: the entry rolls over, and after a few rolls it is indistinguishable from "explained". Margin quantification dies in the degradation of its source: the first figure is measured, the second is copied from the first, the third is an experienced guess, and nobody notices that the wording in the source column has moved from "measured" to "estimated". The exposure audit dies at the manual step: logging the increment depends on the releaser jotting it down, and when things get busy only the total keeps rising. The two-signature rule dies in the relationalization of the second pen: the risk-bearing representative sits with the user long enough that the independent check before signing shrinks into a courtesy initial. One antidote covers all four. Each quarter, draw one closed entry at random and re-audit it backwards, publish the draw, and put the result on the first page of the next quarterly report. Devices do not stay honest by themselves. Someone has to poke them.

docs.title: 11.6 Boundaries with Adjacent Mechanisms
docs.text:
Against practical drift (Chapter 15). Drift describes the fork between practice and rule, which is the question of how the work is done. Normalization describes the fork being redefined as acceptable, which is the question of how it is ruled on. Drift can run without normalization: drift that a register is watching stays in "remediation by date". Normalization usually takes drift as its raw material, but it needs the second step, explain and file. Where both are present, find the fork point first, then find out who filed it.

Against margin erosion (Chapter 25). Eating into margin is an active reduction, a cut, and it leaves a register to check. Normalization is an interpretive slide, carried out in speech, and it usually leaves no register. A single approval to extend an interval is both a cut and a normalization, and the carrier decides which chapter owns it. What lands on paper belongs to Chapter 25. What lives in the tone of a meeting and in custom belongs here.

Against narrative before evidence (Chapter 13). Narrative operates after the conclusion is public: commitments made outward, sides taken inward. Normalization operates in the internal archive layer: filing, classification. The two usually appear as a pair, normalization inside first and narrative outside afterwards. The discriminator is audience. An action filed inward belongs to this chapter. An action promised outward belongs to Chapter 13.

docs.title: 11.7 Five Self-Checks
docs.text:
1. In your process's deviation register, how many entries carry the status "explained"? Pick one. Is its deviation still running now?
  2. Where were you the last time you said "we have always done it this way"? Was there anything in the other person's objection that deserved a register entry?
  3. Of the relaxations you have signed (intervals, limits, waivers), how many rested on material that included records from outside the user?
  4. In your organization, who can state the current cumulative exposure count for a given running-at-risk item? If nobody can, in whose hands is the exposure accumulating?
  5. Take a customary practice you have run for more than two years with no consequence, and walk it through criteria ①②③. If all three hit, what does this chapter call it?

docs.title: Chapter 12 Goal Displacement; Goodhart's Law
docs.text: What this chapter covers: how a metric quietly takes the place of the goal it stands for; three criteria for telling that the mechanism has started; the shape it takes on the ground in four domains; eight weak signals; and four lines of defence for whoever sets a metric. When to turn back: when you are about to set a new KPI, when a polished metrics report lands on your desk, or when something "looks good in the numbers but feels wrong". Estimated reading time: 50 minutes.

docs.title: 12.1 What It Is
docs.text:
A metric is always a stand-in. The goals that matter, safety, health, whether anyone actually learned the material, whether trust is real, whether the assets are worth what the books say, are for the most part not measurable in themselves. So the organization measures something countable and installs it where the goal should be. Goal displacement names the moment the substitute takes over: management attention settles on the countable quantity, the organization starts optimizing the quantity itself, and the optimizing stops improving the thing the quantity stood for. Goodhart's law in its common form: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Charles Goodhart said something narrower in a 1975 lecture at the Bank of England; the familiar sentence was written by Marilyn Strathern ('Improving ratings', European Review 5(3): 305–321, 1997, bibliographic record verified via Crossref). The causal direction is the part people get wrong. The measure did not degrade. The behaviour around it changed.

Three criteria tell you the mechanism is running. Any one of them is enough:

  1. Optimizing actions appear that are specific to the assessed quantity, and their cost is spent on the number rather than on the work.
  2. Those actions do not improve the goal behind the number, and may consume it.
  3. Someone who says so pays for it, in the appraisal or in the meeting.

The three are not parallel. Criterion 1 is the starting point. Any assessed metric attracts optimizing actions; that is rational behaviour, not a disease. Criterion 2 is the watershed, the point where the optimizing action comes off the goal it was supposed to serve. Criterion 3 is the freeze: the separation has been noticed, the noticer has been punished, and the organization's priorities are now on the record. How fast the three arrive depends on how quickly the distance between metric and goal becomes visible. The greater the distance and the later the consequence, the longer the window in which nothing appears to be wrong.

The occasion of Goodhart's observation is worth recording. In 1975, discussing monetary aggregate targets at the Bank of England, he put the point as a piece of regulatory shop talk: any observed statistical regularity will tend to collapse once pressure is placed on it for control purposes. Strathern later rewrote it into the sentence everyone cites. The difference between the two versions usually gets skipped. The original describes a game between the controller and the controlled: the controlled party knows what is being watched and moves real behaviour outside the observation point. The familiar version describes a divergence between measure and goal. This book uses both, because both are happening inside organizations. The first is gameplay, what the assessed do to the metric. The second is drift, what the metric's meaning does to itself over time. Of the four defences in section 12.5, the first two watch gameplay and the last two watch drift.

Donald Campbell, a sociologist, said the same thing a few years before Goodhart, from the angle of educational testing: the more any quantitative indicator is used for social decision-making, the more it will be subject to corruption pressures and the more it will distort and corrupt the social processes it is meant to monitor. Read together, the two sentences show the mechanism ignoring systems and industries alike. Wherever measurement is used to decide people or resources, pressure appears. You do not need to remember who said it first. What you need is the conditional both sentences share: used for decisions. A metric on a wall that nobody looks at provokes no behaviour at all. The entire force of goal displacement comes from the metric's wiring to appraisal, budget and personnel.

Take a metric apart and it has four parts: the definition (what counts as one overdue loan), the sample (which projects enter the rating), the frequency (how often it is measured), and the presentation (what type size, which page). Each part has room for play, and the professionalism of the play rises through that list. Changing the presentation is the crudest move: bad numbers set in small type. Changing the frequency sits in the middle, measuring before the review and stopping after it. Changing the sample is subtler, moving the projects that are about to fail out of the sample. Changing the definition is the professional's move, redefining the start date of "overdue". Goodhart effects do not arrive in step across the four. Play with the presentation and the goal may be unharmed. Play with the definition and the link between metric and goal is usually already severed. Defences can be laid out to match: presentation and frequency get caught by paired indicators (Device 2), sample and definition get stopped by the register of definitions (Device 4). Case 1 in this chapter works on the definition layer, on whether a rescinded loan counts as a loss, and that is why it is misleading rather than merely aggressive accounting. A cut at the definition layer carries a disclosure obligation with it.

Readers of a metrics report come in three kinds, and each has a different failure to guard against. The first reads the trend: the curve is up, so things are fine. Trend is the reading most easily polluted, because gameplay manufactures trends by nature. The second reads rank, its position against peers. Rank moves an organization's attention from the goal to the competition, and goal displacement evolves fastest in a ranking context, because once gameplay spreads among peers, not playing becomes the way to fall behind. The third reads anomalies, caring only about moments of significant deviation. The anomaly reader is the least sensitive to mature gameplay, since mature gameplay keeps numbers inside the normal band and misses every anomaly detector by design. No one reading is sufficient. The workable combination is to have the three readers exchange question lists on a schedule: the trend reader asking the anomaly reader "what has felt wrong lately" usually gets further than any audit report.

One step down the same four parts yields three conditions a metric needs at the moment it is set. It must be reconcilable: the metric's data has to reconcile against an independent source, system logs against reports, an external list against an internal ledger. A metric that will not reconcile has no standing to enter an appraisal. It needs an outside comparison: a comparison series, not collected by the assessed party, designated in advance as the reference for when the metric distorts. And its definition history must be on file: changes to definition, sample, frequency and presentation kept in one place, so the metric can be replayed through time. A metric failing all three can still be used, though only for self-reference, never for appraisal or resource allocation. These three are the four defences projected onto the moment of setting: reconcilability is Device 2, the outside comparison is Device 3, the definition history is Device 4.

docs.title: 12.2 How It Grows
docs.text:
Three conditions generate it.

Condition one: the goal cannot be measured directly. A goal that can be counted needs no proxy. "How many conforming parts did we build this month" can be counted. "How good were this month's decisions" needs a stand-in, say the share of decisions revisited six months later. The further the proxy sits from the real goal, the more room the optimization has to skew.

Condition two: the levels above read only numbers. Management's bandwidth is finite, and reporting across levels compresses into numbers by default (Chapter 16 gives that attenuation its quantitative form). Once the basis of a decision converges on a single number, optimizing that number is the rational choice at every desk in the organization. Nobody breaks a rule. Every level completes what it is assessed on. That is Chapter 17's misaligned incentives arriving as a technical implementation.

Condition three: the assessment cycle is shorter than the real cycle. Loan quality runs in years and the report in quarters. Student growth runs in years and the exam in semesters. Where the two cycles differ, the metric and the goal come apart, because inside the gap the return on optimizing the proxy is certain while the cost of exposure is deferred.

A fourth condition is implicit and usually skipped: the neutral appearance of a number. Numbers do not look like interests. They look like facts. When two departments fight over a metric's definition, the scene presents as a technical discussion, how the sample is drawn, what sits in the denominator, and nobody has to say out loud that this decides their year-end rating. The neutral surface keeps optimizing actions out of moral view. Nobody believes they are cheating; everyone is "getting the data right". This is why goal displacement is more common than open fraud. Fraud needs someone willing to lie. Metric optimization needs ordinary people doing their jobs carefully.

The spread of gameplay is the fastest step in the whole mechanism. Once an optimizing move has been invented, it needs no training to travel. The month-end push, the selective filing, the trick of moving an ugly quantity out of the denominator: these move with rotation, with meetings where one department watches another, with the annual reinterpretation of the assessment. Gameplay is the fastest-travelling knowledge in organizational memory, because it is the only knowledge that pays immediately on acquisition. Design the defence on the assumption that gameplay exists. A metrics system designed in the hope that nobody finds the game fails on the day it goes live.

Condition three has a seasonal form that deserves its own paragraph. Gameplay rises and falls with the assessment calendar. The month-end push, the quarter-end surge, the fiscal-year-end adjustment of a definition are direct projections of the cycle gap. That shape hands an auditor a time window. Check at the trough of the calendar and you see normal operations; check at the peak and you see the game. Sampling points for a metric audit should therefore be secret and random, with the days around the assessment date always included. The practice is cheap. What it encodes is the insight that gameplay is periodic, and only a periodic method will see it.

Composite metrics need a warning of their own. Weighting several sub-metrics into one score is the standard answer to thin management bandwidth, and it widens both entrances to this mechanism at once. Weights are the top layer of the definition: whoever sets them sets the cheapest path for gameplay, and weight changes usually go unlogged, with a lower bar than changing a definition. Composition also hides compensation. A deteriorating sub-metric can be fully cancelled by a flattering one, so an improving safety score may come precisely from a falling count of reported incidents. Three minimum requirements apply to any composite. Weight changes go through the definition register. Every sub-metric is displayed separately. Any jump in the composite can be traced to a named sub-metric. A composite that fails all three is worse to read than its parts.

docs.title: Case 1 (Finance): The Delinquent Loans That Were Moved Off the Books
docs.text:
fi-001.

When and where: May 2019 (the special handling programme launched), August 2019 (the delinquency programme launched), through February 2021 (the end of the period the SEC treats as relevant), with rescissions in practice continuing to the end of August 2020. Orlando, Florida, at the headquarters of Travel + Leisure Co. The complaint was filed on 30 September 2026 in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida, case No. 26-cv-62760, with Litigation Release No. 26657 issued the same day.

What and who: Travel + Leisure Co., formerly Wyndham Destinations, Inc., renamed after its spin-off from Wyndham Worldwide on 31 May 2018 and renamed again to its present name on 17 February 2021, the largest timeshare company in the world, with 797,000 owners and more than 280 resort clubs; since 2014 the company has financed more than half of its timeshare sales itself every year (complaint p.6). The posts involved: senior management responsible for finance and investor relations, who confirmed the rescission target count every quarter (p.10); the sales rescission committee, which reviewed rescission requests beyond the statutory rescission period; the operations departments that executed the rescission coding; and the financial planning staff who built the monthly forecast.

What they were doing: Through late 2018, third-party exit companies grew active, charging owners to terminate contracts after the statutory deadline and often advising them to stop paying outright (complaint p.7). The company tightened rescission approvals and rejected any customer suspected of working with such a firm (p.7). The outcome ran against the tightening. In the first quarter of 2019 delinquency and the loan loss provision rate jumped together, the provision rate rising from 20.4% in the same quarter a year earlier to 22.5% (p.8). On the 1 May 2019 first-quarter earnings call, five analysts pressed on that metric in succession, and management promised on the spot to stop the year-over-year increase and hold the 2019 provision rate at its 2018 level (p.8). That same month the company started a special handling programme that pulled delinquent or defaulted timeshare loans out of the portfolio and rescinded them in bulk, known internally by three names: "late-stage delinquency" rescission, the "late-stage rescission programme", and the "owner care programme" (pp. 9–10). In August it added a further delinquency programme, covering loans tied to customer complaints (p.2). The special handling programme screened the longest delinquency first, ahead of foreclosure (p.10). New rescissions stopped at the end of August 2020 because timeshare sales were falling under the pandemic (p.11). Every loan rescinded in the relevant period fell outside the statutory rescission period, five to seven days in the states concerned, which the company called "late-stage rescission" internally (p.3, p.9).

The decision point:

  1. 1 May 2019, the first-quarter earnings call. Management turned the loan loss provision rate into a public commitment: stop the year-over-year increase, hold the 2019 guidance (complaint p.8). One quarter earlier the metric had appeared in the results at 22.5% against 20.4% (p.8). That sentence converted an internal metric into a public target, and every quarterly number after it had to answer to the sentence.

  2. From May 2019, the monthly forecast. The company wrote a target count into the monthly forecast for how many delinquent or defaulted loans had to be rescinded, calculated backwards: to reach the provision guidance, a given number of defaults had to leave the portfolio (p.10). Senior management confirmed the target count at least once a quarter and then directed the relevant departments to execute it (p.10). The calculation had two inputs, the 2019 guidance holding level with 2018 and the internal 2020 target the company had set for itself (p.10). The carrier was a forecast spreadsheet rather than a set of minutes, and the spreadsheet ran from May 2019 to the end of 2020 (p.10). It carried counts and balances. It carried no loan identities, and no comparison column for what the rate would have been without the rescissions.

  3. August 2019, the weekly meeting of the sales rescission committee. The delinquency programme compiled delinquent and defaulted loans into a "delinquency agenda" spreadsheet circulated before the meeting; every line on it was approved, with no review loan by loan (p.11). The committee's original function was to judge, one loan at a time, whether a request to rescind past the deadline should stand. After this step the judgement was a signature on a whole table. The committee still met and the agenda still went out.

  4. 30 October 2019 to February 2021, seven periodic reports and five calls. The carriers the complaint lists: the MD&A of the 10-Q for the five quarters from 30 September 2019 to 30 September 2020; the quarterly results releases issued with 8-Ks; the MD&A of the 10-K for fiscal 2019 and fiscal 2020; and the calls for the third and fourth quarters of 2019, the third and fourth quarters of 2020, and the full year 2019 (p.12). The improvement was attributed to the customer care phone line, to getting owners back on vacation, to tighter underwriting, and to improvements in the booking system (p.13).

What was visible then: the loan-by-loan list of rescinded loans, with days delinquent and default status; the thresholds were the company's own, 30 days delinquent and 120 days in default (complaint p.7). The list held one particular class of entry: loans coded for rescission within a few days of the 120-day mark (p.10). The delinquency programme's table was grouped by customer complaint, with rescission decoupled from whether a complaint had merit and tied only to delinquency status (p.2, p.11). The "delinquency agenda" spreadsheet and the committee's weekly agenda (p.11). The rescission target count inside the monthly forecast (p.10). The record of the five analysts' questions on 1 May 2019 (p.8). Analyst reports forwarded by investor relations, one stating that the provision rate had a material impact on the stock price (p.8). 10-Q and 8-K drafts, the provisioning worksheets, the call scripts (pp. 12–13). The company's self-set 2020 internal target sat in the same forecast set (p.10). One piece of background was also of record: investors and analysts treated the metric as a barometer of whether the company could hold off the third-party exit firms (pp. 11–12), and the company knew it (p.8). At the end of every quarter these materials sat on the same desk at the same time, a sheet saying how many loans had to go and a draft saying how much the metric had improved. One thing was already blank. The company forecast the effect of rescissions on the metric and never tracked the programme's actual effect on the financial statements (p.2, p.10), so nothing on that desk could answer how much of the improvement came from the rescissions. What became knowable only afterwards: the totals of more than 2,900 loans, roughly $77 million in balance, of which about $34 million was in default (p.3); the age profile, 44% over one year and 11% over two years (p.9); and the fact that in several quarters the programme moved both metrics by more than 5% (p.12).

Stop here. Decide before you turn the page.

You are in that seat now, with the materials above in front of you.

  1. What would you do? Write the action, not "pay more attention".
  2. Which item here are you most likely to miss, and why does it look unimportant?
  3. If you may set one checkpoint, when is it and what does it check?

What happened: on 30 September 2026 the SEC sued and settled on the same day. The company neither admitted nor denied the allegations, accepted a permanent injunction (Securities Act of 1933, 17(a)(2) and (a)(3); Exchange Act of 1934, 13(a) and 12b-20, 13a-1, 13a-11, 13a-13), and paid a civil penalty of $975,000 (Litigation Release 26657). The relevant period, October 2019 to February 2021, is not the same stretch as the rescission operations, May 2019 to December 2020, and the complaint writes the two apart (p.1, p.3). During the relevant period the company raised about $1.65 billion through three private note issuances, and issued $13.5 million of common stock for a 2019 acquisition and $96.8 million of common stock for an employee stock purchase plan (complaint p.14). Against the three questions: the most common answer to the first is "have legal confirm whether the right to rescind is available". The right was available. The complaint alleges non-disclosure, and the rescissions themselves are not among the charges (pp. 1–3), so that answer is a layer off the mark: an available right and a disclosable fact are two different things in the complaint (p.3). The item most easily missed under the second question is the monthly forecast, the only sheet in the case that carries the target and the action in one place. The checkpoint for the third belongs at the first monthly forecast review in May 2019: check whether that line of numbers has a disclosure treatment attached to it, and who signs the sheet.

Options ruled out: disclose both programmes and their quantitative effect on the provision metric (not done; every allegation in the complaint rests on this omission, complaint pp. 1–3). Leave the rescinded loans in the portfolio and provision for them on the normal basis (not chosen; rescission and charge-off happened in the same place, leaving no trace in the accounts, p.3). Have the sales rescission committee review the delinquency agenda loan by loan (the process existed; the delinquency programme routed around it, p.11). Track the programme's actual effect on the financial statements (not done, p.2, p.10). Use the absolute balance of delinquent loans as the external pair for the provision rate (not done; no disclosure in the complaint sets balance beside rate). Confine rescissions to the statutory five-to-seven-day window in each state (not done; every loan rescinded in the relevant period was past it, p.3). Obtain a written opinion from an outside auditor on the accounting for the rescissions (the complaint does not mention any review opinion from an outside auditor). The complaint records behaviour, not the reasons these options were turned down. What can be checked is that none of them happened, and that each carried a cost legible on paper.

Early signals:

  1. 1 May 2019: five analysts pressed on the provision rate in the same call (complaint p.8). The promise to stop the rise and hold guidance absorbed the pressure, and nobody asked how the company meant to stop it.

  2. First quarter 2019: the provision rate at 22.5%, up two percentage points year over year, a move the company itself acknowledged as meaningful to investors (p.8). It was treated as an operating problem and handled by operating means: take loans out of the portfolio, rather than say in the disclosure that the definition had changed.

  3. An analyst report forwarded by investor relations, stating that the provision rate had a material impact on the stock price (p.8). The sentence entered the internal channel and never entered a filed document.

  4. August 2019: the "delinquency agenda" went live and rescission moved from loan-by-loan approval to approval of a whole table (p.11). The simplification looked like an efficiency gain. It is the only written procedural change in the case, and after it no document records why any individual loan was approved.

  5. The age of the rescinded loans, 44% over one year and 11% over two (p.9). These were old accounts. Rescinding them did not improve the quality of new sales; it changed the numerator and the denominator of the current period.

Of the five, the earliest predates the programme's launch and the latest appears in the results release of 30 October 2019 (p.8, p.13).

The point of escalation: the "delinquency agenda" mechanism of August 2019. Judgement loan by loan was replaced by a signature on the whole table, and after that no rescission carried a record of whether it should have been approved (complaint p.11). In the same quarter the first rescissions entered the 10-Q and 8-K treatment. By 26 February 2020 the company described the full-year provision rate as "flat" and claimed it had met guidance (p.13), and the fiscal 2019 10-K carried the same treatment into the annual report (p.12). On 6 May 2020 it said the metric "would have been" the fourth consecutive quarter of year-over-year improvement (p.13). By then the rescission had moved from an operating action to a component of the compliance story. From May 2019 to at least December 2020 the cumulative count passed 2,900 (p.3), with the target reset on the forecast every quarter (p.10): each quarter stacked new rescissions on the last, and backing out would have meant unwinding a stack of spreadsheets. After new rescissions stopped in August 2020, the disclosure did not change its story; the fiscal 2020 10-K and the full-year call still described improvement (p.12). Reversing course would have required restating three years of external statements at once. That is what "cannot turn back" looks like in practice.

Failure chain:

Technical layer: the definition. Whether a loan counted as on the books, and whether it stayed in the portfolio after rescission, was decided by the company's own accounting treatment. Once coded as rescinded, revenue, provision already taken and default balance reversed together, and the accounts read as though the loan had never existed (complaint p.3). The delinquency and default thresholds were the company's own as well, 30 days and 120 days (p.7), and rescissions clustered just short of 120 days (p.10).

Organizational layer: the target count went from the monthly forecast to the executing departments; the delinquency programme bypassed the sales rescission committee's review loan by loan; and the company did not track the programme's actual effect, so no internal document could answer how much of the improvement came from rescissions (p.2, p.10). Of the three layers, only the accounting entries kept a complete record, and what they record is "never happened". What can reconstruct the history is the rescission coding table and the monthly forecast, and neither enters the disclosure process.

Incentive layer: the provision rate sat in external guidance, analysts called it material to the share price, and the May 2019 call turned it into a commitment (p.8). In the same period the third-party exit firms were pushing defaults up, and the company itself used the metric as a barometer of whether it was holding them off (p.7).

At the boundary: the definition layer supplied the action, move it out; the incentive layer supplied the number, how many. The two met in one row of the monthly forecast. The break is that row. It was an operating target and a disclosure treatment at once, and only the first was written into a process.

Minimum counterfactual: on the first monthly forecast of May 2019, add a line reading "provision rate if this month's rescinded loans had stayed in the portfolio", and carry that line unchanged into the MD&A of that quarter's 10-Q. One action, in the month the programme started, needing no luck: the company was already forecasting the effect (complaint p.2), and the data sat on the same sheet. The 10-Q is prepared every quarter and the MD&A written every quarter, so the line has a landing place already built (p.12). The cost is one line of text and one more signature. The line does not stop the rescissions. It makes "what is the metric after the rescissions" into a question somebody has to answer. Answer it and a disclosure obligation exists; leave it blank and the sheet carries a gap. The gatekeeper is the existing quarterly reporting sequence, and no new committee is needed. Fixed afterwards instead, the job becomes a comparison series across five quarters (p.12): one line turns into a restatement, and the restatement then has to explain why the first five quarters said nothing.

Outcome and sources: civil penalty of $975,000, permanent injunction, neither admit nor deny (Litigation Release No. 26657 / AAER-4603, 30 September 2026). Two primary documents, issued the same day, checking each other: SEC v. Travel + Leisure Co., No. 26-cv-62760 (S.D. Fla.), Complaint, 17 pages, paragraphs 1–50, giving fact and page number paragraph by paragraph; and Litigation Release No. 26657, giving the penalties and the list of statutes, a web page without pagination, cited by release number. The two agree on the penalty amount, the list of statutes and the period of conduct (LR text; complaint ¶1, ¶9). The enforcement release page carries a download link to the complaint PDF, which closes the citation chain. Link at Appendix B, fi-001.

Case 1 also repays a separate look at the width of five reporting quarters. At the end of the first quarter the rescission could still be explained as an accounting judgement. Repeated at the end of the second, the judgement was anchored by precedent. By the third quarter it was beginning to look like a process. By the fifth it was a routine component of the financial statements, and apart from the few people who knew all the facts, nobody in the organization still treated it as a decision. That is the temporal shape of this mechanism: the sense of doing something decays with repetition while the undisclosed amount accumulates. The point where the two curves open away from each other is where outside intervention is worth most and an internal brake costs most. A hard rule follows from it. Any accounting choice that affects external disclosure, executed for two consecutive reporting periods, triggers a mandatory outside review, with reviewers including a party from outside the auditors and the disclosure committee. Five quarters of width could have been compressed into half a quarter of argument.

docs.title: Case 2 (Public policy): Ratings That Drifted from Actual Risk
docs.text:
po-003.

When and where: March 2025 (the baseline month for the risk documents) and April 2025 (the month of the rating snapshot), with the report published on 7 October 2026. Washington, D.C. Policy and definitions were set by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Federal CIO office, the dashboard at itdashboard.gov was operated by the General Services Administration (GSA), and the ratings were submitted by the CIOs of 12 agencies.

What and who: OMB's Federal CIO office, which set the rating definitions and the update frequency; GSA's Office of Government-Wide Policy (OGP), which took over dashboard operations in March 2022 (GAO-27-108416 p.5) and handled user feedback, prioritization and releases on three-week iterations (p.25); the CIOs of 12 agencies, together with the CPIC teams, investment managers, project health assessment groups and chief technology officer offices that drafted ratings for them (pp. 43–48); and GAO, which ran the comparison at the request of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform (p.1).

What they were doing: OMB launched the federal IT dashboard in June 2009. In December 2014 FITARA wrote into law that agency CIOs classify major IT investments by risk, and required that an investment rated high risk for four consecutive quarters trigger a review (GAO-27-108416 p.1, p.9). The dashboard covered nearly 600 investments across 26 agencies (p.5). The page carried three classes of rating. Cost and schedule were computed by formula, with a variance of 30% or more red, 10% or more but under 30% yellow, and under 10% green (p.6). The CIO rating was filled in by a person on a 1 to 5 scale, 1 the highest risk and 5 the lowest, then mapped onto five colours (p.6). OMB supplied six factors: risk management, requirements management, contractor oversight, historical performance, human capital, and other (p.7, table 1). Update frequency was not specified in A-11 Section 55 of 25 July 2024; only the version of 29 August 2025 says "at least quarterly" (p.7, footnotes 16 and 17). GAO began the audit in April 2025, took the April snapshot, and used the March risk registers for comparison, on the reasoning that ratings in the month an audit opens are least disturbed by the audit (pp. 3–4). The report summary offers an example: a system already behind schedule that still displays a stale "low risk" on the page may never receive the review it needs (report summary page). In 2015 GAO had already placed IT acquisition and operations management on the federal high-risk list, partly on the reliability of dashboard data (p.2).

The decision point:

  1. April 2025, 53 ratings posted to the dashboard. How each was calculated differed by agency. Treasury added three scores (the operational risk rating, the bureau CIO's integer from 1 to 5, and the CPIC chair's judgement), passed the sum through an overall rating formula and rounded to an integer (p.46, table 17). Education scored the six factors, combined them into a raw score from 1 to 5, and had the CIO review it; where the CIO believed other factors applied, the "CIO discretionary rating" became the final rating outright (p.44). HHS used a self-assessment followed by a "discretionary risk rating and rationale" from the CIO (p.45). GSA ignored risk scores and set a level when any three of eight criteria were met (p.47). VA used a quantified score, 1 point per category out of 5 (p.47). In that same month GSA rated Login.gov "medium" and GAO rated it "high": three risks in the investment's risk register averaged "elevated", and technical issues plus an incomplete data protection implementation remained open as of March 2025 (p.20).
