The mortality denominators are harder still: about 20% die before reaching any hospital, and about 50% die before reaching a specialist centre (§5.2.2).

The patient's path ran alongside those numbers. A 54-year-old man, ordinarily fit; at 18:00, while weightlifting, sudden retrosternal pain with nausea and a sense of impending death, the pain moving to between the shoulder blades; at 18:40 he rang NHS 111, the call handler followed the script and asked about the character of the pain (tearing, severe), he answered that it was severe and lasted no more than 15 to 20 seconds, then agreed to the description crushing, aching, band-like, and took 300 mg of aspirin (§2.2–2.8). At 19:04 an ambulance arrived, crewed principally by a first-year student paramedic (PM2); blood pressure in the two arms measured 127/61 and 114/84 mmHg, 19 minutes apart, with "no signs of abdominal aortic aneurysm" recorded; the ECG showed occasional ectopics and an enlarged cardiac shadow (§2.10–2.11). The crew agreed that everything pointed to muscle pain and conveyed him anyway, to rule out a myocardial infarction (§2.12). He reached AH1 at 20:04, was booked in at 20:12, and sat in the waiting area (§2.13).

The decision point: four irreversible moments.

Moment one, 20:46 to 20:49, triage. EDS entered "chest pain" into the electronic Manchester Triage System (MTS) with observations of pulse 128, blood pressure 108/47 and respiratory rate 17; the system assigned category 2 on a five-level scale, where category 2 requires assessment within 10 minutes, and she signed at 20:49 (§2.17, Appendix 1). After signing he was sent back to the waiting area and entered a cubicle only at about 21:00 (Appendix 1). The MTS chest pain flowchart contains no "aortic pain" discriminator, which is precisely what HSIB's first recommendation set out to add (recommendation R/2020/066). The carrier is the electronic triage record, and the signatory is EDS.

Moment two, 21:21, the first assessment entry. EDACP picked the case up from the electronic board, and triage gave no verbal handover (§2.22). After examining the patient he wrote "looks well", with a differential of musculoskeletal chest pain, chest infection and cardiac chest pain; a Wells score of 0, not suggestive of pulmonary embolism; neither palpation nor movement reproduced the pain, and he was unhappy with his own diagnosis, because the pain would not reproduce and the patient said he felt unwell (§2.23–2.26). The carrier is the 21:21 electronic record. He then handed the patient to FY2, verbally, and ended his shift.

Moment three, 22:48, FY2's entry. The chest X-ray was read as no obvious abnormality, troponin T was 30 ng/l against a normal range of 0–14, and D-dimer was above 3000 ng/ml against a normal range of 0–230; the record notes only negative findings for venous thromboembolism, and the abnormal values were written down without being taken anywhere (§2.28–2.29). At 22:58 an addendum records discomfort, back pain and vomiting (§2.34). Radiology reported the chest X-ray the following day as an enlarged cardiac shadow with a widened mediastinum (§2.28).

Moment four, 23:27, the imaging request. Once MSpR took over she said she had seen a similar case before, suspected dissection, asked for blood pressure in both arms (123 and 100 mmHg, a difference of 23) and requested an emergency CTA at 23:27 (§2.35–2.38); the scan ran at 00:01 and was formally reported at 01:06 as Stanford type A, with the tear extending to the right common iliac artery and the right brachiocephalic artery (§2.42–2.44).

What was visible then: there is no cockpit here, only consulting rooms, and what could be seen was just as limited. The list follows the order of contact.

At the triage desk, 20:46 to 20:49, EDS had the MTS electronic flowchart in front of her: select the presenting complaint "chest pain", click through the items, and the system assigns a category by algorithm. The evidence she could enter was four observations, pulse 128, blood pressure 108/47, respiratory rate 17 and a pain score of 1/10, together with the patient's colour and posture as he sat in the waiting area. She remembered afterwards that she had looked once and thought he was in a bad way (§2.15). The system returned category 2, to be seen within 10 minutes (§2.17). The flowchart has no aortic pain line, and no line anywhere asks for a comparison of the two arms.

At the assessment desk, 21:20 to 21:26, EDACP had no handover, only the triage note and the electronic board (§2.22). What he could see was a complete history (weightlifting, sudden onset, 10 to 15 seconds, left arm and back, a sense of impending death), one examination (neither palpation nor movement reproduced the pain), a Wells score table calculated at 0, and the patient's appearance: looks well, no pain face, no sign of circulatory failure (§2.23–2.24). Of those four, the last was the most persuasive and the least reliable, because it fitted muscle strain after exercise exactly.

At the handover desk, 22:48, FY2 had three new items, the chest X-ray she read as no obvious abnormality, troponin T of 30 and a D-dimer above 3000 (§2.28). She could also see how the patient had changed over three hours: walking about, pale, sweating, vomiting, back pain (§2.33–2.34). Her seniority was second year since qualifying and less than 1 week in the department (§2.27). Of the three new items, two were abnormal and one had been judged normal, and the report records that her entry carried only the negative findings that excluded venous thromboembolism (§2.29).

At the consultant's end, around 22:50, EMC was the most senior person in the department with 18 years behind him. His information on this case amounted to one telephone call: he went to the bedside, the patient was in the toilet, and the examination did not happen (§2.30). His advice to FY2 was that abnormal blood results were worth worrying about, that she should speak to the medical registrar, and that admission might be needed (§2.31).

At the diagnostic end, 23:00 to 23:27, MSpR held the most unusual information of the five: one precedent, a similar case seen before, plus systolic pressures of 123 and 100, a difference of 23 mmHg (§2.35–2.37). In nurse training that figure is taught as significant once it passes 20, and it did not reach the record until 23:21.

What was learned only afterwards: the chest X-ray had in fact shown an enlarged cardiac shadow and a widened mediastinum (§2.28); the CTA showed the dissection extending along most of the aorta to the right common iliac artery and the right brachiocephalic artery (§2.44); scored retrospectively on the ADD-RS he would have had 1 point (§4.9.5.3); and his four hours in the department were shorter than the national mean of 4 to 5 hours (§4.8.7.4).

Stop point:

Stop here. Decide before you turn the page.

  1. What would you do? Write the action, not "pay more attention".
  2. Which item here are you most likely to miss, and why does it look unimportant?
  3. If you may set one checkpoint, when is it and what does it check?

What happened: at 01:57 the transfer vehicle left. About 12 minutes later breathing stopped and the heart stopped soon after; the vehicle diverted to another hospital to collect blood, and on arrival received a message from the regional centre to come immediately, so it turned around without the patient ever leaving the vehicle. The regional centre said that after 32 minutes of CPR nothing more could be done, and death was declared at 03:15 (§2.62–2.67). HSIB made two recommendations: that the Manchester Triage international reference group add "aortic pain" to MTS as a chest pain discriminator, and that the Royal College of Emergency Medicine and the Royal College of Radiologists jointly develop, deploy and evaluate a national recognition and management pathway (R/2020/066, R/2020/067). There were also three safety observations and one safety action, under which NHS Pathways amended the telephone triage algorithm in version 18 (§5.2). Back to the three questions. The most common answer to the first is "more training for emergency doctors". Six people were involved in this case and three of them had more than ten years of experience, while the one who recognized the dissection was in his sixth year since qualifying with a single precedent for this disease to draw on. Training cannot change an exposure of 15 cases a year per person. The item most often missed under the second question is the denominator of 1 in 400 chest pain patients: it says that practice does not make perfect with this disease, and every judgment that the patient looked well was made on that premise. The checkpoint for the third question belongs within 10 minutes of triage: calculate the ADD-RS once, and arrange imaging at 1 point or above.

Options ruled out: adding "aortic pain" to the triage table. The MTS chest pain table had no such item at the time; HSIB made the recommendation in January 2020, and the Manchester Triage international reference group replied on 17 April 2020 that it had been added to four flowcharts, chest pain, back pain, abdominal pain and collapse, with a definition attached ("sudden onset, presenting with severe abdominal or chest pain, which may be sharp, stabbing or tearing..."). A national diagnostic pathway. None existed at the time; the report recommended that the two colleges develop one, and the reply said the working group planned to publish guidance in 2021. Routine CTA for all chest and back pain. The report discusses the cost of that route, which requires balancing detection rate against CTA capacity, and it therefore argues for screening first with a score and D-dimer (§4.9.5.2, 4.9.6.3). The ADD-RS itself. The tool was published and available as an online calculator at the time, and the report's retrospective calculation for this case comes to 1 point (§4.9.5.3); it was never outside the options, it simply went unused. Controlling blood pressure and heart rate before transfer. The report records that this was considered and given up, to save time and to avoid needing a doctor in the vehicle (§5.1.13), while the ICU consultant argued against delay on the grounds that the disease carries a 10% hourly risk of death (§2.50).

Early signals: ① about 2,500 cases a year nationally, with about half dying before reaching a specialist centre (§5.2.2); the reason it was waved through: the disease is intrinsically lethal, and the deaths were booked to the disease. ② neither palpation nor movement reproduced the pain (§2.24); the reason it was waved through: musculoskeletal pain stayed in the differential, and the report describes a tendency not to abandon that diagnosis while exploring more serious cardiopulmonary problems (§5.1.5). ③ troponin of 30 and a D-dimer above 3000 (§2.28); the reason it was waved through: the record said only that venous thromboembolism was excluded, and the abnormal values were never converted into a next action (§2.29). ④ the chest X-ray judged as no obvious abnormality, then read the next day as an enlarged cardiac shadow and a widened mediastinum (§2.28); the reason it was waved through: the on-shift read is taken as the conclusion, and a chest X-ray is a poor test for dissection in any case (§5.1.8). ⑤ the patient walking about the department, saying he felt unwell, vomiting, with back pain (§2.33–2.34); the reason it was waved through: observations and oxygen saturation were normal and he looked well (§2.23, 2.29). ⑥ triaged as category 2 yet placed in the low-dependency area (§5.1.4); the reason it was waved through: category 2 sets a 10-minute assessment time and says nothing about the level of monitoring.

The point of escalation: 22:48. Three lines lay in the record at the same moment, pain that would not reproduce, a D-dimer above 3000 and a troponin of 30, and what FY2 wrote was a direction, chase the bloods and possibly home, resting on a chest X-ray reported as no obvious abnormality (§2.27–2.28). Before that moment, anyone taking the case over who laid the three side by side would have moved toward imaging; after it, the record carried a direction written as exclusion, and later people followed the exclusion.

From that moment to the CTA request at 23:27 lie 39 minutes, and the report records what filled them: EMC advised referral to medicine, FY2 called the medical registrar, went back to the patient and found him vomiting, and the patient's partner also agreed that something was wrong (§2.31–2.32). The force that overturned the direction came from the eye at the bedside, not from the record. The carrier is the 22:48 electronic entry; the step needed nobody's approval and got none. EDACP had gone off shift, and EMC was consulted by telephone only after this point (§2.26, 2.31).

Failure chain: technical layer: the symptoms are non-specific, since 85% of patients have sudden severe chest or back pain that can be described as tearing or as crushing (§1.9); diagnosis rests on imaging alone (§5.2.6); a chest X-ray is unsuited to detecting dissection (§5.1.8); and a dissection can extend from the ascending aorta to the iliac arteries within hours (§2.44). Organizational layer: the triage table lacks an aortic pain item, and the existence of recommendation R/2020/066 is the evidence; triage to assessment had no verbal handover (§2.22); for three hours the patient was carried by EDACP and FY2 while the consultant never examined him (§5.1.6); between diagnosis and transfer there is a further wait of more than an hour for the formal report (§5.1.11); and nationally there is no usable incidence and outcome data, which the report makes a safety observation in its own right (O/2020/053). Incentive layer: chest pain is about 5% of emergency attendances and about 45% of it is cardiac, so throughput and priority sit on that side; the report records that junior doctors may be reluctant to request a CTA out of concern about its availability (§4.9.4.5); and transfer time pressure overrode treatment before transfer (§2.50, §5.1.13). All three layers broke at once. The interface: the epidemiological data is in the report and the checklist line is not, and no post existed to translate data into a line. The two recommendations were meant to create that post, and at the time it had no name.

Minimum counterfactual: before 22:48, calculate the ADD-RS for this patient. The score covers three classes of high-risk feature, predisposing conditions, pain features and examination features, on a 0 to 3 scale; here it comes to 1 point retrospectively, which in the published literature means considering a CTA, even without a D-dimer result at the time (§4.9.5.3). One action, taken in any minute after triage, needing no luck: the score is published with an online calculator, and it measures three facts that can be asked for, a family history of Marfan syndrome or aortic disease, whether the pain was sudden and severe, and an absent pulse or an inter-arm blood pressure difference. Nor does it require the person calculating to trust his own intuition, because the score moves "should I suspect this" from feeling to counting.

Outcome and sources: the patient died at 03:15 the following day, and HSIB issued 2 recommendations, 3 safety observations and 1 safety action (§5.2). One of the report's central findings is blunt: during his time in the department the patient never saw a consultant, and was seen by an advanced care practitioner and an FY2 (§5.1.6). Another is equally blunt: a four-hour delay from arrival to diagnosis is not unusual with this disease (§5.1.10). The inability to produce national incidence and outcome data is a gap the investigation admits to itself (O/2020/053), and the gap is the physical evidence for criterion 2, since a system that cannot count its own numerator is in no position to give its judges feedback. Primary source: HSIB, Delayed recognition of acute aortic dissection, 23 January 2020, link at Appendix B me-015 (archived link, grade A−); this card cites by paragraph number (§) because the report is web-only and sets no page numbers.

The ending of case one is worth a second look, specifically the pilot's self-report that he suspected the runway width illusion had affected him. That report is rare twice over. Survivors of an illusion usually attribute the incident to the wind, the light or how they were feeling that day, and blaming an illusion amounts to admitting that perception itself was wrong, an admission that needs the help of evidence afterwards. Rarer still is blaming the illusion rather than the state of the day, because it shows that the man completed the upgrade from "I made an error" to "human perception errs on narrow runways". After that upgrade the experience remains usable, carrying a note on its range of validity from then on. That is what Device 2 is meant to produce in quantity: experts who know where their confidence comes from, with the confidence intact and the annotation attached.

docs.title: Case 6 (Healthcare): Judgment Alone on Non-Specific Symptoms (Condensed)
docs.text:
me-013. Diagnosis of pulmonary embolism (PE) in an English emergency department. The HSIB investigation report (March 2022, archive snapshot read for this book) drew on 14 serious incident reports, concluded that individual judgment under non-specific symptoms lacked decision support, and made 3 recommendations. The symptom spectrum of PE (breathlessness, chest pain, a fast heart rate) overlaps several common diagnoses, and clinical intuition carried far too much of the sorting load: the judge's experience holds few PE samples (criterion 3), the symptom environment is irregular (criterion 1), and the outcome feedback is broken (criterion 2). The decision point is the moment of individual judgment with no decision support tool present. Minimum counterfactual: embed a standardised scoring tool in the emergency pathway and make its use mandatory. Primary source: HSIB, Clinical decision making: diagnosis of pulmonary embolism in emergency departments, 2022, link at Appendix B me-013 (grade A−).

A number in case two deserves a paragraph of its own: 11 administrative controls. The figure looks generous, and taken apart item by item it is all the same material, procedures, training and prompts, every one of them resting on people having stable attention and stable recognition. Dense stacking of administrative controls has a name in this chapter's frame: transferring the safety load of the system onto people, and then treating human reliability as an input assumption. When the CSB lists reliance on administrative controls as one of its two major safety issues, an investigating body is confirming that the transfer failed, and confirming it at its own level of authority. A conversion rule for the reader: for each administrative control you meet, ask once what guarantees its effectiveness. If the answer comes back to human attention, the control's real weight in that system is close to zero, unless the system has also provided a backup for attention, in the form of interlocks, fault tolerance or a forced wait.

docs.title: Case 7 (Aviation): Three Minutes in Cloud for a VFR Pilot (Condensed)
docs.text:
av-014. A Cessna FR 182 on a private ferry flight, February 2021, Germany. The BFU investigation report (2022, read for this book): the flight entered cloud under visual flight rules, spatial disorientation led to loss of control, the aircraft struck the ground, and the pilot was killed. The environmental premise of visual flight is continuous visual reference to the ground, and cloud removes that premise entirely; with no ground reference the pilot's felt sense of attitude returns systematically wrong answers. This is criterion 1 in its most complete form, since the environment changes wholesale the instant the aircraft enters cloud. The decision point is the decision to keep flying visually in front of a gap in the cloud. Minimum counterfactual: check the route forecast during pre-flight planning, and set a personal line of "no going visual". Primary source: BFU, 2022, link at Appendix B av-014.

Cases five to seven push each of the three criteria to an extreme. Case five is the textbook for criteria 2 and 3, broken feedback plus a low-frequency scenario. Case six is a triple failure zone, with all three criteria satisfied at once. Case seven is the instantaneous, full version of criterion 1, the environment replaced wholesale inside the second it takes to enter cloud. The value of the criteria lies in how they combine. One criterion on its own can be negotiated, through training, experience or remediation; when two or more hold together, any confidence in intuition should be counted as zero until an instrument or a checklist is in place.

Combining them has a second use, which is profiling posts. Run the three criteria over each key judgment post in your organization and most will land in a stable combination. Scheduling and triage posts, with high judgment frequency and fast feedback, usually lack only the environmental upkeep of criterion 1. Purchasing and investment posts, with slow feedback, lack criterion 2. Emergency and safety posts, with once-in-a-lifetime events, lack criterion 3. The combination type decides the combination of defences: a post short of criterion 1 gets a change trigger, short of criterion 2 gets records and review, short of criterion 3 gets instruments and checklists. Draw that map across the whole organization and the budget for intuition defences has an ordering for the first time, with the posts carrying the heaviest combination going first.

The chain rescue in case three deserves a second look as a domain general rule. Serial deaths during rescue from an oxygen-deficient confined space are a recurring category in marine investigation: the first man goes down to the environment, and the second and third go down to the rescue instinct. The mechanism is at its purest in this category. Saving people is one of the strongest social instincts humans have, it is almost always right in open air, and it is fed by dense feedback in a stable environment; a confined space turns the environment's single critical parameter, oxygen, into something that cannot be sensed, and the whole premise of the intuition is pulled away while the surface scene does not change at all. The MAIB report attributes the three deaths to the act of entering the enclosed space itself, which amounts to a ruling: in this setting the correct action is a veto on intuition, and the equipment (a gas detector) and the procedure (call first, then enter) exist to carry out that veto.

The under-deduction in case four reads differently under each criterion. The old calculation table is the specimen for path two, a conversion convention carried through years of tender offers. The new instrument form, short call options appearing in the consideration of an offer, is the rule change of path three, and the internal procedure does not define how the new form converts, which is the system admitting at its own level that judgment is still running on the old library. FINRA's penalty, $80,000 of which $40,000 went to FINRA, is small in scale; the value of the case is its generality. Financial instruments are innovated at a pace that runs steadily ahead of the pace at which internal definitions are updated, and the gap between the two paces is the interval in which this class of case is generated. Device 3's new column on the change form, the list of existing experience affected, is designed for exactly that interval: the day a new position type enters the system, the review of the conversion definition should be triggered.

The risk that went into the PHA with no independent guarantee mechanism deserves one further step along the administrative-control audit. After all 11 controls have been asked what guarantees their effectiveness, most organizations' lists shrink to two or three lines, and what survives is the set of items that carry a genuine independent guarantee. The shrinking is not alarming. It makes the real water level of risk control visible for the first time. What follows visibility is the watershed: add engineering controls, which are expensive, slow and effective, or accept the level and write it into the risk assessment, which is cheap and honest. The worst choice is to leave the list untouched, because the gap between the paper water level and the real one is the stock of future accidents.

One organizational detail in case two is worth enlarging: an operator without experience was placed in an independent post on the grounds that he had completed standard training. That sentence quietly merges two concepts, training hours and intuition built. Standard training delivers explicit knowledge, the rules, the sequence, how to read a label; intuition needs repeated exposure in the environment plus feedback, and the two take construction periods an order of magnitude apart. Scheduling pressure looks only at the first, because the first has a certificate attached that can be checked. A corresponding check for the reader's own organization: in the roster for a key post, is the basis for working independently a certificate or a count of exposures? The first is the system's assumption, and the second is the system's reality.

docs.title: Case 4 (Finance): The Short Options Left Out of the Deduction (Condensed)
docs.text:
fi-012. Cowen and Company. The FINRA penalty of August 2026 (monthly summary PDF read for this book): in a partial tender offer the internal procedure did not define how 100,000 short call options should be converted into a net long position, the calculation followed the old convention, the firm over-reported by 150,000 shares, and the penalty was $80,000, of which $40,000 went to FINRA. The decision point is the moment the net long calculation met a new instrument form. Minimum counterfactual: the internal procedure triggers a review of the conversion definition automatically when a new position type is added. Primary source: FINRA, Disciplinary and Other FINRA Actions – October 2026, 2026, link at Appendix B fi-012.

What the four cases share is this: every judge was fully confident at the moment of judging, and the source of that confidence, visual experience, post common sense, the rescue instinct, the old calculation table, lay inside the range of criterion 1 or criterion 3. Recognizing a failure zone does not require doubting the judge's intelligence. It requires checking which environment the experience behind the judgment was formed in.

docs.title: 4 What Can Be Seen Earliest
docs.text:
Eight weak signals, each with the reason that usually waves it through.

  1. The reasoning behind a decision contains analogy rather than measurement ("this is much like that one back then"). Reason given: "experience is the fastest theory there is."
  2. The environment's rules, equipment or population changed recently, and the people in the key posts did not. Reason: "core competence is transferable."
  3. A veteran answers data in a meeting with seniority ("I have done this for twenty years"). Reason: "respect for practice."
  4. A class of decision has never had feedback: it was made, and nobody has ever checked whether it was right. Reason: "it has always run fine."
  5. Training hours get compressed on the grounds that the system will handle it. Reason: "efficiency." (Chapter 26 develops this.)
  6. A newcomer asks a basic question and the experts present answer vaguely. Reason: "the detail has gone; the direction I am certain of."
  7. The induction period for someone crossing domains is an order of magnitude shorter than the period their old domain took to build. Reason: "he was brought in to step straight in."
  8. The organization keeps no record of its expert judgment: the judgment was made, the basis was not written down, and afterwards nothing can be calibrated. Reason: "the business moves fast."

Items 4 and 8 together are the definition of calibration. No record means no feedback, no feedback means no calibration, and confidence without calibration is only temperament.

Put the eight signals back against this chapter's cases. Signal 1, analogy instead of measurement, maps onto case one, where the sense of when to flare is analogy in its fastest form. Signal 2, environment changed while the post did not, maps onto case two, where the new three-valve screen met an operator population that had not changed. Signal 3, seniority answering data, appears in case five in a variant: experience answering checklisting, with the checklist read as distrust of clinical judgment. Signal 4, decisions without feedback, maps onto case five, where the missed diagnosis killed the patient after transfer and the emergency department never heard about it. Signal 5, compressed training, maps onto case two, where administrative controls replaced depth of training. Signal 7, induction too short across domains, maps onto case two's new operator. Signal 8, unrecorded judgment, maps onto all of them, since the basis of an intuitive judgment cannot be reconstructed after the event.

Read by discovery cost, the eight signals have a reading peculiar to this chapter. Signals 1, 3 and 6 come by ear, in meetings and conversations. Signals 2, 5 and 7 come by eye, from the organization chart and the roster. Signals 4 and 8 come by checking records. A failure-zone audit is therefore a division of labour among three senses: hear the analogies and the seniority talk, see the mismatch between environment and people, check for the absence of feedback and records. The three correspond to a conversation audit, a post audit and an archive audit, and any one of them done alone covers a third of the ground.

The conversation audit has three opening questions for a reader who wants to start on Monday. Ask the expert: "if this judgment is wrong, when is the earliest you would know?" A judgment that cannot name a time has no feedback loop, and criterion 2 lights up. Ask the expert: "when did you last meet a case of this kind?" An answer of never puts the judgment under criterion 3, to be handled as a hypothesis awaiting verification. Ask the team: "if someone more junior made this judgment, how would he get it wrong?" The list of errors in the answer is the list of experience the judgment actually rests on, and the longer that list, the more exposed the judgment is to the failure zone. None of the three needs a tool. All three need a questioner who is not under seniority pressure.

The standard move in an archive audit is to sample judgments, not events. Draw a number of significant judgments at random from the past year and ask one thing about each: how much of the basis was recorded. Most organizations doing this for the first time come out with a glaring empty set, which is not a scandal but a starting point, since the empty set says the organization has no recording system for its judgment assets, and weak signal 8 has something to remediate at last. Sampling judgments reads cleaner than sampling events, because an event arrives with its own demand for attribution, while a judgment sits quietly inside the process and reflects the organization's real habits best.

docs.title: 5 How to Defend Against It
docs.text:
Device 1: an intuition admission form. Add one mandatory line to the review form for significant judgments: "Does the experience this judgment rests on hold in the current environment (rules, equipment, people)? What is the basis?" A judgment that cannot produce a basis is downgraded to a hypothesis awaiting verification, under the tiered release of Chapter 13. The cost is very low, one line. What it stops is the whole class of failure zones.

Device 2: convert intuition into a checklist. A veteran's intuition is an asset, so bring it out and write it as explicit check items, which lets newcomers benefit and lets the veteran be checked. The method is interview extraction: have the expert talk through what he is looking at while he works, and the fixation points recorded become the candidates for check items. Whatever will not go down on paper is marked as the non-reliable part and signed by the expert himself. The signature is the step that matters, because it turns "only tacitly known" from a disclaimer into a risk statement.

Device 3: environmental change triggers retraining. For every change of rules, equipment or interface, list the intuitions that depend on the old environment and assess item by item whether retraining is needed. The interface change in the Shell Monaca case and the instrument innovation in the Cowen case should both have triggered this step. The trigger's carrier is the change form: add a column reading "list of existing experience affected", to be filled in by whoever raises the change.

Device 4: give the failure zone an instrument. A four-gas detector for a confined space, approach aids for a narrow runway, automatic conversion for a net long position: inside a failure zone, replace recognition with measurement. The budget ordering rule is to start with scenes where criterion 1 holds, since failure there is the most complete.

Now put the four devices onto this chapter's cases. Device 1 on case one: add one mandatory line to the approach briefing, "how far is this runway's width from the usual one, and how does the flare reference change". One line, twenty seconds, and what it stops is the entire class of perceptual illusion. Device 2 on case two: ask an experienced operator to say aloud what he is distinguishing while he works the three-valve screen, and write the fixation points down as check items; whatever will not go down gets his signature, "not reliable here", and after that signature the system must be fitted with a physical interlock. Device 3 on case five: every revision of a differential checklist lists the existing judgment habits it affects, and the triage group's habits are compared against it item by item. Device 4 on case six: embed the scoring tool in the emergency system and make its use mandatory, moving the sorting from recognition to measurement.

The failure modes of the devices need writing down as well. The admission form dies of inflation in the answer to "what is the basis", since if anything counts as a basis then nothing was asked. The checklist dies when nobody maintains it after extraction, with the environment moving again and the list standing still, which is where Chapter 15's fork grows. Change-triggered retraining dies when the "experience affected" column stays empty all year. Instrumentation dies when the instrument's alarm gets turned down for the sake of good relations. The four deaths have a single common antidote: put device use into the audit, and have the auditor ask what the device last stopped, leaving aside the question of whether it exists at all. A device that has never stopped anything means either that the environment really is safe or that the device is already dead, and the audit's job is to tell those two apart.

Together the four devices point to one organizational document worth establishing, the intuition asset register. Each row records one significant intuition held by one expert: the environment in which it holds, the check items extracted from it, its failure conditions, and the date it was last reviewed. Maintenance costs little, one pass against the change forms each quarter, and the return is that the organization holds an inventory view of its judgment assets for the first time: whose intuition has been validated in which environment, whose intuition is owed an extraction, and which posts' judgments have no register at all. The intuition asset register belongs to the same family as Chapter 11's deviation ledger and Chapter 12's definition register, since all three turn key states that were scattered across individuals into entries that can be searched, reviewed and handed over.

The order in which the register gets built matters. Start with the posts that hold few people and heavy judgments, such as emergency command, release signatures and investment decisions, then cover the posts that hold many people and scattered judgments, such as front-line operation and review. Every row in the first group can correspond to a major consequence, while the value of the second group is the statistical view that coverage gives. Most organizations start with the second group because people are easier to organize, and the register comes out thick with the critical judgments still unrecorded. The first iron rule of the register is to order by magnitude of consequence, not by headcount.

docs.title: 6 Boundaries with Adjacent Mechanisms
docs.text:
Against extrapolating past the validated domain (Chapter 23): extrapolation carries a conclusion into a new environment, at the data layer, while this chapter carries the judge into a new environment, at the person layer. When a scene occupies both, check the person first, meaning his experience premises, and the conclusion second, meaning its validation boundary. Fixing the person is cheap and fixing the conclusion is expensive.

Against practical drift (Chapter 15): drift is the fork between practice and text, an organizational phenomenon, while the failure zone is one person's recognition capacity crossing its edge, an individual phenomenon. A whole crew can drift together; a failure zone shows up only in specific people. The reverse holds too, since individual intuition inside a drifting organization can stay perfectly precise, precisely executing a practice that has already left the text behind.

Against all the talk that surrounds expert confidence: this chapter has nothing against experience; what it opposes is experience overstepping. The test is always the three criteria rather than an attitude toward experts, which means neither deferring to them nor dismissing what they say because of who says it.

docs.title: 7 The Five Self-Checks
docs.text:
1. Do the two premises, environmental regularity and feedback quality, still hold for the judgment you rely on most? What was the last change to either?
  2. Whose data have you answered with "I have done this for twenty years"? Looking back, was that intuition or a failure zone?
  3. After your team's last environmental change (new system, new rules, new population), which pieces of old experience were reassessed? If there is no list at all, where did the reassessment happen?
  4. Which decisions in your post are once in a lifetime? What are they made with now, measurement or recognition?
  5. Can you write one veteran's intuition as a checklist? Pick one and try it. Will he sign "not reliable here" over the parts that will not go down?

docs.title: Chapter 15 Practical Drift (Snook)
docs.text:
What this chapter covers: how formal procedure and actual practice can diverge for years without producing a casualty; Scott Snook's drift model, its three activating criteria, four settings in the field, and the two-end alignment defence. When to turn back: when what training teaches no longer matches what the site does; before you write a new rule that "must be followed"; after an audit finds that practice and manual disagree. Estimated reading time: 50 minutes.

The hardest thing about spotting practical drift is that it produces no victims while it runs. Every crew works by a method it has worked out for itself, and the work gets done well. Every checklist is ticked as the procedure requires, and the ticks are all there. Studying the 1994 shootdown of a US Army Black Hawk by a friendly fighter, Scott Snook found the frightening shape of the structure: every link in that accident had been running in exactly the same way, every day, before it. He named the phenomenon practical drift. Organizations do not slide into chaos. They drift, each unit toward what is convenient for that unit.

docs.title: 15.1 What it is
docs.text:
Definition: practical drift is the gradual departure of actual practice from formal procedure, where the departure persists over a long period, nobody corrects it, and members of the organization come to regard the fork as normal. The departure is no sudden impulse toward risk. It is a local adaptation to real working conditions. The workload changed, the staffing changed, the tools changed, the manual did not, and reality grew a second method.

Three activating criteria. The mechanism has started if any one of them appears:

  1. Formal procedure and actual practice have diverged for a long time, and the divergence has a substantial history;
  2. The divergence is read as expertise: departing from the manual is treated as proof of professionalism;
  3. Nobody believes he is violating anything, because the rule is written in a form no one could follow.

The third criterion is the dividing line between drift and ordinary violation, and the reason drift's consequences run heavier. A violator knows what he is risking. A drifter does not, because the procedure he bypassed is missing from his risk model altogether.

Snook's book deserves two paragraphs of background, since they explain why a model drawn from military research is not confined to the military. In April 1994, in the northern Iraq no-fly zone, two US Air Force F-15 fighters shot down two US Army Black Hawk helicopters, and the United Nations personnel aboard were all killed. Snook's finding was that every unit taking part in that sortie, the fighter wing, the helicopter detachment, the air traffic control agency and the joint operations centre, was running on its own actual version of the mission; each version departed from the joint task regulation, and each departure had been happening daily for months without consequence. He pictured the organization as two ends of a drift: at one end the baseline practice written in the regulation, at the other the actual practice each unit executed. During a consequence-free stretch, nobody looks at the distance between the two ends.

That background also supplies a key property. Drift happens unit by unit. Each crew, each post, each station drifts on its own, at a speed and in a direction set by local working conditions; the organization holds no single drift quantity that can be read off, because drift keeps no central record. What an accident needs is only to string already-drifted units onto one event chain, and on the day they are strung together every unit is doing what it does on any other day. Snook called this the latent structure of drift: every site on the eve of a disaster is as calm as routine.

Three words need separating under this chapter's usage: deviation, violation, drift. A deviation is a one-off departure, archivable afterwards, the raw material of Chapter 11. A violation is a deliberate bypass of a rule the actor knows exists. Drift is the process by which the fork becomes the default, and the actor gradually loses any sense that the rule exists. The relation is progressive. A deviation is tolerated repeatedly and hardens into a convention; the convention settles into the site's normal way of working; the gap between the normal way and the rule is forgotten, and drift is complete. The best position for a defence line is between the first level and the second, which is where the three-state register for deviation ledgers does its work (Chapter 11, Device 1). The worst position is to start checking for violations after the third level, because by then you face a complete parallel rulebook, and punishing anyone you pick is a misjudgement.

The two-end alignment mentioned at the head of the chapter can now be stated properly. Snook's remedy is not a return to the regulation, since most regulations genuinely lag reality. His remedy is to align baseline and actual at both ends on a regular schedule: either amend the regulation until it can be executed in reality, or resource reality until it can execute the regulation as written. The operative word is regular. Alignment is a calibration act; drift is a continuous process; a single alignment does not stop the next drift. Alignment has to be mounted on the organizational calendar, twice a year and on any change, and become a standing operation the way instrument calibration is. Device 1 in section 15.5, the manual-reality comparison, is that alignment in institutional form.

docs.title: 15.2 How it grows
docs.text:
Four generating conditions, in structure, incentive, time and information.

The structural condition: rules are written by people who do not work the line, and they are written from the design state rather than the operating state. The incentive condition: following the book carries an immediate cost, while the cost of departing is delayed and probabilistic. The time condition: drift needs time, and every "this trip is special, simplify it once" leaves no record behind. The information condition: no comparison mechanism exists, so nobody measures the difference between manual and reality.

Then there is drift's arithmetic. A single departure is usually harmless, which is Chapter 9's point that one broken layer is a fault. The disaster form of drift is several fork points stacking in the same direction on one event chain.

Three features of the dynamics deserve adding.

Drift has a directional bias. It always drifts toward lower immediate cost. Pausing, cross-checking, waiting, reading back: each of these actions costs time now and pays off somewhere else, and the first cut of drift always lands here. To observe an organization's drift direction is to observe how it prices time.

Drift is contagious. A new member meets two demonstrations, the manual version and the site version, and the trainer will teach the site version, because that is the one that gets the job done. Drift therefore copies itself automatically through staff turnover, and every handover is an inoculation. Chapter 30's handover rupture connects to this chapter at exactly that point.

Drift self-organizes a shared understanding of when drifting is allowed. Crews form default terms among themselves: which steps may be dropped when it is busy, which may never be dropped. The understanding is never written down and is executed with fair consistency, and its existence is itself proof that drift is no error; it is the organization revising its rules through action. This is also where prevention gets hard. What you face is not a lapse of memory. It is a parallel rule system, running in fact.

Push the arithmetic one step further and the disaster form appears. Each fork point strung on an event chain passed every safety review on its own, because the object of review is the regulation, not the practice. A drifted organization therefore shows a particular compliance face: the paper system is complete, and the paper system has nothing to do with reality. Three of this chapter's four cases carry that face.

The relation between drift and audit needs its own warning. Routine audit is drift's incubator. The benchmark an audit compares against is a document, and the carrier it inspects is a document as well: records, signatures, ledgers. Drift grows precisely on the layer outside documents. A fully drifted practice can generate a complete set of passing audit evidence, because the drifted organization learned long ago to complete the paperwork. Case 9's working papers and Case 3's surgical checklist are both conforming output from that production line. Two conclusions follow. An organization whose audit finds zero differences is the one whose drift level most deserves suspicion. And audit method has to include site observation and shadow comparison, described in section 15.4; an audit that reads only documents is structurally blind to drift.

docs.title: 15.3 The pattern in four domains
docs.text: This section held four cases when it was first drafted (aviation, maritime, healthcare, construction) and holds nine after expansion; Cases 5 to 9 (aviation, maritime, nuclear, finance) were added. Nine cases cover the hosts drift commonly lives in: the seam between training and design, the seam between scheduling and the body, the seam between tagging and handover, the seam between checklist and pause, the seam between template and object.

docs.title: Case 1 (Aviation): The Logbook in Flight
docs.text:
Case ID: av-020.

When and where: 18:57 local time, 9 March 2023, mountainous terrain near the town of Franklin, Macon County, North Carolina, United States. The helicopter departed Murphy (5NC4) at 18:44 bound for Asheville (NC95), 13 minutes en route (NTSB ERA23LA147 p. 1, p. 4). The flight was at night, in Class G airspace, on a company VFR flight plan, with no air traffic control clearance (p. 4).

What and who: an EC135 P2+ helicopter, registration N558MT, manufactured in 2012, operated by Med-Trans Corporation (MED-TRANS CORPORATION, trading as LifeForce) under Part 135 on-demand air taxi, air medical, holding a Part 135 operating certificate (p. 3). Four people were aboard: one pilot and three passengers, one of whom the report mentions was a flight nurse. The pilot was 51, held a commercial certificate with airplane and helicopter ratings, 4,723 total flight hours, 1,867 on type; his last proficiency check was on 1 March 2023, and his second-class medical carried no limitations (p. 3). He flew single-pilot from the right seat (p. 3). Airframe total time was 6,067.7 hours at the AAIP inspection of 23 February 2023; the emergency locator transmitter was installed and did not activate (pp. 3, 4).

What they were doing: Before departure the pilot worked out the highest obstacle on the route himself, 6,100 ft, with several 5,000 to 5,500 ft peaks along it; he also calculated that the flight would run into the end of evening civil twilight (p. 1). Both calculations were his, and the report contains no second route analysis.

After takeoff he set the autopilot at 5,500 ft and levelled off (p. 1). He then reached for his night vision goggles and found them on the co-pilot's seat, lying under an aircraft logbook. He moved the logbook to the pilot's door pocket, "where it normally was kept" in the report's words, and inside that same movement decided to check the logbook's flight hours against the maintenance hours due (p. 1).

Once the check was under way he noticed the cloud base descending, reset the autopilot to 5,000 ft, and then "put his head back down" into the logbook (p. 1). The flight nurse in the rear asked for an updated arrival time. He looked up and saw the helicopter heading for a tree-covered peak. He pulled aft on the cyclic to climb, the tail boom struck several trees, the vertical stabiliser separated from the tail boom, and he put the helicopter down on a road (p. 1).

Thirteen minutes passed between takeoff and ground contact. In those thirteen minutes the cockpit held one person, and no second pair of eyes was watching the relative position of the altitude, the cloud base and that peak.

A word on the nature of this material. The report runs five pages, its factual section cites no recorded data from the aircraft, and the entire sequence comes from the pilot's statement and the site examination (pp. 1, 5). Whether the helicopter carried recording equipment, and of which kinds, is not stated in the report. Every moment on this card, the level-off, the moving of the logbook, the altitude change, the look up, has a single source. That is not thin reporting. It is the standing condition of this class of investigation when there is no recorder and no second crew member: the sequence can only be retold by the person who lived it, and what he retells is exactly how his attention was allocated at the time.

The decision point: three moments, and not one of them left a document.

Before 18:44 on 9 March, in cockpit preparation, the cruise altitude was set at 5,500 ft. The grounds were his own route data: highest obstacle 6,100 ft, several peaks between 5,000 and 5,500 ft (p. 1). That single choice fixed every margin that followed, because 5,500 ft is level with the highest of those peaks, which leaves zero tolerance. The choice had no paper carrier of the kind a weight and balance sheet provides; the report holds only the pilot's statement.

After takeoff, in the stowage that preceded donning the goggles, the logbook was on the co-pilot's seat with the goggles on top of it, instead of in the pilot's door pocket (p. 1). He moved it to its usual place and then decided to check it there and then. No meeting, no approval, no second person.

After he saw the cloud base descending, he took the autopilot from 5,500 to 5,000 ft and went back head-down into the logbook (p. 1). This is the last reversible moment in the sequence. Changing altitude took a few actions; stopping the check would have taken a few actions. He took the first.

What all three share is the absence of any paper carrier. This is not the author's inference. The investigation was graded Class 4, the NTSB did not travel to the site (p. 5), and the report cites no company operations manual, no training record, no duty regulation. Most cards in this book can name a meeting date and a signatory at the decision point. This one cannot, because on that day the cockpit held one person.

There is a fourth moment of a different kind: the aft cyclic input after he looked up and saw the peak. It lasted on the order of a second, and the report gives it one sentence, that he pulled aft to climb and the tail boom struck several trees (p. 1). It does not belong to drift. It is the compensating action after drift. When a person finds himself at the wrong altitude and on the wrong heading, the action space left is a few seconds wide.

What was visible then: Before the flight on 9 March, what he had in hand was his own computed obstacle data, highest 6,100 ft with several peaks at 5,000 to 5,500 ft, and his own conclusion that the flight would meet the end of evening civil twilight (p. 1).

In flight, what was actually in the cockpit: the autopilot setting at 5,500 ft and later 5,000 ft; the night vision goggles on the co-pilot's seat; the logbook under the goggles; the pilot's door pocket, the logbook's usual place (p. 1). Outside the window, the cloud base, which he himself described as descending (p. 1). On the intercom, the rear medical crew, and the flight nurse's request for an arrival time, the only external input that pulled him out of the head-down state (p. 1).

What was learned afterwards: the distance between the helicopter and the tree-covered peak at the moment he looked up; the separation of the vertical stabiliser from the tail boom after the tail struck trees; the extent of airframe damage from the landing on the road (p. 1, pilot statement and site examination). The K1A5 weather station, 4 nautical miles from the accident site, recorded at 19:15, eighteen minutes after the accident, a cloud base of 5,000 ft, visibility 10 miles, temperature 12 Celsius, dew point 0 Celsius, no precipitation and no obscuration, at a station elevation of 2,020 ft (p. 4). That observation was not on his desk, and the report does not say he consulted that station before departure. It establishes something else: visibility that night was not the obstacle. The obstacle was terrain and a lowered head, present at the same time.

Stop here. Decide before you turn the page.

  1. What would you do? Write the action, not "pay more attention".
  2. Which item here are you most likely to miss, and why does it look unimportant?
  3. If you may set one checkpoint, when is it and what does it check?

What happened: the tail boom struck trees and the vertical stabiliser separated, the helicopter landed on a road, three aboard were slightly injured and one was unhurt, and the airframe was substantially damaged (pp. 1, 4). The NTSB's probable cause, in the report's words, was the pilot's "improper decision to review the aircraft logbook in flight, which resulted in a controlled flight into terrain" (p. 2). The report carries five findings: aircraft control (pilot), mountainous terrain (decision related to conditions), task allocation (pilot), decision-making and judgement (pilot), and task monitoring and vigilance (pilot) (p. 2).

The three questions, looking back. The commonest answer to the first is "check the logbook after landing", and that action costs nothing: the logbook has its place in the door pocket and can be checked on the ground just as well. What the case spent instead was the whole margin of a 13-minute leg. The item most often missed under the second question is the number 5,000 ft. When the cloud base fell he changed altitude, and the route carried peaks of 5,000 to 5,500 ft; that information was in the pre-flight calculation, written by him. The third question lands in pre-flight preparation: check which tasks on this trip must be done in the air, and if you cannot name one, do not carry the object for it into the cockpit.

Options ruled out: the report records neither the alternatives the pilot considered nor any company rule on when the logbook is to be checked. The four items below are built from what was on his desk and from conditions in the report that make them unavailable.

Check the logbook after landing. Zero cost, since the pocket is where it normally lived (p. 1). The report records no rule either forbidding or requiring an in-flight check: at the level where documents exist, the act was neither prohibited nor required, only habitually scheduled.

Have a second person read the figures. This was a Part 135 single-pilot operation, the right seat was empty, and the goggles were lying on it (pp. 1, 3). The option did not exist on this leg.

Hold 5,500 ft and leave the altitude alone. The action the pilot described was a 500 ft descent (p. 1). The report records no consideration of routing around, climbing, or turning back; when the cloud base fell, he did not treat changing altitude and stopping the current task as one act.

Switch to instrument flight. The leg was on a company VFR plan with no clearance in Class G airspace (p. 4). IFR was not part of that day's mode of operation, and changing mode is itself an abort of the mission.

Early signals: no meeting record exists to cite, so the four signals below can only be described by how they were handled, not by what reason dismissed them. This is drift landing on a single-pilot post: there was no second person who needed persuading.

Signal one: the cruise altitude of 5,500 ft, level with peaks of 5,000 to 5,500 ft (p. 1). The signal sat on the pre-flight calculation sheet, and the handling was to fly it as computed.

Signal two: before flight he had already calculated that evening civil twilight would end during the flight (p. 1). Daylight disappearing inside the leg was his own result, and cabin paperwork was then scheduled into the same leg.

Signal three: the pre-flight stowage order had already changed. The logbook had left the door pocket and was lying on the co-pilot's seat, with the goggles on top (p. 1). The signal was an object in the wrong place, and the handling was to move the logbook back and start checking it on the spot.

Signal four: the descending cloud base was seen, and the handling was 500 ft down and the head down again (p. 1). The signal was processed into an altitude number. It was never processed into an action stop.

The point of escalation: in cockpit preparation before 18:44 on 9 March, the logbook was set down on the co-pilot's seat with the night vision goggles on top of it, and was later fetched for checking in flight (p. 1). The report does not record the day this practice began, nor how many times it had been executed before. What can be checked is that one day: it happened, no second person was present, and no one signed.

Failure chain: Technical layer. The autopilot held 5,000 ft; the route carried peaks of 5,000 to 5,500 ft; there was no visual reference while his head was down; at look-up the helicopter was close to a tree-covered peak; aft cyclic, tail boom striking trees, vertical stabiliser separating; a landing on a road and substantial damage (p. 1). Organizational layer. Part 135 single-pilot operation with no second pair of eyes in the cockpit; a company VFR plan with no clearance, so no outside opportunity to warn (pp. 3, 4); no company document in the report governing when the logbook is checked (pp. 1, 5). Incentive layer. En-route time was treated as time available for other work, a point the report does not support with any document and which can only be read from the sequence: he carried the paperwork aboard, and after seeing the cloud base fall he went back to it (p. 1). All three layers broke at once. The junction: the falling cloud base was a technical-layer signal, and the one channel that could translate it into "stop looking down" was another person in the cockpit, a channel that single-pilot operation removes by design.

Minimum counterfactual: put the logbook back in the pilot's door pocket before departure and check it after landing. One action, taken in cockpit preparation before 18:44, with no luck required: the pocket is where the logbook normally lived, and the report says so in those words (p. 1).

Outcome and sources: controlled flight into terrain at 18:57 on 9 March 2023; three people slightly injured, one unhurt, airframe substantially damaged; investigation graded Class 4, the NTSB did not attend the site, and the report was first issued on 6 June 2023 (pp. 1, 5). Primary source: NTSB, Aviation Investigation Final Report, ERA23LA147, 2023; link in Appendix B, av-020.

One layer in this case is worth naming. The act of a crew member going head-down into a logbook has a respectable name in aviation: task management, the business of putting en-route time to use. The material of drift is often exactly this kind of respectable practice wisdom. It makes sense, colleagues vouch for it, it has a record of efficiency, and its only problem is that it was never checked against another rule. Preventing drift does not mean abolishing practice wisdom. It means giving practice wisdom an interface for that check: every clever local practice deserves one question, which accident was the rule you bypassed written for. Answer it, and the practice at least knows what it is betting. Fail to answer it, and the practice is betting against a history nobody has read.

docs.title: Case 2 (Maritime): The Watch Alarm the Music Covered
docs.text:
Case ID: ma-002.

When and where: about 02:38 on 14 October 2025, off Lochinver in Sutherland, Scotland, on the rocky shore at Rubha Rodha. The trawler left Stornoway at 21:30 on 13 October for the fishing grounds (MAIB Report 17/2026 p. 1, p. 2). At the time of the accident it was dark, with slight seas and moderate to good visibility (p. 8).

What and who: the prawn trawler Silver Cloud II (fishing number WK 80), wooden, built in 1972, registered length 15.58 m (overall length 16.55 m), gross tonnage 42, bought in 2024 by Silver Cloud Shellfish Ltd and normally based at Ullapool and Gairloch (pp. 2, 8). Three people were aboard: the skipper, the mate and one deckhand. The skipper and the mate each had about 25 years in fishing, and the deckhand had been aboard about 12 months; all held the certificates Seafish requires, and safety drills were held on board regularly (p. 2). The accident was investigated as a very serious marine casualty (p. 8).

What they were doing: On 10 October the vessel finished a repair period. The skipper helped on site and went home to rest around midnight (p. 2).

At 11:00 on 11 October the vessel sailed from Gairloch to start fishing. The skipper already had influenza-like symptoms at sailing, headache, sore throat, blocked nose and muscle aches, and was taking paracetamol; he judged himself fit to sail (p. 2). Fishing ran until the evening, the vessel entered Ullapool at 23:00, and he went to bed at midnight.

He rose at 03:30 on 12 October and sailed immediately. The mate took the first watch until 05:30, the skipper took over until shooting the gear at 06:30; hauling at 11:30, then fishing through the day; that evening the vessel steamed to an old submarine mooring buoy in Loch Ewe, arriving at 20:30, and he went to bed at 23:00.

At 04:15 on 13 October the vessel left the buoy for the grounds and shot at 06:45; hauling at 11:00 found the net badly damaged, and the decision was taken to go to Stornoway to land the catch and repair, berthing at 15:00. The skipper went to sleep while the mate and deckhand repaired the net, landed the catch and ate. He rose at 21:00, the crew decided to add a night tow to make up for the shot lost that day, and the vessel left port at 21:30 (p. 2).

The mate stood the first two hours in the wheelhouse, and at 23:30 the skipper took over and was left alone. He set a waypoint near the grounds, expected to arrive at 01:15, and engaged the autopilot (p. 2). Between 23:30 and 01:15 he fell asleep in the wheelhouse. The vessel missed the waypoint, held 092 degrees and continued toward the Scottish mainland, and at 02:38 it struck the rocks at Rubha Rodha (p. 2).

The decision point: three moments, none of them signed.

At 11:00 on 11 October, at the Gairloch quay before sailing, he sailed with symptoms. The report's words are that the skipper had influenza-like symptoms at sailing but judged himself fit to sail (p. 2). That judgement involved no medical examination, no review and no second signature. It locked the next three days of rota into a body already running at a discount.

At 21:00 on 13 October, aboard at Stornoway, the crew added a night tow. The background was the badly damaged net found at the 11:00 haul and a shot lost that day (p. 2). The crew made the decision jointly; the report's phrase is "the crew decided". The immediate consequence is written in Table 1: on 13 October, 16 hours 30 minutes of work, a longest unbroken work period of 15 hours, and a longest unbroken rest of 4 hours (p. 4).

At 23:30 on 13 October, in the wheelhouse, the mate handed over and the skipper kept the watch alone. At that point 19 hours 15 minutes had passed since he rose at 04:15 that day (p. 2; the interval follows from the report's narrative). Three people were aboard, the mate had just finished two hours on watch, and the deckhand had been aboard 12 months (p. 2). The decision at that moment was not to call anyone.

None of the three moments has a paper carrier, and the report is blunt about why. MSN 1884 (F) amendment 1 requires work and rest arrangements to be planned and recorded (p. 5), and "a complete record for the four days prior to the vessel's departure could not be obtained" (p. 6). No record means nothing to sign, and without anything to sign, all three decisions are absent from the paper.

What was visible then: Before sailing on 11 October: his own symptoms, four of them, being held down with paracetamol (p. 2); the schedule, a cycle of 10 days at sea and 4 to 5 ashore (p. 4).

Aboard on 13 October: three people available, of whom the mate had about 25 years and the deckhand about 12 months (p. 2); the fact that the net had been badly damaged that day (p. 2); the fact that a shot had been lost (p. 2); the vessel's equipment fit, a watch alarm mounted in the wheelhouse that armed when the autopilot was engaged and needed a button pressed every 4 minutes, with the volume rising if no one intervened for 1 minute after the first alarm, and no visual alarm or audible repeater in the crew accommodation (p. 4).

In the wheelhouse at 23:30 on 13 October: the waypoint and the expected arrival time, the autopilot, and the music that was playing. Also present was a division of labour already customary on that vessel: during trawling the skipper or mate would usually keep the wheelhouse for long stretches, while watches on passage were taken by the mate and the deckhand (p. 4). That night the passage watch fell to the skipper himself. The report records that music was often played on this vessel when hauling and often in the wheelhouse, and that music was playing in the wheelhouse on the night of the accident (p. 4).

What was learned afterwards: the skipper's total rest across three days (6, 6.5 and 7.5 hours) and his longest unbroken rest (6, 3.5 and 4 hours), in Table 1, which the MAIB reconstructed from interviews (p. 4); the missing records for the four days before departure (p. 6); and the judgement that the alarm was highly likely to have been masked by music in the wheelhouse, the report's phrase being highly likely (p. 6). One more item: the period when human alertness falls naturally runs from about 02:00 to 06:00 (p. 5), and the grounding at 02:38 falls inside that window (p. 6).

Stop here. Decide before you turn the page.

  1. What would you do? Write the action, not "pay more attention".
  2. Which item here are you most likely to miss, and why does it look unimportant?
  3. If you may set one checkpoint, when is it and what does it check?

What happened: the vessel grounded at 02:38. The impact and the movement that followed woke the skipper and the crew; an inspection found the fish room flooding to about 1 m and still rising, and the skipper decided to abandon. The three donned life jackets, the deckhand stepped straight onto the rocks, and the mate entered the water on the starboard side and was pulled ashore by the deckhand. The skipper put the engine in neutral, activated the emergency position indicating radio beacon, sent a distress alert by digital selective calling, took the VHF radio, and entered the water on a line to be pulled ashore. At about 03:00 the RNLI lifeboat arrived and recovered all three (pp. 2, 3). There were no injuries; the hull was breached, flooded and partly submerged, then broke up on the rocks and was declared a constructive total loss (pp. 1, 8).

The MAIB made no new recommendations and issued no safety flyer, on the grounds that findings of this kind had recurred repeatedly in earlier investigations: Sustain (16 November 2023, off the entrance to Loch Broom, skipper asleep on watch) and Crystal Stream (6 June 2025) (pp. 5, 7).

The three questions, looking back. The commonest answer to the first is "fit a watch alarm". This vessel had one, and it was not a legal requirement (p. 6, original: although not a requirement on board Silver Cloud II, a watch alarm was fitted). It still did nothing, and the cost of that answer is turning a four-minute button press into an action that may or may not be taken. The item most often missed under the second question is the absence of a repeater in the crew accommodation. It reads like an equipment detail. In fact it decides that this alarm can only wake someone already in the wheelhouse, which makes it structurally useless against the watchkeeper himself falling asleep. The third question lands before 21:00 on 13 October: count the seven-day rest total, and cancel the night tow if it falls short.

Options ruled out: the report records no discussion of alternative arrangements among the crew. The five items below are built from conditions aboard at the time and from facts the report can verify.

Two-person watches. Three people were aboard, and the mate had already stood the first two hours before 23:30 (p. 2), so he was capable of taking over. Single-person watches are not prohibited at this vessel size, though the arrangement runs against MGN 313 (F) guidance on the risk of lone lookout (p. 6). The real cost of this option is the mate's rest, and the mate's rest that day was fragmented as well (p. 4).

Cancel the night tow. The direct cost is one shot of gear, which is exactly what the 21:00 decision set out to recover (p. 2). The report records no one proposing cancellation.

Turn the wheelhouse music off or down. The vessel had no ban on music; it was played routinely when hauling and in the wheelhouse, part of the work (p. 4). MGN 313 (F) lists distractions in the wheelhouse, music systems among them, as a contributory factor in collisions and groundings (p. 5). The guidance was written and the vessel's practice had not followed it: a verifiable fork between text and practice.

Have the deckhand keep him company or take the watch on passage. The third person was in his bunk at the time; the report records that the deckhand had been aboard about 12 months, was building experience, and did not stand trawl watches independently (pp. 2, 4). Passage watches were normally shared by the mate and the deckhand (p. 4), and that night they were not arranged that way.

Fit a repeater for the alarm in the accommodation. That is an equipment modification requiring the owner to spend money (p. 4 records that the vessel had no repeater). The report records no discussion of it.

Early signals: five, each with the account available at the time.

Signal one: sailing with symptoms at 11:00 on 11 October (p. 2). The account available: the symptoms were influenza-like, held down with paracetamol, and he judged himself fit to sail.

Signal two: three days of rest at 6, 6.5 and 7.5 hours, with longest unbroken rest of 6, 3.5 and 4 hours (p. 4, Table 1). The rules require no less than 10 hours in any 24 and no less than 77 hours in any 7 days, with daily rest split into no more than two periods, one of them at least 6 hours (p. 5). Rest on 12 and 13 October was split into three periods each, with longest periods of 3.5 and 4 hours, so both conditions failed at once. The account available: MSN 1884 carries its own exception, allowing an authorised departure for operational reasons provided safety is not harmed (p. 5). That exception had become the default channel.

Signal three: 16.5 hours of work on 13 October, with a longest unbroken stretch of 15 hours (p. 4). The account available: the net broke during the day, a shot was lost, and it had to be made up.

Signal four: the alarm sounded only in the wheelhouse, with no repeater in the accommodation (p. 4). The account available: the equipment was not a legal requirement, and having it at all was a bonus (p. 6).

Signal five: music and alarm sharing one space (p. 4). The account available: music was the normal background of the work, played when hauling and in the wheelhouse.

The point of escalation: two consecutive actions between 21:00 and 23:30 on 13 October. The crew decided on a night tow and the vessel left at 21:30; two hours later the mate handed over and the skipper stayed alone (p. 2). Once the vessel had left, it had no physical means of relieving the watchkeeper before the 01:15 waypoint, and two of the three remaining people were in their bunks. Nothing was signed at this step and nothing was recorded: the work and rest arrangements for that day were never written down (p. 6).

One time gap deserves recording separately. The vessel missed the waypoint at 01:15 and grounded at 02:38, 83 minutes later (p. 2). On the alarm's setting, with the autopilot engaged, a button press was required every 4 minutes, the alarm sounding if it was not pressed and rising in volume after 1 minute without intervention (p. 4). Eighty-three minutes is room for more than twenty alarms. The report does not record whether the alarm sounded that night. It records a conclusion: the crew did not know the skipper had lost the ability to keep watch until the vessel struck (p. 6).

Failure chain: Technical layer. Grounding at 02:38, hull breach, fish room flooding to about 1 m, subsequent break-up (pp. 1, 2). Organizational layer. A single watchkeeper and no structured rota (p. 4, original: an informal watchkeeping arrangement and had no structured rota); no work and rest records, with the four days before departure missing (p. 6); an alarm with no repeater in the accommodation, designed on the assumption that someone in the wheelhouse could hear it (pp. 4, 6). Incentive layer. Catch and trip rhythm: a shot was lost to net damage on 13 October and a tow was added that night to recover it (p. 2); a cycle of 10 days at sea and 4 to 5 ashore, landing catch every two days (p. 4). All three layers broke at once. The junction: the one channel that could carry the fact of the skipper asleep to the accommodation was the alarm, and the alarm was designed to sound only in the wheelhouse, where it was highly likely to be masked by music that night (p. 6). The channel broke at the level of equipment fit and volume, and that level sits on nobody's checklist: the alarm was not broken and the music was not a violation.

Minimum counterfactual: before deciding on the night tow at 21:00 on 13 October, check the rest total against 77 hours in 7 days, and cancel the tow if it falls short. One action, taken two hours before departure, with no luck required: the three days' figures in Table 1 were already in his own routine, and the floor set by the rules is written in MSN 1884 (p. 5).

Outcome and sources: all three rescued, unhurt; the hull breached, flooded, broken up and declared a constructive total loss; the MAIB made no recommendations and issued no safety flyer (pp. 1, 7, 8). Primary source: MAIB, Report 17/2026, Silver Cloud II, August 2026; link in Appendix B, ma-002.

There is a quieter layer in Case 2: the fact that the alarm really was fitted to that vessel. The equipment was real, the function was real, the defence line existed, even though no requirement demanded it (MAIB Report 17/2026 p. 6). What drift does is not dismantle defences. It makes them mismatched. The alarm was kept as its design scenario specifies, a quiet wheelhouse, while the wheelhouse's real scenario, music, had long since stopped being the design scenario. That sentence generalizes into a test question for drift: is this defence line's design scenario still the same scenario as the site today. The difference between the two is the part drift has eaten, and that part appears on no defect list, because the alarm was not broken and the music was not a violation.

docs.title: Case 3 (Healthcare): The Checklist That Drifted (condensed)
docs.text:
me-001. An NHS orthopaedic treatment centre in the United Kingdom. HSIB investigation report (Administering a wrong site nerve block, 2018; the archived snapshot was read and verified for this book): the nerve block for a 69-year-old patient's right ankle operation was injected into the left leg, and the patient was not harmed. The Stop Before You Block checklist was in use and was being filled in, but the way it was executed had evolved from pausing at each item and confirming aloud in both directions to ticking items off as you went. National figure: about 192 wrong-site operations a year. The decision point sits at the moment the checklist was simplified from an item-by-item pause and check to a running tick. Minimum counterfactual: execute the checklist as designed, with a pause and a cross-check at every item. Primary source: HSIB, 2018; link in Appendix B, me-001 (archive link, grade A−).

This condensed case holds the sharpest phenomenon in the chapter. After drift, the checklist still produces complete compliance records. The ticks are real, since every form was signed. The check did not happen, and that is real too. A paper record proves that the form was filled in; it cannot prove that the check took place. The difference between the two is the measure of the pause that got eaten. Device 2, which registers pause-type actions on a separate list, is aimed at exactly that difference: a checklist protects the pauses between the ticks, not the ticks on the paper.

docs.title: Case 4 (Construction): The Safety Space Filled with Cable (condensed)
docs.text:
ce-003. Ickenham station, London Underground. RAIB report (Report 02/2026; the pages were read and verified for this book): a passenger fell onto the track and was struck and killed by a train.
