Gmail has been a free service since 2004, requires a Google account before use, and the account is at once the entry to advertising, YouTube and other products (§6). On the company's statements in the proceedings these advertising entries enter no mail storage, cannot be searched, moved or replied to, are allocated by auction and change with the conversation (§194). Two earlier penalties on the same subject hang on this same path, of 7 December 2020 and 31 December 2021 (§84, §244).

The decision point: three dates, each with a carrier.

The first is 15 December 2020, when the account creation consent mechanism went live. The carrier is the account creation path on google.fr itself; the decision records the date and the two-step and five-step structure, with no signing post appearing (§113, §117). The first path's page is titled "Confirm your personalisation settings and cookies", and it holds two buttons, "Confirm" and "Back" (§118). The asymmetry fixed at that moment is two clicks to accept and six to refuse (§133).

The second is April 2023, when the Gmail advertising entries were restyled. The carrier is the format change on the delivery side, and during the proceedings the company submitted an IPSOS format study it had commissioned, in which 76 percent of respondents found the redesigned advertising not hard to tell apart from messages (§164). The decision records the change as intended to reduce the risk of confusion with messages, and the restricted committee held it insufficient to overturn the legal characterization (§160, §249). The same period holds the second on-site inspection of 5 September 2023 and company submissions of 26 September and 14 November 2023 (§12, §14).

The third is October 2023, when the path was redesigned. Quick personalisation (1 step) was renamed "quick choice (1 step)", two buttons were added, "Refuse all" and "Accept all", and clicking through led to a "Confirm your settings" page that still offered "Confirm" or "Back" (§121). The manual path was renamed "manual choice (4 steps)", with the content of pages 3 and 5 untouched and page 3 still titled "Enable the 'customised ads' parameters to see more relevant ads" (§122, §123). The decision's conclusion splits in two: from that date the freedom limb of consent was no longer missing (§136), and the flow as a whole satisfied the informed limb neither before nor after the redesign, because nowhere from beginning to end did it state that access to the service is conditional on advertising cookies being dropped (§138, §141).

The notice sentence at step 5 of the manual path still comes after the user has picked an advertising type (§124). The order of the three moments is structure first, appearance second, buttons last. The round that added buttons changed the click count and left the disclosure alone, and the choice on page 3 still happens before the explanation on page 5, so a user has to pick an advertising type before learning that what he picked is a whole set of cookies (§143).

What was visible then: the NOYB complaint filed on 24 August 2022 on behalf of three complainants (§7); the full text of resolutions 2020-091 and 2020-092 of 17 September 2020, requiring refusal to be as easy as acceptance and the interface not to highlight one option visually (§97, §101); the Court of Justice's judgment of 25 November 2021 in C-102/20, holding that advertising in an inbox, of the same shape and in the same position as messages, constitutes direct marketing by electronic mail and needs specific, informed consent in advance (§157), with paragraphs 41 to 43 of that judgment giving as grounds the occupation of a line meant for private mail and the resemblance to a message that makes a mistaken click likely (§192), the judgment given nearly a year before the inspection began (§242); paragraph 150 of the Court's judgment of 4 July 2023 in Meta, C-252/21, which writes the equivalent alternative into the test of free consent (§102); its own account scale in the backend, meaning the number of consumer Gmail accounts in France active at least once in the 28 days to 11 December 2022 whose inbox carried a Promotions or Social tab, redacted as [...] in the decision (§241); two prior cases, SAN-2020-012 of 7 December 2020 and SAN-2021-023 of 31 December 2021, same defendant and same subject (§84, §244); the notice on step 5 of account creation, which opens with "if you agree" while the path holds no refuse-all step (§145); its own path's click counts, two to accept and six to refuse, countable on any walkthrough (§133); the path and buttons after the October 2023 redesign (§121); EDPB Opinion 08/2024 of 17 April 2024, which lists free service with generic advertising only as an equivalent alternative and which the company cited in its defence (§101, §114); the report served on 25 July 2024, written submissions of 4 October 2024, 29 January and 28 April 2025, and oral submissions of 26 June 2025 (§16, §17, §20, §23). What became known only afterwards: more than 74 million accounts in France, of which 53 million people were shown the advertising at issue (CNIL press release, 3 September 2025; the corresponding figures are redacted as [...] in the decision, §239, §241); the fine and the daily penalty (§264, §265, §271); and the informed limb still unrepaired after October 2023 (§138).

You are in the seat now, with the material above on the desk.

Stop here. Decide before you turn the page.

  1. What would you do? Write the action, not "pay more attention".
  2. Which item here are you most likely to miss, and why does it look unimportant?
  3. If you may set one checkpoint, when is it and what does it check?

What happened: on 1 September 2025 the restricted committee fined Google LLC 200 million euros and Google Ireland Limited 125 million euros, 325 million euros in total, the two amounts split by company with each covering both violations and no split by violation (§264, §265 and the operative part). It also ordered both to remedy within six months of notification: French users must be made to understand that creating an account necessarily means advertising cookies, and prior consent must be obtained before advertising is inserted between messages; after the deadline the penalty is 100,000 euros a day (§269, §270, §271). The decision was published, with the names removed after two years, and an appeal to the Conseil d'État lies within four months (last page of the operative part). Back to the three questions. The commonest answer to the first is another round of remediation, though two rounds have already shown that the same structure regenerates the same violation, so the third round's output will most likely be a third remediation document. The item most often missed in the second question is the revenue function itself: whether the consent mechanism is bolted onto the architecture or built into it decides whether remediation fixes the boundary or the engine. The correct landing point for the third question is the interface design review, whose mandatory question is "what is the revenue state of this architecture with all consent switched off", a question that forces revenue dependence and compliance boundary into the same room.

Options ruled out: four, each with ready practice at the time.

The first is an explicit cookie wall. The restricted committee says plainly that tying access to the service to cookies is not in itself unlawful, provided consent is free and refusal carries no loss (§127); the decision even gives two sample lines, one for creating a free account and accepting cookies for personalised advertising and content, one for creating a free account and accepting only cookies for generic advertising (§146). The route was there and was not taken, and the decision's assessment is that where the company could have chosen a cookie wall that is unambiguous to users, it chose a path that was complex and ambiguous (§147).

The second is making refusal one step. The "Refuse all" button of October 2023 proves it can be done (§121); it did not appear before the redesign, and after the redesign it solved only the click count (§136).

The third is stating the condition on the first screen. The remediation order requires exactly that sentence (§269); the decision notes that neither path carried it at any time (§141), and that the manual path split it across steps 3 and 5, leaving the user to join the two (§143).

The fourth is making advertising entries plainly unlike messages. The change of April 2023 did part of it (§160); the entries in the Court's case had a grey background and showed no sender (§190), while Gmail's have a white background and a sender name in the same format as messages (§193).

All four leave the revenue model untouched and move disclosure and clicks instead. The decision holds no record of ruling them out.

Early signals: ① The two penalties of 7 December 2020 and 31 December 2021, same defendant and same subject, both on cookie consent under Article 82, the 2021 one naming the inconvenience of refusal on the home pages of google.fr and youtube.com (§84, §244). They were read as a fine on the website banner and not on the account creation flow, a distinction the company itself raised in defence (§28, §34, §35). ② The Court's judgment of 25 November 2021 (§157), given nearly a year before the inspection (§242), was read as a civil judgment about advertising that is not mail, the company arguing against applying it by analogy (§162), and the appearance change was pushed back to April 2023 on that reading (§160). ③ The guidelines of 17 September 2020 required refusal to be as easy as acceptance (§101), and the penalty of 31 December 2021 had already stated as a principle that the two options must take an equal number of operations (§135), while the company's own path still ran two against six (§133). It was read as already offering a refusal path; the decision acknowledges the choice existed and finds the manner of expression distorted it (§134). ④ After the buttons went in during October 2023 the informed limb was still unrepaired (§138), and that was read as remediation complete, with the company arguing that the order no longer served a purpose under Article 82 because the redesign had been finished (§267). ⑤ From September 2024 the company stopped using some cookies connected with personalised advertising (§115, §249), which is a different matter from opting out of all advertising cookies; the decision records it as a mitigating circumstance (§249, §247) without changing the finding, and the account scale kept rising through the same period, with the measurements of 13 May 2023 and 10 September 2024 each higher than the one before (§241).

The point of escalation: the October 2023 redesign is that step. The date is in the decision, the action was adding two buttons and renaming the paths (§121), and no signatory appears. The timing sits after the inspections closed and nine months before the report was served on 25 July 2024 (§16). In the year before, both inspection procedures had run their course (§8, §11, §12), and the April 2023 format change had already been made once (§160). The escalation holds because the redesign closed the freedom limb while fixing the informed limb in place: the path set from then on, and every later claim of compliance landed on "the user can choose", which is the defence's own wording at §267, while the gap the decision finds is exactly that the user does not know he has no choice (§141, §142). Adding the sentence about access being conditional on cookies after the redesign would mean overturning the whole path design of December 2020; leaving it out, every step of the path can be called a choice. The acceptance standard of that round shows here too. The deliverable list is buttons and renaming, and the decision, comparing page by page, records that the content of pages 3 and 5 of the manual path was unchanged (§122), so the deliverable is two buttons live while the running state is whether the user knows what he is choosing. A deliverable can be accepted. A running state can only be sampled.

Failure chain: technical layer. The advertising entries share the size, the white background and the sender format of messages and differ only in a green Ad and the date position, the web version lacks a checkbox, and clicking opens the whole advertisement in the form of a message (§187, §188); account creation holds two paths, two clicks to accept and six to refuse (§133); the October 2023 redesign added buttons and left disclosure split across steps 3 and 5 (§143). Organizational layer. Both changes land on the product path, and the decision records dates and structures only, with no signing post (§113, §121); the joint-controller finding rests on the parent's full ownership and the decision chain and has nothing to do with who signed (§262); the approval column is empty in the decision; remediation was delivered by the party being remediated, out of its own path and its own explanation (§267); after the report was served on 25 July 2024 the company's four rounds of written submissions argued jurisdiction and ne bis in idem (§28, §33, §37), not facts. Incentive layer. Gmail is provided free, and its maintenance and development are funded by the group's advertising revenue, a layer the decision's own text describes as therefore intrinsically connected with the dropping of cookies (§130), and it provides that a party adopting a cookie wall must show its purpose is to keep an economic balance between providing the service and its cost (§129, §131). The difference between the personalised and the generic inventory is recorded as degree of intrusiveness (§109, §110), with the unit price absent from the file; group revenue in 2024 was 350 billion dollars, about 312 billion euros (§263), and the advertising line's own revenue figures are redacted in the published version (§252). All three layers broke at once. The break at the boundary runs between the technical and the incentive layer: every click on the path is at the same time a pricing of inventory, and the ease of the click is decided by the technical implementation.

Minimum counterfactual: when the path went live on 15 December 2020, put the sentence "creating an account requires accepting advertising cookies" on the first screen, beside the two options. One action, on the day the mechanism went live, changing no button and adding one line of copy. The cost is a screen of copy and one copy review, with the two sample lines at paragraph 146 of the decision serving as template; no architecture change, no change to the revenue model, and the six-click asymmetry can be left as it is. The step was doable at the time and did not depend on luck: the guidelines of September 2020 already required clear disclosure (§101), and the remediation order at paragraph 269 requires exactly that sentence. Acceptance takes one person and one pass: open google.fr, walk the first path, see whether the first screen carries the sentence. It does not erase all liability, since the freedom problem before the redesign still stands, and it erases the informed limb, which is the one thing this Article 82 violation lacked from 2020 to 2025 (§138, §153, §154).

Outcome and sources: 325 million euros in total (200 plus 125), two violations found, a six-month remediation period and 100,000 euros a day after it (§264, §265, §269 to §271). Primary source: CNIL restricted committee decision SAN-2025-004 of 1 September 2025, English courtesy translation, PDF of 54 pages; citations in this card are paragraph numbers (§) and page numbers are PDF pages. The decision runs from a cover page with the subject matter and the service record, through Part One on facts and procedure (§1 to §23), Part Two on reasoning, jurisdiction, procedural objections, controller determination, Article 82 and L. 34-5, and Part Three on the fine, the remediation order and publication (§225 to §275), to the operative part on the last page. The translation's header states that the French original prevails where the two differ. Accompanying press release of 3 September 2025; prior cases SAN-2020-012 of 7 December 2020 and SAN-2021-023 of 31 December 2021; Court of Justice C-102/20 of 25 November 2021. The published version carries [...] redactions, and where a figure is redacted this card fills in none (§239, §241, §252). Link at Appendix B sw-007.

Case 5 is the standard portrait of misaligned incentives in the platform economy: the form of the violation upgrades with each remediation while the structure of the conflict persists unchanged. Its sister case (sw-008, Appendix B: FNAC DARTY fined 7 million euros for an app sending browsing data to third parties through an SDK without consent) shows the small and medium version of the same structure, where privacy compliance never covered the third-party SDK chain. As in case 5, the gap sits in the chain rather than in awareness: the compliance team sees its own code and not the code integrated into it.

docs.title: Case 6 (Manufacturing): Fifty Mattresses and Eleven Thousand Bottles of Lotion (condensed)
docs.text: mn-007 and mn-009. Two CPSC recalls of October 2026, pages checked for this book: about 50 Longjili Trading mattresses failing the mandatory flammability standard, and about 11,000 units of RootStim minoxidil hair regrowth liquid missing child-resistant packaging, a PPPA mandatory standard. Both are isomorphic with case 4 in this chapter, the SOOWERY dresser: small-batch import, violation of a mandatory standard, no injury reports, delisting from the platform channel. The reading of a recall sequence three in a row at the incentive layer is this. The compliance cost for a small-batch importer, testing, certification, packaging change, is badly out of proportion to the batch size, and list first and withdraw if caught is for many small sellers a strategy that holds up mathematically. A mandatory standard settles whether a thing may be sold; it does not settle whether anyone verified anything before it went up, and with the verification step empty the standard degrades into a recall catalogue. Minimum counterfactual: mandatory compliance spot testing by the platform on a small seller's first order. Primary source: CPSC, 2026, links at Appendix B mn-007 and mn-009.

docs.title: Case 7 (Finance): Even the Identity Was Borrowed (condensed)
docs.text:
fi-003. Ichcoin Tech Corp. SEC enforcement of August 2026, text checked for this book: an investment adviser practised on forged ADV filing information, using the CRD number of an unrelated 87-year-old individual. The principal-agent chain is pushed to its absurd edge here, since the compliance identity itself, the investment adviser registration, was forged, so the agent the principal faces, regulator and client both, is already broken at the identity layer. It gives the chapter's three questions an extreme test. Is each layer's choice rational? Borrowing an identity is rational inside a fraud frame. Did nobody break a rule? Someone did, and this case enters the territory of intent. On whose head does the summed loss land? On investors and on the 87-year-old whose number was used. The answers push the case to the corruption and fraud side, which is exactly what calibrates the line drawn at the start of the chapter: misalignment changes structure, fraud moves the courts. Primary source: SEC, 2026, link at Appendix B fi-003.

Laid out by industry, the seven cases run audit, tax collection, regional aviation, platform retail, platform data, small-batch manufacturing and adviser identity, and the distribution follows one rule: the more expensive verification is in an industry, the heavier the case. Audit and securities, cases 1 and 7, verify quality in units of years, and their cases end in criminal exposure and large penalties. Platform retail, cases 4 and 6, verifies in units of spot checks, and its cases end in a recall catalogue. Data platforms, case 5, sit between the two and end in a seven-figure euro fine. Verification cost grades the failure style of an industry: expensive verification produces big cases, cheap verification produces catalogues. Inverted, the rule is the budget table for defences. Whichever grade your industry's verification cost sits in is the grade your incentive-layer governance budget should sit in.

One diagnostic tool belongs beside that budget table: principal identification. Every agency relation has a nominal principal, the one who pays, and a real principal, the one who carries the consequence, and the separation between the two is the depth of the misalignment. The nominal principal of an audit is the audited company, the real principal is the reader of the statements. The nominal principal of goods on a platform is the seller, the real principal is the buyer. The nominal principal of regional capacity is the mainline carrier, the real principal is the passenger. The tool is one question: when this thing breaks, who loses most, and who has no seat today? Find that person and you have the legal starting point of every defence in this chapter, since Device 2's whole-result signatory acts, nominally, for this absent party. The absent party's seat is the origin of the whole corporate governance literature, which this chapter does not re-expand; it only notes that any proposal claiming to solve misaligned incentives while giving the absent party no place to speak is circling inside agency upon agency.

docs.title: 4 What Shows Up Earliest
docs.text:
Seven weak signals, each with the reason that usually presses it down.

  1. The phrases "we followed the contract" and "we followed the rules" appear at abnormal density in meeting minutes. Reason given: following the rules is not a fault.
  2. Every piece of bad news reaching a given post comes off another link's ledger. Reason: that is the division of labor.
  3. The beneficiary is the verifier of some problem, and the verification reads "no issues" year after year. Reason: it is running normally.
  4. Decisions with large externalities are never made by anyone who meets the people who carry them. Reason: hierarchical division of labor.
  5. The assessment metrics fight each other, and every side in the fight is winning. Reason: multi-dimensional assessment.
  6. The same structural disease recurs at different suppliers or divisions, and every response is to replace the people. Reason: an execution problem. If replacing people worked, the second occurrence would not have happened.
  7. In contract negotiation, risk clauses get far less time than price clauses. Reason: price is the business.

Put the seven back against this chapter's cases. Signal 2, bad news arriving from another link's ledger, is case 1: the first victim of an audit quality problem is the statement reader, who appears on no ledger of the firm. Signal 3, the beneficiary verifying and finding nothing year after year, covers cases 1 and 4: the party maintaining the client relationship shares a table with the party guarding audit quality, and on the platform the spot check sits on the same side as the listing. Signal 4, deciders who never meet the bearers, is case 3: the designer of the capacity cost structure does not sit in the cockpit on a night approach. Signal 5, metrics fighting while every side wins, is case 2: the revenue metric wins and tax source reality loses. Signal 6, a recurring structural disease handled by replacing people, covers the two firms of case 1 and applies as well to the three recalls of case 6. Signal 7, risk clauses getting short negotiation time, is the native form of the listing terms in case 4.

One indicator of the layer's own deserves writing down: the whole-chain checkup, an extension of question 5 in section 7. Take the most recent loss that crossed a link boundary, write out each layer's choice and its rationality in that layer, and put the summed result and the party carrying it on the last line. The layer-by-layer rationality table is the incentive layer's examination sheet: every row, read alone, is innocent, and the last row is the lesion. It is also the strongest tool for talking to outsiders, since any party shown the table can find on it the evidence of his own correctness and, on the last line, the cost he took part in. The persuasion problem of misaligned incentives is hard exactly there, and that is also where it is solved.

The three questions need operating instructions. For the first, on whether each layer is rational, the material to check is each layer's assessment documents and contracts, never interviews: an interview will say of course we put safety first, an assessment document tells the truth. For the second, on whether anyone broke a rule, the material is the compliance audit's conclusion: an all-green compliance record next to a bad outcome is the signature of the second question holding. For the third, on whose head the loss lands, the material is the consequences chapter of the accident report set against the seating chart of the decision table, and the seat gap shows up in the first comparison of the two lists. All of it is available inside the organization, which makes this one of the lowest-threshold diagnoses in the book: it needs no industry knowledge, only the one act of laying the documents side by side.

docs.title: 5 How to Prevent It
docs.text:
Device 1: externality accounting. Write the foreseeable effect of this layer's decisions on the other parties of the chain into this layer's own assessment. Audit firms get assessed retrospectively on later penalties and litigation records, and the CSRC penalty is an instance of the externality returning to the account, since what it fines is the consideration the audit fee bought. The quality of lawful collection enters the collection agency's assessment weights. What will not fit a quantitative clause goes in as a qualitative item with mandatory reporting at every review.

Device 2: a signatory for the whole result. Every multi-link chain names one role answerable only to the whole: the engagement partner answerable to the readers of the statements, the collection quality officer answerable to the taxpayer's experience, the operations control chief answerable to passenger safety. Its assessment is tied to no output of the layer. An empty title achieves nothing. The person must hold the power to stop (Chapter 18), and the stop must not be subject to performance assessment by any party inside the layer (Chapter 19's protection interface).

Device 3: beneficiary recusal from verification. Whoever benefits from a problem may not act as its verifier, and an arrangement already in place is replaced by external sampling. The whole institutional history of audit independence is the implementation record of this one clause, and its failures always begin with an exception: "this one is special, let the in-house team review it first".

Device 4: a structure-review trigger. When the same failure mode appears at two or more suppliers or divisions, escalation to a structure review is mandatory: examine the contracts and the assessments, not the people. Recurrence is the incentive layer speaking. A problem that yields to a personnel change does not recur, and a problem that recurs never yields to one.

The four devices against this chapter's cases. Device 1 on case 1: add regulatory penalties and litigation lookback to partner assessment, with the 3,679,245.18 yuan of this case as a ready-made lookback entry. Device 2 on case 3: add a co-signing role answerable for passenger safety to the capacity clauses of the mainline and regional contract. Device 3 on case 5: move the verifier of the consent mechanism's remediation from the advertising line to outside it. Device 4 on case 6: the third recall of the same kind triggers a structure review of the platform's small-batch import channel automatically.

The three write-ups for putting an externality back into assessment are worth giving in full. Write-up one is money: final payment, revenue share and settlement cycle tied to verifiable end quality, as described above. Write-up two is a post: the whole-result signatory, assessed on the end result alone, which is Device 2. Write-up three is an account: convert the externality into an internal cost and book it, as a compliance cost line for collection quality or a fatigue risk provision inside the capacity structure. The common enemy of all three is the excuse that it cannot be quantified: the accounting version of write-up three allows interval estimates (Chapter 11's Device 2, the digitizing of margin), and what will not fit a quantitative clause goes in as a qualitative item reported at each review. None of the three is expensive. What is expensive is the reason for refusing to write them, which is that the layer does not want to see its own externality. Seeing it is the first step of every defence in this chapter.

The four failure modes deserve equal space, since each has a respectable way to die. Externality accounting dies of account inflation: the lookback line takes everything, and in the end it is indistinguishable from an ordinary cost line. The whole-result signatory dies of being an empty title: signatures get signed and the stop power is never wired, with no budget veto and no direct reporting line. Whether a signatory is real takes two facts, whether he has ever stopped something and what happened afterwards. Beneficiary recusal dies of spreading exceptions: the list of special cases grows longer every year until recusal is a principle on paper, so every exception needs written approval and a quarterly review in aggregate. The structure-review trigger dies of threshold decay: two or more becomes three, then four, and the trigger becomes a souvenir. All four share one examination question: when did this device last actually fire? A device that cannot produce a date is dead.

docs.title: 6 Boundaries with Adjacent Mechanisms
docs.text:
Against goal displacement (Chapter 12): misaligned incentives is the interest structure, goal displacement is its technical implementation. The criteria divide the work. If what needs changing is the interest structure, meaning who carries the consequence, go to Chapter 17. If the interest structure is sound and the measurement is crooked, stay in Chapter 12. The two often need work at the same time, and the order is to plug the structure first, by beneficiary recusal from verification, and repair the measurement after.

Against diffusion of responsibility (Chapter 18): dilution is nobody being responsible, with the signature chain ownerless; misalignment is someone being responsible in the wrong direction, with the assessment pointing the wrong way. The criterion is one question. Give the responsibility to one named person: does the situation change? If it changes, the disease is dilution. If giving it changes nothing because his assessment forces him to act against it, the disease is misalignment.

Against horizon mismatch (Chapter 28): when the current-period tilt is amplified by short tenure, the horizon dimension stacks on top. The criterion: extend the decision-maker's tenure three times over, would the choice change? If it would, the main disease is in Chapter 28. If it would not, the main disease is in this chapter.

docs.title: 7 Self-Check: Five Questions
docs.text:
1. Write out the assessment objective of every link in your chain and see where the sum points. Does it point at the objective of the whole?
  2. Which problems in your organization have the beneficiary for a verifier? Can you list three?
  3. Has one of your decisions damaged another link's ledger? Did that damage appear in any assessment document of yours?
  4. If your role were given one more line, answerable only for the result of the whole, which line of your present assessment would have to be deleted to make room?
  5. Take an old incident in which every layer was blameless, write out each layer's rational choice in turn, and put the summed result on the last line. That line is the incentive layer's examination report.

(This chapter: 14,553 characters.)

docs.title: Chapter 18 Diffusion of Responsibility
docs.text:
What this chapter covers: how responsibility thins as the number of signatures rises; three criteria, four field sites, and the design of unilateral stop authority together with a ceiling on signature counts. When to turn back: when the organization runs a countersigning workflow, stands up a committee, or hands one matter to three departments. Estimated reading time: 50 minutes.

Responsibility dilutes quietly. Nobody refuses it. It is averaged away in the act of dividing the work. A fraudulent annual report carries four signature lines. A collision in a shipping lane has four classes of party. A level crossing's warning equipment spans two owners. A helicopter's landing rests on two sets of assumptions. Seen afterwards, every party signed, every party covered its own segment, and every party can state exactly what it did. No link in the chain is in charge, and every link sincerely believes that somebody else is watching. This chapter is about that somebody else.

docs.title: 18.1 What It Is
docs.text:
Definition: diffusion of responsibility is the psychological and structural phenomenon in which responsibility thins as the number of participants rises. The structural face is dispersal: staged approval, multi-party signature, committee decision. Each gate added is meant to add a line of defence. What it adds is one more contributor to the assumption that someone else will check. The psychological face is the office version of the bystander effect: the more parties involved, the higher the cost of unilateral intervention and the greater the social risk of making a fuss over nothing. Lay the two together and no link in the chain is in charge.

Three trigger criteria. Any one of them means the mechanism has already started.

  1. Many participants, and the responsibility interfaces between them are not drawn in writing.
  2. Every party can state exactly what it did; no party can state who owns the whole.
  3. The organization holds no unilateral stop authority anywhere.

Criterion 2 has a self-test that is harsh and does work. After an incident the organization's first reflex is to find out who signed. The signature chain carries seven names. Seven signatures mean the step was confirmed seven times, which means not one of the seven confirmations was necessary.

The psychological face has a dated experimental origin. John Darley and Bibb Latané ran a series of experiments in 1968 in which subjects waited alone or in company while smoke came into the room next door, or a person fell next door. Subjects on their own reported the anomaly at a far higher rate than subjects in company. Company did not add up to more vigilance. It diluted each person's inclination to step in. The central variable is structurally identical to this chapter's criteria: the presence of others supplies the assumption that somebody has already dealt with it, and that assumption holds in every head at once. The office version differs in one respect. The others there carry documented roles, so the assumption looks better founded. The experiment also supplies the usable converse. Name one person, even if the only change is that one more person is nominally responsible for raising the alarm, and intervention rates return to the solo level. The antidote has sat in the literature for decades. Replace everybody with a name.

The structural face needs one more definition: what it means to be in charge. The test here is three observable conditions satisfied at once. You know what you are looking at, which is the information state. You know what you are allowed to do, which is the authority state. You know what follows if you do nothing, which is the consequence state. Take away any one and you are not in charge, even where the paperwork carries your name. The VTS operator in Case 1 (ma-008) lacked the second: the boundaries of authority were unclear. The two parties in Case 3 (ce-008) lacked the third and the first: nobody assessed what the equipment actually did to pedestrians. Auditing the three states beats auditing the name of the responsible person, because the paper name is usually written in a clear hand and the three states are usually all empty.

docs.title: 18.2 How It Grows
docs.text:
Three generating conditions.

Condition one is an institutional tradition of multi-party signature and staged approval. The intention is another line of defence; the cost structure of signing decides the behaviour. Checking every prior signature benefits the chain and costs the signer, so a rational signer checks his own cell. Defences stack on paper and run in parallel in practice.

Condition two is layered outsourcing and subcontracting. Each tier down drops the visibility of risk a grade and weakens the responsibility link a grade. Where a subcontract carries service clauses and no risk clauses, nothing but a commercial relationship remains between the tiers.

Condition three is committee decision. The resolution belongs to the collective, execution needs an assignee, and supervision has no post. What a collective passes has no individual claimant by construction, and the credential of having taken part makes each member feel the duty is already discharged.

The tragedy of dilution is that it is asymptomatic in ordinary times. Every link signs, approves and meets. The system looks deeply defended, which is Chapter 22's illusion of redundancy projected onto the responsibility layer. The symptom shows up only at the moment somebody has to call a stop. At that moment seven signatories equal none.

The arithmetic fits in a sentence. Responsibility divides by headcount. The drive to intervene declines by headcount. The two curves run in opposite directions. Let the cost of dealing with a risk be C. With n parties and no written interface, each party perceives its own share of "I ought to act" as roughly C/n. The larger n gets, the smaller each share, and the cheaper the waiting strategy of letting somebody else move first. The equilibrium of waiting strategies is the classic dilution scene: everybody waits and the exposure runs its full length. The design implication is as plain. Either squeeze n to one, a single accountable person, or put each party's perceived share back at C by writing the whole consequence into each party's assessment. Those two moves are Device 1 and Device 2.

n also has a time dimension. Dilution is not static. The participant count grows with the age of the process. A new process has one owner. Every small incident adds a countersignature. Every cross-departmental collaboration adds a party. n climbs monotonically with age, the perceived share falls monotonically, until some unpleasant event drags the chain onto an audit table. That is why old organizations carry the most signatures on their gates and not necessarily the strongest defence. The growth of n records the organization's history of frights; each signature is a souvenir of the last accident, the organizational-design counterpart of Chapter 11's deviation ledger. Device 4, the ceiling on signature counts, is aimed at exactly this monotonic growth. Souvenirs can stay in the minutes. They do not have to stay in the workflow.

Signing has one further behavioural layer: how far a signer rationally checks. Making every signature verify all preceding content grows the cost linearly with chain length while the benefit falls with the marginal contribution of each added signature. A rational signer checks his own cell. Chapter 1 set out that structure; its industry version is the signature chain in Case 4. The patch is not to ask signers to be more conscientious. It is to write the verification protocol into the system. Signatures come in two kinds. A verifying signature means substantive checking of the content in that cell. A passing signature means confirming only that the paper moved through. Mark the two in separate columns, and rule that a passing signature may never be cited as quality evidence. Once the columns exist, the defensive illusion of seven signatures has no raw material left.

The outsourcing chain has a contract-layer patch worth spelling out: vertical continuity of risk clauses. A subcontract usually carries service levels and nothing else. The risk clauses, meaning the duty to notify when something goes wrong, the duty to cooperate with an investigation, and the cap on liability, are signed only between main contractor and client. At the second and third tiers the obligations to risk fall to zero tier by tier. The continuous form is the flow-down clause: the main contractor writes the core risk clauses verbatim into every tier of subcontract, and no tier may override them with looser terms. Flow-down is established practice in aviation maintenance and maritime contracting. It treats the disease in condition two, the tier where nothing but a commercial relationship survives. Checking the penetration rate of flow-down clauses is the first move in auditing an outsourced chain.

docs.title: Case 1 (Maritime): A VTS Whose Staff Did Not Know Their Own Authority
docs.text:
Case ID: ma-008.

When and where: 24 October 2023, 0455 (UTC+2). Eastern German Bight traffic separation scheme, collision point 54°01.5N 007°38.7E, 0.2 nautical miles inside international waters. The watch station was the German Bight vessel traffic service centre at Wilhelmshaven. Wind force 5 to 6 with gusts to 7, visibility between 10 and 31 km, dark (pp. 10, 24, 65).

What and who: the Bahamian bulk carrier Polesie (24,055 gross tons, built 2009, managed by Polska Żegluga Morska P.P., 20 crew, 32,997 tonnes of grain) and the Isle of Man general cargo ship Verity (2,601 gross tons, built 2001, managed by Faversham Ships Ltd, 7 crew, 3,262 tonnes of steel coils). The monitoring party was German Bight Traffic, operated by the Federal Waterways and Shipping Administration under the direction of the Federal Waterways and Shipping Agency (GDWS). Responsibility is recorded by post: the officers of the watch on both ships, the VTS nautical assistant, the VTS nautical supervisor (pp. 10, 32–33).

What they were doing: at 1940 on 23 October Polesie sailed from Hamburg for A Coruña with 32,997 tonnes of grain, draught 10 m, after seven days loading in port. At 2008 the same day Verity sailed from Bremen for Immingham with 3,262 tonnes of steel coils, draught 5.4 m, after five days loading (p. 12).

At 0310 on the 24th the pilots left both ships. On the Polesie bridge were the master, the second officer and a helmsman. The master handed control to the second officer and left. Course 273°, speed 11 knots, time in hand (p. 12). At 0410 the chief officer took the 0400 to 0800 watch. The starboard radar was on 6 nautical mile range with offset display. Verity was already on AIS at CPA 0.15 nautical miles and TCPA 45 minutes. Neither radar had its CPA alarm switched on, and the ARPA had not acquired the target (p. 15).

At 0423 Verity entered the northbound lane on course 335° at 8.3 knots, keeping to the eastern side. At 0444:30 Polesie passed the planned waypoint, where the plan was to alter to 256° onto the westbound lane; she was still making 273°. At 0446:03 she crossed the 256° planned track with no change of course (p. 16). Between 0448:48 and 0449:59 the chief officer entered nine successive course changes on the autopilot, taking the heading from 264° to 245°. The 28° port turn went in instalments, and from another ship or from the VTS screen it did not look like steering (pp. 17, 58).

Over the same period the VTS assistant was monitoring both ships, judged that there was a risk of collision, and noticed that Verity was not acting as the give-way vessel. In the preceding three minutes the assistant had also handled two routine ship reports; the rest of the watch's tasks are unknown. The Channel 79 west sector assistant was absent that night and one supervisor covered two sectors (pp. 17, 36).

The decision point: the first moment sits at the document layer. On 28 October 2013 Coral Ivory and Siderfly collided in the Kiel Canal, and the Federal Bureau of Maritime Casualty Investigation (BSU) recommended in report 330/13 that GDWS study changing the VTS ship-shore duplex channel to simplex (p. 53). Nobody died in that collision. Siderfly was at risk of sinking from damage below the waterline and the canal was shut for three days (p. 53). The report records no formal reply from GDWS. By the time the 2026 report was published, GDWS said a next-generation VTS system was in development with the simplex requirement included, over 2028 to 2034 (p. 69). For the ten years between, the two ships could reach each other only through a shore station relaying words.

The second moment is 0450:09. The assistant called Verity on Channel 80 with the ships less than 1.3 nautical miles apart, CPA 160 m, TCPA 8 minutes 11 seconds. Three sentences: the CPA is very small; what is your intention; under the rules you must take avoiding action (pp. 17, 60). The report notes that the VTS's own post-event report does not explain why the intervention waited until TCPA was down to 7 minutes 28 seconds (p. 60). When the call ended the ships were a nautical mile apart, CPA under 0.2 nautical miles, TCPA 5 minutes 16 seconds (p. 17). The call carried no IALA WARNING marker and the tone was the tone of ordinary conversation (pp. 17, 61).

The third moment runs from 0453:43 to 0454:00. The supervisor called Polesie on Channel 80, confirmed radio contact, then in a raised, urgent voice said "do not go left, do not go left, turn right, Polesie, alter course to starboard" (p. 20). The chief officer answered "yes, starboard", and nine seconds later went to hand steering and hard starboard (p. 21). The VTS post-event report states that the supervisor was acting under Rule 17(c) of the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea (p. 61). The report's analysis holds that the chief officer was more likely acting under Rule 17(b), and that the restriction in 17(c) did not apply in that situation (p. 62). At the moment the instruction went out the ships were under half a nautical mile apart, and the instruction finished within 90 seconds of the collision (pp. 20, 62). Polesie was still inside German territorial waters, where the VTS had authority to instruct her. Half a mile away Verity was already in international waters, where the VTS could only advise (p. 65). Two ships half a mile apart, two sets of authority.

None of the three had a second person check it. The document was issued by GDWS. Both calls were decided by the watchkeeper on duty. Annex A holds only time, call sign and the words as spoken (p. 72).

What was visible then: on the Polesie bridge, both pilots were off the ship and the master was aboard but not on the bridge (p. 12); two tracks on radar and ECDIS, with the CPA and TCPA figures from AIS; the territorial sea baseline drawn on the ECDIS at 0433, the moment Verity passed from German territorial waters into international waters (p. 16); at 0443 a readout of CPA 0.11 nautical miles and TCPA 14 minutes 42 seconds (p. 16); at 0452:37 the Verity AIS icon selected, reading 0.83 nautical miles, CPA 0.2 nautical miles, TCPA 3 minutes 40 seconds (p. 19); four written instructions from the master, one of them "call the master in any doubt", specifying a call at 5 nautical miles or more (p. 30).

At the VTS station: a chart terminal fusing radar and AIS, on whose reconstruction of 0450:09 the two ships show a CPA under 0.1 nautical miles with 8 minutes left (p. 18); the automatic alarm for CPA under 0.5 nautical miles muted because there were too many small craft, with the indication still on screen (p. 35); no German territorial sea boundary on the display (p. 65); Channel 80 duplex, so the shore station could hear the ships but the ships could not hear each other (p. 37); one assistant short on the watch (p. 36); a three-shift rotation with the night shift from 22:00 to 06:00 (p. 35); no written guidance on what to do at which CPA (p. 35).

On the Verity bridge: two X-band radars with ARPA, AIS, ECDIS, BNWAS (p. 30); a steady 8.3 knots along the eastern side of the lane since 0423, nearly 8 nautical miles without a change of course (p. 57); no voyage data recorder, not then required on a ship of 2,601 gross tons (pp. 11, 70).

What became known only afterwards: the 28° port turn by Polesie was hard to make out on radar or by eye (p. 58); Verity was in fact turning into the track of Polesie (p. 59); the CPA between the two ships never exceeded 0.53 nautical miles from entry into the traffic separation scheme to the collision (p. 56); Polesie entered international waters at 0454:18, 1 minute 10 seconds before the collision (pp. 21, 65); had the port turn continued there would have been no collision (p. 61); the investigation found that the chief officer "felt obliged to comply" with the supervisor's instruction (p. 62); the investigation found no evidence that either the operator or the supervisor knew the geographic limits of their authority (p. 65).

You are in the seat now, with the material above in front of you.

Stop here. Decide before you turn the page.

  1. What would you do? Write the action, not "pay more attention".
  2. Which item here are you most likely to miss, and why does it look unimportant?
  3. If you may set one checkpoint, when is it and what does it check?

What happened: at 0455:28 the bulbous bow of Polesie struck Verity on the starboard side at a relative speed of about 12 knots, some 11 m forward of the accommodation (p. 22). Verity sank in 36 m of water, about 5 minutes after the collision. Five of the seven crew died; two were rescued, the second officer and one seaman (pp. 9, 23, 54). The search ran into the night. Four crew were unaccounted for, and two of the bodies were found inside the vessel during the recovery (p. 64).

Go back to the three questions. The commonest answer to the first is to intervene earlier and to use the WARNING marker. In this case the cost of that action does not sit in speaking. It sits in what follows speaking. After the first call at 0450:09 the VTS internal report records that "at 1 nautical mile VTS had no further opportunity to intervene" and that it was "satisfied that the earlier interaction had produced a collision avoidance solution" (p. 36). Three and a half minutes later it spoke again, and that second sentence pulled the chief officer out of a port turn that had already been working. The item most easily missed under the second question is the absent territorial sea boundary on the display. It looks like a charting detail. It was the shared blind spot of all three people on watch that night. The answer to the third question lands before anybody speaks: establish which side of the water the ship is in, then decide whether the sentence is advice or instruction (p. 65).

Options ruled out: a broadcast on Channel 16 so both ships hear the same words. The report states there is no indication that Channel 16 was considered, and concedes that a broadcast has drawbacks, but it does offer a way to clarify what is happening (p. 63). Having the two ships move to a working channel and talk directly: not possible on a duplex Channel 80, which needs a separately agreed channel; the VTS would not be a party to that call, and once advice had been given it would not know what the ships had agreed (pp. 62–63).

A single instruction from the VTS to both ships: on the Verity side the VTS had advisory authority only (p. 65). Intervening before 0450: the VTS internal report sets out as experience that small craft in the area often give way late, need little swinging room and are reluctant to leave their course (p. 36). The experience held, and the price of it was a threshold pushed out to 1.3 nautical miles. Continuing to intervene inside 1 nautical mile: the internal report sets its threshold at "at 1 nautical mile VTS had no further opportunity to intervene" (p. 36). The chief officer carrying the port turn begun at 0452:55 through to the end: the reconstruction shows no collision, but he went to hand steering nine seconds after the supervisor's instruction (pp. 21, 61). The master taking the bridge: his written instructions required a call at 5 nautical miles or more in any doubt (p. 30), and the master was called after the collision (p. 22).

Early signals: 1. On 28 October 2013 Coral Ivory and Siderfly collided in the Kiel Canal, and BSU report 330/13 recommended that GDWS study changing the duplex channel to simplex (p. 53). Reason it was overridden: the canal was closed three days, nobody died, and the recommendation stopped at "study". 2. On 11 February 2015 Ever Smart and Alexandra 1 collided inside the Jebel Ali port limits, and the container ship's bridge sighted the other vessel seconds after the port control call (p. 52). Reason it was overridden: a one-off inside port limits where both pilotage and port control had failed. 3. On 11 December 2013 Paula C and Darya Gayatri collided in the Dover Strait, and the investigation found that a timely and well-meant VHF intervention by the coastguard almost certainly pushed the Paula C officer of the watch into the wrong action (p. 53). Reason it was overridden: blame landed on the officer of the watch for losing situational awareness, and the intervention itself was never questioned. 4. The VTS compulsory refresher scenario VK02-K-GBT-De trains exactly the case of a risk of collision where the VTS does not intervene (p. 36). Reason it was overridden: the training supplies the right answer, and the boundary was only ever exercised in one direction. 5. In 2022 the IMO member state audit of Germany raised no finding or observation on the VTS (p. 36). Reason it was overridden: the external audit passed, so the system was taken as confirmed. 6. A shipowner inspection record of 19 October states that the bridge personnel knew all navigational safety procedures; the master's written instructions were a verbatim copy of the Liverpool to Hamburg version of 12 October, signed by the master and three officers (p. 30). Reason it was overridden: complete paperwork was read as execution.

The point of escalation: 0451:36 to 0451:50. The assistant called Polesie with the sentence: "the Verity on your port side will pass astern of you, he tells me he will turn to starboard and pass astern of you, keep a check on the situation" (p. 19).

Before that sentence each ship held its own picture. Verity held course and speed, expecting Polesie to give way to the lane and let her pass ahead. Polesie expected Verity to pass astern (pp. 57, 19). The two pictures contradicted each other and neither ship had spoken to the other. After that sentence, the Polesie picture had been confirmed by the shore station. The chief officer answered "yes, I will keep a watch, a little to starboard" (p. 19). The report notes that this answer did not meet the closed-loop readback standard of IALA 1132, and that had the assistant used the WARNING marker before the call, the ambiguous reply would not have been let pass (p. 61).

The escalation took the form of a relayed sentence. It sent each ship a confirmation that the other would give way, and the two confirmations pointed opposite ways. It also put the VTS itself in the position of a problem already handed over: for the next four minutes nobody spoke, until 0453:43. In those four minutes Verity only began to turn to starboard at 0452:26, while Polesie at 0451:02 set the autopilot from 245° to 252° and stopped the port turn that was under way (pp. 17, 19). Who approved it: the assistant issued it, the supervisor sat at the same watch station, and there is no record of a review. The words are in Annex A (p. 72).

Failure chain: technical layer. The duplex Channel 80 kept ship from speaking to ship, leaving the VTS as the only channel and reducing it to relaying what was meant (pp. 60, 62). The automatic alarm for CPA under 0.5 nautical miles was muted (p. 35). The terminal did not show the territorial sea boundary (p. 65). Both ships made small incremental alterations on autopilot that did not read as steering at a distance (pp. 56–57). Verity had no voyage data recorder (p. 11). Neither ship had its CPA alarm on. Polesie's seamen were on a lookout rota and by custom did not keep lookout (pp. 15, 29). Whether Verity had an extra lookout that night, the report records as impossible to establish (p. 55).

Organizational layer. Authority was cut into two grades of post, supervisor and assistant, and three grades of measure, traffic information, traffic assistance and instruction, with the assistant empowered to issue instructions only on the supervisor's authority (p. 33). The three sentences at 0450 belong in the files to information and assistance, yet they went past plain notification ("under the rules you must act"), and the authority to instruct was not the assistant's (pp. 17, 33). The ordering rule that traffic assistance is provided when traffic information has failed to achieve its purpose came with no CPA or TCPA threshold and no statement of when to stand back (pp. 34, 62). The supervisor issued the instruction on the basis of Rule 17(c), and the report holds that 17(b) was the rule that applied (pp. 61–62).

Incentive layer. The VTS was not assessed on CPA at all; assessment fell on whether interaction followed procedure and whether records were kept. Four posts of thirty were vacant and the watch ran anyway, with cover arranged "opportunistically" (p. 36). The two ships were assessed on schedule reliability and surface compliance. Both had time in hand that night (p. 55) and both kept the CPA inside 0.5 nautical miles (p. 56).

The seam broke between the document and the experience. The document left blank who must speak at what distance. The watchkeeper filled the blank from experience. In that experience small craft always give way late, so silence read as a judgement.

Minimum counterfactual: add one line on standing back to the intervention clause of VV-WSV 2408. When TCPA falls below 5 minutes, the VTS issues warnings only and no instructions. One action, dated before October 2023, needing no new equipment and no extra staff. The report states plainly that neither VV-WSV 2408 nor VV-GDWS 24-2 gives guidance on the CPA or TCPA at which intervention becomes counterproductive (p. 62). With that line in place, the "turn to starboard" at 0454:00 would not have gone out. The report's reconstruction shows that had the chief officer continued his port turn the ships would not have collided (p. 61). The figure of 5 minutes has support in the report: when the supervisor spoke at 0453:43 the TCPA was under 3 minutes, and the report describes that band as counterproductive for intervention (p. 62). The report did not put the threshold into a recommendation. 2026/117 asks GDWS only to "provide guidance", with no number attached (p. 70). The same line would hold for next time: the decision to stand back becomes citable, and therefore answerable.

Outcome and sources: Verity was a total loss, five people died, Polesie suffered slight damage to bow and starboard side with minor oil pollution (p. 10). The report makes seven recommendations, numbered 2026/115 to 2026/121. The IMO should amend SOLAS Chapter V/20 to bring internationally trading cargo ships of 500 to 3,000 gross tons within the voyage data recorder requirement. GDWS should review the use of duplex channels and provide guidance to intervention staff covering when to intervene, the use of information markers, and when to stand back (p. 70). IALA has revised Guideline 1141 to require shore relay wherever a duplex channel is used (p. 69). The limits of the investigation are also recorded: Verity carried no recorder, key witnesses were not interviewed, and the internal decision process at the VTS could not be reconstructed (pp. 9, 11).

Primary source: MAIB, Report on the investigation of the collision between the bulk carrier Polesie and the general cargo ship Verity, Report No 5/2026, February 2026, 82 pages, with Annex A a translation of the German Bight VTS report and Annex B extracts from the Collision Regulations. Link in Appendix B, ma-008.

The four-party shape of Case 1 is worth reading again against the three states, because it is the complete specimen of this chapter's criteria. Information state: each of the four parties held a fragment (the two ships each knew their own constraints, the VTS could see both tracks), and the whole picture existed only on radar, never in a judgement. Authority state: the authority clauses for operator and supervisor were vague on what could be required, whether it could be enforced, and who carried the failure if enforcement failed, which was the fatal gap on the monitoring side. Consequence state: each bridge knew the physical consequence of a collision, and the assumption that the other would act thinned the urgency of it. Each state has a patch: a common picture table for information, an authority list for authority, and making assumptions explicit for consequence, where the watch rule requires "I think the other will move" to be said aloud, at which point it becomes something that must be verified. The MAIB recommendations fall broadly inside that frame, and the reader can check them against the original.

docs.title: Case 2 (Healthcare): The Incompatibility Only the Registry Knew
docs.text:
me-008. Joint replacement surgery in the English NHS. HSIB report (Implantation of wrong prostheses during joint replacement surgery, 2018; the archived snapshot has been checked against the original for this book). During surgery a 62-year-old patient was implanted with prostheses from different manufacturers that were not compatible with each other, and the defect surfaced days later when data at the national joint registry were matched. Surgical team, instrument supply, pre-operative check, registry entry: each person at each link could explain how his own step met that link's process. The theatre took implants against the implant list, the supplier shipped against the order, the check ran against the checklist. No link carried full responsibility for whether the two components matched each other, because matchability straddled the seam between four links, and seams do not sign.

The stop point is the instant on the operating table between the implantation of the first component and of the second. On the table: implants each carrying its own label, process records showing every link verified, and a registry that nobody thought to query on the spot. What happened: the patient underwent a second operation; the report names the registry's detect-afterwards pattern, and detection afterwards means nobody was responsible beforehand. Primary source: HSIB, 2018, link in Appendix B, me-008 (archived link, grade A−).

"Seams do not sign" can be pushed a step further. The seam went unclaimed because matchability straddles the catalogue systems of two manufacturers, and neither catalogue contains the other. The gap in the information structure comes before the gap in responsibility: even a person who wanted to own it would have no data to check against. The order of repair for seams of this kind is therefore data first, responsibility second. Until a compatibility tool exists, one that queries both catalogues together, naming a responsible person only creates a post with a duty and no instrument. The HSIB report makes the registry's after-the-fact detection a principal finding, which is an acknowledgement that the data layer was missing, and the direction of its recommendations agrees with this chapter's order. The generalisation for the reader: at a check point spanning two systems, ask first whether the tool exists, then whether the responsibility exists. Responsibility written where the tool is absent is written in the air.

docs.title: Case 3 (Construction): The Governance Interface at a Level Crossing
docs.text:
ce-008. The Staniforth Road level crossing of the Supertram network in Sheffield, 22 June 2025. RAIB report (Report 10/2026, pages checked against the original for this book): a tram struck two pedestrians, one seriously injured and one slightly injured, both taken to hospital. The pedestrians did not notice the tram coming, the audible and visual warnings had no effect, and risk management between the infrastructure owner and the operator at the crossing was weak. The crossing's warning equipment straddles the governance interface of two bodies. Ownership of the equipment, its maintenance, its assessment for effectiveness and its actual effect on pedestrians sit on different responsibility lists, and the unworded seam between those lists falls exactly on the question of whether a pedestrian can cross safely.

The stop point is the last moment at which the crossing's warning equipment was assessed on the measure of actual effect on pedestrians. On the table: the equipment status record, which reads normal, the owner's and the operator's respective duty documents, both complete, and the seam between them that neither party has ever signed. What happened: two people went to hospital; the report lists the unclear risk interface among its investigation findings. Primary source: RAIB, Report 10/2026, 2026, link in Appendix B, ce-008.

The governance interface here has one feature worth marking. The equipment status record reads normal. Normal means the equipment has power and is working. What failed was the measure of actual effect on pedestrians, meaning whether the warning is enough for a pedestrian to notice the tram. The split between the two measures falls along the split between the two bodies: the owner manages equipment condition, the operator manages operational safety, and the measure of effect sits in neither assessment. This is the responsibility version of the negative substitution in Chapter 12, where the information channel for the real goal was never wired into either party. The repair copies Chapter 12's general rule: build a quantity for the effect, here a frontline observation of whether pedestrians notice, then assign it an owner under this chapter's device. On governance interfaces like a level crossing the two chapters' defences always arrive as a pair.

docs.title: Case 4 (Finance): The Ex-Post Section Through a Signature Chain
docs.text:
fi-007. The decision against the responsible persons in the Qingyue Technology fraudulent issuance case (〔2026〕No. 59, pages checked against the original for this book): chairman Gao Yudi, warning, a fine of 9 million yuan, an 8-year market ban; executive deputy general manager Mu Xinju, a fine of 9 million yuan, a 6-year ban; chief financial officer and board secretary Zhang Xiaobo, a fine of 6 million yuan, a 5-year ban; supervisory board chairman Wu Lei, a fine of 4 million yuan, a 3-year ban (the same case as fi-006). The penalty decision is a section cut through responsibility diluted in advance. The fraudulent offering document and annual report carried four names, and the four signatures made up the organizational narrative of layer upon layer of checking. Afterwards the regulator took each signature back to its true degree of knowledge, one by one: the layering of signatures was the shape of dilution beforehand and the order of accountability afterwards.

The stop point is the stretch of process in which the fraudulent content was finalised and the four signatures went down in sequence. On the table: what each signatory actually knew, the route by which each document arrived already signed above, and the half step by which each signatory pushed the duty to check onto the signature before or after his own. What happened: fines totalling 28 million yuan, with market bans of 3 to 8 years. Primary source: China Securities Regulatory Commission, 〔2026〕No. 59, 2026, link in Appendix B, fi-007.

The layering in Case 4 has one more thing to read. The fines and ban lengths fall away in strict order down the four signatures, because the regulator prices by degree of knowledge and by the influence of the post. The counterpart of that pricing beforehand is that knowledge and influence ought to weigh a signature. Dilution flattens them into the same undifferentiated "signed". The lesson for a board is written in the pricing. The further down the chain a signature sits, the greater the signatory's information disadvantage, so the designer of the chain owes the lower signatories an independent information route, whether an outside adviser with direct access or a channel for dissent that goes straight up. Without one, the lower signature is only a guarantee given by the upper, and dilution runs from the first signature to the last.

Case 4 and Case 1 of Chapter 17 (fi-008, the audit firm's side of the same issuer) are a mirror pair for this chapter. The firm is the outsourced end of the chain failing, the four company signatures are the core of the chain failing, and the same fraudulent annual report sits between them. The regulator's handling of the two ends, put together, is the full section through dilution: the structural disease at the outsourced end, which is paying for strictness, meets the structural disease at the core, which is the flattening of the signature chain, on one issuer. The two cases are placed side by side so the reader can see the whole-chain shape of dilution. It does not stop at the boundary of an organization, at committees and countersignatures. It also runs between organizations, through commissioning, outsourcing and subcontracting. The instruments that defend against it are the same set. The governance interface register, Device 3, carries across organizations unchanged, and the requirement to name four parties holds across an organizational boundary as well.

docs.title: Case 5 (Public Policy and Administration): Thirteen Years, Four Options, Two (full card)
docs.text:
Case ID: po-005.

When and where: 2000 to June 2026. The Palace of Westminster, London, a Grade I listed building inside a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The report was signed by the Comptroller and Auditor General on 8 June 2026, ordered to be printed on 11 June and published on 15 June, numbered HC 32, session 2026-27 (pp. 1, 3).

What and who: the Restoration and Renewal Programme. The parties involved: the House of Commons and the House of Lords, each of which must approve the scope and funding of Phase 2; the House Commissions, one per House, responsible for that House's administration and services and setting the spending limit for Phase 1; the Clerk of the House of Commons and the Clerk of the Parliaments, corporate officers who serve as accounting officers for the programme; the Client Team, which acts for the Clerks and manages the Delivery Authority day to day and replaced the Sponsor Body in 2023; the Client Board, a joint body of the two House Commissions; the Programme Board, made up of members of both Houses, the two Clerks and external independent experts; the Delivery Authority, responsible for day-to-day delivery; and Strategic Estates, which manages the parliamentary estate and reports through the Director of Operations to the Commissions. Oversight sits with the National Audit Office, and the report is signed by the Comptroller and Auditor General, Gareth Davies (pp. 3, 7–8, 30).

What they were doing: in 2000 the first survey of the plant rooms raised concerns about the building and its services (pp. 6, 16). In 2013 the two Houses established the programme (pp. 7, 17). In 2014 the Commons Commission agreed to proceed with refurbishment of the Northern Estate; in 2016 that Commission decided to give Richmond House to the programme as decant space (p. 28). In January 2018 the Commons voted to approve construction and to vacate the Palace entirely during the works, with a commitment to return as soon as possible; in February the Lords endorsed the approach (p. 17). In 2019 Parliament passed the Parliamentary Buildings (Restoration and Renewal) Act, establishing the Delivery Authority and the Parliamentary Works Sponsor Body and writing in nine scope considerations: value for money, safety and security, environmental protection, accessibility, visitor access, education and other facilities, public engagement, archaeology and historic value, and benefits across the whole of the UK (pp. 17–18). In December 2020 the House Commissions agreed to ask the Sponsor Body to study the implications of continued presence (p. 18). Through 2022 and 2023, over concerns about cost and schedule, the Sponsor Body was replaced by the Client Board and the Client Team (pp. 18, 30). In 2023 the Client Board added two options for construction inside the Palace, EMI and EMI+, and asked Strategic Estates to develop them; the same year the two Clerks said it was uncertain how much longer the Palace could be used as it stands, because the building has no reliable system for stopping the spread of fire (pp. 16, 18). In March 2024 the Client Board published a strategic case that fixed scope at outcome level 4, "reasonably ambitious" (pp. 18–19). In 2025 the Commons Commission required the Northern Estate refurbishment to meet a "Parliamentary grade" standard, raising the refurbishment standard above the minimum intervention originally set (p. 28). In February 2026 the Client Board published the costed options report, the first time four delivery options had been set side by side with complete cost and schedule ranges (p. 8).

The decision point: the first moment is January to February 2018. The vehicle was two votes, the Commons in January and the Lords in February, and the report records only the month. Each House voted separately and neither could stand in for the other. That vote turned "move out" from an option into a premise, and every option since has had to find room between that premise and the commitment to return as soon as possible (p. 17).

The second moment is December 2020. The vehicle was a decision of the House Commissions to ask the Sponsor Body to study the implications of continued presence. The report records the decision in a single line: ask the Sponsor Body to carry out work so as to understand fully the implications of retaining a continued presence in the Palace during construction (p. 18). It sets no deadline for the study's conclusions, and it does not say that the 2018 decision stands if the conclusions come back unfavourable. From that year on, the 2018 premise was open to discussion, and the discussion carried no expiry date.

The third moment is 2022 to 2023. The vehicle was a change of governance: the Sponsor Body was abolished and the Client Board and Client Team took over. The report records the range of years, with no months and no document numbers. The stated reason was to increase members' engagement with the programme, and the remit handed to the successor was "to develop options for the Houses to consider and vote on" (pp. 18, 30). The responsible body changed its name, and the verb in the remit changed from overseeing delivery to developing options. The direction of accounting responsibility appears in the same section: the two Clerks answer to their own House and Commission, not to a minister or to the Treasury (p. 30).

The fourth moment runs from February to June 2026 and is not complete. The vehicle is the costed options report plus a parliamentary debate that has yet to be scheduled. The Client Board asks the Houses to approve cutting the options from four to two, full decant and EMI+, and to authorise a seven-year Phase 1 with a £3bn cap; the target date for the final choice is 2030 (pp. 6, 8–9). The request goes to the Houses, and the debate required for approval has to be scheduled by the government (p. 9). The membership of the Houses keeps changing. The report records that since 2024 the Client Team has met around 542 sitting members, of whom around 283 are sitting Commons members, roughly 43 per cent, and that many of them took no part in the earlier decisions and met the programme at one point only in its development (pp. 10, 19). The date of 2030 was set by the Client Board itself, and the report calls it a target rather than a statutory deadline (pp. 6, 31).

What was visible then: in January 2018, the conclusions of every review since 2000, the current condition of the building and its services, and the option set of full decant with a return as soon as possible. The costs of the four options did not appear until February 2026 (p. 8).

In 2019 the nine scope considerations of the Act sat side by side on one page. The report's comment is that these broad and potentially competing considerations needed clear trade-offs (p. 18).

In December 2020 the table held the NAO's 2020 report on early value-for-money risk (p. 9). The cost and schedule of continued presence had not been estimated, and its range of £14.4bn to £22.0bn over 33 to 45 years did not stand beside the other three options until 2026 (p. 8).

In February 2026 the four ranges were on the record together: full decant £11.1bn to £15.6bn over 19 to 24 years; continued presence £14.4bn to £22.0bn over 33 to 45 years; enhanced maintenance and improvement, or EMI, with the Palace divided into 14 zones and no more than 30 per cent vacated at any one time, £23.3bn to £56.3bn over 52 to 84 years; and EMI+, with the Lords vacating for 8 to 13 years and the Commons borrowing the Lords chamber for no more than 2 years, £19.5bn to £39.2bn over 38 to 61 years (p. 8). Phase 1 in the same month was divided into five work packages: temporary accommodation, at £417m for the Queen Elizabeth II Centre with the acquisition price counted separately and £328m for Richmond House; enabling works at about £691m; early works at about £160m; and pre-construction activity at about £860m (p. 25). Design of the conference centre stood at RIBA stage 2 and the Northern Estate group containing Richmond House at stage 1, and the former had under one month of buffer between completion and handover to operations (pp. 27–28).

What became known only afterwards: the technical feasibility of the two EMI options cannot be confirmed until the next design stage (p. 20); the precise location and quantity of asbestos are unknown (p. 23); the Northern Estate cannot provide temporary accommodation before 2034, pushing completion to 2039 (p. 28); and if the Commons decant were phased, some members and staff would remain on site for about half the duration of a full decant (p. 28).

You are in the seat now, with the material above in front of you.

Stop here. Decide before you turn the page.

  1. What would you do? Write the action, not "pay more attention".
  2. Which item here are you most likely to miss, and why does it look unimportant?
  3. If you may set one checkpoint, when is it and what does it check?

What happened: as of the NAO's June 2026 update, none of the four delivery options had been selected, and both requests, cutting the options to two and authorising a seven-year Phase 1 capped at £3bn, were waiting on debates in the two Houses, which the government schedules (pp. 8–9). The spread between the highest and lowest option was £45.2bn in cost and 65 years in schedule (p. 8). Each year of delay adds £320m to £420m to the programme's overall cost (p. 10). Maintenance of the Palace averaged about £1.5m a week between 2017-18 and 2025-26 and is expected to rise to about £2m a week from 2026-27 to 2029-30; the programme itself is expected to bring that weekly figure down by about £700,000 (p. 17). Go back to the three questions.
