⑤ November 2021 and October 2023 were 23 months apart, and local authorities were asked to redo their spatial and local transport plans between the two documents (NAO p.24). Why it was passed over: the line the report quotes is "just two years after the November 2021 plan".

⑥ Transport for the North's written concerns of September 2024, and the January 2026 internal audit finding that lessons had not been applied consistently (NAO pp.27, 36). Why it was passed over: a governance review was under way, and the lessons were listed as 11 themes and 24 actions.

The point of escalation: October 2023, when the estimated cost of the HS2 Manchester section was transferred into this programme whole while Sheffield, Hull and Bradford were added to the scope (NAO pp.20, 23). What came across was the Millington to Manchester section, including Manchester Airport station and Piccadilly station (NAO pp.17, 22). After that step, cancelling the former HS2 section amounted to cancelling the future north-south line: the September 2024 alternatives study wrote the consequence down plainly, and the January 2026 announcement retained the section on that basis (NAO p.23). The July 2024 King's Speech revived the bill, and the route entered the procedure of legal text (NAO pp.21, 31). The table on page 22 sets the scope of the three announcements side by side, item by item, so which sections were added and which removed is readable at a glance (NAO p.22). That table is the physical evidence of this step. Between "the scope can change" and "this section cannot change" sits one document that transferred a cost. The signatory is the government, and the report names no one.

Failure chain:

Technical layer: the engineering itself did not fail. The break sits between the engineering breakdown and the commitment. In the three-phase plan, phase 2's parliamentary authorisation will not complete until around 2030, and the breakdown assumes the preceding section's scope will not move (NAO p.31). The interface is specific down to a platform: in November 2021 DfT widened the scope and funding of the Transpennine upgrade to include elements this programme would later use, among them a possible extra platform at Huddersfield and a freight passing loop (NAO p.34).

Organizational layer: ministers decide the scope; DfT and two arm's-length bodies deliver; the benefits have to be realised by the housing and communities department, local government and the combined authorities (NAO p.17). As of January 2026 the formal structure that would bring these parties together did not exist (NAO p.29), the delivery committee does not decide (NAO p.29), the sponsor board's effectiveness was challenged in writing in September 2024 (NAO p.27), and the team managing the interfaces explicitly holds no decision rights (NAO p.34).

Incentive layer: each term's books run on financial years, and the spending table is laid out by year (NAO p.25); the commitment runs on the whole programme, and the price base switched from 2019 to 2025 (NAO p.22); the £45 billion ceiling counts from 2026-27 and leaves the £410 million of earlier design spend outside it (NAO p.25). Three sets of units that do not convert: annual spend cannot show a cross-term commitment, a change of price base makes the years incomparable, and a moved start date puts earlier money outside the allowance.

The junction breaks between the organizational and incentive layers. The cost of a change has no one to sign for it, and the organizational layer lacks exactly the structure that could record a signature.

Minimum counterfactual: move the start of the £45 billion ceiling from 2026-27 back to 2015-16, and count both the money already spent and the investment written off by each scope change against that ceiling. One accounting action, inside the same January 2026 decision, requiring no luck: the year-by-year spend data sits in DfT's finance system, and the table on page 25 is its product. With the change, a change of the October 2023 kind would eat into the ceiling in the current period, and scope change would carry a price for the first time. The same ceiling would move written-off design fees from a historical footnote onto a line of the decision table. It does not settle who signs; it settles how much one change costs, a question nobody had answered. The ceiling is an instrument that already exists, and moving its start date needs no legislation, only a different date in the same decision.

Outcome and sources: NAO, Northern Powerhouse Rail, HC 1734, Session 2024-2026, 11 March 2026, 48 pages, ISBN 978-1-78604-664-2; signed by the Comptroller and Auditor General, Gareth Davies, on 3 March 2026. Audit basis: fieldwork from October 2025 to February 2026, 23 interviews, of which 7 with DfT and one each with Network Rail and HS2 Ltd (NAO p.42); document review covering the agendas and minutes of the DfT executive committee, investment committee, programme board and sponsor board (NAO p.44). The report does not cover the wider growth plan for the north or the progress of the Transpennine upgrade itself (NAO p.8). Its classification is a value for money audit, and its conclusions land on whether value for money was obtained, not on who was responsible (NAO p.4). Link in Appendix B, po-007. Every figure in this card comes from that report, and the page numbers are PDF pages.

Every scope change in Case 1 can also be filed term by term against this chapter's criteria: which term made it, the reason given, the previous term's investment written off, the new position of the delivery date. Four columns joined together make a chronicle of horizon mismatch, and the value of the chronicle is its symmetry. Each term's change had an adequate reason inside its own period (strategic adjustment, fiscal constraint, reordered priorities), and read in sequence they show one machine turning: every term changes the scope, and every change pushes the date back. The fuel is at criterion ③, since the cost of a change has no signatory. The previous term's investment is written off with nobody answerable for it on the books, the delivery date moves with nobody signing for the new position. Adding a column for the signatory, with "none" entered, is an action an audit can take immediately. On the day that column comes back empty in run after run, the mechanism is written in ink.

Evidence in ink has a multinational reference to borrow: the UK's national infrastructure commitments mechanism, where commitments are published as a register on a five-year cycle with a delivery status against each one, and the statutory funding of long-term projects in several countries, where the budget source is locked when the commitment is made. Both turn delivery from political will into a registration obligation. The register makes each term's commitments comparable and lets an unfulfilled commitment be named. Naming is not punishment, which needs procedure; its function is to keep a slipped delivery date in public view. A date may slip, but it may not slip out of sight.

docs.title: Case 2 (Manufacturing): This Year's Sales and a Stove Years Later
docs.text:
mn-002. Grade B material: a US Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) recall announcement (recall number 27-051, 29 October 2026) and the manufacturer's recall notice issued the same day. Both are announcement texts, not investigation reports: no design review records, no validation test protocol, no launch decision meeting and no signatories. Where the announcement is silent on an internal decision, this card writes "not in the public record" and fills nothing in.

Case ID: mn-002.

When and where: manufacturing window 14 June 2021 to 20 March 2023 (Ariston recall notice); sales window May 2021 to July 2026, through independent HVAC contractors and wholesale distributors across the United States (CPSC announcement); recall announced 29 October 2026. The failure site is the boiler room or utility room of a user's home, and the site of a licensed technician's service call.

What and who: Ariston Canada Inc. (formerly NTI Boilers Inc., Canada) is the manufacturer, and Ariston Thermo USA LLC (Providence, Rhode Island) the importer (CPSC announcement). The regulators are the US CPSC and Health Canada. After-sales service runs through independent licensed technicians, and the goods move through wholesale distributors. The announcement presses the notice obligation onto four separate roles: owners, selling installers, wholesalers and installing contractors (Ariston recall notice). The job titles and holders of the product safety and compliance functions are not in the announcement.

What they were doing: in 2026 the company was running three things at once. A safety notice in February 2026 on the FTG series, requiring an upgrade kit on every unit manufactured before 8 January 2026 (manufacturer's recall page). Sales of the affected batches had not stopped: the CPSC records sales from May 2021 through to July 2026, at $3,200 to $7,700 a unit (CPSC announcement). A recall of 29 October 2026, issued with repair parts moving into the channel: a new controller, part 6501575600 for FTVN and 6501575700 for TFTN, free to contractors, labour reimbursed under standard service practice, parts arriving about three days after contact (Ariston recall notice). The action required of the channel is two rounds of notice two weeks apart; the action required of wholesalers is to count and quarantine stock and report the list to the manufacturer (Ariston recall notice). On the manufacturer's own figure, the remedy means one visit to each of 6,329 units. All three workstreams share one unit of measure: output by unit, shipment by unit, repair by unit. Nothing is counted in operating cycles or in years installed.

The decision point:

One, 14 June 2021, the start of the manufacturing window. It is the manufacturing start date the announcement gives, and the only carrier of a "design frozen" moment this card can anchor to (Ariston recall notice). The dates, attendees and signed documents of the design review are not in the public record, and this card does not fill them. Ten models are affected: FTVN150, FTVN150C, FTVN199, FTVN199C, TFTN150 and TFTN199 from NTI, and EFTU-150WBN, 150WCN, 199WBN and 199WCN from HTP. The CPSC gives the serial numbers in two ranges, the first beginning in a date-like form and the second carrying a 3260 prefix; how the two ranges map onto the manufacturing window is not explained (CPSC announcement). The start points of the two texts do not line up either: sales records begin in May 2021, manufacturing records on 14 June 2021 (CPSC announcement, Ariston recall notice). The sales ledger and the manufacturing ledger are not on the same basis.

Two, 20 March 2023, the last batch left the factory (Ariston recall notice). For the next 40 months that stock kept selling in the channel, into July 2026 (CPSC announcement). Manufacturing stopped; release did not.

Three, 29 October 2026, the recall announcement (number 27-051). The remedy was settled the same day: replace the controller and revise the software, with the condensate tray replaced only where a technician's visual inspection finds it "appears damaged" (Ariston recall notice). This is the only decision in the case with a date, a text and a signatory, Ariston Canada Inc. issuing jointly with the CPSC and Health Canada. The economics of the remedy were fixed that day too: free per unit, labour reimbursed per visit, parts in about three days, cost following the installed base rather than the output (Ariston recall notice).

Four, 29 October 2026, the second instruction in the same notice: owners must not clear the lockout themselves, and operation may be restored only after assessment by a licensed technician (Ariston recall notice). That writes the field habit of "reset means the heat is back on" into a prohibition for the first time. The same notice leaves a way out: where the unit genuinely has to be used, fit smoke and carbon monoxide alarms first (Ariston recall notice). The sentence concedes that some units will keep running until they are repaired.

What was visible then:

  • Serial numbers and manufacturing records from June 2021: the CPSC gives two serial ranges, Ariston gives start and end dates and a total of "about 6,329" units. The two records cover each other, and their start points differ (CPSC announcement, Ariston recall notice).
  • Sales records from May 2021: channel type, price range and coverage (CPSC announcement).
  • The FTG notice of February 2026, a whole-batch notice drawing its retrospective boundary at "manufactured before 8 January 2026" (manufacturer's recall page). The format is established practice at this company. It has nothing to do with the condensate tray defect; the item shows only that the retrospective mechanism was running.
  • The 34 condensate tray rupture reports accumulated before the recall, 3 with the front cover detaching and 1 with a technician's jaw fractured (CPSC announcement).
  • The mechanism as the announcement describes it: on delayed ignition the tray cracks, unburned gas accumulates in the sealed chamber, and on ignition the front cover detaches suddenly (CPSC announcement). The units are unsafe before repair and must be taken out of service (Ariston recall notice).
  • The post-repair procedure, also in the announcement: replace the parts, inspect visually, run a combustion test with a flue gas analyser, and put a label in a conspicuous place so the next technician can see the unit has been repaired (Ariston recall notice).

Known only afterwards: the date, location and model behind each of the 34 reports; the material, thickness and supplier of the tray; the protocol and duration of design validation and ageing tests; the meetings, signatories and internal assessments behind the launch decision. None of the four is in the public record, and this card does not write them.

You are sitting in this position, with the material above in hand.

Stop here. Decide before you turn the page.

  1. What would you do? Write the action, not "pay more attention".
  2. Which item here are you most likely to miss, and why does it look unimportant?
  3. If you may set one checkpoint, when is it and what does it check?

What happened: 4,726 units in the United States and 2,261 in Canada (CPSC announcement); the manufacturer's own figure is "about 6,329" (Ariston recall notice). The two do not agree, and this card records both without forcing them to reconcile. The known count is 34 rupture reports, 3 front cover detachments and 1 fractured jaw (CPSC announcement); on the manufacturer's figure, 34 reports come to about 0.54% of 6,329 units (the book's calculation from the two announcements). The remedy is a free controller replacement, a technician's visual check of the tray, a combustion test and a label, with parts arriving about three days after contact (Ariston recall notice). The units of the two scales on this batch are the current period in units and unit price, the cross-period in ignition cycles and years installed, with no conversion table between them either.

The three questions, read back. The commonest answer to the first is "lengthen the validation period". In this case that action costs the following: the manufacturing window was only 21 months and the release window 62, so validation set by the manufacturing period cannot reach the fourth or fifth year after installation. The most commonly missed item under the second question is the instruction not to clear the lockout. It reads as an operating tip, and it is the only sentence in the case that records a precursor. The checkpoint under the third belongs at the moment the controller software was finalised, and what it checks is whether reset counts were being recorded.

Options ruled out: the announcement does not say what was considered at the time or on what grounds anything was rejected. The four items below are the boundaries of the option space the text allows one to infer, each with its basis noted, no reasons added. They fall on the product fix, the level of notice, the party executing and the sales cut-off.

One, replacing the condensate tray itself. Not adopted as a general measure: the kit is a controller and software, and the tray is replaced only where it looks damaged (Ariston recall notice).

Two, a safety notice only, with no recall. The same manufacturer used just such an upgrade kit notice for the FTG series in February 2026 (manufacturer's recall page); this time it used a recall, with "stop using immediately" (CPSC announcement).

Three, letting owners reset the unit or repair it themselves. Prohibited in plain terms: no clearing the lockout, no handling it themselves (Ariston recall notice). The cost is that every loss of heat becomes a service call, with the waiting time falling on the household.

Four, selling off the existing stock and then dealing with it. Sales stopped in July 2026, and federal law prohibits the sale of a recalled product (CPSC announcement, Ariston recall notice).

Early signals:

① Delayed ignition trips the lockout. The announcement goes out of its way to say "do not clear any lockout", which indicates that resetting is a common action in the field (Ariston recall notice). A lockout is a state the service procedure can handle on site; reporting it as a fault requires a different protocol. Why it was passed over: a lockout is the most common boiler service call, and a reset is standard practice.

② The tray cracks only after delayed ignition, and a single event leaves a crack in a plastic part visible only with the unit opened up (CPSC announcement). Why it was passed over: handled as a component replacement, inside the warranty terms.

③ Three front cover detachments. That is no longer a component-level fault, since the cover flies off and injury outside the boiler room is plausible. Why it was passed over: 3 events across an installed base of several thousand is about 0.05% (the book's calculation from the announcement figures), and the ratio reads as a one-off.

④ The same manufacturer's safety notice channel had been used three times before, with the retrospective boundary always written as a manufacturing date: the TFT seal in July 2018, the TRX burner door studs in March 2025, the FTG upgrade kit in February 2026 (manufacturer's recall page). The channel works. What is missing is not a channel but a metric that counts resets.

The point of escalation: 29 October 2026, the moment "new controller plus revised software" was chosen as the remedy. Before that, the risk sat in the strength of the tray across 6,329 units. After it, the risk sits in one execution condition, that every unit has been visited once. The announcement can guarantee only two rounds of channel notice and the wholesalers' stock quarantine (Ariston recall notice); reaching the end user still runs through a contractor, and all four roles act on their own initiative. After the recall the units do not move, so the risk scatters across thousands of homes at their installation addresses (CPSC announcement). The announcement also leaves a flexibility clause: some units will keep running until they are repaired (Ariston recall notice). The clause exists to make the recall executable, and its cost is that the risk deadline moves from the recall date to the day the last unit is visited, a day in no document. This step has a date, a text and a signatory, and no way back.

Failure chain:

Technical layer: on delayed ignition the unburned gas accumulates in the sealed chamber, the pressure releases through the front cover when it ignites, and the tray cracks first along that stress path. The remedy changes the ignition control logic and not the tray's strength: between the number of delayed ignitions the controller allows and the number the tray can take, there is no calibrated figure (CPSC announcement, Ariston recall notice). The judgement is by eye, since a technician's visual inspection decides whether the tray is damaged and the announcement sets no quantified criterion (Ariston recall notice). Confirmation after the repair is also a one-off: a combustion test with an analyser and a label, with no further sampling (Ariston recall notice).

Organizational layer: manufacture in Canada, import into the United States, service through an independent contractor network, and a defect information path that runs contractor to wholesaler to manufacturer to regulator. To reach the end user the recall has two rounds of channel notice and nothing else; the requirement on installers is at least two rounds, two weeks apart (Ariston recall notice).

Incentive layer: the current period is measured in units and unit price, at $3,200 to $7,700 a unit; the cost in ignition cycles and years installed. The warranty counts years, fatigue counts cycles, and the two rulers have different sources. The recall's accounts count units and service visits, and they open only after the recall date (CPSC announcement).

The junction breaks between the technical and incentive layers. Because the reset count was never recorded, per-unit accounting looks entirely sound, and the 34 reports are the shape that blank accumulated into.

Minimum counterfactual: before the first production run, make "lockout reset count" a factory-recorded field in the controller, shipped with the unit. One action, taken before June 2021, requiring no luck: the controller already handles the delayed ignition and lockout decision, and the 2026 remedy changes exactly that software (Ariston recall notice). With the record in place, a cumulative reset count reaching a threshold would bring the tray into view without waiting for 34 reports. The same record makes "which batch fails first" into comparable data, and nobody can make that comparison today. The cost is one data field and one software addition; the return is turning 34 reports from a count into a rate. It does not change the strength of the tray, only the date on which it is found. This card does not claim the action was considered at the time.

Outcome and sources: CPSC, NTI and HTP Brand Gas Boilers Recalled Due to Risk of Serious Injury or Death from Fire, Carbon Monoxide (CO) Poisoning and Impact Hazards, recall number 27-051, 29 October 2026; Ariston Canada Inc. (formerly NTI Boilers), recall notice of the same date, ntiboilers.com/safety-recalls/ftvn-tftn-product-recall. Link in Appendix B, mn-002. The two texts were published on the same day and serve as checks on each other: one for the regulatory record, one for execution detail. Grade B: both are announcements without the evidence chain of an investigation report, so the factual statements here stay inside those two texts, and the card describes no internal decision process because no verifiable text exists. Where the two disagree (4,726 plus 2,261 against about 6,329) the figures are recorded side by side without conversion, and no media retelling was used.

The material for Case 2 stops at the announcement, and the protocol and duration of accelerated ageing tests are not in the public record; this passage covers only the general method. An accelerated test compresses time by amplifying stress (high temperature, high humidity, high cycling), and the conversion depends on an ageing model that extrapolates the relation between stress and life. The model's assumptions are the gap between test and reality. The management answer to that gap is settled practice in reliability engineering: keep a real-time tracking sample alongside the accelerated test, a batch of early product held for long-term observation, with measured life backfilling the model's parameters. The cost of the sample is storage and follow-up; the return is a conversion factor for the next generation that stands on measurement. From Case 2's angle, the 34 rupture reports were themselves a late backfill, paid for with a user's stove and a technician's jaw.

Backfilling has a public version in consumer products, in the relation between the CPSC's incident report database (the public report stream at saferproducts.gov) and the trigger for a recall. The stream aggregates use across millions of households into a statistical signal (the six hundred power bank reports in Chapter 16's fourth case were its product), and the timeliness of the signal sets the lag before a recall: a defect with few, scattered reports, like the 34 here, waits longer. Consumer products therefore have a public route out of horizon mismatch. The aggregation speed of defect reports is the error-discovery speed of the whole product line, and the firm-side counterpart is to monitor the stream and aggregate by its own model numbers (Chapter 20's two-way flow of the industry library, on its third appearance here).

docs.title: The Evidence Gap
docs.text:
First-hand deep cases in horizon mismatch run into two difficulties. In political and infrastructure cases the decision chain is scattered through audit and budget documents from several administrations, and the cost of collection and reassembly is high. In corporate cases the forward cost (technical debt, deferred maintenance) is almost never written up as a postmortem, because writing it up hands the successor a bill, which is exactly the self-concealment this mechanism relies on. The A-grade deep cases in this book's library are currently mostly public audits, and the directions for further collection are renewal reviews by legislatures and research on long-tail losses in insurance.

Beside the gap, four extrapolations, labelled mechanism extrapolation rather than case card. Extrapolation one, software technical debt: every expedient implementation borrows time from the future, since the benefit of shipping lands at once and the maintenance cost accrues like quarterly interest; the interest is paid by everyone who takes the code over, the principal by a rewrite years later. The check under criterion ③ is a technical debt ledger (what is owed, at what interest, due when) with a receipt at handover. Extrapolation two, infrastructure maintenance: roads and pipe networks are designed in decades and maintained on annual budgets, and deferred maintenance shows up year by year in the surface and in burst mains (Chapter 29's home ground), while on the books it stays a discretionary line. The check is a deferred maintenance ledger and statutory funding. Extrapolation three, pensions and population: the generational mismatch between contributors and recipients is the century-scale version, with this period's contributions supporting this period's pensions and the generational cost paid by a population structure decades away; the check is actuarial disclosure, together with the political difficulty of a contract between generations. Extrapolation four, the asset management industry: the quarterly cycle of subscriptions and redemptions is mismatched against the multi-year cycle of value investing, and managers are pushed into trading to the rhythm of flows, setting the return on current assets under management against the long-term return. The check is a longer lock-up and a longer performance reconciliation period. The four cover four time scales, from code to civilization, and share one chain of criteria; converting them into real cards is also on the collection list.

The common solution across the extrapolations has a cross-scale abstraction worth stating. The terminal form of governing horizon mismatch is to turn the future cost into today's cash flow (statutory funding, depreciation and amortization, provisions), so that the future line appears in this period's cost table. Cash flow is the only language both markets and politics hear, accounting and budgeting being the common inputs of both systems, and visibility (Device 2) is the forward post of that conversion: first the number, then the money, then the liability. The order cannot be scrambled. Visibility without a number is a slogan, visibility without money is a ledger, visibility with money but no liability is a bad debt.

docs.title: 4 Earliest Signals
docs.text:
Six weak signals, each with the reason it usually gets passed over.

  1. The budget table has no line for future cost, or the line exists in name only. Reason given: "the distant future cannot be estimated."
  2. No table compares the decision-maker's term against the consequence cycle. Reason given: "who would make such a table."
  3. Key milestones cluster before the term boundary, and every benefit milestone sits after it. Reason given: "that is how the plan is staged."
  4. A key post changes hands in mid-project, and the handover contains no unfulfilled obligations. Reason given: "the handover was done to procedure."
  5. "The next five-year plan will deal with it" becomes the closing sentence of this plan. Reason given: "we are phasing delivery."
  6. Maintenance and capability-building spend is classed as discretionary and finishes last in the queue year after year. Reason given: "protect the priorities first." (Chapter 29 picks up here.)

Put the six back against this chapter's cases and extrapolations. Signal one, the missing future cost line, matches Case 1: across the many scope changes on the rail programme, written-off investment was recorded in history and never on the current decision table. Signal two, the absent term comparison, matches everything: a table setting term against consequence cycle is the one table this chapter should standardise, and the absence of that table is criterion ② admitting itself. Signal three, asymmetric milestones, matches Case 2: the launch milestone sits inside the assessment period, the defect exposure milestone outside the warranty. Signal four, a handover without obligations, matches Case 1: the handover between administrations carried no statement of what was being taken on from the previous term's commitments. Signal five, the next five-year plan, matches extrapolation one: every entry in the technical debt ledger is annotated "to be repaid at the next refactor". Signal six, maintenance last, matches extrapolation two: the discretion in a discretionary line is exactly the exit horizon mismatch reserves for itself.

Reorder the six by cost of evidence. Signals one and six are cheapest, needing only the budget table. Signals three and four are middling, needing the plan and the handover documents. Signals two and five are most expensive, needing comparison across terms and textual analysis. The starting recommendation is signal one: open the budget table and look for a column on future cost. Its absence can be confirmed without any permission, and the act of confirming it is the first image of this mechanism inside your own organization.

One snapshot mechanism on the time axis deserves a rule of its own: an interim bill at the midpoint of the term, when the forward liabilities of the current term are made visible and published once. It gives the term a reconciliation point, so the hidden cost of the current period is exposed once in the middle rather than saved as a surprise for the successor, and its institutional prototype is the mid-year budget review in the public sector. The interim bill and Device 1's handover list are the same list at two moments: half at the midpoint, all at exit. The difference between the two, the liability added in the second half of the term, is the trace left by the final-year sprint, and the trace is itself a soft constraint on sprinting.

docs.title: 5 Prevention
docs.text:
Device 1: a bill handover system. When a key post changes hands, the handover is required to contain a list of unfulfilled obligations: what was promised, what is owed, when the cost falls due, where the money is. The list is signed for by the incoming holder, and gaps are completed by the outgoing one, which puts Chapter 30's handover onto a time axis. The force of the list depends on how seriously the signature is taken: signing means the incoming holder confirms the list is true, and a false list can be pursued.

Device 2: make the forward liability visible. The forward cost of technical debt, deferred maintenance, and ageing population and assets is converted each year into a note to the current statements and published. The figure can be disputed; its absence cannot be. Visibility does not buy precision. It buys the change from nothing to something, which gives every postponement a line that can be cited.

Device 3: a cross-period signatory. Create a post accountable for the result five years out (a long-term value officer, a steward of legacy assets), with every assessment metric defined outside the term and the protection of the post written into the charter. The post answers criterion ② directly: the term is shorter than the consequence cycle, and the period of responsibility can still be longer than the term.

Device 4: a milestone symmetry review. At plan approval, check the distribution of milestones: where the gap between a decision milestone and a benefit milestone exceeds the term, require an account of the mechanism that will carry delivery across the gap (a dedicated body, statutory funding, a treaty commitment), and where no account can be given, shorten the commitment.

The four devices against this chapter's cases and extrapolations. Device 1 on Case 1: make the handover between administrations carry a schedule of commitments assumed, with every commitment of the previous term marked carried over, revised or dropped, and a signed reason for each drop. Device 2 on extrapolation two: convert deferred maintenance into an interval figure in the notes to the annual budget, and publish the curve of the backlog year by year. Device 3 on extrapolation three: place the signatory for actuarial disclosure outside the current budget department, with protection of the post in the institution's charter. Device 4 on Case 2: bring the exposure period into the decision table at the product freeze, aligning the launch schedule with the exposure cycle and calibrating the warranty terms to it.

The failure modes of the four devices. The bill handover dies for want of competition over the completeness of the list, since the outgoing holder submits a template of empty lines and the incoming one signs it. The patch is a two-source list: the incoming holder builds his own from his own enquiry, the two are read together, and the differences are the points of suspicion. Visibility of the forward liability dies of drift in the basis, with the method changed every year and the history made incomparable. The patch is a frozen basis with a change register (the same as Device 4 in Chapter 12). The cross-period signatory dies of the ornamental post, where the holder attends ceremonies and never vetoes. The patch is a statutory veto list, naming which decisions require that signature, written into the charter. The milestone symmetry review dies of rhetorical justification, where the account of the cross-period mechanism fills up with vision language. The patch is hard fields: the establishment number of the dedicated body, the account code of the statutory fund, the clause number of the treaty text. If none of the three can be filled in, shorten the commitment. All four patches share one check-up question: at the most recent cross-period commitment, who was in the room on the due date.

The order of installation matters too: Device 2 first (visibility, since the number is the foundation of everything after it), then Device 1 (handover, hanging the list on an existing process), then Device 4 (milestone review, applied to new plans at once), and Device 3 last (the cross-period post, the largest piece of institutional engineering). The order runs opposite to Chapter 27, which starts with the zero-based question, and the reason lies in where each mechanism is cut open: escalation's lesion is in the argument for a decision, mismatch's in the measurement of one. Change the question first in one case, change the ledger first in this one. Neither operation should wait, since the cost of mismatch grows every quarter, so the real answer is to schedule both first steps in the next quarter: one quarter to install the zero-based question and the forward liability note, at almost no cost. The review question is narrower than feasibility: who will be in the room on the due date.

docs.title: 6 Boundaries with Adjacent Mechanisms
docs.text:
With the invisibility of maintenance (Chapter 29): horizon mismatch explains why maintenance gets cut, since the cost of the cut lands outside the term, and the invisibility of maintenance explains why cutting it does not hurt, since the cut cannot be seen. The two chapters use different faces of the same cases: the delay at the Palace of Westminster (po-005) belongs to Chapter 29, and the multi-term structure behind the delay belongs here.

With sunk cost and escalation (Chapter 27): escalation pushes the cost further onto the successor, since the reset project accumulates a fresh set of bills, and horizon mismatch guarantees that the successor can clean up without ever holding the predecessor to account. The criterion: if the decision-maker has to be present in some form to bear the consequence, the structure corrects itself. What fails to correct is this chapter's territory.

With misaligned incentives (Chapter 17): a term shorter than the consequence cycle is misaligned incentives in the time dimension. Chapter 17's accounting for externalities, seen across periods, takes the shape of this chapter's bill handover and forward liability disclosure.

docs.title: 7 Five Self-Checks
docs.text:
1. Of the decisions your organization is making now, which year is the latest in which a cost falls due? Where will the person making the decision be when it does?
  2. How much of your term remains? Of the things you are pushing forward, how many pay off after the term ends?
  3. At the last handover of a post, did you receive a list of unfulfilled obligations? Did you ever hand one over?
  4. In your organization's budget, which line holds the money that must be spent five years from now? If there is no such line, whose surprise is that money turning into?
  5. Would you be willing to come back in five years and give your successor an account of what you are signing off now? List the items you would not.

docs.title: Chapter 29 The Invisibility of Maintenance
docs.text:
What this chapter covers: why maintenance is always the first thing cut, and why the arrears arrive all at once years later; four sites, the backlog booked as a liability, and a wall around the maintenance budget. When to turn back: budget-cut discussions, approvals to run equipment in a known-defective state, and the weeks after some "sudden" failure. Estimated reading time: 50 minutes.

Maintenance is the one class of work whose success is that nothing happens. A gear replaced and a gear left alone turn the same machine just as smoothly today; a seal repaired and a seal ignored leave the same wall just as dry today. Its output is the absence of events, and absence is the only cost line whose value cannot be verified in the period that paid for it. So when budgets tighten, maintenance is cut first. Nobody has to be incompetent for that to happen. It is the only line whose removal leaves no trace in the current quarter. Interest on the deferral compounds with the age of the equipment, and the bill is delivered years later in a single instalment, in the form of a breakdown, a shutdown, a collapse, or an explosion. The public and the people who decide call that an accident.

Put the delivery mechanism more coldly. A maintenance backlog is the one variety of organizational liability that comes with its own detonator. A financial default is procedural, handled through collection, litigation, restructuring. A maintenance default is physical. It accumulates inside the material and is redeemed under stress, and the redemption point is chosen by physics rather than by a creditor. Two consequences follow, and both belong on the page. The timing is not negotiable: no extension, no restructuring, wall thickness at zero is at zero. The damage cannot be apportioned: a collapse does not select who is inside the building. Together they argue that a maintenance backlog should outrank a financial debt of the same size in governance priority. Financial debt can be carried along. Physical debt only presses down. A balance sheet cannot see the difference, which is what Device 2 in this chapter is for: writing the difference into the statement.

The invisibility itself has parts, and the parts differ by role, because each role is blind for its own reason. The user cannot see the waterproofing under the decorative layer. The manager cannot see the backlog scattered across the blank cells of a thousand work orders and asset registers. The auditor cannot see it, because a financial audit reads expenditure and not condition. The regulator cannot see it, because inspection samples cover a fraction of the estate. Stack the four and the backlog acquires the most complete concealment an organization can offer: no role sees the whole of it, and every role believes its own layer is fine. The general tool that breaks the concealment is direct measurement of condition, the measured corrosion depth, wall thickness, insulation resistance. Measurement turns the invisible into a number, and a number breaks all four invisibilities at once. Device 3 in this chapter, the condition trigger, is that breaking made into procedure.

docs.title: 1 What It Is
docs.text:
Definition: the invisibility of maintenance means that time and probability sit between what maintenance produces (availability, service life, safety) and what is spent on it, so that no appraisal period can measure the elasticity. Deferred maintenance is therefore a hidden liability shared by every kind of organization: governments, companies, households.

Three trigger criteria. Any one of them appearing means the mechanism has started:

① Maintenance done well shows no value, and the organization has no mechanism for booking "nothing went wrong" anywhere (the interface to Device 1 of Chapter 20);

② When budgets tighten, the maintenance line is cut first and restored last;

③ The consequences of the backlog arrive concentrated, as sudden failures, and the public and the decision-makers call them accidents.

docs.title: 2 How It Grows
docs.text:
Three generating conditions.

Condition one: no output metric. Time and probability sit between what maintenance produces and what it costs, so elasticity inside an appraisal period is zero. With no output ledger (Chapter 20), maintenance is scored as producing nothing in every budget round.

Condition two: external invisibility. The interior state of equipment, corrosion depth, remaining lubrication, insulation ageing, seal ageing, is invisible to users, visitors and auditors alike. Anything that shows poorly is weak in resource allocation, and maintenance is the least visible of all asset work.

Condition three: the decision-maker's term is shorter than the backlog's maturity (Chapter 28's time condition). The bill for cutting maintenance always lands on the next person, and the next person's appraisal does not cover it either.

docs.title: Case 1 (Aviation): The Debt Loaded into the Cargo Hold
docs.text:
Case ID: av-035.

When and where: 14:13:42 on 11 May 1996 (US Eastern Daylight Time). ValuJet Flight 592 lifted off from Miami International Airport (MIA) and about ten minutes later went into the Florida Everglades; the main impact crater lay roughly 17 miles northwest of MIA (NTSB AAR-97/06 p.15, p.18). The work site is a month earlier: SabreTech's Miami repair station, and ValuJet's cargo area at MIA.

What and who: ValuJet Airlines (a 14 CFR Part 121 carrier); SabreTech, Inc. (a 14 CFR Part 145 domestic repair station, certificate RD3R811L, first issued 3 December 1969, operating under the SabreTech name from 1 February 1996, p.75). In the accident month the station had 265 permanent employees and 351 contract workers, 57 percent contract (p.76); of the 587 people who booked hours against these three MD-80s, 442 came from six labour contractors (p.76). The positions at issue: the mechanic who signed the MECH SIGNOFF block of work card 0069; the SabreTech inspector who signed the Final Inspection block of the non-routine card; the logistics supervisor; the shipping clerk; the receiving clerk; and the three ValuJet technical representatives assigned to the station. Aircraft type DC-9-32, registration N904VJ.

What they were doing: On 31 January 1996 ValuJet bought two MD-82s (N802VV, N803VV), and on 1 February a third, an MD-83 (N830VV). All three were ferried to the SabreTech Miami station for modification and repair (p.18). One task was to check whether the cabin chemical oxygen generators had passed twelve years from the date of manufacture (p.18). The check found that every generator on N830VV expired in 1998 or later, while most of those on N802VV and N803VV were already out of date (p.20). ValuJet therefore ordered all generators on the two aircraft replaced, under engineering order E.O. 15-3520-B0820 and routine work card #0069, "Chemical Oxygen Generator, Removal/Installation" (p.20). The card was taken from the one McDonnell Douglas issued for the same task, with the content unchanged; ValuJet had not used it before (p.20 n.13). Work started in mid-March (p.27). The recorded removals on N802VV came to 72 generators, 67 three-mask and 5 two-mask, most built in 1979 and 1980; N803VV has no serial-by-serial record (p.28). The contract set delivery of N802VV for 24 April and N803VV for 30 April, with $2,500 deducted for each day late (p.27 n.25). A station memorandum of 26 April put all maintenance personnel, management included, on seven-day weeks until the three MD-80s were delivered, because of the workload (p.30 n.29). Sign-off on the cards came on 30 April for N803VV and 5 May for N802VV (p.28). Both aircraft were then added to ValuJet's operations specifications and left: N803VV was added and departed the same day, 1 May, and N802VV was added on 7 May and departed on 9 May (p.28 n.26). On the day the aircraft left, five boxes were still on the floor of the receiving area.

The decision point: The first is the morning of 4 May 1996, when a supervisor handed the mechanic the task of signing card 0069; he signed the N802VV card on 5 May (p.28, p.30). He said the caps were not discussed at the signing, and that his attention was "entirely on the airworthiness of an aircraft with new generators installed" (p.30). The card carried no inspector sign-off block, because the task was not on ValuJet's list of required inspections (p.26). His own count of removals was 30 to 35; the recorded figure for N802VV is 72. According to the station's quality control director, 72 people booked about 910 hours against the work covered by card 0069, the station had no consistent shift handover briefing procedure, and no system tracked which specific tasks each shift performed (p.28, p.29).

The second is the signature in the Final Inspection block of the non-routine card, in the same period. The SabreTech inspector said he knew at the time of signing that the generators needed caps, had raised it with the shop lead, and was told that the SabreTech supervisor and the ValuJet technical representative both knew and "would handle it in the warehouse". He signed after receiving that answer (pp. 30–31).

The third is 7 or 8 May 1996, when the logistics supervisor came to the receiving hold area and ordered the floor cleared. The reason was a prospective customer audit, after another customer had written up the area's housekeeping as deficient; he said he did not know what was in the boxes, and he gave no instruction for disposing of them (p.32).

The fourth is 8 May 1996, when the shipping clerk asked the logistics supervisor whether he should seal the boxes and get them ready for Atlanta. The answer was "Okay, that sounds good to me." (pp. 32–33). The clerk redistributed the generators among five boxes, filled the top of each with 2 to 3 inches of bubble wrap, sealed them, and affixed blank SabreTech address labels and ValuJet COMAT labels reading "aircraft parts" (p.33). The next day he asked the receiving clerk to make out an air waybill and handed him a note asking for "Oxygen Canisters - Empty". The clerk abbreviated Oxygen to Oxy, put Empty in quotation marks, and dated the document 5/10/96 (p.33). On 11 May a truck delivered the shipment to ValuJet's ramp, and ValuJet employees signed for it (pp. 33–34).

What was visible then: ① Work card 0069, a seven-step process, step 2 reading "if the generator has not been expended, install the shipping cap on the firing pin" (p.24). The card omits step 8 of the McDonnell Douglas manual, "store or dispose of the oxygen generator" (p.25). It carries no hazardous materials marking and no requirement for an inspector's signature (p.26). ② Section 2.D of the McDonnell Douglas MD-80 maintenance manual 35-22-01: no generator may be disposed of before it has been fired and fully expended, and disposal requires securing it in a noncombustible fixture, pulling the release pin, and waiting for the shell to cool (p.25). ③ The green "Repairable" tag on the generator itself (Form M021), with "Reason for Removal" reading "out dated", "out of date", "expired" (p.27). ④ The four tag definitions on page 44 of section five of SabreTech's inspection procedures manual: green means awaiting repair, red means scrap awaiting disposal, must be segregated, must carry an inspector's signature (p.77). ⑤ Around 10 April 1996, a ValuJet technical representative saw generators on a parts rack without caps, warned the mechanic that they would catch fire, and suggested disposing of them "with the rest of SabreTech's hazardous waste". He then went to the inspector, the supervisor and the project manager; the boxes were moved more than three weeks after that first approach, and he did not know where they went (p.31). ⑥ The five cartons on the receiving floor on 8 May, and one fact about them: no written procedure at the time required anyone delivering items to that area to state the contents or whether they were hazardous (p.32). Information learned afterwards: of roughly 144 generators removed, only about 6 were reported as expended, and the other 138 or so have no disposal record (p.28); the SabreTech Miami station never trained its employees in hazardous materials recognition or in air transport, and ValuJet's policy of carrying no hazardous materials was never passed to the contractor (p.79, p.136); four other MD-80 operators each had a practice, Alaska requiring on-site firing and disposal from 1992 and American from 1994, Delta and TWA fitting caps and shipping the generators back to base as hazardous materials by COMAT (p.106).

You are in the seat now, with the material above in front of you.

Stop here. Decide before you turn the page.

  1. What would you do? Write the action, not "pay more attention".
  2. Which item here are you most likely to miss, and why does it look unimportant?
  3. If you may set one checkpoint, when is it and what does it check?

What happened: At 14:10:03 the cockpit voice recorder picks up an unidentified sound and the captain asks "What was that?"; at 14:10:22, "we need to go back to Miami"; at 14:11:12 a flight attendant shouts "completely on fire"; at 14:12:45 calls from the ground go unanswered; at 14:13:42 the aircraft hits the ground (pp. 16–17). All 110 people aboard died: 2 pilots, 3 flight attendants, 105 passengers (p.15). The aircraft was destroyed, valued at $4 million; salvage and cleanup cost more than $10 million (p.34). Back to the three questions. The commonest answer to the first is "add a disposal step to the work card", and that step costs nothing, because the McDonnell Douglas card already had step 8 and it was dropped in transcription. The item most easily missed under the second is the pair of quotation marks around Empty: the receiving clerk added them, they look like a spelling habit, and they wrote "unexpended" as "empty". The checkpoint under the third belongs at the moment the maintenance site hands material over to the freight staging area, where no written handover procedure existed (p.32).

Options ruled out: Firing the generators on site: Alaska and American already did so before the accident, SabreTech was doing this task for the first time, the caps were not in stock, and under the contract they were "peculiar expendables" to be supplied by ValuJet or separately agreed (p.29 n.28, p.106). Fitting caps and shipping the generators back to base as hazardous materials: the Delta and TWA practice, which requires the carrier to be authorized to accept hazardous materials, while ValuJet's policy was to carry none (p.106, p.80). Handing the shipment to Dangerous Goods Consultants for packing, labelling and documentation: SabreTech held a contract with the company and the shipping clerk could call it directly, but this shipment never entered that flow (p.80, p.33). Waiting for ValuJet's Atlanta warehouse to decide on disposal: a technical representative called on 9 May to coordinate and was told to wait until 13 May to settle who would do the inventory (p.32). Using the contract's written authorization clause: the service agreement stated that equipment removed and not reinstalled was retained by SabreTech and could be disposed of only with the customer representative's written authorization, and that if no authorization came within thirty days SabreTech had to notify the customer in writing of its intention to dispose of the items (p.32 n.36). That path was written in the same contract. Nobody started it.

Early signals: ① On 10 April 1996 the technical representative saw the uncapped generators and reported them up the chain, to the inspector, the supervisor and the project manager, all three of whom later denied having been approached; the boxes were moved more than three weeks later (p.31). What overrode it: the matter "had already been reported", and each position assumed the next step sat with someone else. ② No caps in stock: a supervisor told the mechanic the company had none (p.29), and another supervisor said nobody had raised the need with him (p.29). What overrode it: this was the first time the task had been done, and under the contract the caps were not SabreTech's stock responsibility. ③ Life-limited parts should have carried a red tag under the manual, meaning scrap, segregated, inspector's signature, and what they actually carried was a green tag, meaning awaiting repair (p.77, p.27); the shipping clerk read green as meaning empty (p.33). What overrode it: the tag read differently at different positions, and no crosswalk table existed. ④ On 22 and 24 December 1995, two fires broke out in packages of expired generators at Delta's Atlanta maintenance station; one was found to have its safety clip not fully inserted, and Delta moved to on-site disposal on 26 January 1996 as a result (p.107 and n.114). What overrode it: the two fires were not reportable to the FAA, and they were not reported. ⑤ On 10 August 1986 a DC-10 at O'Hare was destroyed by a fire from generators packed on the backs of COMAT seatbacks in the cargo hold; the FAA issued a notice on the 13th of that month, the notice lapsed a year later, and no periodic follow-up replaced it (pp. 107–108). What overrode it: a one-time notice. ⑥ On 10 February 1981 the Safety Board recommended, on the same class of cargo hold, that the FAA reassess Class D certification and either require detection and suppression or require a liner able to contain such a fire (A-81-012) (p.41). Fifteen years later the forward hold of this aircraft was still Class D.

The point of escalation: The oral approval of 8 May 1996. Sealing the boxes and labelling them with a COMAT tag reading "aircraft parts" turned five boxes from maintenance residue awaiting disposal into company material: the identity changed from "to be disposed of" to "to be delivered", and the action from "dismantle and destroy" to "transport and deliver". From that moment every downstream position, the receiving clerk, the truck driver, the ramp lead, the hold loader, the first officer, handled company material only. Before it, every node still held an interface for reversal: the card could have had step 8 added, the inspector could have declined to sign, the boxes could have stayed on the rack. After the sealing, one reversal interface remained, the commodity description on the air waybill.

Failure chain: Technical layer: the generator went without its shipping cap, the retaining pin shifted in handling and the generator fired; the shell's operating temperature runs 450 to 500 degrees Fahrenheit (p.21); the DC-9 forward cargo hold is Class D under 14 CFR 25.857(d), a class that requires neither smoke detection nor fixed fire suppression (p.40). Organizational layer: the work card was missing the disposal step (p.25); an item outside the required inspection list had no inspector signature (p.26); a life-limited part carried the wrong tag (p.27, p.77); the receiving area had no written handover procedure (p.32); contractor staff had no hazardous materials training (p.79, p.136); ValuJet technical representatives were contractually barred from supervising or directing the contractor's employees (p.85). Incentive layer: the delivery deadlines and the $2,500 daily penalty (p.27 n.25), the seven-day weeks (p.30 n.29), a customer audit imminent after the area's housekeeping had already been written up (p.32); and the hold had no cargo restraint, so the boxes pressed on the tyres (p.34). One relation between the layers is worth recording: every link in the technical layer is written in a manual, and every link in the organizational layer is written in nobody's job description. The break at the junction sits between the organizational and incentive layers: the floor was cleared to pass an audit, the boxes were sealed to clear the floor, and the missing disposal process was filled that day by the act of shipping.

Minimum counterfactual: On 9 May 1996 the shipping clerk writes not "Oxy Cannisters - Empty" but "Unexpended chemical oxygen generators, oxidizing solid, Class 5.1", and hands the shipment to the contracted dangerous goods agent for documentation. One action, one position, doable that day, no spares needed, no additional approval (p.80 records that the clerk had authority to contact the agent directly), and nobody required to admit a previous error. The downstream consequence is certain: ValuJet's policy was to carry no hazardous materials, so a Class 5.1 oxidizer on the paperwork would have kept this shipment off any aircraft at any receiving dock (p.80).

Outcome and sources: 110 people died (p.15). The report finds SabreTech's failure to prepare, package and identify the unexpended chemical oxygen generators correctly to be a cause of the accident (p.133), and ValuJet's inadequate oversight of SabreTech to be a cause as well (p.137); SabreTech surrendered its repair station certificate on 15 January 1997 (p.96). Primary source: NTSB, Aircraft Accident Report NTSB/AAR-97/06, adopted 1997-08-19, link in Appendix B av-035. Page numbers here are PDF pages (printed page equals PDF page minus 14).

The arrears chain in Case 1 carries one more reading, at the level of industry structure. Outsourced maintenance is the normal form in aviation, especially among low-cost carriers. The efficiency gain is immediate, in labour and in parts. The boundary of quality responsibility stays blurred, with the contractor's disposal process, the carrier's acceptance check and the regulator's classification all three incomplete. The revisions the industry made after ValuJet, hazardous materials classification for maintenance residues and contractor qualification and oversight, were in substance an attempt to restore visibility to the outsourced chain: maintenance can be subcontracted, and responsibility cannot be subcontracted with it. Generalized across industries, wherever maintenance is outsourced, in property, equipment or IT, the acceptance checklist must include disposal items, what happens to the old parts and how the residue is stored. A disposal backlog kills as reliably as a repair backlog.

The blank in the record in Case 2 has a manufacturing-process detail worth enlarging. The opening of the door plug for riveting rework was a legitimate temporary state inside the flow. The backlog is created by the closing of that state going unrecorded: no work record on reinstallation, no trigger for a re-check. Legitimate temporary states are everywhere in manufacturing, openings left for access during servicing, fasteners left loose for a trial fit. Their shared hole is that the closing action has no checkpoint. The fix is at process level: a temporary opening must be registered, opening paired with closing, and any location whose closing is unregistered enters the pre-delivery re-check list automatically. Paired registration turns every legitimate temporary state into a trackable object, and the backlog, an opening never closed, acquires a ledger.

The palace in Case 3 offers a governance comparison worth writing down. The British national heritage system never stopped assessing the building's condition, and the annual reports all describe the ageing. The backlog is a failure to get scheduled. That failure is half Chapter 18 (diffusion of responsibility) and half Chapter 28 (horizon mismatch); this chapter adds a third half, losing the priority competition. In a budget ranking, maintenance competes with growth spending, new projects get ribbon-cuttings, and maintenance gets no ceremony. The competition comes out the same way in most years. The levers that change the result are Device 2 in this chapter, booking the backlog as a liability so the figure is nailed into each year's budget document, and a narrative lever, rewriting maintenance from a cost into the preservation of value, since keeping a heritage building's value is itself an output. Both are slow variables, and the year a slow variable starts sets the year the backlog curve turns. Start one year late and the curve climbs for one more year.

The progressive collapse in Case 4 comes with an engineering point that belongs in this chapter. What makes progressive collapse frightening is the concealment of load transfer: one connection fails, the load quietly reroutes, the overload accumulates in the next member, and nothing shows on the outside. A maintenance backlog runs the same pattern. The interest is never settled, because there is no interim payment event; it moves inside the structure, from this waterproofing to that rebar, from this cover layer to that concrete, and the ledger of the transfers is published only on the day of collapse. The one tool that breaks the transfers is direct condition measurement, Device 3's condition trigger. Measurement is a snapshot of the internal transfers, and the frequency of snapshots sets how long a transfer can hide.

docs.title: Case 2 (Aviation): Assembly Without a Reinstallation Record
docs.text:
av-030. Alaska Airlines 1282, a Boeing 737-9 (N704AL), 5 January 2024, Portland. NTSB investigation report (AIR-25-04; the PDF was downloaded and read for this book): during the climb the left mid-exit door plug separated, the cabin depressurised rapidly, and the aircraft returned safely; 7 passengers were lightly injured, 169 were uninjured, and the airframe was substantially damaged (the report states on page 10 that the four retention bolts "were not located"). The report's safety issue points directly at the state of work on that door during final assembly at the Renton factory: the plug had been opened for riveting rework, and on reinstallation the positioning bolts were missing with no work record. The form the backlog takes here is a blank in the record: one opening of a critical area triggered no human re-check anywhere along the release chain.

Stop at the decision point: the release node after the door was closed and before the aircraft passed into delivery service. On the table: incomplete work-order records, and inspections ticking items off an existing checklist, a checklist with no line reading "reinstallation after opening a critical area must be re-verified". 〔Outcome〕Fleet-wide grounding for inspection, and multiple revisions to the manufacturing process and to regulatory oversight. Primary source: NTSB, AIR-25-04, 2025, link in Appendix B av-030.

docs.title: Case 3 (Public): The Palace, Thirteen Years of Repair Without Work Begun
docs.text:
po-005. The Restoration and Renewal programme for the Palace of Westminster. NAO 2026 update report (pages read for this book): the two Houses established the programme in 2013 and decided in 2018 to decant for the works, and at publication the programme was still in the early stages of the first scheme, seven years and capped at £3 billion. The building's maintenance backlog accumulates in units of a decade: every year's decision to wait was, in its own year, the money-saving decision, and the building's ageing curve does not pause for a budget cycle. World Heritage status means the bill for the backlog is written into every annual report, and the start of work still recedes. A backlog visible to this degree that still cannot be moved is the strongest form of this mechanism: nobody is unaware of it, and knowing does not get it onto the schedule.

Stop at the decision point: the approval moments, budget cycle after budget cycle, at which "the major works will not start this year". On the table: the fiscal room available in that year, the building's condition survey, and the political weight of the scheme. 〔Outcome〕The backlog keeps accumulating and the scheme remains in its early stages. Primary source: NAO, Restoration and Renewal 2026 Update, 2026, link in Appendix B po-005.

docs.title: Case 4 (Construction): A Forty-Year-Old Building's Progressive Collapse
docs.text:
Case ID: ce-009.

When and where: About 1:30 a.m. on 24 June 2021 (US Eastern Daylight Time), Champlain Towers South condominium, Surfside, Florida. The failure began three weeks earlier: in early June 2021, two slab-column connections between garage columns and the pool deck failed in punching shear, one after the other (NIST technical findings, released 2026-06-22).

What and who: Champlain Towers South Condominium Association, Inc., the 136-unit owners' association and its board; Morabito Consultants, the structural engineer retained by the association, which submitted a structural field survey report on 8 October 2018; the Town of Surfside building department and its Building Official; the NIST National Construction Safety Team (NCST). Responsibility sits on three positions: the association board, for repair decisions and apportioning the cost; the retained structural engineer, for inspection and reporting; the building official, for review and clearance. The building was twelve storeys plus a penthouse, 136 units, three joined sections, reinforced concrete flat plate without beams, completed in 1981 (NIST news release, 2026-06-22).

What they were doing: Maintenance work continued throughout, and it still leaked. About fifteen years after completion, around 1996, on evidence of cracking, leakage and rebar corrosion, the association carried out a major repair of the pool deck: most of the original quarry tile was removed and some left in place, a waterproof membrane was laid over the existing sloped concrete topping, and a sand bed and new pavers went on top (NIST technical findings transcript). NIST's wording is that the added pavers and sand put load on a system that was already structurally inadequate. NIST also found that rebar corrosion had been visible more than twenty-five years before the collapse, and had progressed far enough by 1996 and 1997 to require structural repair and waterproofing; problems continued after that repair, with leakage and rust staining still present. A row of large planters stood on the pool deck, planted with palms, and was removed after the 2017 hurricane. In 2018 the association retained a structural engineer to begin the 40-year recertification, several years ahead of the 40-year date; the report of 8 October went to the association treasurer (Miami-Dade grand jury report p.20), and the repair estimates it listed came to more than $14 million (p.21). In April 2021 the board president wrote to the owners: because most of the concrete and waterproofing work lay below ground, "almost the entire ground level" would have to be opened up, including the pool deck, the whole entrance driveway, the ground-level parking, the north-side contractor parking, and the planter landscaping. The letter said the visible damage in the garage and elsewhere had become significantly worse since the initial inspection, and it explained the mechanism: when concrete spalling is visible, the rebar holding it together is rusting and losing section, and the deterioration accelerates (p.21). By April 2021, more than 29 months after the report was received, the association had not started any repair work (p.21).

The decision point: The first is the board's regular meeting of 15 November 2018. The minutes record that the "40-year certification" and the "structural engineer's report" had been discussed and had been reviewed by the then Surfside building official, and they relay that official's finding that the required data had been collected and that the building appeared to be in very good condition (grand jury report p.20, quoting the minutes). That meeting produced no repair project and no vote on a source of funds. The grand jury report records one checkable link: structural repair requires a building permit, and on that basis it notes that the absence of any repair work should not have been invisible to the building official at the permit stage (p.21).

The second is the president's letter to owners in April 2021. It set the scope as opening the entire ground level and the deterioration as accelerating, but gave no start date and no schedule for apportioning the cost (p.21). The letter also stated the trajectory, that the observed concrete damage would multiply over the coming years (p.21). It was written before bids were opened, and not one sentence in it carried a date.

The third is early June 2021. A long horizontal crack opened in the masonry planter wall on the pool deck, with severe damage and displacement where the planter box met the wall; witnesses photographed it, and the same planter in a photograph from fourteen months earlier shows none of that damage (NIST technical findings transcript). In the same period the door from the pool deck to the street-level garage jammed and could not be used. Three things, on one deck, in one stretch of weeks, triggered no structural inspection.

The fourth is the board meeting that had been called to open the repair bids. Per the grand jury report, the building came down thirteen days after that scheduled date (p.21). Thirty-two months had passed since the October 2018 report.

What was visible then: ① The structural field survey report of 8 October 2018, the repair scope it listed, and the estimate above $14 million (pp. 20–21). ② The board minutes of 15 November 2018, including the relayed "very good condition" (p.20). ③ The president's letter to owners of April 2021 (p.21). ④ Visible rust, leakage and concrete spalling in the garage and on the pool deck: NIST records that after the 1996 and 1997 structural repair and waterproofing the problems continued, and leakage and rust staining did not stop (NIST transcript). ⑤ The early June 2021 photographs of the horizontal crack in the planter wall and the displaced planter box, alongside a clean photograph of the same place at the same angle from fourteen months earlier. ⑥ The jammed door. ⑦ A letter that translated spalling into rusting rebar: the April 2021 letter told every owner what to look for, and after it the rust in the garage was no longer invisible to a non-engineer (p.21). Information learned afterwards: the first punching shear failure came in early June and the second in mid-June, and for the two or three weeks after that load rerouted across the deck (NIST news release); the collapse began at the pool deck, not at the tower; corrosion was measured across hundreds of rebar samples, with moderate to severe corrosion concentrated under the planters and where chloride-bearing water had wetted the concrete (NIST transcript).

You are in the seat now, with the material above in front of you.

Stop here. Decide before you turn the page.

  1. What would you do? Write the action, not "pay more attention".
  2. Which item here are you most likely to miss, and why does it look unimportant?
  3. If you may set one checkpoint, when is it and what does it check?

What happened: At about 1:30 a.m. on 24 June 2021 the middle and east sections of the building collapsed, only the west section remained standing, and 98 people died (NIST news release; grand jury report p.4). NIST excluded several possible triggers: vibration from construction at a neighbouring site, foundation failure and sinkhole settlement, hurricane and storm surge, impact loads such as a dropped load or an explosion, and overload from the roofing work under way at the time of collapse (NIST news release). Back to the three questions. The commonest answer to the first is "call the engineer when the planters cracked", an action whose cost is one site visit, when the association already had a structural engineer of record. The item most easily missed under the second is the major repair of around 1996 itself, which looks like evidence that maintenance was done and in fact added load at the connections. The checkpoint under the third belongs on abnormal displacement of non-structural components: a jammed door, a long crack in a planter wall, a displaced planter box, three at once on the same deck for about three weeks, with no procedure at the time treating them as a structural signal.

Options ruled out: Replacing the pool deck waterproofing together with the sloped topping: what was chosen around 1996 was a membrane over the old topping, then sand, then pavers (NIST transcript). Starting repairs as soon as the report arrived: bids above $14 million apportioned across 136 units, and twenty-nine months passed after the report without work starting (grand jury report p.21). Inspecting earlier: the association had already done the inspection ahead of time, and that link was not the missing one (p.21). A structural emergency inspection of the planter damage in early June 2021: there were photographs, witnesses and a jammed door, and no procedure defined abnormal displacement of a non-structural component as a trigger for structural inspection (NIST transcript). Opening the bids and signing the contract at the pace then in force: even signed in mid-June, the work was months away and would have come after the June failure (grand jury report p.21).

Early signals: ① Leakage and rust staining continued after the 1996 and 1997 repair (NIST transcript): treated as a cosmetic problem, patched and repainted each time. ② The same repair added a sand bed and new pavers, raising the dead load: recorded as an improvement. ③ The report of 8 October 2018 and the building official's relayed "very good condition" (p.20): the report entered the recertification flow, and that flow ends at submission, not at construction. ④ "The deterioration is accelerating" in the April 2021 letter (p.21): written into an explanatory letter to owners, and into no engineering deadline. ⑤ The horizontal crack in the planter wall and the displaced planter box in early June 2021 (NIST transcript): entered the repair channel for planters and doors, and not the structural one; the photograph from fourteen months earlier, at the same angle, was clean. ⑥ The row of large planters on the pool deck is not on the original drawings: NIST compared the drawings with aerial photography and confirmed the planters are absent from them; they held palms for most of the building's life, the palms were removed after the 2017 hurricane, and the planters stayed. The addition never entered any record of structural change, and its load stayed on the slab.

The point of escalation: The pool deck repair of around 1996. The action was to remove part of the tile, lay a membrane over the old sloped topping, then sand, then new pavers, and the association initiated it: NIST's words are that evidence of cracking, leakage and rebar corrosion prompted the association to carry out a major repair of the pool deck. That step did two things at once, adding dead load to connections already short of capacity and turning waterproofing into a layer stacked on a layer. The construction detail stays in the record too: only most of the original tile was removed, some stayed in place, and the membrane went over the old sloped topping. The repair stopped at the surface. For the next twenty-five years every leak and every rust stain happened on top of that assembly, and each repaint reinforced it.

Failure chain: Technical layer: the punching shear margin at the slab-column connections was close to zero as built (NIST news release); load was added around 1996; rebar corroded in a chloride environment and connection capacity fell with it (NIST transcript: moderate corrosion alone can significantly reduce the capacity of a connection); in early June 2021 came the K-13.1 punching shear failure, with the slab held by membrane action and the adjacent connections, load rerouted, and a second failure in mid-June; on 24 June the south edge of the pool deck pulled away from the supporting wall, the north edge broke away from the face of the mid-rise tower, two tower connections were pulled out, the middle section collapsed progressively, and the east section followed (NIST news release). Organizational layer: the 40-year recertification is a submission regime, the report is submitted, the official comments orally, and the repair need not become a project (grand jury report pp. 20–21); the vote on the repair budget and the determination of structural safety sat in two separate flows; abnormal displacement of a non-structural component appeared in no inspection trigger (NIST transcript). Incentive layer: $14 million across 136 units; and doing the inspection early lengthened the gap between report and construction, October 2018 to June 2021, thirty-two months (p.21). The break at the junction sits between the organizational and incentive layers: the report moved the state from unknown to known, but "known" had no corresponding action and no date, and the calendar of the funding vote was not the calendar of physical failure.

Minimum counterfactual: In early June 2021, within forty-eight hours of the horizontal crack, the displaced planter box and the jammed door, have the structural engineer of record inspect the slab-column connections at the pool deck and put the conclusion in writing. One action, doable at the time: the engineer was of record, the contract relationship existed, no new budget approval was needed (grand jury report pp. 20–21); triggering it took one phone call, and nobody had to first admit the building was dangerous. What the inspection looks at is specific: deflection of the slab around the columns, diagonal cracking in the connection zone, and rust-staining cracks or water marks on the soffit, which are exactly the appearances NIST later identified as the punching shear failure (NIST transcript).
