Time pressure medium, because complications show up over weeks and months. Scale multi-team, because one operation is run jointly by surgery, anaesthesia and nursing. Regulatory density dense. Three rows hit: 16, 18 (a multi-party signature structure), 32 (dense regulation, and the department's safety meeting agenda is dominated by violation notices). Filters: evidence keeps 18 and 32 (the three-party check runs with the signature as the completion mark and the content check left to individual diligence, so 18 holds; six consecutive months of minutes discuss violation events and not one near miss, so 32 holds). Level demotes 16 to a reporting item, because the cross-department reporting structure is not something a head nurse can move. The time window transfers nothing. Main list: 18, 32.

Set the two instances side by side and one thing shows. Same six parameters, and the software team's main list lands on information and redundancy while the nursing unit's lands on structure and compliance. The difference in combination decides which chapters get read. The table does not hand you the answer. It takes you off random reading.

The table also works as a ninety-minute meeting. Everyone fills their own copy beforehand, fifteen minutes. In the room each parameter is called out with its basis read aloud, about sixty minutes for six parameters. Before people leave, one item only: the two parameters with the widest disagreement become actions, fifteen minutes. The discipline comes from the rehearsal meeting in Chapter 39. Argue with the basis, never with the person.

Of the three filters, the level filter is the one most often skipped, so here is a small worked case. A mid-level engineer at a platform company fills the table and the main list comes back with Chapter 28, horizon mismatch: the platform's exit clauses are missing, the consequence cycle clearly outlasts the tenure of the decision-makers, and the criteria hold one by one. The level filter then asks its question, and the engineer cannot move the exit clauses, which belong to the financing structure and the board. Chapter 28's destination is a report, written in the shape of a finding: the criteria one by one, the evidence each points to, the facts verified, and the action recommended at the decision level, in a form the layer above can read. All of Chapter 16's techniques for the upward channel apply. Copy yourself on one baseline as well: a known structural risk that has been written down counts as doing your duty, and one that has not been written down is complicity. Here the level filter's real function shows. It converts "what I cannot defend against" into "what I can report", which is why the main list only ever holds locks you actually have keys to.

docs.title: 35.5 Printable Version
docs.text:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Situating Table   date: ______   filled by: ______   object: ______    │
│ 1  Coupling: low / medium / high            basis: __________          │
│ 2  Redundancy reality: high / medium / low  basis: __________          │
│ 3  Incentive: aligned / partly / systemically misaligned               │
│    basis: __________                                                   │
│ 4  Time pressure: short / medium / long     basis: __________          │
│ 5  Scale: single point / multi-team / network  basis: ________         │
│ 6  Regulatory density: none or sparse / dense / dense but captured     │
│    basis: __________                                                   │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Rows hit (against the table in 35.3):  Ch. ____  ____________          │
│                                       Ch. ____  ____________           │
│                                       Ch. ____  ____________           │
│ Main list after screening (2 or 3):   ____________________             │
│ Carried to the ledger, recipient:     ____________________             │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Filling discipline: every level needs a basis, one sentence is enough, and a level without a basis gets filled at the most dangerous setting. Chapter 36 takes over from here: fifteen minutes in the library, ten minutes writing the conclusion, and the output is "which three deaths I most resemble".

docs.title: 35.6 The Six Parameters at Organizational Level
docs.text:
The personal version is complete on its own. The organizational version turns it into a quarterly rolling instrument. Each quarter, every owner of a key project or system fills one sheet, and the sheets aggregate upward to the governance layer, which reads trend rather than single sheets. Is coupling rising or falling? Is redundancy reality improving or degrading? Has incentive direction worsened? A parameter's quarterly trend carries far more than a single reading. A single reading locates; a trend warns.

The second organizational use is the distribution chart: a bar chart for each parameter by level across all projects, counting how many projects sit at high coupling, how many at low redundancy, how many at systemic misalignment. The extreme quadrant, the count of projects where high coupling, low redundancy and systemic misalignment hit together, is the organization's heaviest risk carrier. That carrier list sets the topic priority for the rehearsal meeting in Chapter 39.

The third use is entry positioning for new projects. At approval, the project owner fills one sheet as an attachment, standing beside the exit clauses and the list of irreversible points as the three documents of approval. Entry positioning hangs the warning on the project from day one, instead of waiting for the first anomaly to open the book.

Calibration data only accumulates value in a format. The recommended minimum is one line per record: date, object, six levels, chapters hit, revisit column. The revisit column gets two fields six months after the fill. Whether the object showed symptoms, meaning what happened, or an explicit statement that nothing did. Whether the hit held, where a symptom matching the mechanism of the hit chapter counts as a hit and a mismatch is recorded as a deviation with the mechanism that actually ran. Version control for the map follows from this. The table in 35.3 carries a version number, governance reviews hits and deviations once a quarter, and a row is revised only after three or more deviations accumulate, with the calibration source attached to the revision. The rule has one purpose: to make the table more accurate with use instead of leaving it at factory precision. Three years of calibration data carries a by-product. Your organization's own mechanism bias will show, the same two or three chapters hit repeatedly by similar objects, and that bias is the organization's failure fingerprint. The topic list for the rehearsal meeting in Chapter 39 is drawn straight from it.

Three typical fingerprints recur in high-frequency situations, listed for quick comparison.

Fingerprint A: an internet product in growth. Coupling medium to high, redundancy medium, incentive partly misaligned, time short, scale climbing, regulation sparse. Hits 16, 22, 24 and 33 at high frequency. The theme is expansion turning yesterday's redundancy into today's single point: during a scale climb, the backup that was enough last year does not cover this year's added dependency surface.

Fingerprint B: a heavily regulated operating unit (hospital, nuclear power, aviation maintenance). Coupling high, redundancy medium, incentive partly misaligned, time medium to long, scale multi-team, regulation dense or dense but captured. Hits 18 and 32 at high frequency, adding 31 where the capture evidence is sufficient. The theme is the feeling of compliance taking the place of the safety question, with the fact of passing every inspection read as evidence that the whole is safe.

Fingerprint C: long-cycle infrastructure (buildings, pipe networks, platform foundations). Coupling high, redundancy low to medium, incentive often systemically misaligned, time long, scale network, regulation dense with rules that update slowly. Hits 21, 25, 28 and 29 at high frequency. The theme is invisible maintenance meeting horizon mismatch: the consequence lands in the next person's tenure while the cut happens in this period's budget.

Fingerprints save time. A reader whose situation closely resembles one can read that fingerprint's chapters in the order of their hit frequency, then come back and complete the evidence for all six parameters as a check. A fingerprint is a starting point; evidence is the landing place. Where the two conflict, trust the evidence.

A rarer result is also real: six parameters filled, rows compared, no row hit. An empty result has three explanations, in order of probability. The likeliest is optimistic filling, a variant of error one, and the fix is to go back to the evidence lists with attention on incentive and redundancy, the two places where self-image pulls the level. The next is a genuinely clean situation: low coupling, real redundancy, aligned incentives, a sane tempo, controllable scale, effective regulation. Such combinations exist, mostly in small stable teams, and the table's job is done, with an annual refill. The one that deserves most suspicion is the third: every parameter green and the felt sense uneasy. Return to the line at the head of this chapter, where the numbers look good and the feeling is wrong. Unease usually comes from a dimension that has not been parameterized yet, the state of a key person, a process awkwardness nobody can name. Write it down as a candidate parameter for the next fill. An empty result is information, and the order for handling it: doubt the table first, doubt yourself second, trust the result last.

docs.title: 35.7 The Limits of the Table
docs.text:
No table can be exhaustive. Four limits are known and stated here to prevent misuse.

Limit one: the six parameters compress, and compression loses information. Dimensions outside parameters one to six (team culture, leadership style, an external shock) are not in the table. Lost information does not become unimportant; it falls outside this table's remit.

Limit two: three levels is coarse, and the world is continuous. The coarse grain leaves room for subjective judgment at the boundary, and the counter is the basis field. A level with a written basis at least lets a reviewer judge your judgment.

Limit three: the trigger regions overlap, and one combination hitting several rows is normal. Several hits does not mean all of them are running. The table gives candidates, not a diagnosis, and diagnosis goes back to each mechanism chapter and checks its criteria one by one.

Limit four: the table does not replace intuition. It is a tool, and the judgment of the person holding it is the core. Chapter 14's warning about the failure zone applies to the table as well: where the environment is irregular or feedback is delayed, your locating intuition may itself be off, and in that case the table deserves more weight than the intuition does.

The common conclusion from all four: the table is a first screen, not a final review. Its value is compressing twenty-four chapters into two or three, which gives attention a starting point. What lies past those chapters, going back to the chapter, checking the criteria, finding the evidence, is not the table's work. It is yours.

docs.title: 35.8 Five Common Filling Errors
docs.text:
Error one: optimistic levels. The sign is an empty basis field, or a basis that states a wish ("redundancy: high, we are planning a remote disaster-recovery site"). The design already carries a counter, since a level with no basis gets the most dangerous setting. What actually works is cross-filling: two fillers' difference in levels is more conspicuous than any reminder.

Error two: filling the target state. The organization is mid-reform and the filler writes the post-reform picture. Keep two sheets apart. A present-state sheet locates mechanisms; a target-state sheet argues the reform; the difference between their levels is exactly what the reform is buying. Mixed into one sheet, every warning misses, because you compared an organization that does not exist yet against the trigger regions.

Error three: filling once. The sheet gets treated as a one-off diagnosis and filed. Mechanisms run dynamically and parameters move: expansion raises scale, layoffs lower redundancy, a new appraisal scheme worsens incentives. Put the table on a rhythm, quarterly routine plus event triggers, where a new appraisal scheme, an organizational expansion or a serious accident reported in your industry each earns a refill. The event-triggered sheet usually carries more information than several quarterly ones, because the event has just changed your situation.

Error four: taking a hit for a diagnosis. Main list of two or three chapters in hand, the reader skips the criteria and starts installing prevention. The table gives candidates. Diagnosis goes back to section 1 of each chapter and checks the entry criteria one by one, keeping what has concrete evidence and demoting what does not. Prevention installed past the criteria is a placebo.

Error five: filling it and not showing it. The sheet goes into a drawer because the levels look bad. The table's value to one person is finding risk, and its value to the organization is trend and distribution. Both depend on being seen. A sheet nobody sees is a sheet not filled: its whole information content has improved the filler's intuition, and Chapter 14 has just said under what conditions intuition fails.

Same table, different roles, different centre of gravity. Four common roles are worth separating.

Line engineer: what you can move is the technical layer and the organizational layer. Incentive direction will most likely come out partly or systemically misaligned, and by the level filter that is not a level you can change; it is material for a report. The engineer's version of the table therefore produces two columns: what can be defended (mechanisms in the technical and organizational layers, with the prevention section attached) and what can be reported (mechanisms in the incentive layer, written as a report with concrete evidence). Keep the columns apart and the table does not turn into a complaint list.

Middle manager: you are the direct operator of four of the six parameters (incentive, time, scale, regulation), and your filling accuracy sets the quality of the organizational roll-up. The error you are most likely to commit is error two, filling the target state, because you are usually the person executing the reform. The counter is to have your direct reports cross-fill your sheet. Their level for incentive direction sits closer to the truth than your own.

Executive and board member: your seat suits two parameters, scale and regulation, whose evidence is on your desk. The other four should come from the middle-management roll-up rather than your own pen. The core output of the executive version is the distribution chart (section 35.6) and the list of extreme-quadrant carriers. A single sheet is of limited use to an executive; the distribution is your view.

External role, audit, investment due diligence or regulation: you are filling in the situation of the subject, and the self-assessment standard is discounted because you do not hold their ledger. Work by evidence availability, dropping a level where evidence is missing. Where you cannot get evidence, assume nothing optimistic, start at medium and mark it "not visible from outside". The greatest value of an external fill is comparison: set your sheet against the subject's own, parameter by parameter, and the widest gap becomes the first item on the due-diligence question list.

The shared discipline for all four roles is one line. Fill the parameters you have evidence for, and cite the other parameters from whoever filled them. The higher the role, the easier it is to fill the line's levels from imagination, and the table distorts upward along the power gradient the way information attenuates upward through the hierarchy (Chapter 16).

A concrete schedule for landing it.

Week one: each core project lead fills a present-state sheet, one cross-fill happens, and the pair produces a main list and a draft action list. The week does not aim at an organizational roll-up; it aims at every sheet having a basis field.

Quarter one: two things inside three months. Turn the "read the chapter" item on the action list into one two-hour collective close reading, with a presenter for each hit chapter and a written answer afterwards from each participant, which level they now fill differently. Run one revisit cycle as well, recording the state of the previous round's objects in the revisit column, even if the first round's conclusion is "no symptoms, hit holds".

Year one: after four quarters, governance should hold four things. A map with a version number. At least three rounds of calibration data. One distribution chart. At least one rehearsal meeting scheduled off the distribution chart (Chapter 39). With all four, the table has turned from a sheet of paper into a system. Missing any one, it is still paper.

The most common break point in the schedule is the second quarter, when the first round's novelty is gone and nobody fills the revisit column. The counter is to write the revisit into the standing agenda of the quarterly meeting, ten minutes, never skipped. Agenda status is the only reliable defence against forgetting, and it shares a base principle with the invisibility of maintenance in Chapter 29: anything without a routine carrier disappears into busyness.

docs.title: Five Self-Checks
docs.text:
1. Fill the table in 35.5 in five minutes. Which incentive direction level do you get, and would you show the basis to your team?
  2. Of the six parameters, which do you answer with least confidence, and what kind of information are you missing that leaves it uncertain?
  3. In your situation, which rows of the 35.3 table hit, and of those chapters, which have you never read?
  4. Has your organization run a rollout into a new environment in the past year? Did anyone list what had changed relative to the pilot?
  5. Which level did you give time pressure? Think of your last decision to compress a verification process: does the reason given then still hold?

docs.title: 35.9 Where the Table Sits in the Book's Toolchain
docs.text: The table is the first link, and four things hang off it downstream. The thirty-minute walkthrough of Chapter 36 takes the table's output as its input: the first half of the walkthrough list, which three deaths, comes straight off the main list. A walkthrough without the table picks topics from memory, memory picks wherever the last accident happened, and that place is not necessarily where the mechanism is most active. Chapter 37's review questions are chosen by hit mechanism. Running the questions for all twenty-four chapters is unrealistic, so the design questions belonging to the hit chapters get asked first, and the question list carries chapter numbers for selection by number. Chapter 38's postmortem template uses mechanism names as archive tags: every postmortem writes "mechanism: Chapter X" in its conclusion field, archived postmortems aggregate by mechanism, and the aggregate feeds calibration of the 35.3 map, which closes the chain into a loop. Chapter 39's rehearsal topics come from the extreme quadrant of the distribution chart, since the quarterly organizational roll-up of section 35.6 produces the heavy-risk carrier list and the rehearsal schedules off it, one carrier per session. The mark of a full circuit: a real hazard found in a rehearsal, archived through a postmortem, becomes one calibration record in the map. Read the four together and the table's role is clear. It turns "read a thick book" into "read two or three chapters and do three concrete things". The rest of the toolchain each holds one segment, and together they are an organization's mechanism warning and rehearsal system.

docs.title: Chapter 36 Thirty Minutes Before the Decision
docs.text: What this chapter covers: the full run from the position table to a conclusion page reading "these are the three deaths I most resemble", in a time box of 5 + 15 + 10 minutes, with a walkthrough of a synthetic example end to end. When to turn back: before any decision that touches a point of no return (Chapter 7); and when you want other people to use this procedure and need to hand them a minimum version. Estimated reading time: 30 minutes.

docs.title: 36.1 The Procedure at a Glance
docs.text:
The thirty-minute procedure is the executable form of the position table (Chapter 35) and the master gate for all the mechanism material in this book. It does one thing. Before a point of no return, it converts "which kinds of death do I most resemble" from diffuse anxiety into three specific mechanism names and three corresponding checking actions.

The compressed version for emergencies is worth giving up front as well. Each of the three time boxes shrinks to a third: two minutes filling the table, with only two parameters, incentives and time; five minutes in the library, checking only the first criterion of the first mechanism that hits; three minutes writing the conclusion, with only the likeliest death and one action. The ten-minute version produces one death and one action instead of three, and it is a hundred times better than zero minutes. Its precondition is a real emergency, a decision window measured in hours. If your window is measured in days, run the full thirty. A sense of emergency is not an emergency: often it is the amplifier from Chapter 13, narrative before evidence. The more you feel there is no time, the more you need the procedure.

One numerical coincidence in the design is worth naming. Five plus fifteen plus ten is thirty, and thirty minutes is roughly the limit at which attention stays at high quality on a single task. Beyond thirty, fatigue degrades the judgment you bring to the library search. Short of thirty, the table and the search lack depth. Thirty minutes is the optimum between cognitive load and judgment quality. Nobody designed the number that way; it was noticed afterwards, when the finished procedure was looked at as a whole and turned out to sit on the sweet spot of cognitive science. That is why it should not be compressed to fifteen, where quality fails, nor stretched to sixty, where fatigue cancels the gain. Thirty minutes is thirty minutes: physics, not a preference.

The three time boxes:

Stage Time Action Output Fill the table 5 minutes Six-parameter positioning (Chapter 35, table 35.5) 6 grades with evidence Search the library 15 minutes Against the hit mechanism chapters: criteria, weak signals, comparison cases Candidates narrowed to 2–3 mechanisms Write the conclusion 10 minutes Three-paragraph conclusion page One page: three deaths, three checking actions, check person

The threshold for using the procedure: the decision touches a point of no return (signature, go-live, announcement, external commitment), or the commitment is large enough that withdrawal would draw on second-tier resources. Ordinary decisions below that threshold do not need the full run. Copy the format of the conclusion page instead, three deaths plus checking actions, and use it in a five-minute spoken version.

Timing has its own rules. Run the procedure before the decision point, and leave at least one overnight gap (Chapter 7, the cooling-off period). Run it after the meeting and the output is postmortem material. Run it before and the output is armour.

There is a deeper reason for that difference. The person who runs the procedure before the meeting is still inside the information fog, and the discipline of Chapter 6 comes naturally: you have no outcome to lean on, so judgment is forced to start from what was visible. Run it afterwards and all three disciplines fail. You already know the outcome, and creeping determinism paves every fork in the road into a highway. So the thirty-minute procedure has one legal timing: before the decision. What happens afterwards is a postmortem (Chapter 38), not a thirty-minute procedure. The two have different purposes, and armour and teaching material should not be packed in the same box.

Ten minutes of preparation come before the clock starts. They do not count toward the thirty, but without them the procedure idles. Four items.

Materials: the numbers the decision turns on, budget, schedule, dependencies, and the record of comparable past decisions, on one page at most. The thirty minutes will not digest a fifty-page feasibility report. It needs the conclusions and numbers you have already digested. If materials are missing, the gap is handled under the Chapter 35 evidence checklist: whichever class of number is missing, that parameter gets the most dangerous grade.

Room: a table you can write on and a stretch of time nobody interrupts. The three time boxes do not tolerate handling messages at the same time. Phone silent, and the thirty minutes marked on the calendar as non-displaceable. Displacement is the most common way this procedure dies. It looks postponable at any moment, and after the third postponement the decision point has arrived.

Role: confirm the candidate check person, against the standard in 36.4. Asking in advance works better than asking afterwards, because advance notice leaves the other person room to decline or to name someone better. Asked afterwards, only obligation remains.

Entrance: write one sentence answering "which point of no return does this decision touch", using the Chapter 7 test: signature, go-live, announcement, external commitment, or withdrawal drawing on second-tier resources. The sentence goes at the top of the table. A decision whose point of no return you cannot name usually fails the threshold; take the spoken version and leave it there.

Two patches for the compressed version. The first: compression applies to time boxes only, and the check person is never dropped. The ten-minute output of one death and one action still carries a name and a time; a compressed page without a checker is self-comfort. The second: when a decision run in compressed form came out fine, give it a full thirty minutes later. Walk the judgment again with time to spare, and put the difference into the team's card library, meaning the mechanisms the full run caught that the compressed run missed. Compression is an emergency posture. Routine compression is routine myopia.

docs.title: 36.2 The First Five Minutes: Filling the Table
docs.text:
Fill the six grades on the printable version at Chapter 35, 35.5. The discipline has one line: every grade carries evidence, and a grade with no evidence is filled at the most dangerous setting. A parameter you cannot write evidence for inside five minutes is exactly where your information is darkest, and that fact is worth recording. Section 36.6 comes back to it.

The common error is turning the table into a statement of position. For "incentives: aligned", the evidence cannot be "our team has a good atmosphere". It has to point at a specific appraisal clause, and the test of that clause is whether the role that creates the risk bears the consequence. No clause, and the starting grade is partial misalignment.

docs.title: 36.3 The Middle Fifteen Minutes: Searching the Library
docs.text:
Take the 3–6 mechanisms, by chapter number, that the 35.3 table hit. Run three fixed actions on each, at a budget of 2–3 minutes per mechanism. The actions can be that fast because every chapter in Part Three has the same skeleton, in the same positions (writing standard, section 10).

Action one: check the activation criteria (section 1 of the chapter). Each mechanism chapter gives three criteria of the form "present means already started". Ask of each one: is there identifiable evidence of this in my situation? All three absent, and the mechanism leaves the main list.

Action two: scan the weak-signal list (section 4). Each chapter carries 6–10 weak signals, and each signal comes with the reason it was pressed down at the time. Any hit gets marked. Two hits or more, and the mechanism moves to the head of the main list.

Action three: read one comparison case (section 3 plus Appendix B). Read only the case card's decision-point paragraph and its minimum counterfactual paragraph, not the whole account. The purpose is to give the candidate mechanism a concrete face, so that when you discard it you are not discarding something you simply could not picture happening.

At fifteen minutes you should be holding a main list of 2–3 mechanisms, each with criterion evidence, 1–3 watch items where there is suspicion but no evidence, and the names of the mechanisms you moved off. Removal leaves a trace as well. Three months on, at the postmortem, the judgment "this one did not look like us" is itself up for examination.

docs.title: 36.4 The Last Ten Minutes: Writing the Conclusion Page
docs.text:
Three fixed paragraphs, one page.

Paragraph one: the three deaths I most resemble. One line each: mechanism name with chapter number, one sentence describing the situation, and the criterion evidence that hit. A worked example: "Practical drift (Chapter 15): the spot-check procedure went live three months ago and runs at 2% while the rule says 5%, and nobody has the authority to change the difference (criterion 1 hit)."

Paragraph two: one checking action per death. The action must be completable before the decision point and it must leave an artifact. Example: "Before go-live, pull the actual execution rate of spot checks against the written value; if the gap exceeds half, the switch does not ship." One action per death, the same discipline as the minimum counterfactual. Three actions equal zero actions.

Paragraph three: check person and time. State who verifies paragraph two's output, and at what hour.

For the artifact, use a sticky note or a message rather than a formal document. The ceremony of a formal document is what makes people postpone writing the page. The note has three lines: three deaths, three actions, one check person with a time. It goes on the desk or is pinned in the project tool. A visible conclusion page is ten times more useful than one filed in a folder, and the Chapter 30 register works on the same principle: visibility is a tool's oxygen. A conclusion page without a check person is a diary, not a tool.

The check person is a key design element of this thirty-minute choreography and deserves its own explanation. The role does three things. It is a time lock: the action you wrote has to appear in the checker's calendar, or it stays words. It supplies an outside view: the checker sits outside your decision chain, so he reads your artifact without your bias. It is an escalation channel: if he finds the action undone or the result abnormal, he has the right to report it upward, a miniature of the stop authority in Chapter 18. The selection standard: no stake in the decision, time to look, and knows what abnormal looks like. People who meet all three are easier to find than you expect. A quality person on another team, a PM on the neighbouring project, or your own manager, as long as he will spend five minutes.

Fifteen minutes of library search only runs if the stock has been arranged beforehand. Three speed tricks.

Trick one: criterion cards. Make one card for each mechanism chapter you have hit, three activation criteria on the front and eight weak signals on the back. The source is a transcription of sections 1 and 4, and making the card is itself a close reading. After a dozen of your frequently used mechanisms, the first two actions become flipping cards instead of flipping the book.

Trick two: pre-marking. In the two or three chapters you use most, highlight the comparison case's decision-point paragraph and its minimum counterfactual paragraph. Action three then changes from finding the paragraph to reading the mark.

Trick three: a fixed format for the trace. Record every search on the same line: mechanism, criterion entries hit, weak-signal entries hit, reason for removal. A fixed format is what lets a postmortem three months later compare the judgment then against the facts now.

docs.title: 36.5 Walkthrough of a Synthetic Example
docs.text:
The following scene is a teaching composite, not a real case, and exists to show how the three time boxes join.

Scene: a payments team decides to replace manual line-by-line review of refunds with automatic approval plus 5% spot checks. Decision point: the act of flipping the configuration switch. Point of no return: automatic approval takes effect and users begin receiving refunds nobody reviewed.

Filling the table, 5 minutes. Coupling: medium, since a wrong refund hits a single transaction and the support queue, and a payment can be stopped by hand but volume would drown the staff. Realness of redundancy: low, since the automatic rule's backstop is a manual console on the same code, with no independent check line. Incentives: partly misaligned, since support hours are this group's appraisal item while the loss is carried by risk. Time pressure: short, since it must ship before the promotion. Scale: multi-team, with payments, risk and support involved. Regulatory density: dense, since payments is subject to regulatory examination and rule changes must leave a trace. Every grade has identifiable evidence.

Searching the library, 15 minutes. The 35.3 table hits four rows: 15, practical drift, time short plus rule against workload; 11, normalization of deviance, a spot-check ratio that is nominal and a consequence that arrives late; 12, goal displacement, the hours metric outweighing the loss; 26, automation and skill decay, manual review skill going unused. Action one, criteria: Chapter 12 criterion 3, "somebody has been penalized for pointing this out", has no evidence yet, so the mechanism drops to a watch item. Chapter 15 criterion 1, "the same deviation twice or more", hits, since last month brought two cases of "spot-check ratio temporarily lowered during peak" with no change process. Chapter 11 criterion 2 hits, since the per-transaction loss is small and has always been explained as contained. Action two, weak signals: Chapter 15 hits two, training teaching something different from the manual, and new hires learning from the old hands. Action three, a case: the practical-drift comparison case confirms the shape, a fork that came from a rule written and not followed.

Writing the conclusion page, 10 minutes. The three deaths are practical drift (15), normalization of deviance (11), and automation and skill decay (26, promoted from watch item, on the argument that manual review skill decays as it goes unused and six months from now nobody may be able to run the rollback switch by hand). Actions: (1) before go-live, pull the actual spot-check execution rate for the last three months and compare it with the written value; if the gap exceeds half, do not ship; (2) add an independent check line beside the automatic rule, keeping refunds above a threshold on manual review, drawn from a heterogeneous source; (3) keep one manual review drill a month and write proficiency into the shift handover. Check person: the risk interface verifies (1) at the go-live review, and the duty manager verifies (3) monthly.

The most valuable part of this page is action 2. It comes from none of the three mechanism texts. It surfaced structurally once the three mechanisms had been located, as the obvious repair: put back the independent redundancy that is missing. What the procedure produces is three concrete actions with named checkers, and the vocabulary is a side effect.

Each of the three paragraphs also has a sample for a different class of decision. Copy the format.

Infrastructure sample, data-centre migration. Death one, hidden coupling (Chapter 21): the migration list carries no dependency on the old backup system, and the criterion "nobody can state the full blast radius" hits. Action: run a full dependency scan before migration and compare it against the oral interviews. Death two, the illusion of redundancy (Chapter 22): the standby hall and the primary hall sit with the same carrier, and the criterion "same-source backup" hits. Action: run the switchover drill once under conditions where the standby hall is actually carrying production traffic. Death three, handover rupture (Chapter 30): the migration window crosses a quarter boundary and the on-call roster changes over it. Action: the handover page of the migration manual gets a signed cross-check before the changeover. Check person: the platform lead verifies all three at the migration review.

Hiring sample, a key post. Death one, where intuitive expertise breaks down (Chapter 14): the interviewer's judgment comes from a highly regular interview environment. Action: add a work-sample test built on the same structure as the job's real tasks. Death two, narrative before evidence (Chapter 13): the requisition is already announced externally and the candidate profile was publicly committed at announcement. Action: hand the evidence list behind the hiring standard to a third-party colleague for review before the final round. Check person: the HR interface verifies before the offer goes out.

Contract sample, a supplier agreement. Death one, horizon mismatch (Chapter 28): the term runs five years while the counterparty's financial health moves on a quarterly cycle. Action: add an annual financial-health review clause and an exit clause. Death two, crossing a scale threshold (Chapter 24): the single supplier's share will pass four in ten. Action: prequalification of a second supplier starts in the same period as signing. Check person: legal verifies before the seal is applied.

What the three samples share: every death points at a criterion, every action has an artifact and a time of verification, and the whole thing fits on one page.

With the walkthrough finished, the three boxes deserve a commentary each, because the example hides design intentions that are easy to read past.

On the filling box. The heaviest grade among the six is realness of redundancy at low. Look at how the evidence is written: the backstop is a manual console on the same code, with no independent check line. That one sentence does two jobs. It evidences the grade, and it already implies the repair, an independent check line from a heterogeneous source. Good evidence carries its own repair clue. Weak evidence, "the backstop feels shaky", is a record of mood.

On the library box. Chapter 12 was demoted to a watch item because criterion 3 had no evidence. The move is worth enlarging. A mechanism with incomplete criteria can still be a real mechanism, and watch item means "current evidence does not support it", not "it is not happening". Watch items belong in the margin of the conclusion page; this example did not write them there, but it kept the trace. Searching has always included exclusion. Knowing which mechanism lacks evidence is worth, defensively, as much as knowing which one is confirmed.

On the writing box. Action 3, the monthly manual drill, serves death three, skill decay, and its verification rhythm is monthly, decoupled from the decision itself. That shows the page can hold two classes of action: one-off actions before the decision point, such as pulling the execution data, and periodic actions after it, such as the monthly drill. Both need a checker, and only the check time differs. The example wrote both because an automation decision naturally produces periodic after-effects, which is the theme of Chapter 26.

The method has a source. Research on prospective hindsight shows that when a task is framed as "imagine the event has already happened, then work back to its causes", people list significantly more causes, and better ones, than when they are asked directly what could go wrong (Mitchell, Russo & Pennington, Journal of Behavioral Decision Making 2(1): 25–38, 1989; Crossref record checked). The writing section of the thirty-minute procedure borrows that effect directly: "which three deaths do I most resemble" is a hindsight question. Gary Klein developed it into the premortem, and Chapter 39 of this book is his ninety-minute version. The thirty-minute version here compresses the effect onto a decision at personal scale, and the price of the compression is a single viewpoint. One person cannot run past his own group's blind spots, which is why 36.4 insists on an external check person.

docs.title: 36.6bis The Cross-Check List for the Conclusion Page
docs.text:
Five minutes of cross-check after the page is written, the same instrument as cross-filling: ask a colleague with no connection to the decision to go through it. Five items, one at a time.

  1. Does every death point at a criterion entry, Chapter X, criterion 1, 2 or 3? A death you cannot point at is a story. Go back to the library.
  2. Does every action have an artifact? The artifact can be data, a record, a drill result. It cannot be "awareness", "atmosphere" or "attention".
  3. Can every action be given a date on a calendar? An action you cannot date has no owner.
  4. Does the check person meet all three standards: no stake, has time, recognises abnormal? Miss any one and change the person.
  5. Do the three deaths cover different layers (the three layers of Chapter 9)? Three deaths all on one layer, all technical for instance, mean the search missed organizational and incentive candidates. Go back and search again.

Passing means all five. Two failures mean the page gets rewritten. Four failures mean the procedure itself has gone out of shape, and you go back to the 36.2 preparation list and start over. The checker signs initials in the box; the cross-check stays under ten minutes, because above that nobody uses it.

The page also needs lifecycle management. Once the actions have been verified, archive the note in a public place, a fixed column in the project tool, tagged twice: decision object and mechanisms hit. At the end of each quarter, pull the archive statistics, three numbers only: usage (is anyone using it at all), the rate of actions verified on time, and the cross-check item that fails most often. Each number maps to one improvement action. Low usage sends you back to step one of the rollout. A low verification rate sends you to the check person's time commitment. The frequent failure sends you to the cross-check list itself. Statistics stop there, and a dashboard would be over-engineering.

docs.title: 36.6 Three Ways to Fail
docs.text:
Failure one: filling the table with the evidence skipped. A grade with no evidence is decoration, and the whole procedure fails with it. The test is easy. Show your table to a colleague with no connection to the decision and ask which grade he does not believe.

Failure two: the library search turning into browsing cases. Stopping to read the stories blows the fifteen minutes. Read only the decision-point paragraph and the minimum counterfactual. The purpose is screening mechanisms, a case is a calibrator, and one calibrator is enough.

The calibrator deserves one more step of explanation. Case calibration exists to prevent matching mechanisms on paper. Without a comparison case, people tend to match any situation to the mechanism they know best. The case anchors the match to concrete detail from the scene, and anchored matching is more accurate. That is not theory; it is the common sense of information retrieval, where a query carrying an example beats a query of keywords.

Failure three: the page reading "heighten attention, keep tracking". An eight-word conclusion equals zero actions. Test: does paragraph two contain a checking action you can date on a calendar? If not, rewrite it.

A warning that runs the other way. The procedure can also do harm. Exploratory decisions (Part Six, Chapter 40) are not for this procedure, because in a situation that needs trial and error, rehearsing death kills the attempt. Judge whether your decision is exploratory or operational with the three criteria in Chapter 40, and only then decide whether to spend the thirty minutes.

One successful usage is left to write. The first run of the thirty-minute procedure must have someone alongside. What a first-timer needs most is a person who has been through it, and that person has exactly one job: when you state your evidence, ask how you know. That single question doubles the honesty of the table. The companion needs no formal appointment; any colleague who has read Chapter 35 will do, and a reading group, a training session or a morning stand-up can manufacture companions in batches. Someone alongside the first time, alone the third, teaching others by the fifth. After those three steps the thirty minutes stops being a tool and becomes a habit.

docs.title: 36.7 Five Common Questions
docs.text:
Question one: the decision maker has no thirty minutes. Delegate the run. An assistant or the team fills the table and searches the library from the materials, and the decision maker joins for the last ten minutes only. The delegated version loses honesty in the table, since an assistant writing your evidence will soften it a grade. The counter is one extra question from the check person at the page: which of the six grades do you disagree with. Disagreements get refilled.

Question two: a superior overrules the action. An overrule is one of the procedure's normal outputs: the procedure put the risk on the table, and the table is where the decision chain decides. The page then gains one line: the action overruled, the reason for the overrule, and a signature reading "risk acknowledged". That line turns an overrule from a default into a trace, and a trace is itself a defence. The diffusion of responsibility from Chapter 18 is held off here by one sticky note.

Question three: several decisions run in parallel. Order them by the timing of their points of no return, and run the nearest one first. Parallel decisions share the same library stock, the criterion cards and the pre-marking, so the second thirty minutes usually runs shorter than the first. Never compress several decisions into one thirty minutes. The time budget of the three boxes is designed for one decision.

Question four: a remote team. Turn the boxes into a shared-document relay. The table and the search are done asynchronously, and the conclusion page is written face to face in a fifteen-minute video call. The remote version loses on action three, where the screen weakens the case's sense of place. The counter: one person reads the case aloud and everyone else only listens, since reading aloud forces slow reading and slow reading restores the sense of place.

The common ground under the four: every stage may change shape, and two things may never be dropped, the evidence column and the check person. The first keeps the table true, the second keeps the action happening. Delegation, relay and asynchrony are changes of carrier, not changes of procedure.

Question five: does this procedure make an organization timid. Teams that have run a large number of conclusion pages report one complaint: having to think of three deaths every time, is this teaching people not to decide. The answer sits in the output. The page produces three actions and a signature, and once the actions are done the decision proceeds as it would have. The procedure blocks two things only. It blocks the case where the actions will not be done and the decision is pushed through anyway, and blocking that is its job. It blocks exploratory decisions that wandered into it, which is the reverse warning in 36.6. Caution and timidity are told apart by output: caution produces actions, timidity produces delay. The procedure recognises actions only. One measurement note while we are here: in teams that run conclusion pages, the number of decisions does not fall. What falls is the number of firefights afterwards and the frequency of "we never thought of that" in postmortems. Those two are what the procedure actually buys.

docs.title: 36.8 Division of Labour with the Chapter 39 Premortem
docs.text: The thirty-minute procedure and the ninety-minute premortem (Chapter 39) are two specifications of one family, split along three axes. Scale: the thirty-minute version serves a single decision, the premortem serves a project or a class of carrier (the extreme quadrant of the parameter map in 35.6). People: the thirty-minute version can be run alone, the premortem needs at least five, since diversity of viewpoint is its fuel and a solo premortem is a longer self-conversation. Timing: the thirty-minute version sits against the decision point, days before it; the premortem sits against project milestones, kickoff, architecture freeze, a month before launch. The outputs differ too: a three-line note against a hazard list with owners attached. The usual order is premortem first, thirty minutes later. Hazards found at the premortem enter the project's checkpoints, and as a checkpoint approaches, each individual decision near it runs its own thirty minutes. With both levels running, an organization's protection at points of no return has scan precision at the single decision and coverage breadth at the project level.

docs.title: 36.9 Three Steps to Roll It Out
docs.text:
The thirty-minute procedure lives easily in one person and dies easily in an organization. Rollout takes three steps.

Step one: a pilot group. Pick a team where decisions are dense: product, operations, post-investment. Two or three people run it ten times. The pilot tracks two numbers only: how many runs, and which of the five cross-check items fails most. After ten runs, hold one postmortem and turn the mechanisms this team hits most into a team criterion card, a team library of its own, with a higher hit rate than the generic one.

Step two: make the template library and the card library public. The pilot's criterion cards, sample pages and cross-check list go into the organization's shared template library, placed inside tools everyone already passes through: the project kickoff process, a fixed step in the release process. No standalone knowledge base: nobody passes through a knowledge base, and only what you pass through gets used.

Step three: a quarterly sample. Governance pulls five archived pages each quarter and looks at two things, the rate of actions verified and the completeness of criterion citation. The result does not enter anyone's individual appraisal, because the moment it does, filling the table becomes a statement of position and the error 36.2 warned about returns. It has two uses only: adding to the card library and fixing the procedure. Rollout fails in a highly consistent shape. Step one has nobody alongside, and a lonely tool does not survive its third use. Step two puts the templates in a knowledge base nobody passes. Step three turns the sample into an appraisal, and an appraisal forces acting. Follow the three steps and dodge those three pits, and after a year the conclusion page turns up in the organization's everyday vocabulary. At that point the tool has grown into the organization.

How the page interfaces with the governance processes already in place decides whether it is one more sheet of paper laid on top or part of the skeleton. Three interface points.

Interface one: the review meeting. If the organization holds kickoff reviews, architecture reviews or change reviews, the page's three paragraphs become the fixed first page of the review pack, with the rest of the pack unchanged. That first page turns a review from hearing a report into confronting risk: reviewers read the three deaths first and judge whether a worse one was missed, and a missed one goes onto the first page before anyone discusses approval. No charter change is needed, only one more sheet.

Interface two: the approval chain. The check person's signature box and the approval chain's sign-off box are different instruments and should not be merged. Sign-off is an act of authority, agree or not. Checking is an act of fact: did the action happen, does the artifact exist. Merged, the checker becomes the Nth signer and the factual content thins out, which is the Chapter 18 mechanism replicated at tool level. The correct merge is one required field in the approval chain, named "conclusion page archive number". No number, no passage.

Interface three: the postmortem. The postmortem of Chapter 38 looks back at the judgment made at the decision point, and the conclusion page is the snapshot of that judgment. The first move of the postmortem is to pull the archived page and check it line by line against what happened: how many of the three deaths occurred, how many of the three actions held, did the checker actually check at the time. The page gives the postmortem a primary record to compare against, and the ceiling on postmortem quality rises with it.

Common to all three: a new tool does not build its own stove. It makes itself one page and one field inside a process that already runs. Grafting outlives building.

A sample quarter with both specifications in use. At the start of the month, one project-level premortem, ninety minutes, with the hazard list going into the checkpoints. Mid-month, each decision near a checkpoint runs its thirty minutes: the spot-check switch, the canary percentage, the wording of an announcement, one note each. At month end, ten minutes with the month's notes and the premortem list side by side, marking where the two agree on mechanisms. A mechanism hit by both is the main theme in that project, and its criterion card belongs in the front row of the team library. The calendar demonstrates one thing. The two specifications do not compete for time; they compete for coverage. The premortem sweeps area, the thirty minutes sweep point, and coverage is complete only when the two line up.

docs.title: Five Self-Checks
docs.text:
1. On the irreversible decision nearest to hand, which of the three time boxes can you not actually run? Is the obstacle time or authority?
  2. The last external commitment you signed off without the overnight gap: looking back, was it worth it?
  3. Can the actions in paragraph two of your conclusion page be dated on a calendar? Which one cannot?
  4. Who on your team would make a good check person? Does that person have the authority to stop something?
  5. What does action 2 in the synthetic example, adding an independent check line, correspond to in your own system? Does it exist today?

The check-person role has an organization-level version worth giving larger readers: a roster. The checker should not always be the same person, because a fixed checker turns the role into a formality. The logic matches the real drill of personnel redundancy in Chapter 22, and each rotation refreshes the checker's understanding as well. The rotation period follows decision frequency, monthly for dense teams and quarterly for sparse ones. The roster hangs in the team's scheduling system, on the same layer as the on-call roster. Treating checking as a kind of duty says by itself how much weight it carries, and duty cannot be skipped.

An upgrade path follows the five questions. Once the individual version is fluent, build the team version. What changes is that the library stage becomes a collective activity: each member claims one mechanism and checks its criteria, and five minutes later the group reports. Collective search hits more criteria, because different people associate different evidence with the same criterion, and the fifteen minutes usually turn up 1–2 more effective criterion hits than the solo version. The team version is more manual and suits decisions with high irreversibility. Low-risk decisions stay on the individual version.

A last paragraph for the reader still deciding whether to use any of this. The entire cost is one afternoon-tea slot and one page of sticky note; the entire output is three concrete checking actions. Cost against output, this is the best ratio in the book, cheaper than any ledger, drill or audit, because it needs thirty minutes before a decision and no project, no budget, no cross-department coordination. It is a tool one person can start alone. If you finish the book and want to carry away one thing you can use tomorrow, carry this chapter.

docs.title: Chapter 37 Design Review Question List
docs.text:
What this chapter covers: 130 review questions in groups, a general set plus the twenty-four mechanisms, each one carrying a note on what it means when you cannot answer. Use it with the locator table in Chapter 35: pick the groups your situation hits, then take the questions one at a time. When to come back to it: design reviews, decision meetings, due-diligence interviews, and any time you are setting an exam for a team below you. Reading time: about 50 minutes.

The question list is a toolbox. It comes off the shelf when needed and goes back, and nobody reads it through in one sitting. There are two occasions for taking it out. The first is a design review: ten minutes before the meeting, the questions for the mechanisms in play are copied into the agenda, and the review changes from a presentation with an audience into a pass down a list. The second is a self-check, one person walking their own system through the questions one at a time. The output of a self-check is the list of questions that could not be answered, and that list is the finding. A question nobody in the design ever considered is itself a gap.

Every question is worded for an answer out of knowledge: can you answer this, as distinct from have you done this. The first form points at knowledge, the second at process. Process on file with knowledge missing is the most common failure shape in this book, and it is practical drift (Chapter 15) seen through a review question.

The list has a second use, in training. Hand a newcomer the questions and send them to interview the veterans. The newcomer learns the structure and logic of the system; the veterans get asked things they never considered. Both sides gain. The barrier is as low as a barrier gets, because nothing has to be taught to anybody. Hand over the list. The list teaches by itself.

Three rules, and they fit on three lines. Rule one: questions are used in groups. Take the mechanism groups the locator table hits, add the general group, and stop at twenty to thirty questions for one review; reading the whole table is an editing act, not a review act. Rule two: the arrow after each question gives the meaning of a failure to answer, and that meaning goes into the minutes, where it does more work than a follow-up question. Rule three: answers must land on dated evidence, and a verbal assurance counts as no answer.

Where the library came from is worth stating once. Not one of the 130 questions came out of theoretical reasoning. All of them were traced back from the decision-point field of this book's case cards: what material lay on the table at that decision point, and which question nobody asked out loud. That unasked question was then rewritten into a form you can put to yourself today. On the Alaska 261 card, the question lying next to the decision point was "whose inspection record is the extension based on" (the information source was the operator alone), and it became the prototype for question 3 of the Chapter 11 group. On the Travel + Leisure card it was "who independently reviewed the change in the counting rule", which became question 7 of the general group. On the Grafton card it was "once the alarm sounds, who has to stop what they are doing", which is question 2 of the Chapter 16 group. This provenance tells you what kind of document you are holding: an index to the decision points of a case collection, with a site behind every question that paid real tuition. It also explains the wording. Almost every organization in those cases had processes and had documents. What they lacked was somebody at the decision point asking the question and demanding an answer.

The relation to the trigger criteria needs drawing as well. A mechanism chapter's criteria answer whether the mechanism is running. A question answers whether your organization holds any knowledge about that mechanism. A criterion hit requires evidence. A question answered with "I do not know" requires only the admission. In a self-check the two tools divide the work: questions screen for black holes in knowledge, criteria confirm whether the mechanism is actually operating. Questions first, criteria second, because screening a black hole costs far less than collecting evidence, and the cheaper instrument belongs in front.

docs.title: The General Ten (run this group first in any review)
docs.text:
1. At which second does this action become irreversible? → No answer means the decision-maker has not yet met the irreversible point (Chapter 7).
  2. Who holds the last second-confirmation slot before that point, and what does that person check? → No answer means the defence is nominal.
  3. Which of the items the decision rests on carry a timestamp? → None of them means the decision stands on retelling (Chapter 6).
  4. If every dollar committed were written off tomorrow, who loses most? → No answer means nobody has costed the exit (Chapter 27).
  5. Who holds the unilateral right to stop this, and in which document is it written? → No answer means the right does not exist (Chapter 18).
  6. Was the last anomaly of this class attributed in the register? → No answer means the anomaly was explained away (Chapter 8, rung one).
  7. Who independently reviewed the last change in the counting rule? → No answer means the ruler is being swapped (Chapter 12; Chapter 8, rung five).
  8. When was the critical dependency list (third parties, suppliers, single systems) last updated? → No list means the dependencies are invisible (Chapters 21 and 33).
  9. What happened, professionally, to the last person who stopped a project? → No answer means stopping is a career risk (Chapters 19 and 27).
  10. Where does the person who pays for today's decision in three years sit now? → No answer means horizon mismatch is running (Chapter 28).

docs.title: Normalization of Deviance (Chapter 11)
docs.text:
1. How many times has a deviation of this class occurred, and on what basis was each occurrence judged to have no consequence? → No register means normalization is already running.
  2. In "there is still enough margin", is the margin a number or an adjective? → An adjective means the standard is softening.
  3. When was the inspection standard last relaxed, and who approved it? → No answer means the relaxation was done in the dark.
  4. How was the last question a newcomer raised about the old practice handled? → "It has always been done this way" means criterion ③ is hit.
  5. Which release action can be completed without writing down why it is acceptable this time? → If one exists, release leaves no trace.

docs.title: Goal Displacement; Goodhart's Law (Chapter 12)
docs.text:
1. How is this metric being optimized right now? Name three actual workarounds. → Cannot name three means you have not been on the floor.
  2. How long is the footnote to the metric's definition, and who has the authority to interpret it? → A swelling footnote means the definition is drifting.
  3. What happened afterwards to the last person who said the metric was distorted? → If they paid a price, criterion ③ is hit.
  4. Which observation channel that cannot be scored is still running, and who reads it? → None means the organization has only the ruler left.
  5. Has anyone written the list of differences between this metric and the goal it stands for? → Never written means the substitution runs unmonitored.

docs.title: Narrative before Evidence (Chapter 13)
docs.text:
1. How many independent explanatory paths did the current conclusion pass through before it was fixed? → One means there is no competing hypothesis.
  2. Whose job description includes "responsible for overturning this"? → Nobody means refutation has no post.
  3. Is the hypothesis written in a form that can be overturned, with the evidence that would make you drop it named? → Cannot write that means it cannot be falsified.
  4. How much evidence must an objection produce before it counts? → A higher bar than the proponent faces means the burden is asymmetric.
  5. When did the early conclusion first enter a formal document? → Before the data was complete means the narrative closed its books early.

docs.title: Where Intuitive Expertise Breaks Down (Chapter 14)
docs.text:
1. Does the experience this judgment rests on still hold in the current environment of rules, technology and people? → No mandatory check means running exposed.
  2. How often do the rules of this environment change? → Fast change plus a practice built on experience puts you in the failure zone.
  3. How long is the feedback loop on this class of decision, and who can afford to wait for it? → Longer than six months means no learning loop.
  4. When did someone last answer data with "I have done this for twenty years"? → If it happened, criterion ① is hit.
  5. In a new field, is the first move analogy or measurement? → Analogy means intuition is out of bounds.

docs.title: Practical Drift (Chapter 15)
docs.text:
1. When was the diff between the manual and actual practice last run? → Never means drift is invisible.
  2. Are newcomers trained from the manual or from a senior hand? → The senior hand means drift is passing down the generations.
  3. Which rule can nobody in fact follow? → No answer means nobody dares admit it.
  4. What is the immediate consequence of breaking that procedure? → None means drift has a place to grow.
  5. Who approves the informed violation, and under what name? → Oral custom means a violation with no owner.

docs.title: Information Attenuation up the Hierarchy (Chapter 16)
docs.text:
1. Where do the front-line version and the decision layer's version differ, item by item? → No answer means attenuation has passed the midpoint.
  2. What channel carries information around the hierarchy, and who is responsible for reading it? → No channel means you hear retellings only.
  3. Is the ratio of adjectives to numbers in reporting moving which way? → More adjectives means packaging in progress.
  4. How many layers does bad news cross from the front line to the decision, and what does each layer delete? → If you cannot say what is deleted, every layer deletes.
  5. What happened to the last person who reported over their manager's head? → If they were dealt with, the channel is dead.

docs.title: Misaligned Incentives (Chapter 17)
docs.text:
1. Have the performance schemes of each layer been read side by side? Which clause is the angle between them? → Never read side by side means the misalignment is invisible.
  2. Whose account carries the externality of this layer's decision? → Nobody's means the cost is discharged for free.
  3. Who is responsible for the overall result, and does that person hold real authority or only the blame seat? → No authority means decoration.
  4. Between the decision-maker's tenure and the cycle of the consequence, which is longer? → The shorter tenure means rational neglect.
  5. How dense are "per the contract" and "per the rules" in the minutes? → High density means behaviour is taking cover in the contract.

docs.title: Diffusion of Responsibility (Chapter 18)
docs.text:
1. In whose contract or job description does the stop authority sit, and at which clause? → No clause means stopping depends on courage.
  2. How many people are on the signature chain, and what exactly does each one sign? → If you cannot say what each one signs, the signatures are idling.
  3. What is the organization's first question after an accident? → "Who signed" in place of "where did it break" confirms a culture of diffusion.
  4. How many layers of subcontracting, and who holds inspection rights at each layer? → If you cannot count the layers, it is a black box.
  5. For a resolution the committee passed, who executes, who supervises, who closes it out? → All three in one seat means nobody owns the resolution.

docs.title: Why the Truth-Teller Goes First (Chapter 19)
docs.text:
1. What is the three-year usage record of the internal reporting or dissent channel? → Zero use means the problems are present and nobody says so.
  2. Where is the person who last raised a sharp question now? → Gone or marginalized means criterion ② is hit.
  3. Who signs the performance review unilaterally? → The direct manager alone means the alarm is wired to the manager's mood.
  4. Which questions have become bound to which leader's reputation? → Cannot list them means the binding runs deep.
  5. How many of the organization's alarms (independent oversight, rotating audit, external assessment) still sound? → All silent means the only alarm left is the accident.

docs.title: The Slack of Success (Chapter 20)
docs.text:
1. Which inputs have shown no visible output value for a long time? Is there a list? → No list means they are being read as surplus.
  2. Has "this has never caused a problem" been used as grounds for a cut? → If it has, criterion ② is hit.
  3. After the last cut to defensive spending, how long until an accident appeared? → Within two years means criterion ③ is hit.
  4. In the finance ledger, does "nothing happened" count as output or as no output? → No output means it will be cut inside the budget cycle.
  5. Who was last rewarded for "nothing happened"? → Nobody means this work runs on self-amusement.

docs.title: Hidden Coupling (Chapter 21)
docs.text:
1. When was the real dependency graph last drawn, by whom, and has anyone checked it? → No graph means the coupling is invisible.
  2. Which systems share something "unimportant" (power, accounts, database tables, domains, people)? → Cannot list three means the sharing has never been examined.
  3. Where is the post-mortem of the last cause-unknown outage filed? → Not filed means the clues are evaporating.
  4. Can "who does this outage affect" be answered automatically? → If not, the blast radius is guessed.
  5. Who holds the list of acquisitions, outsourced pieces and legacy connections? → No owner marks the deepest coupling.

docs.title: The Illusion of Redundancy (Chapter 22)
docs.text:
1. What is the list of items the backup shares with the primary system (same vendor, same drawings, same crew)? → No list means common origin has never been faced.
  2. When was failover last rehearsed at peak load? → Never means the rehearsal is a performance.
  3. Has the redundancy been verified on its own, by turning the primary off? → Afraid to turn it off means the redundancy is unproven.
  4. Has anyone walked through the scenario where both systems fail at once? → Never considered means common-cause failure runs exposed.
  5. Does the integrator's contract carry a redundancy liability clause? → Not written means you bought the redundancy on the drawing.

docs.title: Extrapolating Past the Validated Domain (Chapter 23)
docs.text:
1. Which page of the scale-up plan holds the section "what changed from the pilot"? → No such section means the extrapolation was never declared.
  2. Does the difference list say, item by item, why each difference does not affect the conclusion? → Hand-waved means the differences were never digested.
  3. Has "we validated this at A" been used as grounds for skipping checks? → If so, criterion ③ is hit.
  4. Who listed the differences in the new environment, and when? → Nobody did means differences are found by accident.
  5. Is the valid boundary of the extrapolation written into the final conclusion? → Not written means the next extrapolation follows.

docs.title: Crossing a Scale Threshold (Chapter 24)
docs.text:
1. Where is the re-validation record for the core assumptions at the last order-of-magnitude jump? → No record means the assumptions run exposed.
  2. Is coordination cost measured, in meetings, management layers and interface documents? → Unmeasured means the non-linearity is invisible.
  3. Which practices had already changed character at twice the scale? → No answer means the change is unknowable.
  4. Why was the extra management layer added? → For communication means a threshold signal.
  5. Is there a record of veterans saying "it was not like this before"? → No record means the organization is losing its control group.

docs.title: Margin Erosion (Chapter 25)
docs.text:
1. Where is the design margin register, and who maintains it? → No register means the cuts cannot accumulate.
  2. Has anyone read the list of past cuts as a whole? → Per-event reading only means nobody holds the total.
  3. What is the quantified basis for "still enough"? → No number means criterion ③ is hit.
  4. Who would stop the fifth cut? → Nobody means a straight slide.
  5. Can the original design value of the margin still be found? → If it cannot, the reference point is gone.

docs.title: Automation and Skill Decay (Chapter 26)
docs.text:
1. What is the mandatory frequency of manual operation, and when was it last recorded? → No frequency means the skill is decaying on its own.
  2. What share of training is takeover scenarios? → A low share with high automation means the takeover lands at the hardest moment.
  3. When did "the system handles it" become a reason not to practise? → If it has, criterion ③ is hit.
  4. The manual assumes actions people know; how do you verify they still know them? → No verification means the assumption is expiring.
  5. Is the threshold for leaving automatic mode written down, and rehearsed? → Neither means the takeover is improvised.

docs.title: Sunk Cost and Escalation (Chapter 27)
docs.text:
1. Which section of the project charter holds the exit condition, and who adjudicates it? → Not written means the only exit is a coup.
  2. When did "we have already put in this much" last appear as a main argument, and in which meeting? → Frequent appearance means escalation is running.
  3. Who is the external adjudicator, and do they have a stake in the project? → None means you judge yourself.
  4. Who last adjusted the re-forecast assumptions in the optimistic direction? → One-sided adjustment means the model serves the conclusion.
  5. What happened, career-wise, to the last person who argued for exit? → Moved aside means exit has a price.

docs.title: Horizon Mismatch (Chapter 28)
docs.text:
1. Does the budget have a line for future cost? → If not, the far cost never enters the account.
  2. Has anyone drawn the decision-maker's tenure and the consequence cycle on one chart? → Never drawn means the mismatch is never faced.
  3. Who signs off on the cross-period result? → Nobody does means a commons.
  4. How does a long-dated liability show up in the current-period statement? → If it does not, the ledger is forgetting on people's behalf.
  5. Does the bill list the next incumbent will inherit exist? → If it does not, handover is where blame gets passed.

docs.title: The Invisibility of Maintenance (Chapter 29)
docs.text:
1. Where is the three-year curve of maintenance as a share of budget? → Falling year on year with a constant asset count means the criterion is hit.
  2. Is the maintenance register auditable, in what was done, when, and against which standard? → Not auditable means soft spending.
  3. In the maintenance ledger, does "nothing happened" count as output? → If it does not, you lose every budget review.
  4. Who signed the last decision to cut maintenance? → A signer who did not know the consequence means delayed settlement.
  5. When was the maintenance standard last updated against the vendor manual? → A version cycle behind means the standard is expiring.

docs.title: Handover Rupture (Chapter 30)
docs.text:
1. Does documentation exist for why key processes are done this way? → If only the how exists, the judgment is being lost.
  2. Does the handover list carry a column for what has gone wrong here before? → If it does not, the lessons leave with the person.
  3. After the veteran leaves, what channel carries questions beginning with why? → No channel means the rupture is a fact.
  4. Can you list the places where the documentation states conclusions only? → If you cannot, the blind spots are unknown.
  5. What answer did the last newcomer get when asking why? → "It has always been like this" means criterion ③ is hit.

docs.title: Regulatory Lag and Capture (Chapter 31)
docs.text:
1. What share of the regulator's information comes from the regulated? → A dominant share means the structural condition for capture is present.
  2. What is the lag between the last rule update and the change in technology? → A generation means lag is now normal.
  3. Has anyone computed the ratio of penalty to profit from violation? → Below 1 means the fine is a membership fee.
  4. What is the record of people moving between regulator and regulated? → Frequent movement both ways means the revolving door turns.
  5. Who drafted the key clause? → The regulated party means drafting power has leaked out.

docs.title: Compliant and Unsafe (Chapter 32)
docs.text:
1. Who owns the gaps between inspection items? → Nobody means the gaps are free.
  2. After a compliance check, has anyone asked whether the compliant items taken together are safe? → Never asked means nobody owns the whole.
  3. Are safety meeting agendas built on violations or on risk? → Violations only means a Safety-I loop.
  4. Has a compliance certificate ever stood in for a safety judgment? → If so, criterion ③ is hit.
  5. Is the list of exceptions and waivers getting longer or shorter? → Longer means the rules are failing while the paper stays clean.

docs.title: Cascading Failure (Chapter 33)
docs.text:
1. Does the risk register carry a line for third-party dependency? → If not, someone else's risk is not risk.
  2. Do you know who your key supplier's supplier is? → Not knowing means two layers down is a black box.
  3. Has the isolation and degradation plan been rehearsed? → No rehearsal means a cascade takes everything.
  4. Has anyone estimated the exit cost of a single-source supplier? → Not estimated means exit capacity is evaporating.
  5. Has a third party's accident ever entered your own post-mortem? → Never means the learning radius stops at your wall.

docs.title: Path Lock-in (Chapter 34)
docs.text:
1. When was the last exercise on what you would choose if you started from zero today? → Never means locked in without knowing it.
  2. How much has the current estimate of migration cost risen against three years ago? → Rising without review means the lock is deepening.
  3. When did an alternative last appear in a selection review? → Long ago means the evaluation has become ritual.
  4. Does anyone book the benefits of the lock-in, in compatibility, network effect and scale? → Booking the pain only means the exercise will be distorted.
  5. Is the trigger condition for breaking the lock written down? → No trigger means the lock has no keyhole.

docs.title: How to Run the Review Meeting
docs.text:
The pass has a fixed method, in four steps.

Step one, grouping, ten minutes, done by the chair beforehand. Take the mechanism groups the locator table hits, add the general group, land on 20 to 30 questions, and copy them into the agenda. Under each question leave three lines: answer, evidence (date plus source), verdict (answerable, black, refused).
