Action claim, minutes 70 to 85. Every selected death passes three columns on the spot: action, check date, claimant. The trap is the collective claim, the one that says our group will watch it. The chair has to force out a single name, and an action with no name becomes an escalation item there and then. Escalation items carry a recipient and a deadline as well, and an item with two blank columns does not go into the minutes.

Close, minutes 85 to 90. The chair reads the one page aloud, then asks one last question: how will this page be verified in three months. The answer goes into the footer, with the review date and the comparison method. An output with no verification plan is, by Chapter 38's standard, a dead document.

Three details on preparing the pack. The first item may reuse an organizational conclusion instead of a newly filled page, as long as the date it was filled is marked; a page older than a year gets refilled before the meeting. The second item is chosen by similar mechanism, not similar project: a first launch with no precedent in this project takes same-mechanism records from other projects, since same class means the same class of death, not the same line of business. The third item is the one that most often fails. Most organizations have no dependency graph sitting ready, and the substitutes go in order of preference: an auto-generated dependency list, an annex to an architecture review, and only then a hand-drawn sketch. A project with none of the three has produced the premortem's finding number one before the meeting started, that its dependencies are invisible, and that finding is written up as one known death in the pack.

One distribution rule. Send conclusions, not the raw library. A thirty-page log gets read by nobody, which makes sending it the same as sending nothing. The conclusion page stays inside three pages, the raw library goes out as a link, and whoever wants depth fetches it.

docs.title: 39.3 The Script
docs.text:
Time Step Action 0-10 Opening The chair reads the script and the rules, and announces the assumption that the project has already failed 10-25 Independent writing Everyone silent, each writes "how we died", three entries minimum per person 25-55 Round-robin Each person reads his deaths in turn, record the item, not the argument, exhaust first and classify later 55-70 Classification Hang individual deaths on candidate mechanisms, new ones added in the room (pointing back to Part Three chapter numbers) 70-85 Action claim One defensive action per selected death, claimant and date claimed in the room 85-90 Close The chair reads the one-pager, objections itemized, meeting ends

The opening words are the chair's, and there are three of them, fixed. "This meeting assumes that three months from now the project has failed. We do one thing: name the causes of death." "Everything said is recorded and nothing is rebutted. Rebuttal starts after minute seventy." "At the end of every death I will ask what its earliest visible signal was." The second sentence is the floor the rest of the meeting stands on. The number one cause of a failed premortem is rebuttal arriving early: the first speaker finishes, gets explained away, and everyone behind him closes his mouth.

The independent write is the key component of Klein's method: write before speaking, so that the senior person's account cannot anchor the room. This is Chapter 13's narrative before evidence, in meeting form. The silence rule runs to the end of the block: the chair does not speak, and the highest-ranking person hands in his pen last.

Classification uses the mapping table in Section 35.3 and the question sets in Chapter 37. The chair opens with a sample from the ten general questions, which turns Section 36.2's library lookup into an oral examination, and any answer that hits a question goes into the evidence column of the one page on the spot.

Action claiming follows Chapter 36: one action per death; the action has to be markable as a date on a calendar; the claimant needs the authority to execute or the authority to escalate. A death with no action becomes an escalation item, with the recipient and the deadline written in. Only two things may leave a premortem, an action with a claimant and a report with a recipient.

One worked sheet follows, a teaching composite rather than a real project. The format can be copied.

Premortem one-pager | Subject: warehouse automation, phase two go-live | Irreversible point: 11-20, 08:00, the cutover switch | Chair: L.W., Quality (not a project member)

Death one: practical drift (Chapter 15). The emergency rollback procedure is written in five steps; execution in practice follows the three-step drill version. Defensive action: redo the rollback drill under 5% real traffic. Check date: 11-13. Claimant: K.Z., platform team.

Death two: hidden coupling (Chapter 21). The legacy warehouse system's reconciliation job still connects directly to the new database, and after cutover the reconciliation windows overlap and lock the table. Defensive action: complete the historical integration list with a dependency scan, and delay cutover until it clears. Check date: 11-15. Claimant: D.M., architecture team.

Death three: handover rupture (Chapter 30). Cutover day falls the day after a shift change, and nobody on the duty roster has been through a previous cutover in full. Defensive action: two-person duty on cutover day plus a cutover manual handover page. Check date: 11-18. Claimant: S.H., operations team.

Escalation item: incentives point the wrong way (partly misaligned, the Chapter 17 group). The go-live milestone bonus structure makes the gain from compressing testing immediately visible. Recipient: general manager of the business unit. Deadline: written reply by 11-12.

Footer: review date 12-20, comparison by checking the three deaths one by one against the cutover log (owner L.W.). Objection items, two: see minutes.

What the sheet shows is the interlock between columns. Every death carries a chapter number, every action a date, every escalation item a recipient. The whole page is under three hundred words and takes ten minutes to write, and its entire value is paid out on 20 December, when it is read back: how many of the three deaths hit, how many of the three actions blocked something. That review is the premortem's second meeting.

docs.title: 39.4 Records and the Close
docs.text:
Minutes follow the minimum standard in Section 38.4 of Chapter 38, with four columns added for this meeting: the death list with mechanism chapter numbers, the defensive actions, the verifier and date, and the objection items. Objection items are the line between a premortem and an ordinary review. An opinion rejected in the room is recorded with the reason for the rejection, and three months later those entries are the first batch of evidence for the postmortem.

The one-pager goes to everyone within 24 hours of the meeting, copied to both sides' superiors. A premortem that is not copied upward is a tea party: defensive actions need resources and calendar space, and neither arrives by a route that bypasses the level above. The copy also carries a design intent that has to be explained to the people receiving it. A superior who receives the page has exactly two correct moves: assign resources to the actions, or state a position on a particular death and leave a record. Demanding an item-by-item verdict is too much. Expecting silent acceptance is also wrong. The footer keeps one line for a reply, filled with agreement to the actions and the schedule, or a comment on individual items, five words being enough. The reply line is what makes the copy a two-way commitment: the level below discloses, the level above catches. A one-pager whose reply line is blank twice in a row goes straight to governance before the next meeting, reported by the chair. A failed copy is measured, not guessed by feel.

docs.title: 39.5 After the Meeting
docs.text:
Follow-up has two items. Defensive actions enter the anomaly ledger with a 30-day review point, because the reason an action did not run is itself a diagnosis: no resources, no authority, or an action that was written as a wish. And the deaths identified at the premortem enter the comparison column of the postmortem template: at project close or at failure, the team checks item by item what was rehearsed, what happened, and why the rehearsal did not stop it. That comparison is the only feedback loop this institution has for improving itself. Skip it and the premortem degrades into a rite.

The three failure forms can be detected from the feel of a single meeting, and the chair can carry three questions.

Question one: in the first five minutes, did the highest-ranking person speak? A word before the silent writing block means form one, the credit-claiming meeting, at better than even odds, because he has already set the frame of the agenda. The fix belongs to the next meeting: the chair talks to him beforehand and asks him to hand in first and speak last.

Question two: what share of the death entries name a person? Past twenty percent carrying specific names, form one has crossed with blame and the meeting has left autopsy logic. The fix is on the spot: the chair restates the recording rule, and entries with names move to oral clarification and stay out of the minutes.

Question three: how many minutes did the claim block take? Under ten, the meeting was form three, going through the motions: thirty minutes reading deaths, ten minutes claiming in a hurry, and the output has had its teeth pulled. The fix is to set the next timetable backwards, locking minute 70 as the moment claiming must start, and cutting the death list to three rather than letting claims run out of time.

One indicator runs across meetings: the hit rate of the death lists, meaning the share of deaths that actually happened at the three-month review. The healthy band is twenty to forty percent. Zero means the premortem is writing safe words. Above half means the problem at this project level is severe enough that no rehearsal was needed to see it, and the meeting should escalate to governance. A team that lands outside the band three sessions running has a problem in the composition of the room, meaning homogeneous information, rather than in the process, and should change the people under test two of Section 39.1 before holding it again.

The psychological boundary deserves stating, so the tool is not overrated. It solves one problem precisely: social pressure that suppresses bad news, which was Klein's core experimental finding, and both the independent writing and the already-dead framing are designed around that suppression. Three classes of problem it does not solve, and the organization needs other instruments for each.

Patch one, knowledge blind spots. A problem nobody in the room can write cannot be rehearsed: if no one knows a coupling exists, it will not appear on the list. Only an outside view and materials can light that area, which is why the three-item pack is not optional. The premortem's value equals the knowledge boundary of the participants plus the boundary of the materials, and meeting technique can approach that ceiling but not break it.

Patch two, incentive-layer deaths. Participants go soft on their own incentive structure, since writing that our appraisal scheme caused the compressed testing is writing the exam question for one's own boss, and incentive entries come out systematically thin. The remedy is the escalation channel the chair keeps open in Section 39.3, plus one direct question during classification: one level up, is this an incentive problem? Asking by name is more reliable than waiting for volunteers.

Patch three, insufficient diversity in the room. Five people from the same role, the same tenure and the same background produce five similar lists, and independence buys nothing. Diversity here means information trajectory, not demographics: someone who worked in another industry, someone transferred in from downstream, someone less than six months in the post, each of them carries a path nobody else in the room knows. The organizer selects on trajectory, and where the room cannot supply it, the external reviewer slot in Section 39.2 fills it.

What the three patches share: the premortem is an amplifier, and what it amplifies is the knowledge and the viewpoints carried into the room. Its output ceiling is fixed before the meeting, by materials and by people. A well-run meeting cannot rescue a compromised preparation.

docs.title: 39.8 Where Chairs Come From
docs.text:
Chair supply is the bottleneck on institutionalizing the premortem. Everyone has sat in meetings. People who will make the project lead keep quiet for twenty-five minutes on script have to be grown. Three steps.

Step one, observation. A new chair sits in on two sessions with a counting task: how many times a rebuttal arrived early, how many minutes the claim block used, how many entries carried names. The task is designed to make him see the gap between script and room, and the gap list becomes his first textbook.

Step two, co-chairing. In real meetings the new chair gets an experienced co-chair. The split: the chair holds the process, the co-chair records items and keeps the clock. When the chair slips, letting a rebuttal through or missing the closing question, the co-chair does one thing during the meeting, which is pass a note, and one thing after, a ten-minute review. Chair errors get reviewed within forty-eight hours. Left longer, they become convention.

Step three, rotation and rating. Chairs rotate through the organization on the same logic as Chapter 36's verifier rotation. After each meeting the participants score three dimensions: process held, rebuttals intercepted, claims and close. A chair with stable scores across three rounds enters the organization's chair pool, and the pool stays at five or more. An organization with one good chair loses its premortems the day that person transfers.

The selection advice runs against intuition: the best chairs are often technical leads from other teams, not full-time safety or quality staff. A full-time functionary chairing tends to turn the meeting into an inspection; a peer technical lead keeps it a discussion among peers. Both kinds belong in the pool, at a suggested ratio of two to three.

Venue and equipment need practical specifications, because a small failure here drags down a large block.

Venue: a wall you can stick things to is a requirement, whether a whiteboard, glass, or a large sheet of paper taped up. Death entries have to hang, physically or digitally. Notes lying flat on a table have no public visibility and classification cannot run. Remote sessions use a shared whiteboard, with the rule unchanged: once an item is posted, deletion leaves a trace, struck through rather than removed, which prevents disputes about the record after the meeting.

Materials: three colours of sticky notes, each colour enough for fifteen per person; dot stickers for voting, three per person; a timer at the chair's hand, page turned when it rings. Check the day before. A chair who leaves the room to find sticky notes comes back to a meeting that has changed flavour.

Seating: no head of table, the chair sits at the side. The respondent, meaning the project lead, is placed deliberately furthest from the wall, so the path of reading items and hanging them crosses his field of view. The arrangement reminds the room physically that this meeting is about the project and also about him, and neither of those needs to be handled gently.

Remote sessions add three rules: cameras on, since reading faces is part of the work; whiteboard write access opened to everyone before the meeting, so each person posts his own in the silent block; and stricter timing, because online meetings lose time discipline by default, with the chair announcing the clock once per block.

Three challenges come up, and the chair should have an answer ready for each.

"This death cannot happen, we already have a defence." Do not argue. Record it with a note attached, respondent says a defence exists, and test the evidence for that defence in the classification block, using question two of the ten general questions, the second-to-last confirmation point.

"This meeting is talking the project down." Go back to the second opening sentence, death assumed and nothing rebutted, and add one line: a death not named today will have to be named in three months, with interest.

"I am the project lead, I say how this meeting runs." The chair should be holding an authorisation obtained before the meeting, the chairing authority in Section 39.2, and now uses it. Authority is not debated in the room. The line is: we run on script, and objections go to my superior after the meeting.

docs.title: 39.9 Data Flow and the Toolchain
docs.text:
Four destinations carry the premortem's data inside the book's toolchain, listed here so the data does not die in the minutes.

Destination one, defensive actions into the anomaly ledger, as in Section 39.5, with the 30-day review point watched by the steward. Destination two, the chapter-number distribution of the death list into the calibration data of Chapter 35's mapping table: when premortems on one class of situation keep hitting the same two or three chapters, that is the failure fingerprint of the class, and Section 35.6 describes the organizational use. Destination three, off-vocabulary deaths and recurring variants into Chapter 37's supplement channel for the question bank, under rule one, that increments come from postmortems, with the premortem as the second increment source. A death that will not fit the vocabulary, if it is real, is worth a new question, and the question bank's boundary expands with each premortem. Destination four, the three-month hit comparison into the comparison column of Chapter 38's postmortem: the premortem list is the first thing a postmortem cites.

All four destinations sit under one steward, the same one who holds the question bank and the ledger, reconciled once a quarter. Completeness has a simple test: pull a random one-pager from a year ago and try to find, within ten minutes, the execution status of its actions, its review conclusion and its citation in a postmortem. If all three come up, the toolchain is alive. If not, the premortem was a meeting, however lively, and not a system.

docs.title: 39.7 Three Variants
docs.text:
Micro, thirty minutes, three to five people. For medium irreversible points, an architecture change or an important release. Compression: silent writing and round-robin reading merge into write and post, post and read; classification is cut, with the micro version tagging mechanisms directly and running no collision; the claim block keeps its full fifteen minutes. Output is half a page: three deaths, three actions, three check dates. The difference from Chapter 36's thirty-minute process is the number of people. There is no case where three to five people each run the personal process and then combine the pages to better effect than a micro session. If they can sit in one room, hold the meeting.

Twin, two ninety-minute sessions a week apart. For mergers, outsourcing switches, platform migrations, situations with a wide dependency surface. The first session runs standard and produces the death list. The week between is the organizer's, filling in materials against that list: dependency scans, supplier financial checks, historical incident searches. The second session is a death hearing, not a repeat: each death passes through the new evidence and is confirmed, upgraded or withdrawn, with a reason required for withdrawal. The logic is investigation. The first session produces hypotheses, the interval collects evidence, the second produces conclusions. A large situation rehearsed in one sitting produces an output that is half true by necessity. Split it in two with one pass for evidence and the quality doubles.

Anonymous written version, one week, asynchronous. For situations with high political temperature or teams that cannot meet across time zones. The organizer sends an anonymous form, three deaths, each tagged to a layer. After the deadline the chair classifies and tags chapter numbers independently, and the output goes out as a premortem report, deaths unsigned, classification reasons stated. What is lost is the collision block, meaning the associations that verbal exchange sparks. The remedy is a second round: after the report goes out, one round of anonymous additions is opened, for entries written after reading other people's deaths, and it usually recovers two or three more. The anonymous version produces less than a same-room version in quality, and far more than a same-room version where nobody dares say the true thing. When the temperature is not ready, anonymity is the only form that collects real deaths.

The three variants share one page format, one follow-up rule with actions into the ledger and a 30-day review, and one hit-rate statistic. Variants upgrade. A micro session whose deaths tag to more than three chapter numbers upgrades to standard; a standard session that cannot check its dependency surface upgrades to twin. The upgrade test is a single number: if more than thirty percent of the last output's deaths could not claim an action, the situation is larger than the meeting format, and the format upgrades.

The 30-day review point has a fifteen-minute micro format of its own. It is not a self-check email. It is three people standing at the ledger for fifteen minutes: was the action executed, checked against the output; if not, was the cause resources, authority, or an action written as a wish, one of the three, written into the ledger; and a wishful action gets rewritten into an executable one, following item two of Chapter 36's cross-check list. The commonest finding at thirty days is the third: actions claimed at the premortem turn out to have been wishes when the time comes to land them. That finding feeds the next claim block, where the chair spends two minutes on historical cases of wishful actions, and the quality of claiming improves visibly. One task remains: the first pass at the hit grade, happened, partly or not, which the three-month formal grading revises later.

docs.title: 39.6 The Three Failure Forms
docs.text:
Form one, the credit-claiming meeting. Symptoms: the death list is all "customers too demanding" and "the market changed", and the defensive actions are all "strengthen communication". The disease is a chair who is not independent and rebuttal that arrives early. The fix is a new chair and a reread of the second opening sentence.

Form two, the anxiety meeting. Symptoms: the death list runs without end and not one entry claims an action. The disease is treating the premortem as confession. The fix is the rule that an action which cannot be claimed becomes an escalation item, which forces convergence, and the meeting ends at ninety minutes.

Form three, going through the motions. Symptoms: the one-pager is identical to the last one. The disease is that the premortem has no interface with the ledger or the postmortem, meaning the two items in Section 39.5 were never executed. The fix is to put the hit rate of the previous premortem's deaths on the first page of this meeting.

The premortem is not a one-off rite but a machine that needs maintenance, and its maintenance record is the comparison of successive one-pagers. Without the comparison, the third session slides to form three by necessity.

docs.title: Appendix: A One-Page Agenda
docs.text:
Premortem · Agenda (90 minutes)
Subject: ____   Irreversible point: ____   Chair: ____ (not a project member)
Sent 24 hours before: positioning table conclusion page / last 3 ledger entries / dependency graph
0-10    Opening: the three script sentences, read aloud
10-25   Silent writing of deaths (at least 3 per person)
25-55   Round-robin reading, record only, no rebuttal
55-70   Tag mechanisms (Section 35.3 table) + sample from the ten general questions
70-85   Action claim (one per death: action / check date / claimant)
85-90   Close: read the one-pager; itemise objections
24 hours after: one-pager to all staff and both superiors; actions into the ledger

Voting and priority need their own note, because this step decides the quality of the one page. The default rule is three dot stickers per person, voted on the deaths each person agrees with most, all three allowed on one death. After the ranking the chair does one thing: check the distribution across layers. If the top three all sit in one layer, usually the technical layer, because technical deaths are the easiest to write and the safest to name, he forces one from each of the other two layers into the top three. This is a targeted correction of the room's comfort zone, since organizational and incentive deaths are hard to write and will be absent without force. The two forced nominations are marked on the page as the chair's nomination and carry the same weight as the voted entries. The list stays at three to five entries, and beyond five the merging is done by action, since one action that defends several deaths is written once. Chapter 36 gave the principle: three actions equal zero actions, and five actions equal two and a half.

Hit-rate counting is specified down to the operation. On the review date, the one in the footer, the review owner pulls the actual cutover or close-out records and grades each death on the list in three bands: happened, meaning the process described actually appeared; partly happened, meaning a variant of the mechanism appeared with different details; did not happen. The bands are counted separately and the hit rate counts only happened. The grades go into the annotation column of the one page, which is not rewritten, only annotated in a different pen colour, and the annotated page is filed into the ledger. In the annual tally two numbers stand side by side: the organization-wide hit rate, and the count of happened entries that an action blocked. The first measures the premortem's eye and the second measures the defence's execution, and reading them separately is what keeps either from contaminating the other.

An annual calendar for the organization, as a model. Quarterly routine: one standard session, its topic taken from the extreme-quadrant carriers on Chapter 35's parameter distribution chart (Section 35.6), plus however many micro sessions the quarter produces, decided by each team with the organization counting pages only. The quarterly standard session sits in the second week of the quarter's first month, clear of quarter-end delivery pressure, with time to prepare the pack.

Event-triggered: after a peer's major accident bulletin, add a session for projects carrying a similar mechanism on site, with the third pack item replaced by the bulletin itself. The value of the trigger is a psychological window. An external accident makes bad news fully legitimate for a while, and deaths that cannot be said in ordinary weeks can be said in that window. The window expires: not held within two weeks of the bulletin, and the temperature falls back.

Milestone-fixed: one month before go-live, one month before a closing, one month before an outsourcing switch, three points written into the project template as an institution, by adding one line to the initiation checklist, premortem scheduled. The point of the template is to move the meeting from remembered to unmissable. Institutional memory does not run on people's memory.

Annual summary: hit rates across all pages, chair pool ratings, distribution of variants used, one page to governance. The most important line in that report is the absence count, listing the large irreversible points that have no premortem record. The absence list needs reading more than the hit list does, since the risk of a session that never happened is uncovered in full.

The calendar's total cost can be counted. Four standard sessions a year at six hours each including preparation, plus micro sessions and triggered ones, comes to about eighty person-hours a year for an organization of a hundred people. Against the organizational cost of one real accident, which is the order-of-magnitude table in Chapter 1, the arithmetic does not need doing a second time.

docs.title: 39.10 The Close
docs.text:
The ninety minutes, accounted for at the end: the premortem spends one meeting's time to buy the chance of converting "we never thought of it" into "we thought of it and did not stop it", before the irreversible point arrives. The gap between those two states is an order of magnitude, because the first only becomes visible after the point is passed, and the second still has an action with a name on it. The book's tools close the loop at this chapter: Chapter 35 positioning, which says what to defend against; Chapter 36 the personal walkthrough, which says how one person defends; Chapter 37 the question pass, which measures the cognitive stock; Chapter 38 the postmortem, which books the tuition already paid; this chapter's premortem, which saves the tuition not yet paid. The five share one discipline: translate vague unease into statements with sources and actions with dates. The premortem is the only meeting among the five, and the only one that needs other people to cooperate, which is why it is the easiest to criticize as a fuss and why it has the lowest cost per session and the highest output per session of the set. The reason to hold one never needed more evidence, since Chapter 7's list of irreversible points is the whole of it: every real irreversible point added to that list deserves one more page.

Three points on using the agenda. The agenda goes out with the pack 24 hours ahead, and participants arrive holding a filled conclusion page from the positioning table, because a participant who skipped the personal thirty minutes will spend the first ten minutes of silent writing trying to recall project details. The time boundaries in the agenda are hard: the chair's timer answers to the agenda and not to the mood, an overrunning block cuts content in the room, cutting items and keeping claims, and no block is extended. The post-meeting action on the last line, the one-pager out within 24 hours, is done by the chair personally, since a delegated send quietly shortens the copy list.

One suggestion for the first session: start with a small and real micro version, on a medium irreversible point a team actually faces, and ten minutes after the meeting have everyone score it on three dimensions, freedom to speak, quality of entries, hardness of claims, then fix the low scores before the next one. The first meeting aims at walking the full process, not at meeting the standard. An organization that has walked it once faces half the resistance at the second session, because the doubt in the room has changed from what use is this meeting to what about the one we failed to stop last time. The second doubt is the healthy one: it means the output has entered the mental ledger.

Five objections follow, which the sponsor will meet in full, usually the person who read this book and wants to bring the process in.

"The project team knows its own risks best, so an outside chair is formalism." The team knows the part of the risk that has already been discussed. The premortem wants the part that has not been discussed, and independent writing and an outside chair are both doors onto that part.

"There is not that much to rehearse, our project is small." Small projects take the micro version, thirty minutes. The test is withdrawal cost, and plenty of small projects carry a withdrawal cost that has nothing to do with size.

"We can write it down, but nobody will act, the actions never land." A death that cannot claim an action becomes an escalation item, and escalation items have recipients and deadlines. If escalation also draws no response, that fact deserves escalation on its own, by Chapter 19's test, and the premortem has merely measured a deafness the organization already had.

"Meeting time costs too much." A wrong comparison will always look expensive. The comparison is the historical accident cost of the same class of irreversible point, and Section 38.7's organizational profile holds the numbers ready.

"A premortem makes people nervous." Look at which kind does: the hazard sealed in the corridor after the meeting, or the hazard written on a page with a claimant's name. Nerves come from unease that has nowhere to go, and the page is where it goes.

One ordering suggestion for the sponsor, after the five answers. The first step in promoting premortems has always been a team willing to try and one real decision, not a policy document. A policy brought to a meeting with no sample behind it draws an objection list much longer than this chapter's. With one fully walked micro sample in hand, a one-pager, three deaths, three actions and a review conclusion thirty days later, the policy discussion changes from whether to hold these meetings to how to hold them well, and once the question changes most of the resistance goes with it. The book's five usage chapters follow the same order. The positioning table and the thirty-minute process run without approval. The question pass borrows an existing review meeting. The postmortem rewrite starts with the next postmortem and costs no approval. The premortem comes last, because it needs people and authority. Moving from tools that need no approval to tools that need approval is itself a ladder of rising resistance, climbed in order, and every step of that ladder has a section of this chapter as a handrail. An organization that has climbed all five no longer holds Part Three's twenty-four chapters as a book. It has its own ledger, its own card library, its own hit rate, and an external book has grown into an internal system.

docs.title: The Five Self-Checks
docs.text:
1. Of the three items in the premortem pack for your nearest irreversible decision, how many do you hold right now?
  2. If that meeting were held tomorrow, who chairs it, and would he dare make the project lead keep quiet for twenty-five minutes?
  3. At the last review meeting you attended, were the objections recorded or explained away?
  4. The last premortem one-pager: did it go to both sides' superiors?
  5. If you have organized premortems, where is the comparison table of successive one-pagers? With no comparison, which session will you start backfilling from?

docs.title: Chapter 40 The Failures Worth Encouraging
docs.text:
What this chapter covers: three checkable criteria that separate exploratory failure from preventable failure, and the two symmetrical diseases that follow a badly drawn line, dressing preventable failure up as trial and error, or punishing exploratory failure as dereliction. When to turn back: when you are setting the accountability standard for failure; when you hear "we need to be tolerant of failure", or "zero tolerance". Estimated reading time: 30 minutes.

Every page of this book is about preventing failure. Not one of them says failure is forbidden. This chapter draws the boundary of what should be encouraged: which failures deserve encouragement, which deserve sanction, and where the line sits.

An encouraged failure has to pass three criteria. One: the cost stays inside a budget, and the exploration budget is money that gets spent until it runs out, not a hole with no bottom. Two: the knowledge produced can be coded, and what was learned can be written down rather than only felt. Three: the failure did not touch a point of no return (Chapter 7: once you have signed, gone live, announced, the action has stopped being exploration). All three hit, and the failure deserves encouragement. The form of that encouragement is a public postmortem, recognition for the team, and the lesson entered in the knowledge base.

A failure worth sanctioning also has three criteria. One: a known rule was broken (the rule exists, you knew it, you broke it, which makes the act a violation and not an exploration). Two: it was concealed after the fact (worse than the failure itself, by the logic of Chapter 19). Three: the same failure repeated (Chapter 11: when the same class of anomaly appears a second time and draws the same explanation again, the first step of the ladder is already in motion).

Between the three encouraging criteria and the three sanctioning ones lies a grey zone: cost over budget but knowledge of value, a point of no return touched but a new opportunity found by accident. Discretion over the grey zone belongs to the governance layer, and the decision goes into the case library, so the next grey-zone event has a precedent to consult. The grey zone exists because the line between encouragement and sanction is not a physical line. Organizations draw it in each instance, and each drawing leaves a trace. The traces are the organization's boundary history.

Before the criteria are used, three worked examples (pedagogical composites, not cases from the library) are worth filling in, because the sharpness of a criterion only shows against a filled form.

Case A. A team trials a new caching strategy in production without declaring it, saves budget, and on the third day a cache avalanche takes the service down for two hours. Criterion one, information increment: "cache stampede will avalanche" is already cited in the operations manual, so the information is pseudo-information, and the failure is preventable. Criterion two, cost constraint: no paper existed beforehand, undeclared, preventable. Criterion three, path declaration: no document, preventable. All three point at preventable, whatever the team lead calls it. Handling: ledger, postmortem, structural accountability.

Case B. A team declares a pilot on a new material, with a maximum loss of 500,000 written on the paper and three indicators named as stop-loss. Eight months later the indicators have not been met, the project closes, and the loss comes to 470,000. Information increment: the failure threshold of this material under this working condition is a new proposition, so this is exploration. Cost constraint: the actual loss sits inside the paper. Path declaration: the failure happened on the declared path. All three hit, exploratory. Handling: public postmortem, information into the library, recognition for the team.

Case C. A team declares a pilot with a paper ceiling of 300,000, then goes past the ceiling to 800,000 mid-course to catch a market window, and the direction later proves sound. Criterion one: the direction was sound, so the information is real. Criterion two: 1.6 times past the paper, a miss. Criterion three: over the limit while staying on the path, a miss. Two misses, so it is handled as preventable, but the postmortem records one separate line: the direction judgment was correct. Whether the direction was right and whether the process was lawful are two accounts, and an organization that adds them together learns neither the direction nor the discipline. The taste of the grey zone appears here, and 40.6 comes back to it.

What the three examples teach in common: every document used to check a criterion is a pre-event document, which is what stops the urge to reword the story afterwards. The declaration holds the same position in this system that preregistration holds in an experiment. It turns exploration from a retrospective figure of speech into a status held in advance.

docs.title: 40.1 One Boundary, Two Diseases
docs.text:
Failure is not one category. It is two.

A failed clinical trial, a closed product line, a technology route disproved: these are prices an organization pays to buy information. Shipping with a known defect, skipping verification, ignoring an alarm: these are the consequences of a known rule being broken. The information in the first kind did not exist before the failure. The information in the second kind was written into the rules before the failure happened. The two need opposite governance. Exploratory failure wants a budget, a declaration, and a reward for the information it produced. Preventable failure wants a ledger, a postmortem, and accountability traced back to structure. An organization that runs both through one standard will develop one of two diseases, and often both at once.

Disease one: preventable failure dressed up as exploration. A launch that skipped verification becomes "moving fast and testing cheaply". A gamble that ignored the alarm becomes "the courage to commit". An operation with no record becomes "agile". The dressing keeps preventable failure out of the ledger, so the same death recurs, and each recurrence arrives with the sentence "we learned a great deal".

Disease two: exploratory failure punished as dereliction. A team that tried and failed is held to account, nobody declares the next attempt, and exploration moves underground. Failure continues. It simply stops being recorded and stops being discussed. The organization's visible failure count falls while its information flow stops.

Both diseases point at the same boundary. The test is not the size of the failure, and not the attitude of the person who owned it. It is three objective conditions that anyone can check.

docs.title: 40.2 The Three Criteria
docs.text:
Criterion one: information increment. Did this failure produce a piece of information that did not exist before it?

The information from exploratory failure takes the form "this road does not go through": the drug does nothing at the target, the market will not pay this price, this architecture cannot hold this scale. The "information" from preventable failure is pseudo-information: weak mortar will hollow out, an alarm that has rung for two hours is an instruction to go and look, low tyre pressure will burst a tyre. Those rules existed before the failure, in a standard, a manual, or an industry lesson. The check: write the cause of the failure in one sentence and ask whether that sentence is a citation of some existing document. A citation means preventable. A new proposition means exploration.

Criterion two: cost constraint. Was the cost of the failure bounded in advance?

Exploratory failure is information bought under a capped bet. A phase-one trial of a few hundred subjects, one prototype, one pilot city: the cost appears in a budget and the ceiling can be calculated. The cost of preventable failure has no ceiling. Its size is set by luck, and a run of quiet years only means its turn has not come. The check: ask whether a piece of paper existed before the event stating the maximum loss. If it existed and the actual loss fell inside it, exploration. If there was no paper, or the loss ran far past it, preventable.

Criterion three: path declaration. When the failure happened, was it on a path declared beforehand?

Declaration is what turns an attempt into an organizational decision instead of a personal adventure. The plan, the boundary, the stop-loss point and the approver all sit in a document. A failure inside the declared path gets exploratory governance. A failure on a departure from that path, a skipped step, an exceeded limit, a private modification, gets preventable governance, however much the intention resembled innovation. The check: take out the pre-event declaration and see whether the failing action appears on it. If no document exists, the default is preventable, because nothing can show the attempt was controlled.

How the criteria are used: all three hit, exploratory. Any one miss, preventable. A grey zone, two hits and one weak, may be marked "pending classification", but it must be entered in the ledger. Being unclassified is allowed. Being unrecorded is not.

The point of the criteria is to prevent the after-the-fact explanation. The urge to relabel a preventable failure as exploration never goes away, and since every criterion points at a pre-event document, the relabelling has nothing to work with.

Now the exploratory trio, item by item.

Portfolio management. The path limit starts from an operational formula: the number of paths open at one time does not exceed what the organization can honestly postmortem at the same time. For most teams the real number is three to five. The limit is checked monthly. When the limit is full and someone wants a new path, the only legal move is to close an old one, and running over the limit is not permitted. What the limit prevents is not waste. It prevents the dilution of attention, because an organization splitting attention five ways, a fifth each, has five paths running naked.

Loss budget. Three tiers. A small note, where a single path's loss cannot exceed a tenth of the team's quarterly budget, is approved by the team. A medium note, between a tenth and a half, is countersigned one level up. A large note, above a half, is approved by the governance layer. The tiers make the cost of deciding proportional to the cost of being wrong: small notes open fast and close fast, large notes open slowly and close under scrutiny. The mandatory review triggered by an overrun has its own detail: additions freeze on the day the line is crossed, a review conclusion is due within 48 hours, and the review asks two questions only. Is the reason to continue new evidence or old hope (Chapter 13), and who is delaying the stop-loss.

Quick funeral. Once the speed of falsification becomes a metric, the reverse game starts: stop-loss lines set low so that paths can be closed quickly and look decisive. The declarant sets the stop-loss line, the budget approver reviews it, and the two rights are kept apart. One ritual is worth keeping at the funeral: the closed path gets a hundred-character epitaph (what was learned, under what conditions this road reopens) and the epitaph goes into the knowledge base. The epitaph is the final product of exploratory failure. A failure that can produce a hundred characters has completed the information purchase. A failure that cannot produce them has not even closed its books.

The preventable trio is already laid out elsewhere (ledger in Chapter 11, postmortem in Chapter 38, structural accountability in Chapter 9). One item is unique to this chapter: keep the two ledgers apart. Put exploratory entries and anomaly entries in one book and two years later nobody can say which failure was money spent on information and which was a fee paid for nothing. A shared book is the breeding ground for prettification, and grey-zone entries are the easiest of all to paint over as exploration once they sit in a mixed book. Separate books, separate colours, separate field definitions for the mechanism column. This is infrastructure-level separation, and it works on the same principle as the separation of the postmortem system from the personnel system in Chapter 38: where a cultural promise will not hold, a permission group will.

Criterion one needs one more layer, because pseudo-information has an in-house variant. A rule sits in an industry standard or a vendor manual, and this organization never internalized it. Nobody read it, or someone read it and it never entered a procedure. The cause of the failure is still "a citation of an existing document", so the failure is handled as preventable. That lenient reading attracts objections ("we genuinely did not know"), and there are two reasons to hold it. The criterion system exists to protect the structure of the pre-event paper, and accepting "a rule nobody read does not count" would reward ignorance, making illiteracy a passport into exploration. And information unknown to this organization was available at low cost, one search, so the claim of information increment does not stand. The humane side of the lenient reading sits in Chapter 9: structural accountability runs as usual (why did this rule never enter a procedure, which is a matter for the ledger and the postmortem), while the treatment of individuals goes through the fair-culture substitution test. Leniency and mercy are two different things. The criteria settle the account. The culture sets the penalty.

docs.title: 40.3 Governance of the Two Classes
docs.text:
The exploratory trio: portfolio management (a cap on the number of paths open at once, read as a portfolio rather than case by case), loss budget (each path states its maximum loss in advance, and a breach triggers mandatory review), quick funeral (the speed of falsification is the metric, one month to disprove beating a year to confirm, and delayed falsification is the largest cost in exploratory governance).

The preventable trio: ledger (every event entered, tagged with a mechanism chapter number), postmortem (the Chapter 38 template), structural accountability (ask about process and incentives, not only about people). The two systems share one infrastructure: records, ledger, independent review (Section 38.4). They differ in standard and consequence.

Here is the minimum design of a declaration system, so that criterion three can actually be applied. One page, five required fields.

Field one: hypothesis. One sentence stating what proposition this attempt tests ("this adhesive holds under working condition XXX"). An attempt whose proposition cannot be written does not enter the process. An action that cannot say what it tests has no information increment to offer and falls outside criterion one by construction.

Field two: boundary. In what scope, under what conditions, for how long. This field is the paper against which criterion three checks the failing action.

Field three: maximum loss. Money, person-hours, and the largest impact on existing business, in numbers. This sheet is the whole of criterion two.

Field four: stop-loss point. Which signal means stop. The signal must be observable (an indicator, a date, an event), and "stop when it feels wrong" is not a stop-loss point.

Field five: information outlet. Where the learning gets written and who uses it. This field moves the codability requirement of criterion one to the front: decide where the learning goes before the fact, and afterwards there will be more than a feeling.

Approval has a time discipline. Small note, 48 hours. Medium, one week. Large, two weeks. Past the deadline, the default is refusal, because an approval process that dies of delay is worth exactly as much as no process. Both decisions are written in two lines. An approval gives a reason that can be tested later, since the approver is also declaring a judgment. A refusal has to name a specific defect in one of the five fields ("the boundary is too wide", "the stop-loss is not observable"). Refusals of the "not for now" kind are not allowed, because a refusal with no information pushes the declarant back into an undeclared attempt.

A declared attempt enters the exploratory ledger, and a failure goes through the exploratory governance of 40.3. Changing the boundary or the stop-loss mid-course requires a change declaration: edit the paper, leave the trace. Verbal changes are prohibited, because a paper amended by mouth leaves criterion three with nothing to check afterwards.

Declaration rates do not rise on exhortation. They rise on three structural changes.

Change one: make the win rate visible. How many refused declarations came back on a different path and succeeded, and how many epitaphs from closed paths were later cited by other projects. Publish both numbers. Declarants have to see the system produce value before they keep paying the cost of a page.

Change two: make refusal cost something. An approver who rejects a declaration signs the ledger, and the annual statistics report each approver's refusal rate alongside the number of times work went around the process and then had an incident. Approval becomes a recorded judgment, and a careless refuser becomes visible too.

Change three: decouple the declaration window from the performance cycle. The flood of declarations before a review and the drought after it show that declaring has been filed as a performance act. Decouple by keeping the declaration ledger out of the appraisal numerator and denominator, the same rule the postmortem runs on, and let appraisal look only at the portfolio's final output.

The three changes share one logic. The enemy of the declaration rate was never laziness. It is a negative expected return on declaring. Fix visibility, liability and timing, and the return turns positive, and behaviour walks over on its own.

docs.title: 40.5bis Organizational Detectors
docs.text:
Both diseases have detectors at the organizational scale, and they find the condition earlier than case-by-case diagnosis does.

Disease one has three. Detector A: the ratio of exploratory entries to anomaly entries in the two ledgers. Where exploratory entries dominate to an implausible degree, with more than eight in ten failures described as exploration, the criteria are being used as rhetoric rather than as a check. Detector B: the frequency of "we learned a great deal" set against the completion rate of the mechanism field's chapter number. Said often, and no chapter number to show, is evidence of prettification. Detector C: the annual inventory of large undeclared losses. Every one it turns up is direct evidence of a case that slipped past the dressing.

Disease two has three as well. Detector A: the annual curve of declaration count. Flat or falling while business volume rises means declaring is dying. Detector B: tracking behaviour after a refusal. What share of refused teams came back on a different path, which is healthy, and what share simply went ahead, which is the disease presenting. Detector C: one question in internal recruitment interviews, "would you say in advance here that you were about to attempt something that might fail". The pause before the answer is the reading.

Both sets are read the same way. Ignore the culture as stated. Look at the shape of the ledger and the curve of behaviour. Both diseases are early on paper and late in personnel files.

Four interfaces with the rest of the book, so that this chapter's criteria do not contradict the twenty-odd chapters before it.

Interface one, with Chapter 20 (the slack of success). What slack consumes is defensive investment: inspection, maintenance, redundancy. This chapter's exploration budget is informational investment. Both kinds of money look useless while nothing goes wrong, and both get cut easily, but the reasons for cutting differ and the diseases they prevent are unrelated. Book them as separate lines. Protect defensive investment with the Chapter 20 questions and the exploration budget with this chapter's portfolio management. Book them together and whoever wants to cut will always find a line that looks useless.

Interface two, with Chapter 27 (sunk cost and escalation). Additional spending on an exploration and additional spending on an escalation are indistinguishable in the cash flow. The distinction is the pre-event paper. An addition inside the declared boundary, with the stop-loss point not yet triggered, is the normal rhythm of exploration. An addition after the stop-loss point has triggered is escalation, and the external adjudicator of Chapter 27 takes over. Criterion three's paper does its second job here: the first job settled the character of the failure, exploration or violation, and the second settles the rhythm, continue or stop.

Interface three, with Chapter 13 (narrative before evidence). The declaration is the antonym of a narrative: it forces the proposition to be fixed before the data arrives, and fixed in falsifiable form. The quality of a team's declarations can stand as a proxy for that team's immunity to Chapter 13. A declaration with a vague proposition is almost certain to slide into narrative reconstruction after it fails.

Interface four, with Chapter 36 (the reverse reminder from the thirty-minute procedure). Chapter 36 said that exploratory decisions are not served by the death rehearsal, because a rehearsal looks for preventable ways to die and an exploratory decision has no preventable death to find. That gives the two chapters a precise division of labour: operational decisions use the rehearsal to find death, exploratory decisions use the declaration to buy life. One instrument manages dying and one manages living, and an organization needs both. An organization with only one installed is either over-cautious or running naked.

The common thread through all four: these criteria are not a loose sheet. They close the loop of the book's mechanism system on the side that permits failure. The other half of that loop, preventable failure, occupies twenty-odd chapters. This chapter supplies the missing side, and only then is the system drawn complete.

The accounting detail behind criterion two deserves its own passage, because "how much do we write as the maximum loss" is the field most easily gamed in any declaration system. The motive to write it small is obvious: a lower paper ceiling is easier to approve and lighter to answer for once it is breached. Three countermeasures.

Countermeasure one: define maximum loss as inclusive of spillover. Direct spend plus the largest impact on existing business (downtime, recall, compensation), verified by the budget approver, not calculated by the declarant. Estimate the spillover with the cascading-failure approach of Chapter 33: if this path fails, who receives it along the dependencies.

Countermeasure two: decouple the paper ceiling from the penalty. A breach is handled under the ledger logic of Chapter 11 (entry, postmortem, structural accountability) rather than fined by the size of the overrun. Once the overrun amount is tied to the penalty, declarants learn a reverse skill and write the paper enormously high to stay under it, which destroys the budget. Accountability always attaches to "no paper" and "concealed", and the amount itself is only a number in the postmortem.

Countermeasure three: audit the loss definition after the fact. Each quarter, pull two closed paths and check whether the calculation of actual loss matches the definition used on the paper. A paper that counted spillover and a postmortem that counted only direct spend is a silent overrun. Definition audit guards against bookkeeping compliance, where the ceiling was never breached because the definition went on a diet first.

The principle under all three: criterion two protects the structure of the capped bet. How large the bet is remains a matter for both parties to agree, and any unilateral change after agreement, writing it smaller or counting it smaller, hollows the structure out.

docs.title: 40.10 Three Misreadings
docs.text:
Misreading one: encouraging failure means raising the failure rate. The objective function of the criteria was never the number of failures. It is the unit price of information: the same piece of information bought as cheaply as possible. Portfolio management and the quick funeral press the unit price down, and the failure rate falls behind it, because once pseudo-exploration leaves, the remaining failures are all money spent on information. An organization that reads this chapter as "fail more often" has installed the shell of the policy without the core of the criteria.

Misreading two: a tolerant organization needs no accountability. The other half of the criteria, the three preventable ones, is printed on the same sheet as the three encouraging ones. The more exploration you encourage, the harder the preventable standard has to be nailed down, or violators will spend the exploration allowance (Section 40.1 explains why the two diseases usually arrive together). The fair-culture spectrum in high-hazard industries, graded between pure no-blame and full accountability, is structurally the same as these criteria: the grade is set by intent and by the substitution test, whether another person would have done the same. This chapter moves the material for that judgment forward into a pre-event paper, so the judgment returns to a document instead of a memory.

Misreading three: a declaration system kills inspiration. The improvised attempt born of inspiration is in fact the declaration system's best customer. One page, five fields, and an inspiration that can fill them is worth pursuing, while an "inspiration" that cannot state a proposition is usually an impulse. The system does not filter out inspiration. It filters out impulses wearing inspiration's clothes. Real gold is occasionally among the filtered impulses, and that is the insurance premium of the system, an order of magnitude cheaper than the tail cost of undeclared attempts.

The common antidote to all three: go back to the criteria. The criteria do not reward failure and do not punish failure. They separate two accounts, money spent on information and fees paid for nothing. An organization that keeps the accounts apart can afford to spend from both.

docs.title: 40.9 A Compliance and Legal Addendum
docs.text:
In heavily regulated industries the declaration needs one more layer: a mapping against the rules. Three additions.

Addition one: put a "rule mapping" field ahead of field five. It lists the current rule clauses this attempt touches, and the expected compliance position (inside current rules, exemption required, not covered). Mapping turns legal from the last veto into the person who draws the boundary in advance. The regulatory lag of Chapter 31 meets the demand for exploration here: the ground the rules do not cover is the lawful space for exploration, and it is the reason regulatory sandboxes exist.

Addition two: file the exemption in step. Where an exemption is needed, the exemption application goes in with the exploration declaration, rather than being sorted out after a failure. An exemption obtained afterwards looks no different to a regulator than a violation (the compliance logic of Chapter 32), while filing both together moves the boundary dispute ahead of the loss.

Addition three: design the transparency strategy toward the regulator in advance, deciding what range and what wording will be disclosed, which precedents and epitaphs the regulator may see. Do not decide this during an inspection. Chapter 31 described how a single information source produces capture, and a regulated party voluntarily supplying structured exploration information is one of the few available levers for changing the composition of that source: when the regulator can see where your exploration boundary runs, a rule update has somewhere to land.

The floor under this section is one sentence. Every freedom this chapter grants rests on a pre-event paper, and in a regulated industry the paper carries one more layer than elsewhere. Freedom costs more there. The structure of the criteria applies unchanged.

docs.title: 40.8 The Morphology of Encouragement
docs.text:
For an exploratory failure that hits all three criteria, the word "encouragement" has to become something concrete. Three forms, each with its taboo.

Form one: the postmortem changes specification. An exploratory failure enters the Chapter 38 template with the mechanism field tagged "exploratory path disproved". The session does not hunt for structural defects. It extracts the proposition and the evidence: which later judgments this falsification changed. Taboo: letting preventable-accountability questions into an exploratory postmortem. Wrong book, wrong questions.

Form two: courtesy toward the information. The epitaph enters the knowledge base, the proposition enters the case library, and the falsification feeds the position table and the question library, so a failed path leaves the question library one question larger. What receives the courtesy is the information, not the feelings: a citation can omit the word "brave" and must include "the proposition is falsified, evidence number X". Taboo: turning the person who ran the exploratory failure into a tragic hero. Hero narrative loads the next attempt with a performance obligation, and people suppress stop-loss signals to live up to it. The calmer the wording of the courtesy, the more durable the system.

Form three: renewal of the budget. A failure does not shrink that team's exploration budget, because the budget is assessed on portfolio performance rather than on a single path. Taboo: letting renewal become automatic. For a team whose last three epitaphs produced no codable information, renewal comes with conditions, a change of proposition domain or a change of the person holding the proposition. The whole design target of the encouragement machinery is one thing: the next person dares to declare, and must declare by the rules. Calibrate the three forms to that target and encouragement will not deform.

Portfolio management has one internal structure still to explain: the relation between paths. Inside the limit, a hedged pair is allowed, two paths with opposite propositions open at once, each with an independent stop-loss. The value of a hedge is that its information output runs in both directions: whichever side is falsified, the opposite proposition strengthens. The hedge has one rule. The two paths may not share a data source for their stop-loss signals. A shared stop-loss is the common-cause failure of Chapter 22 replayed in an exploration setting: the data source goes down and both stop-losses go blind at once. Beyond the portfolio view, the paths also need a read on crowding out. Once a star path absorbs the attention, the stop-loss signals on the others get read late, because attention is a resource. Add one question to the monthly portfolio check: in the past month, how many times was each path's ledger opened. The spread in those counts is the reading on crowding out.

docs.title: 40.4 Counterexample: Three Marks of Prettification
docs.text:
Mark one: the story contains no criteria. When you hear "that trial was valuable", ask three questions. Where is the pre-event declaration, what maximum loss was written, and what was the information increment. Three blanks and the prettification is confirmed. A real explorer is boring before the fact (documents, limits, stop-loss points) and talks about value afterwards. The prettifier runs in reverse: nothing before, all meaning after.

Mark two: the cost only becomes known afterwards. The cost of exploratory failure is capped in advance. The cost of a prettified failure is startling afterwards. Whenever "trial and error" appears in the same breath as "far over budget", handle it as preventable.

Mark three: the same death appears a second time. Exploratory failure is the purchase of information, and one piece of information should not be bought twice. A pattern that recurs means the first round's information never reached the ledger, or that what happened was not information but dereliction.

There is a fourth mark, and it lives in the language. Prettified accounts are dense with unverifiable sentences: "the whole industry is like this", "the direction was right, execution was the problem". Whether the direction was right is exactly what the proposition and the stop-loss in the declaration were meant to answer. Whether execution was the problem is exactly what the ledger and the postmortem were meant to answer. Each sentence has a paper it belongs on. Saying them out loud while avoiding the paper is an admission that the paper holds nothing in your favour. When you hear either sentence, ask which version of the declaration carries the proposition. The absence of an answer is the fourth mark.

docs.title: 40.5 Counterexample Two: What Punishing Exploration Costs
docs.text: An organization that punishes exploration loses more than a few attempts. It loses the declaration system. Once a person who ran an exploratory failure is publicly held to account, rational practitioners stop declaring, because declaring leaves evidence, and shift to undeclared attempts: success becomes performance and failure becomes an incident. The organization's real exposure is unchanged and its visibility falls to zero. This is the form that information attenuation up the hierarchy (Chapter 16) takes on innovation topics. The governance test follows: look at an organization's declaration rate rather than its failure rate. A low failure rate with a low declaration rate is usually not safety. It is silence.

docs.title: 40.6 The Grey Zone and the Precedent Library
docs.text:
The grey zone deserves full operational detail, because it is the ground both diseases fight over. The prettifier wants to read the grey zone as exploration. The fault-finder wants to read it as dereliction. The precedent library is the governing form for the grey zone.

Six columns per entry: a de-identified summary of the event; the result of the three criterion checks, which hit and which missed; the point in dispute, with each side's reading; the governance layer's ruling and its reasons; the after-the-fact verification, meaning a look two years later at whether this class of behaviour became more or less common after the ruling; and the precedent number. The fifth column is what distinguishes a precedent library from an ordinary case library. The consequence of a ruling is tracked, and the ruling itself is submitted for testing.

Three operating rules. Rule one: the ruling is made by the governance layer, but the right to open a case sits with the front line. Any team whose failure was judged preventable may apply for grey-zone review, and the review is free, does not overturn the original finding, and only adds a precedent. Rule two: precedents carry retrieval value and no force of law. When the next grey zone appears, precedents inform the discussion and the ruling is made fresh, because the criterion check has to rest on that event's own pre-event papers. Rule three: the library is reviewed once a year, in both directions. Check whether any precedent now rewards a disguised violation, which means the ruling was too loose, and whether any precedent punishes real exploration, which means the ruling was too strict.

A forecast of scale: a functioning organization produces roughly one to three grey-zone events a year. The library grows slowly, and each entry that appears is a developing agent for the organization's values. What counts as exploration here and what counts as dereliction is answered more honestly in a precedent than on a culture poster.

docs.title: 40.7 The Criteria at Every Level
docs.text:
The three criteria are not confined to the project level. They run upward and downward, changing shape a little at each level.

The individual career level. Personal exploratory failure, a change of field, learning a new skill, testing a side business, takes the same three criteria: a budget (living costs and time set aside), a declaration (candour with family or a partner), a stop-loss point. The individual version catches the same diseases. A preventable repeated mistake gets dressed as "I am experimenting" (the third fall into the same pit), or necessary exploration gets punished as "not serious work", where criterion three means declaring to yourself.

The industry level. The regulatory sandbox is a declaration system at industry scale: a limit (caps on users and on money), a declaration (the plan for entering the sandbox is published), a stop-loss (the exit clause). The sandbox shows the three criteria are executable at that scale too. Industry-level diseases have their analogues: dressing up consumers as free test subjects ("innovation always has someone paying for it"), and the fault-finding that bans every new business form ("no precedent means it is a violation"). Both refuse the dull device of declaring in advance, and both want the freedom to explain afterwards.

Cross-level consistency has one test question. Take a single matter and ask "where is the paper" at four levels: individual, team, organization, industry. If the answers thin out as you go up, the declaration system has failed at the top, and nobody up there dares ask for paper on exploration. This is the horizon mismatch of Chapter 28 projected onto exploration: the consequences of senior exploration already take longer to arrive, and without paper the bet has no boundary at all.

One recommendation on sequence, the same shape as the other usage chapters. Start with the one-page declaration template. Try it in a team that genuinely has an exploration need, where one path reaching closure inside a quarter makes a complete sample. Run the criteria three times for real, the way Cases A, B and C are run, and only then discuss the organization's policy standard. The wrong order looks like this: policy first, so the organization paints the slogan ("we are tolerant of failure"), the slogan lands with no criteria and no template to catch it, and six months later the slogan is fuel for disease one. Template first, criteria with it, policy last. This is the same rollout ladder as earlier chapters: cost rises from zero, resistance rises from zero, and you climb in order.

Closing. This is the only chapter in the book whose main business is saying what not to defend against. The twenty-four mechanisms and every device work to shrink an organization's exposure. This chapter opens one controlled hole in that exposure: paper sets its size, declaration sets its position, and the epitaph collects its output. An organization without the hole relieves the pressure somewhere else, since undeclared attempts are water seeping through a crack in the foundation. An organization with an uncontrolled hole takes preventable failure in through it. The whole job of the criteria is to make the hole a valve: three criteria open it, three criteria close it, and the grey zone goes to precedent. Put together, the book's position on failure is one line. For the unknown, buy. For the known, defend. Between buying and defending, the paper is explicit.

Those four words, the paper is explicit, are also the whole deliverable of this chapter: one template, two sets of criteria, an empty precedent register, and the blank cells waiting for your organization's first declaration. On the day the first cell is filled, the book's position on failure moves off the page and into your ledger, which is a more solid milestone than any reaction you might have to finishing a chapter. The criteria stop being three lines to be read and become a form in use. A form speaks for itself, and more accurately than this chapter does.

If your answers to the five questions cluster on the third one, no loss budget, then your organization's exploration is currently running with no paper at all, and the first sheet is the starting point. If they cluster on the second, no declaration channel, fix the channel before discussing tolerance, because an organization with no channel can only be tolerant of buried mines. Both are jobs you can start within a week: the template sits one section before 40.5bis, the channel hangs off the existing approval flow, and the budget starts at one percent of next quarter's project budget. A low starting point does no harm. The virtue of a criterion system is that it holds for small organizations too: a three-person team can still cap its exploration at three paths, declare on one page, and enter epitaphs in a register. The value of a system is in its structure, and structure does not discount for scale.

docs.title: Five Self-Checks
docs.text:
1. Take the last failure your organization publicly praised for "daring to try". Run the three criteria on it. How many does it pass?
  2. Take the last failure your organization held someone to account for. Was there a declaration before it? Having no declaration channel is itself the finding.
  3. Does your team have the concept of a loss budget? Of the attempts running now, how many have a sheet stating a maximum loss?
  4. How long did it take the last attempt to be falsified? Is that period getting longer or shorter?
  5. Which process does a failure declaration travel through in your organization? If the answer is "there is no process", who is running undeclared attempts right now?

docs.title: Chapter 41 Normal Accidents and Black Swans
docs.text:
What this chapter covers: what Perrow's normal accident theory and Taleb's black swan theory each explain and each fail to explain, and where this book's mechanism layer sits between the two. When to turn back: when someone ends a discussion with "that is an inherent property of the system", or "that was a black swan nobody could have foreseen". Estimated reading time: 30 minutes.

This chapter deals with the boundary of the book's own method. Perrow's normal accident theory says the accidents of some systems are structural necessities. Black swan theory says some events cannot be predicted. If both are right, what use are these tools?

The answer comes in two layers.

Layer one: this book never promises to eliminate failure. It promises to move failure from invisible to visible. Visible is not the same as controllable, and visible failure still happens. What visibility buys is traceability, comprehension, and a response plan prepared in advance. Invisible failure is the expensive kind, because you do not know it has arrived. Perrow's structural necessity refers to the interaction of the technical layer with the organizational layer. He did not claim that misalignment in the incentive layer is also necessary, and the incentive layer is where this book has the most room to act: change the appraisal, change the contract, change who signs. Those are within human reach.

Layer two: Taleb's black swan is about the limits of cognition. Unpredictable events do exist. Most organizational failure, though, is not a black swan but a grey rhino, and the record skew of Chapter 2 is what makes a grey rhino look like a black swan. Not knowing is not the same as unknowable. The grey rhino has already been written up as a report in someone else's industry, and your ignorance is a failure that circulates rather than a limit of cognition.

The two conclusions combine into one practical instruction: sort risk into three classes. Class one is preventable and measurable, and it takes the twenty-four chapters of Part Three; most organizational failure lives here. Class two is measurable but not preventable, structural risk; it takes emergency preparation and redundancy design, and the point of Chapter 22 is that measuring it at least lets you prepare. Class three is neither measurable nor preventable, the true black swan; it takes organizational resilience, meaning the intertemporal responsibility of Chapter 28, the knowledge pack of Chapter 30, and the supply chain resilience of Chapter 33. Resilience is not defence against a named risk. It keeps the organization from shattering when an unnamed one arrives. The sorting is itself the first act of prevention. Most organizations talk about classes two and three as one thing, and the result is that neither class gets a countermeasure of its own.

The genealogy of both theories is worth setting out, so the reader knows what is in hand. Perrow's book appeared four years after Three Mile Island, and its immediate motive was dissatisfaction with the nuclear industry's safety narrative of the time, that small probability plus multiple defences equals safe enough. He pressed organization theory, engineering and historical material into a two-dimensional frame, interactive complexity and tight coupling, and used it to triage systems. Over the following forty years that frame produced a whole literature of criticism and inheritance.
