Practical drift (Chapter 15). Aviation carries the densest procedure set in the world, which makes the fork between formal process and actual practice the most instructive one to study. Samples: an air ambulance crew looking down in flight to consult the record book (av-020, the behaviour chain complete); getting out of an R22 with the engine running becoming routine (av-010, where the manufacturer's safety notice had stated the risk years before); a 737 whose takeoff performance was computed for the full runway while the takeoff ran from an intersection, with nobody stepping in (av-028). Every generating condition for practical drift is present here. The rules are written by people who do not fly, the workload is heavy, and a violation almost never carries a consequence.

Margin erosion (Chapter 25). Samples: approved extensions of the horizontal stabiliser lubrication and inspection intervals (av-034, where the cut had a document, an approver, and delivered itself flight by flight); a 747 freighter cargo door left unsealed in rain, letting water reach the electronics bay (av-026, no recheck required of the fairing and the seals). Aviation keeps a ledger tradition for margins. The ledger is held by the operator, and regulatory approval is the legal channel through which a margin gets cut.

Automation and skill decay (Chapter 26). Samples: the autothrottle inadvertently shut off during Asiana 214's visual approach (av-031); a helicopter cleared to a helipad that landed on a runway instead (av-017, no reconfirmation before final approach). Automation dependence combined with compressed training hours is the failure path this industry has validated most often. The industry's own countermeasures, manual-flying quotas and scenario-based simulator training, are worth taking as a complete set by anyone borrowing from this page.

docs.title: 5 What Outsiders Most Easily Mislearn
docs.text:
Mislearning one: taking the checklist for a culture. An aviation checklist works because three supports sit under it. The person signing has the authority to stop the line. Findings are recorded, and the record is not used to assign blame. Missed checks get caught by a data system, FDM, flight data monitoring. Remove the three and the checklist decays into a signature campaign (Chapter 32, compliant and unsafe). Transplanting the form without the system is the commonest cross-industry mis-transplant there is.

Mislearning two: taking one case's lesson for the mechanism. The safety recommendations at the end of a report address specific conditions; lift one out (say, "improve communication") and you have taken the prescription without seeing the patient. The right use is the mechanism field on the case card. Classify first, meaning decide which chapter the case hangs on, then read Section 5 of that chapter for the countermeasures.

Mislearning three: mistaking aviation's transparency for the industry norm. Aviation can publish full reports because a disaster paid for the institution (Chapter 4). Arguing inside your own organization that aviation publishes, so why can't we, points in the right direction. Do not overestimate how easy the publishing is. Behind every page of a public report stands a statutory power to investigate.

(First draft of this page: 2,325 characters.)

docs.title: 6 Three Questions from Readers Outside the Field
docs.text:
What use is an aviation case to me, when my industry has no airworthiness rules? The use sits in the mechanism, not the regulation. Normalization of deviance (Chapter 11) and margin erosion (Chapter 25) are isomorphic across industries; the regulation is only the parameter.

Aviation's accident rate is already low, so is there anything left to learn? The low rate is an institutional output, produced by the four devices of Chapter 3. What you learn is the mechanics of the institution, and copying the clauses is not the same exercise.

Isn't this too technical, all that airworthiness vocabulary? The twelve fields of the case card have already flattened the vocabulary into a sequence of actions. The one-sentence event description in field two is written for a reader outside the field, and the technical detail stays in the body text for verification.

The common answer to all three: aviation is the best specimen library of mechanisms in the book because its records are the best (Chapter 3), and for no other reason.

How to use the list: when a new accident bulletin from this domain arrives, guess the mechanism against this table before reading. Your hit rate is your familiarity with the accent of failure in this domain. Then read the report and check the guess. Where you guessed wrong is the layer of industry skin still between you and the domain.

docs.title: 8 How This Page Gets Updated
docs.text: A domain page is a live document. Once a year, take the new Grade A and Grade B reports in aviation and check them against the five columns here and against the distribution in Section 7. A mechanism that has not appeared before gets a new line in Section 4. A shift in frequency gets an updated count in Section 7. A new Grade A case goes into the library under the field standard of Chapter 5. The trigger, the owner and the review date go into the user's calendar (Chapter 39). Like any ledger, a domain page that is not updated is dead.

docs.title: 9 The Starter Kit
docs.text: Three items for a reader new to aviation. Entry case: av-001, the parked 787 whose emergency locator transmitter lithium battery caught fire and damaged the aft fuselage (AAIB, 2015, link in Appendix B). Read that one first for the house style and granularity of a report in this domain. Entry data source: the primary libraries listed in the aviation part of. Find the entry points, bookmark them, visit once a quarter. Entry mechanism: start from the first row of the table in Section 7 and read the mechanism chapter against a case in this domain. Read one mechanism twice, once in the chapter for the criteria and once here for the parameters. Working through the three items takes about one working day and leaves you with a first coordinate system for the domain.

docs.title: 10 Reservations
docs.text: Three limits apply to everything judged on this page. The book's case library samples toward events with rich public records, and the record skew is the subject of Chapter 2. The frequency ordering of mechanisms reflects the distribution inside this library, not the true distribution in the domain. Institutions and technology in the domain keep moving, so this page has a shelf life measured in years, and a reader quoting it should state the year of the quotation. All three limits are the book's general disclaimer, and the threshold check of Chapter 1 applies to the book itself as well.

docs.title: 11 How the Three Layers Sound in Aviation
docs.text: Read aviation cases through the three-layer model of Chapter 9 and one accent stands out. Breakpoints at the organizational and incentive layers rarely appear alone; they almost always arrive together with a missing signal at the technical layer. The reason is the density of the four recording devices (Chapter 3). A technical signal nearly always leaves a trace, and the failure sits in whether the organization translated it, which is breakpoint one in Chapter 9. The typical incentive-layer form is the tension between a business model paid per departure and the redundancy that safety needs (Chapter 17, av-032), and that line is tightest in the regional carrier system. For a reviewer: on the nine-cell walkthrough of an aviation case, the incentive cell most often needs to be traced back to the day the commercial model was signed, which is the longest retrospective reach of any intervention.

docs.title: 13 Closing Address
docs.text:
The last word for aviation's governing layer. The four devices are thick enough already. What this domain has left to improve sits at the execution end rather than the recording end: tracking whether safety recommendations actually land (the implementation-rate logic of Chapter 19), and the real effect of training (the manual-flying quota of Chapter 26). Those two are where the next stage of spending pays. The value of these cases does not lie in telling aviation how to work, since aviation is more professional at this than the book is. It lies in letting other industries take away the mechanics: the four devices of Chapter 3, the protection logic of Chapter 19, the freshness regime of Chapter 26. Aviation's position in this book is that of a template rather than a specimen.

Aviation holds the most cases of any domain, 41 in the av series. That reflects where aviation sits in the library: the main ground on which the mechanisms are validated, with all twenty-four mechanisms having at least one aviation sample. A reader who wants to learn the whole mechanism set from a single domain should pick aviation for coverage. The same coverage has a side effect worth naming. It can leave the impression that failure happens only in industries with a formal investigation system. Read Chapter 2 (calibrating for record skew) after this page, or aviation's transparency will be mistaken for the normal state of the world.

docs.title: 16 Closing Notes on the Aviation Page
docs.text: This page is the largest of the domain pages because its public material is the thickest. Formal reports from NTSB, AAIB, JTSB, BEA and BFU form a band of evidence that compares across borders, and one mechanism can be evidenced repeatedly, in different chapters of different reports. One warning goes with the material. Thick material breeds aviation exceptionalism, the belief that this industry prevents failure because of resources no one else has. Aviation's actual distinction is a single thing: the institutional density of mandatory reporting and independent investigation (first among the five precedent domains of Chapter 3). Institutional density can be borrowed by other domains. The thickness of the reports is only its output. When you meet any device on this page, ask first where it snags in another industry. Most of the time the answer is institutional density, and that answer can be changed.

docs.title: Chemical & Process | ch
docs.text: Five columns: record quality, feedback delay, coupling, the three deadliest mechanisms, and what outsiders most easily mislearn.

docs.title: 1 Record Quality
docs.text: The U.S. Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board (CSB) is the primary benchmark in this domain. It investigates and does not prosecute, publishes reports in full, tracks its recommendations, and attaches an animated reconstruction to each case page (retrieval route in). The UK HSE regime covers occupational and process safety. On the Chinese side, the Ministry of Emergency Management's section for reports on especially serious accidents carries the full text of State Council investigation team reports (Qingdao 11·22, Kunshan 8·2 and others), while accidents beneath that grade usually appear as bulletins rather than full reports. The Chinese part of this book's chemical sample is layered accordingly, with ch-007 and ch-008 as Grade A full texts. Overall: material on major accidents is rich, material on small and medium accidents depends on company records, and the public sample leans toward the heavy tail.

docs.title: 2 Feedback Delay
docs.text: Three layers coexist. At the process layer, loss of control is measured in seconds and minutes (runaway reaction, leaking vapour cloud) and feedback arrives almost at once. At the equipment layer, degradation (corrosion, fatigue, seal ageing) runs in months and years. At the management layer, arrears in maintenance, in classification and in regulatory coverage run in decades, and they settle in a single payment usually shaped like a major accident (the dust workshop of ch-008, the regulatory gap of ch-002). A chemical decision maker faces the whole spectrum of delays at once, and budgets and appraisals naturally favour the fast-feedback layer.

docs.title: 3 Coupling
docs.text: Coupling inside the plant is high. Pipelines, utilities and tankage interleave in one physical space, so a small fault can amplify along a process route; the relief line in ch-005 became the channel through which an explosion travelled. Coupling across the boundary rises with the distance to the community: the evacuation radius of a toxic release connects a plant decision straight to public emergency response. Single units are physically segregated by design, and shared utilities (power, nitrogen, steam, the effluent system) are the classic gathering place for dark lines.

docs.title: 4 The Three Deadliest Mechanisms
docs.text: Hidden coupling (Chapter 21): a relief system tied back into the process (ch-005), and the dark lines that run through shared utilities. Margin erosion (Chapter 25): reactivity testing that never happened, relief capacity sized too small, a process safety management system absent altogether (ch-006). Compliant and unsafe (Chapter 32): after a building's hazardous-area classification was entered wrong, every inspection round still passed (ch-008); inside a regulatory gap, several layers of inspection each covered one segment and nobody covered the seams (ch-002). Next in frequency: normalization of deviance (Chapter 11, the 32 alarms in ch-001) and information attenuation up the hierarchy (Chapter 16, the reporting chain in ch-007).

docs.title: 5 What Outsiders Most Easily Mislearn
docs.text:
Mislearning one: taking a hazardous chemicals permit for safety management. A permit covers the moment of admission; process safety management covers the whole of operation. The cost difference between the two is a factor of ten.

Mislearning two: taking the CSB animation for the complete truth of an event. The animation is a communication tool. The evidence chain lives in the body of the report and in the case file.

Mislearning three: learning only from the countermeasures to big accidents. Small and medium releases and near misses carry most of the learning available in this domain, and they are exactly what gets recorded least (Chapter 2, record skew). Learning from major accidents alone is training everyday decisions on a tail distribution.

docs.title: 6 Three Questions from Readers Outside the Field
docs.text:
Is a chemical plant explosion really that far from me? The commercial equivalents of these mechanisms sit close by. A dust workshop maps onto dust in woodworking and food processing, a runaway reaction onto any exothermic process, a gap in storage and transport onto any warehouse compliance regime. Mechanism has no boundary.

The CSB only covers the United States, so is there anything to learn from Chinese chemical cases? Yes. ch-007 and ch-008 are both Chinese Grade A full-text reports, and a State Council investigation team report is complete in structure with its list of accountability public. The Chinese chemical record is more usable than most readers assume.

Isn't safety spending in chemicals just money burnt? Safety spending is another form of insurance premium. The cost of not spending settles as an accident; the direct economic loss in ch-008 was 351 million yuan. The arithmetic is in Section 2 of this chapter and in Chapter 29.

docs.title: 10 Reservations
docs.text: Three limits apply to everything judged on this page. The book's case library samples toward events with rich public records, and the record skew is the subject of Chapter 2. The frequency ordering of mechanisms reflects the distribution inside this library, not the true distribution in the domain. Institutions and technology in the domain keep moving, so this page has a shelf life measured in years, and a reader quoting it should state the year of the quotation. All three limits are the book's general disclaimer, and the threshold check of Chapter 1 applies to the book itself as well.

docs.title: 11 How the Three Layers Sound in This Domain
docs.text: The accent in chemical cases is that the physical layer is the loudest. Process upsets, dust explosions and vapour clouds present a technical failure at physical scale, in tonnes and megawatts. Two review traps follow. The drama of the physical layer absorbs all the attention, so breakpoints at the organizational and incentive layers get mentioned in passing; the misclassified building in ch-008 and the absent process safety management system in ch-006 both sit at the organizational or incentive layer. Public and press attention then goes to whose operating error it was, while the value the CSB adds is precisely in pushing attribution up to structure. For a reviewer: on the nine-cell walkthrough of a chemical case, the evidence in the incentive row has to reach back to the process selection and contract structure of the plant's construction phase. The retrospective reach is the longest on the page, and the return is the largest.

docs.title: 13 Closing Address
docs.text:
The lessons of this domain compress into one sentence: the physical world does not negotiate over its margin. Reactivity testing cannot be skipped, relief design cannot be sized on an estimate, a misclassified building has to be corrected on purpose. Each of those is an entry in the margin ledger of Chapter 25, and chemical margins are the most physical in the book. No software rolls them back and no announcement recalls them. After the signature and the startup, the reactor tied to the grid and the tank roof sealed, the only move left is to have worked through the decision table of Chapter 7 before the irreversible point. A chemical reader who prints that table and tapes it up in the control room has taken the most concrete deliverable this chapter offers.

Nine cases is a small number, and the density of lessons in them is among the highest in the book: 97 dead, 62 dead, 14 dead, 4 dead, 2 dead. Chemical Grade A cases almost all carry fatalities. That is not evidence that chemistry is more dangerous. It is the filing threshold of the domain filtering out the light accidents (Chapter 2). The lessons of a small chemical accident settle inside the company, where no outsider sees them, and that is the shape of the record skew here. What you are reading is the part of the iceberg above water. For the volume below it, consider that the 5 recommendations of ch-006 were rated unacceptable: a company can refuse even a CSB recommendation, so the internal lessons of a small accident travel outward even less.

docs.title: 14 How the Mechanisms Vary in This Domain
docs.text:
The chemical variation on the invisibility of maintenance. Maintenance arrears in this domain come with a physical amplifier built in. Read the general criteria in the local language: no output measure for maintenance reads as "the turnaround window yields to the production schedule" (the exhaust fan in ch-001 went unrepaired for months, on the grounds that a shutdown loss counted against the appraisal); budget pressure reads as "the utility refurbishment slips down the schedule" (the dust collection system in ch-008). One criterion is specific to this domain: verification of what a turnaround delivered. The work light left in the explosion-proof area (ch-005) sits outside the general weak-signal list, and the local list needs an added line on whether the closeout of a turnaround has a record of leftover items. The point of the variation: maintenance failure in chemicals does not decay. A year of arrears is paid in tonnes.

The chemical variation on extrapolating past the validated domain. The direction of extrapolation is fixed here: from rated conditions toward boundary conditions. The lesson of ch-003 is that a grid outage was extrapolated into "the backup supply will hold", and a flood level into "the cold store will not be inundated"; every hop of that extrapolation was written into the emergency plan, and no one was responsible for the hop distance. The lesson of ch-006 runs the other way: reaction calorimetry from a small-scale test was extrapolated to a production reactor, and relief capacity was designed on the old data. The reading discipline for this domain: wherever a plan or a design document contains "shall", "as customary" or "with reference to a similar unit", there is an extrapolation point. Register each one (the first device of Chapter 23).

The chemical variation on normalization of deviance. Alarms are the main ground on which normalization happens here. The 32 alarms in ch-001 were acknowledged one by one over several hours, and an acknowledgement costs two seconds on the DCS. The convenience of acknowledging an alarm is itself an accelerator of normalization in this domain. How to read it: sort the alarm list into three classes by response type (an operator must attend, the process needs adjusting, information only), and a rising share in the information-only class is a weak signal. Reading that needs no specialist knowledge, only a DCS report. The line connects to the three-state register of the first device in Chapter 11: alarm entries get three states and no more, and the fourth state, acknowledged but not actioned, is forbidden.

docs.title: 15 Cross-Reading Suggestions
docs.text: The highest return comes from reading this page against three others. Against the nuclear page: the two domains share three kinds of site, the tag, the alarm and the overhaul, and the independent verification device on the nuclear page (the lesson of nu-002) transfers directly into chemical isolation management for turnarounds. Against the manufacturing page: the recall machinery of the mn series and chemical process safety share the language of batch traceability, and the discussion of mandatory standards on the manufacturing page (a variation on Chapter 32, compliant and unsafe) and the misclassification in ch-008 stand as footnotes to one another. Against the public policy page: read ch-007 (Qingdao) alongside the large-project chapter of the po series to see how the mechanisms of emergency decision making stack up on the seam between government and company. All three pairings point at one sentence: chemical failures rarely stay inside chemicals.

docs.title: Nuclear & Energy | nu
docs.text: Five columns: record quality, feedback delay, coupling, the three deadliest mechanisms, and what outsiders most easily mislearn. The case library for this domain has not been collected yet, so this page sets the frame first: the institutional picture and the mechanism judgements rest on the institutional analysis of Chapter 3. The empty case slots show up as a wholly empty column in Appendix A and will be filled once the collection is done.

docs.title: 1 Record Quality
docs.text: Institutional depth here is the greatest of any industry, and the public face is split in two. Mandatory reporting and international sharing: the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and the OECD Nuclear Energy Agency run the Incident Reporting System (IRS) together, and operating events from member states enter a shared pool; the U.S. NRC requires licensees to submit operating event reports (10 CFR Part 50.73). The other half is closed: the reports and assessments of the World Association of Nuclear Operators (WANO) are proprietary, circulating inside the industry and invisible from outside. What the open world can get is each regulator's own documents, NRC inspection reports and event reports, French ASN notices, with the depth of detail set by the country in question; retrieval routes and the direction for filling the gaps are in.

docs.title: 2 Feedback Delay
docs.text: The longest in any industry. Design defects and material ageing return their feedback over decades. Operating events return theirs in months, filtered through several layers of review. Organizational and safety-culture consequences take longer still: the lessons of Chernobyl and Fukushima entered operating practice on a scale of decades. The one short-feedback layer is training and the simulator. This domain has almost no fast feedback, and all of its learning depends on institutional memory (Chapter 30).

docs.title: 3 Coupling
docs.text: Perrow classes nuclear power as the archetype of a system that is high on both interactive complexity and tight coupling: the interactions between subsystems exceed anyone's full understanding, and failures travel faster than any intervention. Seventy years of defence amount to taming that coupling inside multiple physical barriers and defence in depth. Nuclear is therefore the other example of high coupling held down by institutions, standing alongside aviation but with different instruments: aviation through investigation, nuclear through physical barriers and redundancy. Coupling between plants is low, since sites are independent. Coupling across generations is high: designs carry over, standards carry over, and lesson sharing depends on international systems.

docs.title: 4 The Three Deadliest Mechanisms (from Institutional Analysis, Case Slots Pending)
docs.text: The illusion of redundancy (Chapter 22): common-cause failure of multiple defences is the standard shape of a nuclear accident, where common cause means an external event or a systemic design or cultural defect, and the shared-source failure of standby power and emergency systems is the most studied lesson in the field. Handover rupture (Chapter 30): passing operating experience between generations depends on closed industry systems (WANO, INPO), and institutionalizing organizational memory is the lifeline of this domain. Regulatory lag and capture (Chapter 31): licence extensions for design life and the certification of new reactor types keep a standing tension between the rules and the technology. This column will be revised against actual cases once the collection is done.

docs.title: 5 What Outsiders Most Easily Mislearn
docs.text:
Mislearning one: reading WANO's closed doors as an absence of failure records. The internal record density here may be the highest in the world; it is simply not published. Concluding that nuclear offers nothing to learn is a double misjudgement.

Mislearning two: taking the INES scale for a linear measure of severity. It is logarithmic, and it tracks international public impact more than loss.

Mislearning three: taking the visible layers of defence in depth for the actual line of defence. The common-cause check of Chapter 22 is a life-and-death question in a nuclear setting, and treating it as a compliance exercise is the error.

docs.title: 6 Three Questions from Readers Outside the Field
docs.text:
What use is a nuclear case to an industry that is not nuclear? Nuclear is the archetype of defence in depth and conservative decision making. Its redundancy design, its graded event regime and its mechanism for sharing operating experience are all reference frames for other industries (Chapter 3).

The safety record is so good, is there anything left to learn? Precisely because the recording threshold is so low, with even an INES level 0 entered, this domain holds the thickest near-miss library anywhere. The learning value of near misses is the subject of Chapter 2: a low threshold produces earlier lessons rather than more records.

What do the event levels mean? INES runs 0 to 7 on a severity scale, 0 having no safety significance and 7 a major release. Every nuclear case in this book sits between 1 and 3, and the lower levels carry the higher density of lessons: they are numerous, fully detailed, and most of them came out of luck rather than defence.

docs.title: 11 How the Three Layers Sound in This Domain
docs.text: The accent here is that the organizational layer is the thickest. Procedures, tags, watchkeeping, review levels: the density of organizational defence is the highest of any industry, and the INPO and WANO assessment systems are a complete model of organizational audit. Two consequences follow. A break at the organizational layer alone is very unlikely in a nuclear case, since that layer almost always catches it, so real failure almost always needs the incentive layer to cooperate: a budget cut leaves the organizational gate unrepaired for years, and appraisal pressure makes conservative decision making give way. For a reviewer: on the three-layer walkthrough of a nuclear case, the technical breakpoint usually enters only at the last moment, and before that there is a long rope running through the organizational and incentive layers. The far end of the rope is often a budget meeting ten years back.

docs.title: 13 Closing Address
docs.text:
One line for the nuclear reader: this industry has already installed the four devices to their limit (Chapter 3), and the real value of its cases for this book is the view of what residual risk looks like once defence density has hit the ceiling. The residual no longer comes from a missing record or an absent independent investigation, since both are there. It comes from the slow loosening of the organizational and incentive layers (Chapter 25 and Chapter 28). The nuclear case tells the reader that an institution is a starting point, and that keeping it running is the work. That is also why this book treats nuclear cases with the most caution, with an evidence grade and an archival source marked on every one.

Four cases make this one of the thinnest domains in the book, and the thinness is itself a result of success: operating events run into the tens of thousands, major accidents into single digits. The INES grading lets a reader calibrate severity precisely. Level 1, which covers nu-001, nu-002 and nu-003, marks an operating anomaly; level 3 and above is an accident. The value of low-level cases was set out in Chapter 2: they are near misses turned into text. The recording regime of this industry converts what other industries leave unrecorded into a written record, and that is this domain's particular contribution to the book. Few cases do not mean few lessons. Lesson density is lessons divided by cases, and nuclear has the highest lesson density of any domain here.

docs.title: 14 How the Mechanisms Vary in This Domain
docs.text:
The nuclear variation on practical drift. Drift here happens almost entirely at the interface between paperwork and action, and the tag is the largest such interface. The two tagging errors in nu-001 and nu-002 share one shape: the logic on the tag sheet was right, the physical match was wrong, the wrong valve or the wrong cabinet was tagged, and the compensatory measures were recorded on paper with nobody going to the site to verify them. How to read it: whether the verification action was independent, a second pair of eyes, is the core detection point for drift in this domain. Independent verification is a written requirement of nuclear safety culture; what varies in practice is the density with which it is executed. The general criterion, that the rule is written so that nobody can follow it, barely holds here, since nuclear has a surplus of rules. The local criterion for drift has to be rewritten as: the rule set is complete and the verification step is omitted by custom.

The nuclear variation on normalization of deviance. Normalization happens mainly on temporary exemptions for unavailable equipment. The technical specifications of a unit set hard limits on how long key equipment may be unavailable (the 24 hours in nu-001), and going past the limit requires a shutdown or a power reduction, so recovery just inside the limit becomes standard practice: the item comes back at hour 23 and 50 minutes, and the next cycle runs the same way. How to read it: take the distribution of recovery times against the limit, meaning the share of recoveries that land between hour 20 and hour 24. A share that is improbably high says the limit is being used as a target rather than a boundary, which is goal displacement (Chapter 12) mirrored into nuclear. The three-state register needs a fourth column here: how the item was restored, really or on paper.

The nuclear variation on the invisibility of maintenance. The maintenance ledger here is the thickest in any industry; the thin one is the verification ledger. The lesson of nu-003, samples lost and an unregistered sealed source, shows another kind of maintenance: the ledger for sources and samples is kept by hand, the entry depends on an individual researcher's diligence, and the institution has no stock-count mechanism. How to read it: the frequency of a stock reconciliation audit, meaning the three-way check that the ledger has it, the site has it, and nothing is on site that the ledger lacks, is the right indicator for invisible maintenance in this domain. An audit that reads repair records and never reconciles stock is thick and hollow.

docs.title: 15 Cross-Reading Suggestions
docs.text: The first priority is reading this page against the chemical page: tagging, alarms and overhauls are the same three kinds of site in both, and the three variations in Section 14 of the chemical page can each be converted back into nuclear terms. Against the aerospace page: read the discussion of review culture in mi-001, where the flight rationale goes into the ledger, alongside the operating experience feedback system of nuclear (the WGOF tradition at OECD/NEA), and the different institutional densities with which two high-reliability industries handle precedent evidence become visible. Against the healthcare page: read the piped oxygen supply in me-011 against the utility redundancy here, and the gap between the two industries in the verification density of life-support systems shows up plainly. Healthcare can borrow the whole vocabulary of independent verification from this page.

docs.title: Healthcare | me
docs.text: Five columns: record quality, feedback delay, coupling, the three deadliest mechanisms, and what outsiders most easily mislearn.

docs.title: 1 Record Quality
docs.text:
The latecomer that built the institution properly is the United Kingdom. The Health Services Safety Investigations Body (HSSIB, formerly HSIB) runs its investigations on the aviation pattern, and its reports carry the event sequence, the safety recommendations, and a national figure to anchor them, such as "roughly 192 wrong-site surgeries nationwide each year". Every me case in this book comes out of that archive. The original site was unreachable from the network used to collect material for this book, so the reports were read through Internet Archive snapshots, and records which snapshot stands behind which case.

The American material is a step removed. AHRQ's Patient Safety Network (PSNet) and Web&M&M publish case commentaries, secondary curation written for teaching, strong on framing and weak as evidence. On the device side the FDA's MAUDE database holds reports in volume, with single-entry quality uneven.

China's health commission bulletins are available only intermittently. The workable substitute is the judgment in a medical damage liability dispute, which supplies a dated sequence, expert opinion, and a finding on causation, at the price of a legal frame wrapped around a clinical event (Chapter 3).

The verdict: full-text investigation is best in the UK, and its narrative depth is unusual because the patient's identity is protected while the whole chain stays legible. The sample per case is small, which is why the national figure carries as much weight as the report itself.

docs.title: 2 Feedback Delay
docs.text:
Three layers, and they run at wildly different speeds. At the medication and surgical layer feedback is counted in minutes: a wrong site or a wrong concentration shows on the table or by the end of the day. At the process layer it is counted in weeks and months: follow-up that does not happen, results that nobody claims, with the twelve-day reporting delay of me-005 as the type specimen. At the system layer it is counted in years: how far the reconciliation routine has drifted, what the identification-event rate is doing.

What separates healthcare from the rest of the book is the spread inside a single shift. One nurse's day holds second-scale and year-scale risk at the same time, and a reflex trained at one scale misfires at the other.

docs.title: 3 Coupling
docs.text: Inside a hospital, coupling is moderate. Processes are templated closely enough that a defect replicates isomorphically from ward to ward, and physical separation is comparatively generous, so a bad process does not take the building down with it. Across the industry, coupling is high. A process validated at one hospital gets adopted nationally and the defects travel with it: the medication-error shapes of me-001 through me-003 recur across HSIB's national figures instead of staying local. A national protocol is a single point with national reach. The colour coding of injectable medicines is the standing example; when the coding fails, it fails everywhere at once.

docs.title: 4 The Three Deadliest Mechanisms
docs.text:
Handover rupture (Chapter 30). Healthcare carries the densest handover surface in the book: shift to shift, ward to theatre, hospital to community, road to resuscitation room. me-006 carries an identity error from the prehospital crew into a duplicate record in the emergency department. me-005 leaves an abnormal chest film with no owner for twelve days. Every one of those surfaces is a candidate rupture, and the number of surfaces, not the diligence of the staff, sets the exposure.

Compliant and unsafe (Chapter 32). The paperwork is done while the act is not. me-001's Stop Before You Block was signed off as the block went into the wrong leg. me-002 walked around the concentration coding system with an ordinary choice of syringe.

The illusion of redundancy (Chapter 22). me-003 took out two defences in one event: the purple syringe that was meant to mark the route, and the second pair of eyes that was meant to catch it.

Next in frequency, diffusion of responsibility (Chapter 18). me-008's incompatible implant came to light afterwards through a registry.

docs.title: 5 What Outsiders Most Easily Mislearn
docs.text:
Mislearning one: treating individual accountability as system improvement. Healthcare's review culture has been occupied for decades by the question of who was at fault, and the institutional innovation at HSSIB is the separation of investigation from blame. That structure is the transferable asset. No particular checklist is.

Mislearning two: imagining that a hospital's strict processes are strict in execution. A checklist in use and a check performed are two different states, and the gap between them is where several cases in this book live (Chapter 32).

Mislearning three: undervaluing the national figure. A single hospital's case teaches little on its own; the real contribution of an HSSIB report is a national frequency to divide by. Any lesson learned at one site should be read against that base before it is generalised.

docs.title: 6 Three Questions from Readers Outside the Field
docs.text:
Are the healthcare cases only for clinicians? No, and the reason is structural. Healthcare is the prototype site for decisions taken under time pressure, on incomplete information, with a lethal consequence attached, and the mechanisms transfer whole. A triage priority conflict and a medication check that breaks at a handover are shapes a trading desk or a control room meets as well.

Will the hierarchy make the cases hard to follow? The twelve fields have already flattened clinical language into actions. A block injected into the wrong leg, a chest report that arrives twelve days late: the sequence is readable by anyone. Terminology stays in the source report for those who want it.

Is the blame culture in medicine especially heavy? It varies widely by jurisdiction, and the second-victim problem, the injury done to the clinician who made the error, is a public topic in medicine earlier than anywhere else. The repair work on blame culture started here first, and its lessons travel (Chapter 19).

Then read and check. The places you guessed wrong mark the thickness of industry skin still between you and the field.

docs.text:
A domain page is a live document. Once a year, take the Grade A and Grade B reports added to this domain, walk them against the five columns above and the table in Section 7, and revise. A mechanism that appears for the first time gets a line in Section 4. A shift in frequency updates the counts in Section 7. A new Grade A case goes into the library against the field standard of Chapter 5.

The trigger, the owner, and the review date belong in the user's calendar (Chapter 39). A domain page that is not updated is dead in the same way a ledger is: the information does not rot, it simply stops describing the field.

docs.title: 9 The Starter Kit
docs.text:
Three items for a reader new to this domain, about one working day in total.

The entry case is me-001, a nerve block for right ankle surgery injected into the left leg, investigated by HSIB (the predecessor of HSSIB) in 2018, with the link in Appendix B. Read it first for the format and the grain of the reports in this field.

The entry source is the first-hand library listed under Healthcare in. Find the entrance, bookmark it, visit once a quarter.

The entry mechanism is the first line of the Section 7 table. Read the mechanism chapter beside the case from this domain and take the pair twice, once for the criterion in the chapter and once for the parameters here. When the three items are done you own a first coordinate system for the field.

docs.title: 10 Reservations
docs.text:
Three limits apply to every judgement on this page. The book's case library samples toward events with rich public records, which is the record skew of Chapter 2. The frequency ranking in Section 7 describes the book's library, not the true distribution of the domain. Institutions and technology both move, so this page has a shelf life measured in years, and a citation should carry the year it was read.

All three are the book's general disclaimer, and the threshold check of Chapter 1 applies to this book as much as to anything it examines.

docs.title: 11 How the Three Layers Sound in This Domain
docs.text:
The accent here is breakpoint one, the place where a technical signal never gets translated by the organizational layer, and it is the most crowded of the three. A clinical signal, whether a symptom, a laboratory value, or an imaging finding, reaches an organizational action such as a consultation, a referral, or a follow-up only through several translations: triage, handover, report routing. Each translation is a high-incidence breakpoint, and me-005's delayed chest film and me-016's broken discharge information both sit at one. The incentive layer takes the form of bed occupancy and turnover targets, with rewards going to the teams that move patients fastest, and that tension acts directly on handover quality.

For the reviewer: in a healthcare nine-cell table the organizational layer usually holds the densest evidence, because the record system timestamps itself, while the technical layer often surfaces only in post-mortem pathology. Getting the timeline right is the whole of the walkthrough.

docs.title: 13 Closing Address
docs.text:
The last word to the governance layer in healthcare. The HSSIB reports are among the strongest accident analysis texts produced anywhere, and what they share is a method: no blame, and a system diagram instead of a verdict. The largest lesson in this book's healthcare cases belongs to system designers. me-005's ownership of follow-up, me-013's decision support, me-015's triage differential: in each case the defence lands on a structure, not on a person. That is the HSSIB method, and it is the spirit of the Systems Engineering Initiative for Patient Safety. A clinical reader who carries the structural analysis back to his own department has taken the chapter's delivery.

The cases on this page come from independent HSIB investigation, and their common quality is a full reconstruction plus recommendations pitched at system level. The method, with its no-blame frame, its systems analysis, and its publicly tracked recommendations, is the most mature institutional experiment in safety that medicine has run, and these cases show what kind of knowledge product it yields. An HSIB report reads like a postmortem written with the nine-cell table; the three-layer analysis of Chapter 9 is its standard structure. For a medical student the practical use is to read these reports as an advanced form of case teaching. What is learned is systems thinking, and systems thinking is the safety net under clinical skill: the denser the net, the safer the patient.

docs.title: 14 How the Mechanisms Vary in This Domain
docs.text:
Handover rupture at maximum density. One inpatient admission passes through a dozen handovers (prehospital, emergency, ward, imaging, theatre, nursing shift), and every one of them reorganises the information once. me-005 and me-006 stand for the two lesions. In the first, a result has no owner and the loop never closes. In the second, the key is wrong and the record duplicates. The local measure is closure rate rather than record thickness: of the result-type messages sent out, how many were explicitly received and acted on within the window. Count it by department, and put Chapter 30's device wherever the rate falls below the threshold. Rupture in healthcare almost never presents as not knowing. It presents as assuming the other side knew.

Normalization with a moral shell. "For the patient" is the most common licence for compressing a check in this domain. In me-011, where the piped oxygen supply fell short, the emergency itself exempted the verification steps. In me-016, where a three-month-old deteriorated after discharge, discharge criteria applied in bulk absorbed one infant's abnormality into the mean. The local instrument is a register with two columns, emergency exemption and convention exemption, counting every check skipped under the heading of urgency or of routine. The monthly totals are a thermometer for normalization. Exemptions cannot be abolished, since resuscitation is what it is, but each one must carry a name and a time. Anonymous exemption is the incubator.

Truth-telling against a steeper gradient than any firm's. me-015 and me-016 both contain a junior doubt that was never escalated, and the authority structure of a medical team is what kept it where it was. The only reliable indicator of health here is the dissent record of departmental meetings: who raised a different view on which case, and what happened to it afterwards. An anonymous survey cannot measure a culture. Chapter 19's list of alarms has its healthcare counterpart in one question: is the difficult-case conference actually discussing the case, or endorsing it?

docs.title: 15 Cross-Reading Suggestions
docs.text:
Healthcare against maritime is the most surprising pair in the book. Both run small teams, high pressure, and explicit rank, and the bridge and the theatre turn out to share one problem in attention management: ma-002's alarm masked by music reads beside me-001's checklist degraded to a signature.

Against Drugs and Devices: me-014's misread morphine concentration and the recalls in the ph series meet at the same design question, since the error space of a device label and the error space of a drug label are one space. Chapter 26 deserves conservative handling in this domain; me-013 shows what an absent decision support costs, and it does not follow that decision support is a cure.

Against nuclear and energy: see the cross-reading section on that page.

docs.title: Drugs and Devices | ph
docs.text: Five columns: record quality, feedback delay, coupling, the three deadliest mechanisms, and what outsiders most easily mislearn.

docs.title: 1 Record Quality
docs.text:
This domain runs on mandatory reporting plus a public database (Chapter 3), and the American first-hand channel is the most complete of the three. Recall and enforcement reports can be pulled programmatically through the openFDA interface, across the drug, device, and food databases, and every ph case in this book was checked against those API records. The device adverse event database (MAUDE) varies in quality entry by entry and makes up for it in volume. An FDA safety communication that carries an investigation timeline can be graded strong.

Europe routes through the EMA and the national agencies. China's NMPA notices, recalls, and annual adverse reaction reports are the standard outlet, and the detail per entry is thinner.

The verdict: rich in signals and thin in review. What this domain records is the event. Why it happened is mostly left out, which is Section 3.5's pattern of signal detection standing in for accident investigation.

docs.title: 2 Feedback Delay
docs.text:
The structural feature of the field is that delays are long. Clinical trial feedback is counted in years. Post-market risk feedback is counted in years too, since an adverse reaction signal needs epidemiological verification between accumulation and confirmation. Feedback on device fatigue and ageing tracks intensity of use rather than the calendar.

The distribution and use end moves faster: recalls are executed, adverse events are reported. The reporting rate itself is disturbed by how aware the reporter is and how hard the causal link is to judge. The common illusion among decision makers is to read "no signal yet" as "no risk yet".

docs.title: 3 Coupling
docs.text:
Global distribution means simultaneous global exposure. A device enters several countries through a reprocessing protocol (ph-007). A packaging defect in one component enters hospitals across the United States inside a kit (ph-008).

Regulatory coupling comes next. One licensing decision, or the absence of one (ph-005), is exported along the distribution network to every market that recognises the licence or has no corresponding review of its own.

Production coupling concentrates at sterility assurance. A sterility failure is batch-level and crosses company boundaries (the kit case of Chapter 33).

docs.title: 4 The Three Deadliest Mechanisms
docs.text:
Extrapolating past the validated domain (Chapter 23). A single-use device is reprocessed and reused (ph-007). An unlicensed model reaches distribution (ph-005). A device built for one concentration scale is used on another, which is the same failure as me-002 on the clinical side.

Cascading failure (Chapter 33). The kit model carries a component defect across company lines (ph-008).

Regulatory lag and capture (Chapter 31). Marketing without a licence, reporting that lags by years (two years in ph-004), and new product forms landing outside the old classification.

Next in frequency, normalization of deviance (Chapter 11). The missing sterility assurance in ph-001 stays invisible until the consequence arrives.

docs.title: 5 What Outsiders Most Easily Mislearn
docs.text:
Mislearning one: reading the recall database as a safety ranking. Reporting culture, adjudication criteria, and product volumes are not standardised across firms or countries, so a comparison of recall counts means nothing.

Mislearning two: taking the absence of adverse event reports as evidence of safety. In a field where the reporting rate sits far below the true rate, silence carries no information.

Mislearning three: reading the Class designation as the size of the loss. Class describes an assumption about the severity of the health hazard, not the scale of the damage done. Small volume spread wide and large volume held narrow are different arithmetic entirely: the two units of ph-004 and the 5.9 million pieces of mn-006 sit at the two ends of the same page of the manual.

docs.title: 6 Three Questions from Readers Outside the Field
docs.text:
What does a drug recall have to do with me, when I do not make drugs? Recalls are the most complete textbook of supply chain failure available: one defect travelling from component to finished product, which is ph-008's kit model. Any industry with a supply chain stands on the same propagation path.

What can a database like MAUDE tell me? The density of risk, not its size. A report count is not an incidence count, and the distinction between signal and evidence in Chapter 3 is compulsory reading before the database is used.

How does marketing without a licence (ph-005) happen? The shape of a gate that fails is the same in every industry: the licence status was never hard-checked inside the system, and the design of the release system is Chapter 31. Drug and device cases display gate failure more clearly than any other material in the book.

docs.text:
Three items for a reader new to this domain, about one working day in total.

The entry case is ph-001, semaglutide injection recalled for insufficient sterility assurance, FDA, 2025, with the link in Appendix B. Read it first for the format and the grain of the reports in this field.

docs.title: 10 Reservations
docs.text:
Three limits apply to every judgement on this page. The book's case library samples toward events with rich public records, which is the record skew of Chapter 2. The frequency ranking in Section 7 describes the book's library, not the true distribution of the domain. Institutions and technology both move, so this page has a shelf life measured in years, and a citation should carry the year it was read.

All three are the book's general disclaimer, and the threshold check of Chapter 1 applies to this book as much as to anything it examines.

docs.title: 11 How the Three Layers Sound in This Domain
docs.text:
The accent in drugs and devices is that the incentive-layer breakpoint is the one that pays first. Design choice and supply contract are fixed before the product reaches the market, and the failure is repaid years later in the form of a recall: ph-007's reprocessing protocol stretches the original manufacturer's boundary outward, and ph-008's kit model lets a component defect travel between firms. The lookback from an incentive breakpoint here is the longest in the book, running from the recall date back to the date the contract was signed, a distance counted in years, with the evidence scattered between contract files and test records.

For the reviewer: in a nine-cell walkthrough of a drug or device case, the incentive cell should be read for the contract clauses as closely as for the appraisal scheme, and specifically for the weight given to price against the weight given to quality. The lesson of ma-001 applies in this industry as it does in any other.

docs.title: 13 Closing Address
docs.text:
One line for readers inside the industry. The failure chain in drugs and devices runs from a component supplier's packaging line all the way into a patient's vein, and a break at any link ends at the patient: ph-008's kit, ph-005's unlicensed distribution, ph-004's cold chain drift. Every link sits in the register of Chapter 33. The component supplier's name and the post that owns it belong in your risk register, and a supplier who is not on the register is a risk that is not on the register. The last step for a reader here is to open the supplier list and run it through Chapter 33's criteria. That step is available today.

The cases on this page come from the FDA recall and enforcement database, and every API record has been checked for this book. The structured format gives this domain an unusually complete evidence chain, since recall number, product code, distribution scope, and remedy are each a field, which makes these the finest-grained case records in the book. The case count is moderate, and the lessons run the full length from component to shelf: ph-008's kit model is the most complete display of supply chain failure the book contains, and one case read through one supply chain beats ten cases each seen in part. There is a dividend for readers here, because the FDA publishes an open API and a monitoring script is a weekend's work; Chapter 39's automation advice has its most direct technical entry at this point.

docs.title: 14 How the Mechanisms Vary in This Domain
docs.text:
Compliant and unsafe, the drug variation. Almost all ten recalls in the ph series came out of routine compliance inspection and market surveillance, which means the recall is the system working. The peculiar form here is a timing mismatch: the moment the compliance certificate covers and the period in which the risk is live do not coincide. In ph-001 the problem sits inside production batches while the inspection happens off site. In ph-010, where the Tyvek seal carries voids, the problem sits in drift of the packaging line parameters while periodic inspection samples by batch.

The local reading: the sampling density of compliance against the coverage needed for process parameter drift is the measure of whether compliance feeling equals safety in this field. A jurisdiction with many recalls is not a jurisdiction with high risk, since recall visibility is the positive form of the record skew in Chapter 2, and this point runs against outside intuition.

Extrapolation, the drug variation. In this domain extrapolation happens on the storage and transport chain. ph-004, where enoxaparin went outside its temperature range, carries the lesson: the conditions covered by the registration studies and the conditions of the real logistics network are two different distributions, the duration of exposure at the excursion point decides the quality outcome, and most quality systems handle an excursion as a binary event rather than accumulating a duration distribution. The reading: a temperature chain report that gives only the number of excursions, without duration and batch linkage, makes the extrapolation risk invisible. Chapter 23's Device 1 has its counterpart here in a table comparing registered conditions against actual logistics conditions, updated once a year.

Maintenance invisibility, the device variation. In devices it shows up as ageing of the reprocessing validation. ph-007's cracked trocars carry the lesson: the reprocessing protocol for a reused device is validated against a design life, and the gap between actual reuse counts and the validated count is tracked by nobody. The reading: set the reprocessing count ledger against the validated count ceiling, since use beyond the ceiling is a weak signal peculiar to this field. Read beside the consumer recalls of the mn series, where mn-006's forty-year-old product cracked, and the general property becomes visible: a validation has a shelf life. Devices count uses, consumer goods count years.

docs.title: 15 Cross-Reading Suggestions
docs.text:
Drugs and devices against healthcare is the first pairing to take, because the user end and the manufacturing end are two halves of one chain; me-014 and ph-009 meet at the design of a label.

Against manufacturing: the recall regimes of the mn and ph series share the language of CPSC and FDA, and the standards discussion in section 14 of the manufacturing page applies here without modification.

Against software: batch record traceability read beside deployment rollback shows that the two industries put their irreversible point in different places, drugs at the moment of injection and software at the moment of the push, while the management of the validation window before that point is one problem in both.

docs.title: Construction and Infrastructure | ce
docs.text: Five columns: record quality, feedback delay, coupling, the three deadliest mechanisms, and what outsiders most easily mislearn.

docs.title: 1 Record Quality
docs.text:
The sample for independent investigation of transport infrastructure is the UK's Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB). Reports sit in full on the gov.uk platform, and a formal report carries the maintenance and decision sequence, not just the physics, which is why the ce cases in this book rest mainly on RAIB material. The American benchmark for building failure is NIST's post-disaster investigation, with the Surfside condominium as the reference case and a technical conclusion that took five years to reach. Construction-phase safety in the UK falls to HSE.

On the Chinese side, the Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development and the Ministry of Transport issue mainly bulletins, and the availability of an investigation report for a major bridge or building accident varies from case to case.

The verdict: transport infrastructure has the most thoroughly institutionalised record of the three. Building and municipal work records its events after the fact, in assessment reports, and the record of maintenance decisions during operation is thin. That thinness is Chapter 29 appearing in a building context.

docs.title: 2 Feedback Delay
docs.text:
This domain has the widest spread in the book. At the structural layer, feedback from concrete carbonation, rebar corrosion, and bolt fatigue is counted in decades, as in the fatigue fracture of ce-002's baseplate bolts. At the construction layer it is counted in hours: a mistake in a lift or a pour shows on the spot.

Operating decisions, such as the platform inspection in ce-007 or the occupation of the recess in ce-003, give their feedback in years, and the normal state in between is no accident at all. The public usually calls the resulting event sudden. Every investigation report in this field spends its pages refuting that word.

docs.title: 3 Coupling
docs.text:
Coupling to the public is higher here than in any other domain, because the asset is public. A railway, a bridge, a level crossing: when one fails it acts directly on people who never chose to be exposed (the train collision in ce-001, the pedestrians at the crossing in ce-008, the collapse of the condominium in ce-009).

Cross-system coupling is dense as well. Civil works, track, signalling, power supply, and communications share one constrained space, and ce-003, where communications cable filled the refuge recess, is coupling in its physical form. Isolation measures exist, in the shape of single-line block closure and structural redundancy. They fail through accumulation, as maintenance and occupation both draw the isolation down (Chapter 25).

docs.title: 4 The Three Deadliest Mechanisms
docs.text:
The invisibility of maintenance (Chapter 29). Surfside's structural debt (ce-009), the bolt failure at Audenshaw that nobody recorded (ce-002), the rulebook at Denbigh Hall that did not cover the scenario in front of it (ce-005).

The illusion of redundancy (Chapter 22). At Talerddig both sanding systems failed, automatic and manual together (ce-001). At Ealing Broadway the door obstruction detection and the anti-drag measure came up empty in the same event (ce-006).

Diffusion of responsibility (Chapter 18). The level crossing warning sits on an interface between asset owner and operator (ce-008), and facilities held in common by several parties have governance gaps built into their ownership.

Next in frequency, practical drift (Chapter 15). Inspection degrades into a signature in ce-003 and ce-007.

docs.title: 5 What Outsiders Most Easily Mislearn
docs.text:
Mislearning one: reading accident rate as a measure of construction quality. Most infrastructure failure happens in the operating period, which is more than nine tenths of the life cycle, so construction quality is the opening chapter of the story. Learning infrastructure through a construction lens means reading only the title page.

Mislearning two: taking "once in a hundred years" as evidence that protection is adequate. That phrase and the margin arithmetic of Chapter 25 combine into the scenario Chapter 22 exists to describe.

Mislearning three: underestimating the accumulation of permitted occupation. A recess, a space under a bridge, a safety clearance: each temporary occupation looks harmless alone, and together they are the full cause of an event like ce-003. The public sees only the last one.

docs.title: 6 Three Questions from Readers Outside the Field
docs.text:
What use is a building accident to a reader outside construction? Buildings are the prototype of multi-party governance. One building involves owner, managing agent, designer, contractor, supervisor, and regulator, and the accountability interfaces of Chapter 18 are drawn most completely in building cases. Any industry that coordinates across organisations can read itself into them.

Is a collapse like Surfside a low-probability event? A collapse is the settlement of a debt. Decades of deferred maintenance are cleared in one tide, so what looks like low probability is high-certainty accumulation (Chapter 25).

What has a bridge or a tunnel to do with the management of an office block? The mechanism is the same: structural margin eaten away, inspection reduced to attendance, repairs shelved. Only the scale differs, and the invisibility of maintenance in Chapter 29 holds for any owner of a physical asset.

docs.title: 7 Mechanism Distribution at a Glance
docs.text:
The book holds 9 cases in construction and infrastructure. Distribution by mechanism, largest first:

  • the illusion of redundancy (4): ce-001, ce-003, ce-006, ce-008
  • compliant and unsafe (4): ce-002, ce-004, ce-007, ce-009
  • practical drift (4): ce-003, ce-005, ce-006, ce-007
  • the invisibility of maintenance (3): ce-001, ce-002, ce-009
  • information attenuation up the hierarchy (2): ce-002, ce-006
  • handover rupture (2): ce-004, ce-005
  • extrapolating past the validated domain (1): ce-001
  • diffusion of responsibility (1): ce-008
  • cascading failure (1): ce-009

How to use the list: on any new incident notice from this domain, guess the mechanism from the list before reading the report. The hit rate is your familiarity with the domain's accent. Then read and check. The places you guessed wrong mark the thickness of industry skin still between you and the field.

docs.title: 8 How This Page Gets Updated
docs.text:
A domain page is a live document. Once a year, take the Grade A and Grade B reports added to this domain, walk them against the five columns above and the table in Section 7, and revise. A mechanism that appears for the first time gets a line in Section 4. A shift in frequency updates the counts in Section 7. A new Grade A case goes into the library against the field standard of Chapter 5.

The trigger, the owner, and the review date belong in the user's calendar (Chapter 39). A domain page that is not updated is dead in the same way a ledger is: the information does not rot, it simply stops describing the field.

docs.title: 9 The Starter Kit
docs.text:
Three items for a reader new to this domain, about one working day in total.

The entry case is ce-001, two passenger trains on wet rail, braking short, a head-on collision, investigated by RAIB in 2026, with the link in Appendix B. Read it first for the format and the grain of the reports in this field.

The entry source is the first-hand library listed under Construction and Infrastructure in. Find the entrance, bookmark it, visit once a quarter.

The entry mechanism is the first line of the Section 7 table. Read the mechanism chapter beside the case from this domain and take the pair twice, once for the criterion in the chapter and once for the parameters here. When the three items are done you own a first coordinate system for the field.

docs.title: 10 Reservations
docs.text:
Three limits apply to every judgement on this page. The book's case library samples toward events with rich public records, which is the record skew of Chapter 2. The frequency ranking in Section 7 describes the book's library, not the true distribution of the domain. Institutions and technology both move, so this page has a shelf life measured in years, and a citation should carry the year it was read.

All three are the book's general disclaimer, and the threshold check of Chapter 1 applies to this book as much as to anything it examines.

docs.title: 11 How the Three Layers Sound in This Domain
docs.text:
The accent here is the deepest interweaving of the incentive layer with the timeline. Design margin, maintenance debt, and deferred repair all grow inside the incentive layer on a scale of decades: the structural debt at Surfside ran for several decades, and po-005's scheme was put off for thirteen years. The technical breakpoints of a building, concrete spalling and a fractured bolt, are the terminal outlet of that debt. Trace to the root and the physical evidence turns out to be the endpoint, while the ledger is the path.

For the reviewer: in a building case's nine-cell walkthrough the incentive row almost always contains a multi-owner governance interface (Chapter 18). Finding no single person to hold accountable is not a dereliction of duty; it is the true shape of the governance structure, and the repair of that structure is Chapter 18's subject.

docs.text:

docs.title: 13 Closing Address
docs.text:
The hardest lesson this domain hands a reader is the irreversibility of margin. Concrete cannot be un-poured and a pile cannot be re-driven, so the irreversible conclusion of Chapter 7's decision table holds permanently here. There is one exit from that: do the checking before the irreversible point. Surfside's structural repair assessment and the sign-off on the Westminster scheme both waited; every deferral pushed the irreversible point backwards and the consequence forwards. The self-check for a reader in this field is to pull out the structural inspection report on his own project and read it again in the margin ledger format of Chapter 25. Look for the line that says no repair needed. That line is where the reader should stop.

The cases here span unusually long periods. Surfside's debt ran for decades, the Westminster scheme for thirteen years, and nobody knows how long the recess at Ickenham had been filling up. On that time scale Chapter 25, margin erosion, and Chapter 28, horizon mismatch, run in their most primitive form: no software can be restarted and no contract terminated at speed, and the curing period of concrete is the cooling-off period of governance, in which every decision collects interest for more than ten years. The lookback in these cases is the longest of any domain in the book, and the incentive-layer evidence in a nine-cell walkthrough often reaches back beyond ten years, which asks the reviewer for the skills of an archival historian. Chapter 33's register, in this field, is the building archive.

docs.title: 14 How the Mechanisms Vary in This Domain
docs.text:
Maintenance invisibility, the infrastructure variation. The asset has a century of life, and the debt is settled across generations, which makes Chapter 29's horizon mismatch reach the largest scale in the book. In ce-002 the fatigue fracture of a bolt at Audenshaw entered no maintenance ledger and no report, the assurance system did not notice it for years, and the indicator stayed at zero while the target got worse.

The reading: the first question about maintenance visibility here is the overlap between the list of items the ledger covers and the list of structurally critical parts, meaning whether the critical parts are on the ledger at all. The second question is the ratio of inspection interval to component life, since an interval longer than the life means there is no inspection. Surfside (ce-009) pushes the variation to its limit: the gap between the repairs named in the structural assessment and the repairs actually done was accumulated by nobody until physics settled it.

Hidden coupling, the infrastructure variation. The carrier of coupling here is space, and ce-003, the platform recess filled with cable, is the cleanest teaching case in the book: every occupation went through a compliance approval, and the safety function was spent in the course of being compliant.

The reading: dual-register recording of space, one register engineering and one safety function, is Chapter 21's Device 1 in its infrastructure form. The same volume of space holds one state on the engineering drawing and another in the safety ledger, and a conflict between the two is the weak signal. Service pipes under a bridge, tunnel clearances, platform recesses, and escape routes are the four classes to register first.

Practical drift, the infrastructure variation. ce-005, the reverse shunt with no rule to follow, shows the distinctive form: in a non-standard scenario there is no procedure to drift from. Forward work has a method, while reverse, temporary, and non-standard work is improvised on the spot, and the failures in this domain concentrate exactly there. The reading: the prior-authorisation regime for non-standard work, meaning whether anyone approved it and on what information, is the substitute question for drift in this field. ce-006 and ce-007 show the other half: in standard scenarios the strength of execution decays with time, and the four-year absence of the ramp was carried by the fact that nothing had ever gone wrong.

docs.title: 15 Cross-Reading Suggestions
docs.text:
Construction and public policy is the first pairing, since the HS2 programme, Westminster, and Northern Powerhouse Rail in the po series are all infrastructure projects. The mechanism of operating an asset lives in the ce series and the mechanism of deciding about one lives in the po series, and only the two pages together give a full life cycle.

Against maritime: ce-009's progressive collapse and the pipework ageing of ma-004 share the language of silent accumulation, corrosion and fatigue.

Against software: the occupation approval here read beside the permission changes of sw-002 shows that the cumulative effect of legitimate actions is a source of failure common to physical and digital networks.

docs.title: Maritime and Transport | ma
docs.text: Five columns: record quality, feedback delay, coupling, the three deadliest mechanisms, and what outsiders most easily learn wrong.

docs.title: 1 Record quality
docs.text: The UK Marine Accident Investigation Branch is the global sample. Reports sit in full text on the gov.uk platform in two tracks, formal reports and general investigations, and all 13 ma cases in this book come from its 2026 output. The investigation runs independent of the maritime judiciary (Chapter 3). The IMO framework sets the principles, but jurisdiction fragments along flag lines: the same accident under a different flag can end with no public text at all (Section 3.4). The notification channel of China's Maritime Safety Administration is of limited availability [: pending verification]. Overall: small and medium vessels under flags of convenience are the dark zone of the record, while the small fishing boats inside MAIB jurisdiction form the densest sample of small-accident records anywhere. Nine of the 13 cases here are fishing vessels and small workboats. That ratio is the MAIB's value in one line. It turned the failures of unimportant people into searchable knowledge.

docs.title: 2 Feedback delay
docs.text: Operational feedback runs in seconds and minutes (a watchkeeper dozing off, a grounding, a collision), and the shape matches aviation. Maintenance and fatigue feedback runs in weeks and months: the sleep debt in ma-013 built up over a single week, and the sea water piping in ma-004 went aboard in 1998. Institutional feedback, meaning flag-state regulation and the survey system, runs in years. Fishing has a structure of its own. Voyage economics make "carry on" the default (Chapter 27), so the delay gets absorbed as a matter of course.

docs.title: 3 Coupling
docs.text: Inside one vessel, coupling is moderate. Propulsion, power, windlass and firefighting form physical chains, and ma-001 is the textbook form: loss of electrical power took the anchor with it. Between vessels, coupling climbs steeply in close-quarters work (the tanker and the fishing vessel in ma-005, the collision inside a traffic separation scheme in ma-008). Coupling to the outside world changes with the water. Coastal and traffic areas wire a single-vessel accident straight into the public order of the waterway through vessel traffic services, and the edge of VTS authority is a regular scene for diffusion of responsibility (ma-008).

docs.title: 4 The three deadliest mechanisms
docs.text: Practical drift (Chapter 15): the watch alarm buried under music (ma-002), a master alone on watch and asleep (ma-003), a new procedure executed off its own script (ma-007). The invisibility of maintenance (Chapter 29): sea water piping installed in 1998 (ma-004), the non-OEM bearing that left the anchor useless after a power failure (ma-001), an inspection gap on a lifting chain (ma-013). Margin erosion (Chapter 25): freeing ports cut smaller year after year (ma-009), working posture hardened into habit (ma-012). Next in frequency come normalization of deviance (the give-way assumption in ma-005) and handover rupture (the VTS authority boundary in ma-008).

docs.title: 5 What outsiders most easily learn wrong
docs.text: Wrong lesson one: build the picture of the industry from large ships and cruise liners. Most hulls in the world merchant and fishing fleets have no modern bridge and no redundancy, and half the lessons in MAIB reports come from vessels under 25 metres. Wrong lesson two: read flag-state registration as a regulatory guarantee (the fragmentation in Chapter 3). Wrong lesson three: discount small accidents as report material. Capsize and man-overboard cases from fishing boats are the best teaching material available on single-person, single-point, low-cost defence. The defences are cheap (a watch alarm, an immersion suit, a second anchor), the failures are cheap and fatal, and the sense of proportion across industries is all inside them.

docs.title: 6 Three questions from an outsider
docs.text: Question one: what do fishing and small-boat cases offer deep-sea shipping? The mechanism does not pick a hull size. Fatigue on watch, custom standing in for assessment, emergency equipment failing at the moment it is needed: the small-boat detail is the most complete, MAIB investigates a small accident with the seriousness it gives a large one, and a small case is a transparent specimen of a large mechanism. Question two: why do maritime reports always mention the flag state? Jurisdiction fragmentation is the institutional feature of this field, and the flag decides who investigates. Chapter 3 describes the fragmentation and carries the retrieval countermeasures. Question three: does any of this carry to road freight? Watchkeeping, handover, deferred maintenance, cascading failure, and the non-OEM bearing chain of ma-001 hold in any mode of transport. Distance and fatigue are the trade's common enemies.

docs.text:
This domain holds 13 cases, distributed as follows, most frequent first:

  • Margin erosion (7): ma-003, ma-004, ma-005, ma-008, ma-009, ma-011, ma-013
  • Practical drift (6): ma-002, ma-003, ma-007, ma-009, ma-011, ma-012
  • Invisibility of maintenance (4): ma-001, ma-004, ma-006, ma-013
  • Illusion of redundancy (3): ma-002, ma-006, ma-009
  • Cascading failure (1): ma-001
