How to use the list: when a new bulletin lands, guess the mechanism against this table before reading the report. Your hit rate is your familiarity with the field's accent. Then read the text and check. Where you guessed wrong is the industry skin still sitting between you and the domain.

docs.title: 8 How this page is updated
docs.text: A domain page is a live document. Once a year, take the new A and B grade reports in Maritime and Transport and check them against the five columns and the list in section 7. A mechanism that appears for the first time gets a line in section 4. A shift in frequency gets a new count in section 7. A new A-grade case enters the library under the field standards of Chapter 5. Trigger, owner and review date go into the user's calendar (Chapter 39). A domain page, like the ledger, is dead the moment nobody updates it.

docs.title: 9 The starter kit
docs.text: Three items for a reader new to Maritime and Transport. Entry case: ma-001 (a non-OEM bearing wore early and the generator was destroyed by fire; MAIB, 2026; link at Appendix B). Read it first for the house style and the grain size of a report in this field. Entry data source: the primary collection listed under maritime and transport in. Find the entrance, bookmark it, visit once a quarter. Entry mechanism: start with the top row of the section 7 list and read that chapter against a case from here. One mechanism gets two passes, once in the mechanism chapter for the criteria, once in this domain for the local parameters. The three items take about one working day, and at the end of it you own a first coordinate system for the field.

docs.title: 10 Reservations
docs.text: Three limits sit on the judgments above. The case library samples toward events with rich public records, and the skew is described in Chapter 2. The frequency order reflects this book's library, not the true distribution in the field. Institutions and technology move, so this page has a shelf life measured in years, and any citation of it should carry the year. Those three are the book's general disclaimer, and the threshold check of Chapter 1 applies to this book as much as to any other artifact.

docs.title: 11 The three layers in the maritime accent
docs.text: The maritime accent is heaviest at the organizational layer. On fishing boats, inland craft and small vessels, operating procedure exists largely as custom rather than text: outboard work with no assessment in ma-012, a watch with no reserve in ma-003. Custom standing in for text makes practical drift in Chapter 15 and the escalation ladder of Chapter 8 almost impossible to separate here, because the end point of drift is custom, and custom is itself the first step of the ladder. For the reviewer: in the nine-box walkthrough of a maritime case, run the custom archaeology in the organizational box first, asking which generation of vessel the custom started on. The answer points at Chapter 30, handover rupture. Custom cannot be traced back for the plain reason that it was never written down.

docs.text:

How to use the lookup: guess the mechanism from the section 7 distribution, then come here to find the chapter that carries the criteria and the countermeasures. The table does not replace the reading. It is a map, not the journey.

docs.title: 13 Closing note
docs.text:
A last piece of advice for maritime readers. The density of cases proves a commonplace: a small boat does not mean a small lesson. MAIB investigated each of these sinkings with the same care, Report 8/2026 through Report 17/2026, every one public in full, and that seriousness about small accidents is the field's institutional wealth. Small accidents in other industries still get a line in the news and nothing more. The largest lesson the maritime cases hold for a reader outside the field is that the risk of custom is no fishing peculiarity. Any industry leaning on oral tradition rather than written standards sits somewhere on ma-012's extension line. Does your operation have ma-012-style outboard work, a high-risk act nobody has written down? The answer is in the blank space of your work instruction.

One more feature of this page is the hull span, from ro-ro ships of tens of thousands of tonnes down to fishing boats of tens of tonnes. A wide hull span carries a wide mechanism span, and the same water produces failures from a ro-ro's radio link dropping to a trawler's freeing ports cut smaller. Reading across the span trains you to strip the equipment parameters and look only at structure. The result of that training: hand any maritime bulletin, whatever the size of the ship, and within a minute you can place it among this book's mechanisms. The method is simple. Cover the vessel name and the tonnage, read only the process description, and repeat ten times. Recognition then runs without deliberate effort.

docs.title: 14 How the mechanisms vary here
docs.text:
Normalization of deviance, maritime variation: the fatigue and dozing cases (ma-002, ma-003) compress the scene to its minimum, one person, deep night, no second pair of eyes. Read it this way: the watch alarm is this field's own device, and its effectiveness has to be verified under worst-case audibility. The lesson of ma-002 is that passing a monthly test does not mean audible beneath music. Single-handed watchkeeping passes on flag-state rules, and the gap between compliance and safety is filled with physical exhaustion, which makes maritime the small-organization template of Chapter 32, compliant and unsafe. One further reading rule: if the handling of a dozing event stops at "educate the person", normalization has already started. The person is processed and the structure is left as it was.

The invisibility of maintenance, maritime variation: ma-001 (a non-OEM bearing wearing early), ma-004 (ageing sea water piping) and ma-006 (an unsupported suction pipe) make a maintenance spectrum of spare-part quality, component life and installation workmanship. The maintenance economics of a small owner is the structural constraint of the field: maintenance spending is far more sensitive to freight rates there than at a large operator. Read it this way: the comparison between what class survey covers and where failures actually land is the right measure of maintenance visibility, and the share of failure points outside survey coverage is the blind-spot rate of the system. ma-013 (a lifting chain parting) pushes the blind spot into lifting gear accessories. Survey covers primary structure, deck rigging depends on crew self-inspection, and the failure landed precisely in the fatigue band of self-inspection.

The illusion of redundancy, maritime variation: ma-010, three dead in succession in a rescue vessel's oxygen-deficient anchor chain locker, is the book's heaviest case of the rescuer becoming the victim. Confined-space management failed on an emergency response vessel, and the urgency of a rescue exempted the gas testing procedure. Read it this way: the collapse in enforcement of the confined-space entry permit in rescue scenes is the variant of the illusion of redundancy, where the procedural layer of redundancy is absent in the one scene that needs it most.

docs.title: 15 Reading in pairs
docs.text: Read the maritime page against the healthcare page (small teams, high pressure, steep hierarchy; see the paired-reading section there). Against manufacturing: ma-001's non-OEM part reads well beside the supply-chain quality cases in the mn series, where the rule that the source of a part decides the life of the part holds in both. Against construction, see the paired-reading section on that page. Against aviation: av-019 (a hydraulic failure and an out-of-rule ferry flight) reads against the sail-while-sick structure of the ma series, since the ferry segment of aviation and the fishing segment of maritime are both low points in their own regulatory density. Put the low-point cases side by side and the correlation between regulatory density and failure density shows up as one of the most stable empirical regularities in the book.

docs.title: Software and Internet Services | sw
docs.text: Five columns: record quality, feedback delay, coupling, the three deadliest mechanisms, and what outsiders most easily learn wrong.

docs.title: 1 Record quality
docs.text: The world's only public postmortem ecosystem that no statute requires (the exception in Chapter 4). Vendor postmortems, the kind Cloudflare and GitHub publish along with monthly availability reports, give a timeline and a narrative of decisions; that is D-grade material, and the depth is substantial. Regulatory penalty documents from CNIL, the FTC and the ICO cover the data compliance side at C grade. The 9 sw cases here are made up of vendor postmortems (6) and regulatory penalties (3). The gap is security incidents. Intrusions and breaches almost never get a public postmortem, because the postmortem text doubles as an attack manual and legal liability has no ceiling; the public postmortem library has also been shrinking in recent years (Section 4.2). Retrieval channels are in, where blog scraping that times out should be retried with curl.

docs.title: 2 Feedback delay
docs.text: The shortest in any industry. Change feedback arrives in seconds and minutes, since a canary release exposes the fault on a percentage of traffic first. Incident feedback arrives in minutes, through monitoring and alerting. Postmortem feedback arrives in weeks. That speed is the material basis of software's postmortem culture: feedback fast enough to carry a high-frequency learning loop. Inside the field the useful distinction is control plane against data plane. Data plane failures report back fast; control plane failures (dashboards, permissions, configuration) report back just as fast but are more easily underestimated, and the retry storm in sw-004 happened in the control plane.

docs.title: 3 Coupling
docs.text: Coupling at global infrastructure scale. A single vendor's edge network carries distribution and security for traffic across the internet, as the three global events sw-001 to sw-003 show, and a shared substrate turns one point of semantic ambiguity into simultaneous failure for thousands of customers. Automated coupling adds a second layer: changes propagate by themselves (the feature file in sw-002 spreading with the deployment) and client retries amplify a fault (sw-004). Isolation measures are real (regionalization, canaries, rollback), yet common-mode failure keeps penetrating them, because the same configuration system, the same permission model or the same cleanup job sits underneath. The conclusion on coupling matches aviation's. High coupling has been pushed down by engineering, and the pushing down is a continuous process that carries a cost.

docs.title: 4 The three deadliest mechanisms
docs.text: Hidden coupling (Chapter 21): a database permission change doubles the feature file (sw-002), a retry storm (sw-004), the empty-parameter semantics of a BYOIP cleanup (sw-003). Crossing a scale threshold (Chapter 24): record load breaks capacity that was calibrated on historical peaks (sw-005), bulk abuse of a registration system (the mirrored form of fi-004). Cascading failure (Chapter 33): downstream synchronization failing because the automation was shared. Next in frequency come misaligned incentives (the structural conflict in the data compliance cases sw-007 and sw-008) and practical drift (operations and documentation diverging).

docs.title: 5 What outsiders most easily learn wrong
docs.text: Wrong lesson one: read postmortem culture as proof that the industry is safe. Postmortems mostly cover availability incidents that fell ill and recovered, not security incidents and not commercial failure, which is the boundary drawn in Chapter 4. Wrong lesson two: copy the word blameless without the machinery behind it. A blameless postmortem with no anonymization process and no separation from performance review is blameless rhetoric, the name-reality gap of Section 4.2. Wrong lesson three: treat fast rollback as a universal answer. Software can roll back because deployment is atomic and state can be versioned. Writing rollback into another industry's emergency plan without asking whether our state can be versioned is the commonest error in cross-industry transplant, and Chapter 4 states the four conditions that decide it.

docs.title: 6 Three questions from an outsider
docs.text: Question one: what use is software's postmortem practice outside software? Software is the only living sample of a public postmortem culture, and Chapter 4 takes it apart. The blameless process, the game day exercise and the status page are all parts that travel, and Chapter 4 gives the conditions under which transplanting them works. Question two: are cloud platform outages far from my business? If your business depends on any cloud service or SaaS product, you are the downstream party in the cases on this page (Chapter 33, cascading failure). Do those providers appear on your supplier list? Question three: how can a software fault be isomorphic to a chemical explosion? The three layers of the failure chain do not care about industry. A bug in the technical layer, a missing review in the organizational layer, launch pressure in the incentive layer: when all three break at once the shape is the same, which is why Chapter 9 puts the two industries inside one model.

docs.title: 7 Mechanism distribution at a glance
docs.text:
This domain holds 9 cases, distributed as follows, most frequent first:

  • Hidden coupling (6): sw-001, sw-002, sw-003, sw-004, sw-006, sw-008
  • Cascading failure (3): sw-003, sw-004, sw-005
  • Margin erosion (2): sw-001, sw-009
  • Crossing a scale threshold (2): sw-002, sw-005
  • Misaligned incentives (2): sw-007, sw-008
  • Extrapolating past the validated domain (1): sw-001
  • Illusion of redundancy (1): sw-006

docs.title: 11 The three layers in the software accent
docs.text: The software accent is that the technical break is the youngest of the three. Code and configuration breakpoints travel from deploy to exposure in hours and days (the empty parameter in sw-003, the regular expression in sw-001), and the breakpoints in the organizational and incentive layers are just as young: the design of a monitoring blind spot, the approval exemption granted under launch pressure. The entire history of the industry is a few decades. The practical consequence for the nine-box walkthrough is that one table shows a full set of young breakpoints at every layer. Elsewhere a decade of evolution is needed to lay them down; software does it in a single release. The walkthrough is therefore efficient, and the lesson density is correspondingly high.

docs.title: 13 Closing note
docs.text:
A last piece of advice for software readers. The public postmortem culture is the industry's gift to everyone else (Chapter 4), but the gift's shelf life depends on conditions inside the industry, and the warning at the end of Chapter 4 is that culture has no legislative moat. Two self-checks. When was your organization's last public postmortem? If you cannot answer, the public culture is shrinking where you work. Does your blameless commitment have any isolation from the IT system, in the sense of Chapter 8? Software has already proved this can grow. Keep the four conditions of Chapter 4 in place and it will not be a flash in the pan.

The cases on this page share a feature no other industry has: the party writes its own postmortem. Cloudflare's and GitHub's texts are published in full, with technical detail reaching down to API parameters and individual lines of code, which would be unthinkable elsewhere and is itself one of the objects Chapter 4 studies. The reading advice is to read them in series. One company, four cases, sw-001 through sw-004: read four in a row and a single organization's failure fingerprint appears. The root cause differs every time and the propagation path repeats its pattern. Recognizing that pattern is the advanced training for a software reader, and what it produces is sensitivity to the fingerprint of your own organization. One more observation: every case here sits at a top platform. Outages at small and mid-size software companies get no public postmortem, so survivorship skew runs in this field too.

docs.title: 14 How the mechanisms vary here
docs.text:
Hidden coupling, software variation: the coupling cases share one signature, in that whoever executes the change does not know what the change touched. The lesson in sw-002 (a database permission change pushing the feature file past its limit) and sw-003 (a cleanup defect withdrawing prefixes by mistake) both sit in the coverage of the dependency graph: the dependencies of the permission system, the routing system and the cleanup job were never modelled. Read it this way: the reach rate of a change, meaning the ratio of the impact surface declared beforehand to the one found afterwards, is Chapter 21's criterion expressed as a number here. Software coupling is more hidden than chemical coupling in one respect: dependencies grow by themselves as versions drift (library upgrades, configuration merges), so a manual inventory decays faster than in any other industry. Automatic generation of the dependency graph is therefore a floor requirement, not an optimization.

Crossing a scale threshold, software variation: sw-005 (record load breaking an under-provisioned component) and sw-004 (a retry storm overwhelming the tenant service) show the two scales of software, load magnitude and feedback speed. Feedback here is measured in seconds, the fastest in the book, while capacity decisions are validated on a quarterly cycle through load testing. That mismatch of cycles is the structure of scale failure in software. Read it this way: component coverage between the load test environment and production, meaning how many components have never met real pressure. The lesson of sw-005 is that the weak component sat outside that coverage. The retry storm adds a layer specific to software: a defence (retry) becomes an amplifier under abnormal conditions, so any automatic retry needs a circuit breaker and jitter. That rule is the field's correction to the concept of redundancy in Chapter 22.

Regulatory lag and capture, software variation: sw-007 through sw-009, the three CNIL cases, show the enforcement style of data regulation. Fines are set as a share of turnover, remediation orders come as a system, and violations are found through complaints and audits. Read it this way: the ratio of compliance cost to violation benefit is badly asymmetric here, since the marginal return on using data is high and the chance of being caught is low, and the escalation of fines in the GDPR era is regulation catching up. Chapter 31's criterion, that rules update more slowly than the business, is measured in generations in this field, as the ratio of platform iteration cycle to legislative cycle. The sense that regulation is dense and still late is stronger for readers here than in any other field.

docs.title: 15 Reading in pairs
docs.text: Read the software page against the public policy page, where po-003's dashboard rating and sw-004's dashboard retry make a mutual irony: in both, the metric layer has become the new failure surface. Against finance: the sw and fi enforcement cases share a time structure of long behavioural period and short discovery period, and fi-004's shell advisers beside sw-007's cookie consent shows compliance formalized in the same shape in two industries. Against manufacturing: software change management beside the manufacturing change order shows how far apart the two industries sit in the maturity of one device, since the change order is a more complete instrument than the software change approval.

docs.title: Finance | fi
docs.text: Five columns: record quality, feedback delay, coupling, the three deadliest mechanisms, and what outsiders most easily learn wrong.

docs.title: 1 Record quality
docs.text: Enforcement documents are the gold mine. The SEC publishes litigation releases case by case, numbered and citable (5 fi cases here); FINRA's monthly disciplinary summary PDF covers the middle and long tail of brokerage violations; the CSRC publishes administrative penalty decisions in full (4 fi cases here, with body pages that can be scraped while the list page is loaded dynamically, all of it recorded in). UK FCA final notices were unreachable from this book's network environment [pending verification]. The structural gap is that enforcement documents record what got caught. The build-up of systemic risk, meaning leverage, concentration and liquidity mismatch, has almost no full text before it breaks: the material for a 2008-class event is a commission report written afterwards, not a supervisory document written before. Overall verdict: micro-level violations are recorded in great thickness, and macro-level risk depends on post-crisis ratification.

docs.title: 2 Feedback delay
docs.text: Two clocks. On the market clock, price and liquidity feedback arrives in seconds, which produces the illusion of the high-frequency stop-loss; most risk does not report back on the market clock at all. On the regulatory clock, violation feedback arrives in years (the conduct period in fi-001 ran 2019–2021 with the penalty in 2026; the bulk fraud in fi-004 ran 2025–2026 up to indictment), and risk feedback arrives in cycles, since credit losses are invisible during a boom. The career incentives of a financial decision-maker are perfectly mismatched to the regulatory clock: the bonus is paid on the market clock and the penalty lands on the regulatory clock.

docs.title: 3 Coupling
docs.text: The highest of any domain. Institutions are wired to each other through interbank liabilities, clearing and collateral networks, so a single default travels along the clearing chain. On the asset side they are wired through common holdings, which makes the diversification that rises and falls together a pseudo-diversification. On the information side, market sentiment transmits infection instantly. The isolation devices of finance, meaning margin, clearing houses and deposit insurance, essentially convert coupling from disorderly into orderly. Coupling itself never goes away; it is institutionalized into a settleable form. The supplier line of a risk register corresponds here to the counterparty line, and the checklist in Chapter 33 is a life-and-death document in this field.

docs.title: 4 The three deadliest mechanisms
docs.text: Misaligned incentives (Chapter 17): the tension inside audit independence, where two firms failed in succession on the same subject (fi-008, fi-009), and the structural conflict between sales and risk control. Goal displacement (Chapter 12): the beautification of loan loss metrics (fi-001), and a risk rating that departs from actual risk, 24 of 53 (the GAO case in Chapter 12, the public edition of financial governance). Regulatory lag and capture (Chapter 31): fractional share trading falling outside an old classification (fi-011), bulk registration fraud (fi-004), the compliance gap around an AI financing narrative (fi-002). Next in frequency come narrative before evidence (the offering frauds in fi-002 and fi-005) and diffusion of responsibility (the four-signature chain in fi-007).

docs.title: 5 What outsiders most easily learn wrong
docs.text: Wrong lesson one: read penalty documents as moral evidence. They record violations that can be proved, not the whole of an organizational culture, and using them to judge culture carries the same sample bias as the survivorship skew in Chapter 2. Wrong lesson two: rank severity by the size of the fine. The $125,000 in fi-013 and the $17.78 million in fi-005 do not measure the same dimension. Wrong lesson three: take diversification for safety. Diversification that synchronizes across peers is a single exposure under stress (Chapter 33), and most of the simultaneous failure of diversified portfolios in financial history carries a common factor's name.

docs.title: 6 Three questions from an outsider
docs.text: Question one: what use are financial institution cases to an ordinary investor? A due diligence checklist grows straight out of them: auditor independence, cross-checking against the rating, the signs of a backlog of alerts. The five-step audit in Chapter 12 is a ready tool for investors. Question two: the fines look light, $125,000 against 2.56 million trades, so is breaking the rules a good trade? That is criterion 3 shown as arithmetic, where the fine becomes a membership fee (Chapter 31). A light penalty is not grounds for feeling lucky. It is evidence that supervision failed. Question three: is the compliance vocabulary too hard? The action sequences in these cases, cancel the order, release it, report it, are ordinary commercial actions, and the terms live in the source document titles. The mechanism layer is readable by anyone.

docs.title: 11 The three layers in the finance accent
docs.text: The finance accent is that the incentive-layer breakpoint is the clearest of the three. Nearly every penalty decision describes one: the provisioning pressure in fi-001, the offering narrative in fi-005, the arbitrage of a rule gap in fi-011. The decision is itself the official confirmation of an incentive-layer breakpoint, which is why evidence grades in this field run high by nature, since C-grade documents are produced by a process that runs automatically. For the reviewer: in the nine-box walkthrough, the incentive row has the most complete evidence, and the decision can be quoted directly. The bottleneck is usually the technical layer instead, because the detail of the trading system gets compressed when the decision is written.

docs.title: 13 Closing note
docs.text:
A last piece of advice for finance readers. The lesson of these cases condenses to one word, basis. The accounting basis in fi-001, the classification basis in fi-011, the conversion basis in fi-012, the audit basis in fi-008: financial failure almost never happens at the trading layer. It happens at the definition layer, and the definition layer is the battlefield of Chapter 12. The self-check is to open your own metric definition document, walk it line by line with the basis-change register format from Chapter 12, and ask whether each change of basis is recorded. A basis change with no record is a potential fi-001.

These cases carry an evidential advantage no other domain has. A penalty decision is a statutory document: SEC, FINRA, CNIL and CSRC decisions all pass through legal process, sit at evidence grade C, and their facts have been tested. The cases on this page therefore rank above the D and E grade cases of other industries as a matter of course. There is also a reading technique. The findings of fact are the section worth close reading, because they record the regulator's list of established facts rather than legal argument, and the basis of that list is the regulator's own visibility boundary (Chapter 31). The case count is moderate and the amounts span widely, from €80,000 to €325 million; the way to read that span is in Chapter 31 as well. What matters is the ratio of penalty to gain. The absolute figure is only the yearly dues on a membership.

docs.title: 14 How the mechanisms vary here
docs.text:
Goal displacement, finance variation: fi-001, the timeshare loan rescissions, is the archetype case of Chapter 12, and the variation specific to finance is that the metric coincides with the regulatory report. One number both assesses people inside the firm and gets disclosed to the regulator, so once displacement happens the distortion enters two loops at once. Read it this way: the disclosure obligation list for basis changes, meaning which metrics require an explanation to investors when their basis changes, is the core compliance asset of this field, and the failure point in fi-001 was the missing disclosure. A self-check for the reader: does the metric you are responsible for have a basis sensitivity note, saying which accounting judgments move the number and by how much.

Narrative before evidence, finance variation: fi-002 (an AI startup overstating model feasibility) and fi-005 (a cannabis company fraud) show the narrative pressure of a fundraising scene, where the funding window, the competitive story and the founder's reputation all push toward an optimistic description of prospects. Read it this way: the ratio of narrative strength in an offering document to the support of the underlying evidence is the right object of due diligence, which is Chapter 37's question used in diligence. fi-003 and fi-004, a forged ADV and shell adviser entities, show the industrialized form of narrative: once false filings can be produced programmatically, supervisory verification density has to be matched to the production rate, and that is the point of the SEC's bulk cases.

Misaligned incentives, finance variation: fi-008 and fi-009, two accounting firms failing on the same subject one after the other, are the structural form of the mechanism inside professional service intermediaries. The audit fee is paid by the audited party, so the economic foundation of independence tilts by construction. Read it this way: audit opinion shopping, measured by the frequency and stated reasons for changing auditors, and the quality curve across an auditor's tenure, are the two correct observation points on the incentive structure here. fi-010 through fi-013, filing errors and alerts closed in seconds, show the incentive layer of the compliance post: the cost of a compliance action is immediate and the probability of regulatory discovery is discounted. The SEC's monthly penalty summary, the main source for the fi series, is exactly the institutional device that raises that discovery probability.

docs.title: 15 Reading in pairs
docs.text: Read the finance page against the software page (see the paired-reading section there). Against public policy: po-008, the central budget execution audit, reads beside the fi enforcement cases, where audit works as the same device on the state's books and on the market's books. Against startups: the deaths in the st series read beside the offering frauds in fi, where the health of the narrative market along the funding chain depends on the density of due diligence and disclosure. Read those two domain pages together and they amount to a financing risk manual.

docs.title: Startups and Products | st
docs.text: Five columns: record quality, feedback delay, coupling, the three deadliest mechanisms, and what outsiders most easily mislearn.

docs.title: 1 Record Quality
docs.text: The worst record in the book, and structurally so: the extreme form of the survival skew described in Chapter 2. First-hand material is mostly the founder's own postmortem (all four st cases here were collected and verified through Failory Cemetery, and all four carry the founder's own words). The sample is self-selected, the attribution self-reported, and the writing sits under emotional and legal constraint at once (non-disclosure agreements, refund clauses). Bankruptcy and liquidation filings give a factual skeleton with no narrative attached. Media retellings do not count as evidence, and the Chapter 19 rule applies to them too. The gap has a shape: the fastest and largest deaths, the cash-burnout type, are the least postmortemed. Read this domain's failure material with the three quality checks of Chapter 2 running the whole way.

docs.title: 2 Feedback Delay
docs.text: The cash-flow clock is measured in months and it is not linear: when financing tightens, every company's runway shortens at the same time (st-004's Xinja attributed its shutdown directly to "an increasingly difficult funding environment"). Product-market fit is measured in quarters, but the growth narrative defers the reading (st-001's Atrium kept expanding while fit had not arrived). The regulatory clock, in crypto and fintech, runs in years and is exogenous (st-002's Koinex, where a freeze on banking channels carried regulatory uncertainty straight into the business). What separates this domain from the others is that the distribution of its feedback delays is set by variables the company does not control.

docs.title: 3 Coupling
docs.text: Coupling between individual companies is low: one death does not directly infect the next. Coupling inside the ecosystem is high. The funding environment, channel policies and platform rules are an upstream shared by the whole industry, the form Chapter 33 describes as dependency concentrated on the VC cycle. For platform startups coupling rises with success. A company dependent on one acquisition channel, one cloud vendor, one ecosystem buys that dependence cheap while it is small, and discovers at scale that it has bought its own jugular (Chapter 33).

docs.title: 4 The Three Deadliest Mechanisms
docs.text: Sunk cost and escalation (Chapter 27): money kept going in after product-market fit had failed to arrive (st-001, where the founder's own sentence is the most honest line of postmortem in this book). Narrative before evidence (Chapter 13): the growth story ran ahead of the product (st-003). Horizon mismatch (Chapter 28): the cost cycle of the acquisition model set against the cycle of the funding environment (st-004). Next in frequency: regulatory lag and capture (st-002's banking channels) and crossing a scale threshold (organisation and product failing on two fronts during expansion).

docs.title: 5 What Outsiders Most Easily Mislearn
docs.text: Wrong lesson one: taking the attribution in a postmortem for the truth. A founder's account passes three filters, self-report bias, confidentiality clauses, and the needs of the story being told. Read a postmortem for the information environment of the time; do not read it for the cause of death. Wrong lesson two: treating a survivor's lesson list as the complete set (Section 2.2: what is missing is the deadliest death, and cash exhaustion, co-founder rupture and a regulatory veto have the lowest rates of appearance in public postmortems). Wrong lesson three: taking one case for a method. "Raise densely, validate quickly" appears in the sample as both success and st-001-style failure, and one case cannot give you the prior probability. The book returns to this point repeatedly. In this domain it is loudest.

docs.title: 6 Three Questions from Readers Outside the Field
docs.text:
Why is the evidence grade in startup cases so low? Public documents on startup death are thin by nature, and the survival skew of Chapter 4 is heaviest here. Every startup case in this book is marked E and used only to illustrate a mechanism. Marking the grade honestly is the protection the book offers its startup readers.

Is the method for a product failure the same as for a safety accident? The analysis of decision points and points of no return applies without change (Chapter 7: shipping, expanding, betting on a new market are all points of no return). narrative before evidence in Chapter 13 is at its most typical in a funding round. The method has no boundary.

Will studying failure make a founder more afraid to start? The aim is to make the cost of failure predictable. A founder who knows how each road ends tends to test faster than one who does not. Chapter 40 deals with the failures that should be encouraged. Fear comes from the unknown, and the unknown is what a case library removes.

docs.title: 11 How the Three Layers Sound in Startups
docs.text: The three-layer accent in startups is that all three layers are young at once and each accelerates the others. The founder's intuition (Chapter 14) becomes a product decision directly, in the technical layer. The product story becomes a funding promise directly (Chapter 13). The funding arrives and becomes an expansion budget directly (Chapter 27). The coupling distance between layers, ten years in a large company, compresses to eighteen months in a startup, and the life cycles of st-001 and st-003 are samples of that compression ratio. For the reviewer: in a startup case the time column of the nine-cell walkthrough comes out shockingly short, and the break in the incentive layer and the break in the technical layer can fall in the same month. A nine-cell table spanning a few months reads like an incident flash. The density of the lesson does not thin because the page is short.

docs.title: 13 Closing Address
docs.text:
A last word for founders: a low evidence grade is no reason to discount a case. Because the survival skew is heaviest in this domain, one startup failure honestly marked E is worth more than ten success books put together. The self-check for a startup reader is to run the decision table of Chapter 7 over your next point of no return: shipping, signing the lease, hiring the tenth person. The output of that check is not a stop order. It is an awareness of where the door closes behind you, and a founder who knows what they are doing gets up fastest after a fall. Chapter 40, on the failures worth encouraging, is waiting.

The cases on this page carry the lowest evidence grade in the book, E, and they come from startup graveyards such as Failory Cemetery: a CEO's words quoted, the page assembled by media. A low grade is no reason to leave them out. A grade A report on a startup failure does not exist, because a company that has fallen does not write its own investigation report. This is the survival skew of Chapter 4. The value of an E grade startup case is the first-handness of the CEO's words. Assembled by media they may be, but the tone and the logic survive, and the speaker's frame of understanding is part of the lesson. Treat the E mark as an alarm. Where the evidence is thin, complete it with your own judgement, and the completing is the startup education.

docs.title: 14 How the Mechanisms Vary in This Domain
docs.text:
The startup variation of sunk cost and escalation: the three funding deaths in the st volume (Atrium, ScaleFactor, Xinja, with Koinex outside them as an environment type) share one escalation signature, in which the size of the raise becomes the collateral of the promise. Atrium's $75 million and ScaleFactor's $103 million turned into irreversible organisational commitments the moment the money landed: expansion, pricing, headcount. The cost of a strategic turn is amplified by the size of the raise. How to read the variation: the first major pivot after a raise is more hostage to sunk cost than any decision made before it, and the test is the frequency with which "already invested" appears as an argument in the pivot meeting's materials. The external adjudicator of Chapter 27 has a startup counterpart, the board, and the board's independent authority over a pivot is the most valuable governance device in this domain.

The startup variation of narrative before evidence: narrative pressure here comes with a timetable, the funding round, and the moment the narrative closes is predictable, the final draft of the pitch deck. The lessons in the st volume cluster around the speed at which narrative and product evidence come apart. The gap between ScaleFactor's promise of automated bookkeeping and the degree of automation actually in the product was invisible inside the funding narrative. How to read the variation: if the power to define the core metric (what counts as "automated", what counts as an "active user") sits entirely with the side telling the story, the evidence system has already failed. The Chapter 13 device has a startup counterpart: write the definition of the core metric into an annex of the financing documents, so the definition itself becomes a disclosure.

The startup variation of horizon mismatch: Koinex is the template for an environment mismatch, where the ratio between the product cycle (weeks) and the regulatory cycle (months to years) deteriorates sharply and the premise of the business model is pulled out from under it. How to read the variation: list every dependency on regulation and platform policy in the business plan (banking rails, app stores, cloud terms), and assess the single-point exposure and substitutability of each one beforehand. The st volume shows that default optimism about these dependencies is an industry-wide habit. Xinja, which returned its licence, is the reverse case: it identified that the expected value of continuing was negative and exited, the cleanest stop-loss in the book's startup volume.

docs.title: 15 Cross-Reading Suggestions
docs.text: Read this page against finance first, as the two ends of the financing chain (see the cross-reading section on the finance page). Against software: read the product deaths of the st volume beside the operational deaths of the sw volume. Startups die of product-market mismatch, mature companies die of scale and coupling, and the two mechanism sets barely intersect; read together they show how organisational maturity maps onto failure type. Against public policy: read Koinex beside the regulatory decisions in the po volume. A single firm's survival hangs on a public policy timetable, and policy uncertainty is itself part of a startup's risk exposure.

docs.title: Public Policy and Administration | po
docs.text: Five columns: record quality, feedback delay, coupling, the three deadliest mechanisms, and what outsiders most easily mislearn.

docs.title: 1 Record Quality
docs.text: The public reports of audit institutions are this domain's distinctive asset. The US GAO and the UK NAO track the failure of government projects audit by audit, year by year and period by period, so one project accumulates several reports across several years (HS2 and the VA electronic health record each have multiple records in this book's library). The annual audit work report of China's National Audit Office is submitted to the National People's Congress in the name of the State Council and published as a PDF (po-008). The value takes a different form from other investigations: what is recorded is not a single accident but the year-on-year divergence between plan and execution, a public edition of feedback delay. Royal commissions and commissions of inquiry, the deep reviews of major administrative failure, are scattered across countries. Assessment: strong on tracking, weak on narrative. Read the domain by project, whole series at a time, aligned by year.

docs.title: 2 Feedback Delay
docs.text: The longest in the book. Policy feedback is measured in decades (po-007's rail plan went more than ten years without being delivered), project governance in years (GAO's annual comparison), fiscal execution in years (the annual audit report). The institutional consequence: the decision-maker's term (Chapter 28) is naturally shorter than the cycle of the policy's consequences, and intertemporal debt (maintenance arrears, ageing populations and assets, committed obligations) has no line item in the budget. po-005's restoration arrears at Westminster are one form of it.

docs.title: 3 Coupling
docs.text: Coupling inside a project is low to moderate: it can be phased, a section can be stopped. Coupling between policies is high. The same object is acted on by successive governments, several departments and several layers of governance, and the cost of a scope change is absorbed by whoever comes next (po-007). Cross-domain coupling becomes visible in a crisis. The cost of a public project's failure, service interruption and fiscal loss, is borne by an unspecified public, which makes public failure a political event by construction, and makes the pressure of narrative before evidence heaviest here.

docs.title: 4 The Three Deadliest Mechanisms
docs.text: Sunk cost and escalation (Chapter 27): HS2's two resets and the cancellation of phase 2, with £46.8 billion already spent serving as the argument for continuing (po-004). Goal displacement (Chapter 12): an IT dashboard whose risk ratings diverged from actual risk (po-003), and a conceptual schedule handed to the oversight body (po-002). Diffusion of responsibility (Chapter 18): thirteen years without an agreed plan for the restoration, with authority split (po-005), and scope swinging across governments with nobody answerable for delivery (po-007). Next in frequency: the invisibility of maintenance (po-005), and information attenuation up the hierarchy (po-008's early-collection incentive and its information structure).

docs.title: 5 What Outsiders Most Easily Mislearn
docs.text: Wrong lesson one: reading a single audit report as event news. The value of a GAO or NAO report lies in the series. Five years of reports on one project, read together, are what reveal metric drift and accumulating arrears; the latest report alone is a lab result with no medical history behind it. Wrong lesson two: attributing project failure to "government inefficiency". The attributions in audit reports are structural: governance structure, definitions, incentives. Mechanisms that are isomorphic across the public and private sectors (Chapters 12, 17, 27) simply keep a different set of books in the public domain. Wrong lesson three: underestimating the deterrent value of public audit. Periodic tracking plus published implementation rates for recommendations (Chapter 19) is one of the few workable intertemporal accountability devices the public domain has.

docs.title: 6 Three Questions from Readers Outside the Field
docs.text:
What use are public policy cases to a corporate manager? Horizon mismatch, diffusion of responsibility and path lock-in are all isomorphic inside large corporate projects. HS2 across several governments and a multi-vendor IT programme running for years are the same failure chain. Read Chapters 24, 27 and 28 together.

Are audit office and NAO reports worth reading outside the public sector? Yes. The reports are complete in structure, graded in evidence and numbered in recommendation, which makes them the best models available of what a competent failure report looks like (Chapter 3).

Accountability here is visible. Where is the organizational learning? Public accountability is step one. Step two is tracking whether the recommendations land. Of po-002's 18 recommendations, 4 were implemented, and tracking that rate is itself a learning tool (the implementation-rate logic of Chapter 19).

docs.title: 9 The Starter Kit
docs.text: Three items for a reader new to public policy and administration. Entry case: po-001 (air traffic control modernisation with no full-life-cycle cost estimate, and 138 systems whose schedules do not line up; GAO, 2026, link in Appendix B). Read that one first for the house style and granularity of a report in this domain. Entry data source: the primary libraries listed in the public policy and administration part of. Find the entry points, bookmark them, visit once a quarter. Entry mechanism: start from the first row of the table in Section 7 and read the mechanism chapter against a case in this domain. Read one mechanism twice, once in the chapter for the criteria and once here for the parameters. Working through the three items takes about one working day and leaves you with a first coordinate system for the domain.

docs.title: 10 Reservations
docs.text: Three limits apply to everything judged on this page. The book's case library samples toward events with rich public records, and the record skew is the subject of Chapter 2. The frequency ordering of mechanisms reflects the distribution inside this library, not the true distribution in the domain. Institutions and technology in the domain keep moving, so this page has a shelf life measured in years, and a reader quoting it should state the year of the quotation. All three limits are the book's general disclaimer, and the threshold check of Chapter 1 applies to the book itself as well.

docs.title: 11 How the Three Layers Sound in Public Policy
docs.text: The three-layer accent in public policy is that the break in the incentive layer keeps time with elections and changes of government. po-007's scope changes, po-004's reset and escalation and po-005's shelved plan all beat to a change of government or a budget cycle. Chapter 28's term mismatch reaches its purest form here. A company at least inherits a continuous KPI; a public project's KPI resets to zero when the government changes. For the reviewer: in the nine-cell walkthrough, the incentive-layer cell should record the election year and the decision year. Their overlap is the time seed of the failure, and a project with heavy overlap carries horizon mismatch in its design from the start.

docs.title: 13 Closing Address
docs.text:
A last word for policy readers: what these cases ask for is a mechanism designed to outlive a change of government. po-005's statutory deadline, po-007's trail of recorded changes, and po-004's zero-base re-ask are three designs in that family, each immune to an election. The vaccine costs one page of legislation or one clause in a charter. Its absence cost thirteen years of shelving and tens of billions of pounds of overrun. The self-check for a public project reader is to pull out the approval document and find which page the exit clause is on. If it is not page one, the accent in Section 11 is the agenda for your next budget meeting.

The cases on this page come from the NAO and the GAO, the supreme audit institutions of two countries, and their reports are highly standardised: findings numbered one by one, recommendations tracked one by one, evidence itemised. Public audit reports are the most disciplined evidence format among the book's sources, and Chapter 3 sets out their institutional value. One feature is peculiar to this page: what gets audited is usually an institution rather than a company. HS2 is not a company, and the VA EHRM is not a person. An institutional case has to be walked across governments, agencies and budget cycles, so the nine-cell table of Chapter 9 expands into a timeline matrix, one nine-cell per government, with each change of government acting as a line break. Bring a timeline. An institutional case without one does not read.

docs.title: 14 How the Mechanisms Vary in This Domain
docs.text:
The public policy variation of horizon mismatch: the big projects of the po volume (HS2, Westminster, Northern Powerhouse Rail) push Chapter 28 to the largest scale in the book. The decision-maker's election cycle runs in years, the project's consequence cycle runs in generations, and the mismatch multiplier is far beyond anything in a company. How to read the variation: does a full-life-cycle cost estimate exist in the approval document (po-001's lesson, 138 systems and no full-life-cycle estimate), and who triggers a reset (po-004's two resets). The device to argue for is a cross-term project contract, with scope, budget band and decision gates written into legislation or a cross-party agreement. Its weak point is politics itself, since the next government need not honour the last one's contract, so a policy project's register should be designed on the assumption that the contract will be torn up, with exit clauses to match.

The public policy variation of sunk cost and escalation: po-006, Sizewell C, shows the distinctive defence of policy escalation. The argument that a new model reduces risk is itself the narrative vehicle for escalation, while the fact that no comparable project has escaped staged overruns is put in a footnote. How to read the variation: the distribution of fact and narrative across the approval document, whether the decisive fact sits in the body or in a footnote, is a fast way to identify policy escalation. The external adjudicator of Chapter 27 becomes parliament and the audit office here. po-008 shows the annual audit acting as a continuous external adjudication of the national ledger, and the rate at which its recommendations are implemented is the core indicator of a system's capacity to correct itself.

The public policy variation of the invisibility of maintenance: po-005, thirteen years without a settled plan for the Palace of Westminster, is the template at political scale. The beneficiaries of the restoration are future users, who have no vote. The people who bear the cost are the current fiscal year, and they hold every veto. Here the invisibility is produced by the political structure itself; no manager has to be careless for it to happen. How to read the variation: a compulsion to report condition, meaning periodic, public and budget-linked condition assessment, is the only visibility device that works in this domain. po-002, with 4 of 18 recommendations implemented, shows that recommendation tracking already has a mature form here, in the GAO's recommendation ledger, and that publishing the implementation rate is itself the device.

docs.title: 15 Cross-Reading Suggestions
docs.text: Read this page against construction and infrastructure first (see the cross-reading section of that page). Against finance: read po-008 beside the enforcement cases of the fi volume, as the two ends of the audit device. Against startups: read the resets of policy projects beside the stop-losses of the st volume. Admitting failure costs an order of magnitude more in politics than in business, because a public admission hands ammunition to the opposition, and that extra cost is the structural reason policy projects escalate harder.

docs.title: Military | mi
docs.text: Five columns: record quality, feedback delay, coupling, the three deadliest mechanisms, and what outsiders most easily mislearn. Public first-hand material is scarce in this domain. The case library holds one case (mi-001, a space mission provisionally filed here) and the judgements of the framework are marked as awaiting collection.

docs.title: 1 Record Quality
docs.text: The thinnest public record in the book, and thin for institutional reasons: military accident investigations are mostly classified, and what is published comes as accident notices, declassified archives and select committee reports. The usable public samples are these. Independent investigation of space missions, where the Columbia Accident Investigation Board report is published in full and mi-001 is drawn from it, since NASA is a civil-military system and the investigation regime for crewed spaceflight is isomorphic with aviation's. Annual safety reports from national defence safety bodies, where the US military's safety centres publish statistics and lesson summaries while the deep case studies are mostly restricted. Historical declassified archives, with a time lag measured in decades. Collection directions are listed in (declassified archive collections and defence safety publications). Assessment: the structural judgement is trustworthy, in that the investigative institutions exist; the case material is still to be gathered.

docs.title: 2 Feedback Delay
docs.text: Training and equipment operation give feedback on a mission cycle. Equipment acquisition gives feedback in decades, a heavier horizon mismatch than public infrastructure. Organisational culture gives feedback across generations. Crewed systems give feedback immediately and irreversibly, with the points of no return of Chapter 7 operating in their harshest form, which is why military aviation and spaceflight produced the world's strictest checklists and the Crew Resource Management regime. Institutional density runs in proportion to the irreversibility of the consequence.

docs.title: 3 Coupling
docs.text: Coupling inside a mission system is high and peculiar. In combat and in training, communications, identification, the chain of command and the rules of engagement couple under pressure and on incomplete information. The 1994 Black Hawk shootdown is the prototype case for Snook's theory of practical drift (Chapter 15), where the divergences inside each link add up at an accidental intersection. Coupling across units is constrained by establishment and doctrine, and the interface in joint operations is a high-incidence break point (Chapter 30).

docs.title: 4 The Three Deadliest Mechanisms (from CAIB and the Public Literature, Case Slots Pending)
docs.text: Normalization of deviance (Chapter 11): CAIB's review of the "in-family" classification of foam shedding (mi-001) is itself a specimen of normalization inside a military-grade organisation, and mission standards that move a step at a time through success are a disease of high-risk organisations generally. Diffusion of responsibility (Chapter 18): the separation of the command chain from the safety oversight chain, and committee-style mission review. Information attenuation up the hierarchy (Chapter 16): the filtering of upward information under mission pressure recurs throughout published military investigation reports. To be revised once the collection is done.

docs.title: 5 What Outsiders Most Easily Mislearn
docs.text: Wrong lesson one: taking the availability of declassified files for the whole truth. What can be declassified has passed a double filter of time and classification, the military form of the record skew in Chapter 2, and statistical inference drawn from declassified material needs unusual care about its sample. Wrong lesson two: imagining military discipline as a vaccine against drift. Snook's finding runs the other way: drift inside a disciplined organisation takes the form of each link doing the right thing by its own logic, and discipline does not produce alignment by itself. Wrong lesson three: using a space case as an aviation case. The institutional isomorphism of CAIB and the NTSB, independent investigation, full publication, tracked recommendations, is worth learning, but the one-shot mission structure of spaceflight means its feedback cannot be compared directly with the repetitive operations of civil aviation.

docs.title: 6 Three Questions from Readers Outside the Field
docs.text:
Are military cases open to outside readers? What is public is the redacted version of an investigation report. CAIB was a congressionally mandated independent investigation and is published in full. The organisational and incentive-layer lessons transfer completely. Technical detail is abstract where classification applies, which does not impede learning the mechanism.

Does a rank culture distort the lessons? Rank culture is the hardest testbed available for Chapter 19, on why the truth-teller goes first. CAIB's organisational analysis of Columbia reads most powerfully against exactly that background: a blameless review was still possible inside a strong rank culture, and the comparison drawn from the software industry shows this is not a cultural destiny.

Where should a reader moving from military to civilian work start? With mi-001, Columbia. The report is a complete sample that reads outside the industry, and its organisational analysis is isomorphic with failure in any large organisation.

docs.text: Three limits apply to everything judged on this page. The book's case library samples toward events with rich public records, and the record skew is the subject of Chapter 2. Institutions and technology in the domain keep moving, so this page has a shelf life measured in years, and a reader quoting it should state the year of the quotation. docs.title: 11 How the Three Layers Sound in the Military
docs.text: The three-layer accent in military cases is the highest rank density in the organisational layer. Every link in the chain of command is a translation, and Chapter 16's attenuation is institutionalised in military systems as the briefing. More translations do not mean information must decay, because the briefing format is a mature answer to translation loss: read-back, confirmation, standard phraseology. The civilian portability of the format is discussed in Chapters 16 and 30. For the reviewer: the technical-layer cell in a military case is often abstract because of classification, and abstract does not mean absent. Evidence in the organisational and incentive layers still carries the walk-through. Write "classified" in the cell, following the blank-cell discipline of Chapter 9.

docs.title: 12 Case to Mechanism Chapter, Quick Reference
docs.text:
Case ID Mechanism chapter One line mi-001 Chapter 11 Normalization of Deviance External tank foam struck the left wing; the vehicle broke up on reentry

How to use the table: on a news item or a bulletin from this domain, guess the mechanism from the distribution in Section 7, then use this table to reach the criteria and countermeasures in the chapter. The table does not replace reading. It is a map, not the journey.

docs.title: 13 Closing Address
docs.text:
A last word for readers of military cases: the public versions (CAIB, the military-related parts of JTSB) are the densest samples of organisational failure available. Rank culture, information pressure, cross-agency coordination, the whole set of difficulties is present. For a non-military reader their value is that of a mirror: how strong is your organisation's rank culture, how often has cross-agency coordination dropped the line, and does mi-001's organisational lesson have a counterpart where you work. The mechanism mapping here (Chapters 11, 13, 18, 19) is cross-industry public property, and classification blocks technical detail without blocking the structural lesson.

This page holds one case, mi-001, Columbia, and the CAIB report, but that one case carries the weight of a small library. The report runs to ten volumes, and volume one alone is over 500 pages; the book cites pp. 39 and 122–129 of it. CAIB's organisational analysis chapters are the deepest writing on normalization of deviance anywhere in the book, and easier to read than Vaughan's original because they are verified after the fact. There is a second reason this page is thin. How public a military investigation is depends on who authorised it: a congressionally mandated investigation such as CAIB is published in full, while an investigation kept inside the military, such as av-019, the Xinjiang Yaxin general aviation report, was never published in full and could not enter the main text. The selection standard is therefore a double threshold, an accident large enough and an investigation open enough. What survives the double filter is the densest evidence in the book, and mi-001's weight was stated at the start of this page.

docs.title: 14 How the Mechanisms Vary in This Domain
docs.text:
The military variation of normalization of deviance: mi-001 is one of the origin cases of the book's work on normalization, and the distinctive form here is the flight rationale regime, in which risks that cannot be ruled out are written into the flight release document one at a time until the release document itself becomes the ledger of normalization. How to read the variation: the age distribution of "accepted risk" entries in the release documents, meaning how old the oldest entry is, is the domain's normalization thermometer. The older the entry, the more the risk assessment rests on past releases rather than current evidence. CAIB tabulated the flight-by-flight history of foam shedding (Chapter 11 cites p.124), which is precisely this thermometer made into an object.

The military variation of narrative before evidence: the review culture around mi-001, where a foam strike was filed as a maintenance problem rather than a safety problem, shows the power of narrative classification. Which category a phenomenon is put into decides which processing pipeline it enters and what level of resource it can command. How to read the variation: does the risk classification standard provide a channel and a record for reclassification requests, who approves a downgraded classification, and on what evidence. The density of the paper trail on classification changes is the domain's measure of narrative immunity. The neighbouring av-017, a helicopter cleared for the helipad that landed on the runway, adds a second blind spot from a militarised organisation, academy-owned and under quasi-military management: the clearance travelled on a single-channel radio, and a clearance with no check is no clearance.

The military variation of diffusion of responsibility: a multi-layer command structure is a natural hot spot for Chapter 18. In mi-001's lessons, jurisdiction over the foam problem circulated for years among the project office, the space shuttle programme and the contractor, and each layer could name a specific reason why the responsibility was not its own. How to read the variation: a single-claimant rule for cross-layer risk entries, where each entry carries one and only one name at or above a stated rank, is the targeted device for this domain. An entry that circulates for ten years with the same claimant is a healthy signal. A claimant that changes automatically as the organisation chart changes is a symptom.

docs.title: 15 Cross-Reading Suggestions
docs.text: Read this page against aviation first (mi-001 and the av volume share the language of airworthiness and release, and aviation's mandatory reporting system is the clearest proof of the institutional domestication this page discusses). Against public policy: read mi-001's project governance beside the big projects of the po volume, where the governance defects of very large technical projects are isomorphic on both sides of the civil-military line. Against nuclear: the safety culture literatures of the two industries reference each other, with CAIB and the Chernobyl and Fukushima investigation reports citing one another, and readers of this page should take the independent verification variation in Section 14 of the nuclear page with them.

docs.title: Manufacturing and Supply Chain | mn
docs.text: Five columns: record quality, feedback delay, coupling, the three deadliest mechanisms, what outsiders most easily mislearn.

docs.title: 1 Record Quality
docs.text:
Recall notices carry this domain. In the United States, CPSC covers consumer products and NHTSA covers motor vehicles, both publishing case by case. All 7 mn cases in this book come from CPSC pages; NHTSA returned 403 in this book's network environment, which records. Notices from the Defect Product Recall Center under China's State Administration for Market Regulation are only partly reachable. Quality incident investigations run deeper, automotive consent orders and defect investigation reports among them, but availability varies case by case, and the NHTSA consent orders were never obtained here.

The overall verdict: notices are plentiful and thin. A reason, a quantity, a count of incident reports. Everything that would explain why the design failed is missing, so mechanism attribution falls to the reader. That is the job the mechanism index does in this domain.

docs.title: 2 Feedback Delay
docs.text:
Three clocks run at once, at very different speeds.

Harm to the user moves in months and years: the product reaches the user, the defect shows itself, the report is filed, the regulator learns. mn-001's 600 incident reports are the shape of that chain on record. Quality on the factory floor moves in hours and batches: first-article inspection, sampling, line checks. Design defects move in product generations, and mn-006's French press had been selling for 50 years before the accounting came due.

Channel volume stretches the middle clock out of shape. At a fixed defect rate, exposures grow nonlinearly with units shipped (Chapter 24), and the delay between shipment and harm deforms with it.

docs.title: 3 Coupling
docs.text:
Channel coupling rises with volume. One e-commerce channel carries a single batch into hundreds of thousands of households (mn-003). Supply chain coupling is the second axis (Chapter 33): a component maker's defect travels through contract assembly into the brand's product, as with mn-002's Ariston boiler, and structurally the same way through the drug kit in ph-008.

Coupling across products is low, since most consumer goods are independent of one another. The dark thread is the invisible family: one contract factory serving several brands. Recall notices never carry the factory's name, so a defect spanning several brands appears as several unrelated notices. Tracing has to work from batch numbers and process signatures.

docs.title: 4 The Three Deadliest Mechanisms
docs.text:
Crossing a scale threshold (Chapter 24): 338,000 units recalled within a year of launch (mn-003); 5.9 million glass carafes accumulated over 50 years (mn-006).

Misaligned incentives (Chapter 17): the mismatch between the cost of listing speed and the cost of compliance checking (mn-004, mn-007).

Margin erosion (Chapter 25): material and structural margins narrow with each round of cost optimization, and the defect stays invisible until thermal runaway, tipping or shatter (mn-001).

Next in frequency: hidden coupling and cascading failure, both present in mn-002's cracked condensate tray and its delayed ignition.

docs.title: 5 What Outsiders Most Easily Mislearn
docs.text:
Misreading one: treating a recall as evidence of bad quality. A recall is a signal that monitoring and enforcement are working. In a market where the recall regime is thin, the same products appear in no database at all, which is the record skew of Chapter 2.

Misreading two: taking the recall count for the size of the risk. 338,000 heaters against 17 ignitions. Order-of-magnitude thinking needs usage hours in the denominator, and the notice never supplies them.

Misreading three: watching the assembler only. The root cause usually sits two or three tiers down, at mn-002's manufacturer Ariston or at the BD components inside the drug kit. Chapter 33's dependency inventory has to reach the process and material layer to be worth anything here.

docs.title: 6 Three Questions from Outside the Industry
docs.text:
Question one: what does manufacturing recall practice offer a service business? The full chain, detect, assess, report, recall, trace, is structurally the same as fault management in services. Services have recalls too: the apology notice, the compensation scheme, the root-cause fix. The mn cases' problems with recall lag and granularity have a counterpart in every industry.

Question two: how is a cascading supply chain failure prevented? Chapter 33's four devices, register, price, drill, debrief, are general parts. mn-001's six hundred reports are the bill for a register that did not exist.

Question three: why do violations continue when mandatory standards exist, STURDY and PPPA among them? Standards govern design and channels govern listing. The coverage rate of a standard and the inspection rate at listing are two separate variables, and Chapter 17's incentive mismatch concentrates in small-batch import channels.

Three items for a reader new to the domain.

Starter case: mn-001, a power bank's lithium battery in thermal runaway, recalled after 600 incident reports (CPSC, 2026, link at Appendix B). Read it first for the form and granularity of reporting in this domain.

docs.title: 10 Reservations
docs.text:
Three limits apply to every judgement on this page.

The case base over-samples events with rich public records, which is the record skew of Chapter 2. The frequency ordering reflects the distribution of this book's cases, not the true distribution in the industry. Institutions and technology change, so the page's shelf life is counted in years, and a reader citing it should state the year of citation. All three are the book's general disclaimer, and Chapter 1's threshold check applies to this book as much as to anyone else's system.

docs.title: 11 The Three Layers in a Manufacturing Accent
docs.text:
The manufacturing accent sits in the incentive layer, where the breakpoints are the most fragmented. Compliance cost on small imports, sampling coverage on platforms, margin pressure at contract factories. In the mn cases these breakpoints never appear as one large decision. They are diffused through the channel as tens of thousands of small pricing decisions.

Fragmented breakpoints cannot be repaired one at a time. Product-by-product management does not scale, because the products cannot be handled one at a time. Only the structural methods of Chapter 17 work at this layer: payment terms, compliance spot checks, performance bonds. Manage the rules and the products take care of themselves.
